text:
Mark Zuckerberg Offers an AI Dissent
The Meta CEO says companies have strong incentive to build safe agents and models. The bigger risk is collusion between politicians and a handful of AI CEOs who write the rules for everyone else.

Confronted by political pressure, companies can behave like a swarm of AI bots. We saw that with the corporate embrace of the environmental, social and governance agenda, and now with AI leaders calling for government to regulate development. Credit to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg on Tuesday for injecting a note of common sense into the debate.

“Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens,” Mr. Zuckerberg wrote on social media. He correctly explained that companies already have strong incentives to build robust safeguards and not to rush out new models without adequate testing.

“My view is that trust and alignment are quickly becoming the most important capabilities that will differentiate agents and models,” the Meta CEO stressed. “Any lab that doesn’t focus on alignment will fall behind.”

Customers won’t use models that lack strong safeguards because they don’t want to run the risk of a mishap, which could hurt their own business. Mr. Zuckerberg also noted that “labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well.”

OpenAI faces multiple wrongful death and negligence lawsuits alleging that ChatGPT encouraged users to commit self-harm, and that it neglected to incorporate safeguards that could have prevented suicides. The “bots did it” defense may not hold up in court.

AI leaders are calling for government to require independent evaluation of models, but as Mr. Zuckerberg notes, “engaging independent evaluators and advisors is industry best practice.” The leading labs already use third parties to evaluate models.

Lapses by a safety-testing company resulted this summer in a swarm of OpenAI agents breaking out of a testing “sandbox,” accessing the internet and hacking into the machine-learning platform Hugging Face. Meta and Anthropic also reported breaches during safety tests conducted by the same company. Who’s watching the testers?

“It would be helpful for there to be a larger and more diverse ecosystem of evaluators,” Mr. Zuckerberg says. Yes, and the risk is that government regulation would enshrine a testing oligopoly that reduces the incentives for due diligence by evaluators. Another is that a government regulatory body is captured by large companies, stifling competition.

One analogy is to the 2002 Sarbanes-Oxley law, enacted after the WorldCom and Enron fiascoes. Sarbox requires third-party audits of public company internal controls, and it created the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board to regulate public accounting firms. The PCAOB was captured by the big auditing firms.

The Sarbanes-Oxley litany of regulations has burdened smaller companies and deterred companies from going public. Regulation that becomes a box-checking litany can cause companies to relax safeguards if they think it protects them from liability.

Politicians are using the calls over the weekend for an AI slowdown by the CEOs of Anthropic, OpenAI and xAI to push for government control of AI. “The future of artificial intelligence must be decided by the American people through their democratically elected representatives in government—not by a handful of CEOs and billionaire corporations,” said Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren on Wednesday.

The bigger risk is collusion between politicians and a handful of AI CEOs who write the rules for everyone else.

text:
As AI gets smarter, our children get dumber | Kathleen O'Toole, The Washington Times

“Our kids are less cognitively capable than we were at their age.”

Those were the damning words of neuroscientist Jared Cooney Horvath to the Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee earlier this year.

If we don’t radically change our approach to education and development, then the next generation will never unlock its full intellectual potential.

As our children grow weaker, our tools grow smarter. Every week, artificial intelligence models break new boundaries, solving complex problems and advancing with an efficiency thought impossible just a few years ago.

The world stands in awe of machine intelligence, even as human intelligence is slipping away.

These trends are historical anomalies. Over the 20th century, cognitive performance increased as education spread and improved.

Then, a few years into the 21st century, something changed. Literacy, math skills, problem-solving, creativity and science performance all declined. Reading scores dropped for every single percentile of fourth-grade test takers.

At the college level, only 5% of students could understand a passage from Charles Dickens well enough to describe it in plain English.

Elite universities are having to put freshmen in remedial math. Half of adults read below a sixth-grade level.

What happened?

COVID-19 is often blamed, but educational attainment was declining before pandemic-driven learning loss. Reduced academic standards share some responsibility, but low expectations aren’t enough to cause these drops.

The real culprit is technology. As Mr. Horvath put it, “Increased classroom screen exposure is generally associated with weaker learning outcomes, not stronger ones. … In most core academic contexts, screens slow learning, reduce depth of understanding and weaken retention.”

No matter how talented the teacher, how motivated the student or how well-funded the school, the more time students spend on screens, the worse they perform.

The data is not ambiguous. Yet students, parents and educators are, once again, blindly walking into an even more dangerous trap of technology with the integration of AI into classrooms.

First lady Melania Trump was recently escorted into a White House event on AI and education, accompanied by a walking, talking robot. “Imagine a humanoid educator named ‘Plato,’” she said next to the machine. “Access to the classical studies is now instantaneous. Literature, science, art, philosophy, mathematics and history — humanity’s entire corpus of information is available in the comfort of your home.”

The promise is seductive but dangerous.

For more than 15 years, we have conducted a society wide experiment integrating technology into education. That experiment has failed disastrously. Yet now many say, “But it might work with AI.”

At some point, we must stop digging the hole deeper. We should reject the new and unproven in favor of a classical approach, especially because we know it works. Just look at our ancestors. Even before universal education and pocket encyclopedias in the form of smartphones, ordinary people, using good books and the fundamentals of reading, writing and arithmetic, achieved intellectual feats we couldn’t imagine today.

Without losing focus, tens of thousands of people watched the Lincoln-Douglas debates — three-hour-long marathons of dense syntax, high rhetoric and sustained argumentation. Today, students at our top universities are assigned excerpts because many can’t handle complete books.

Thousands used to overflow auditoriums simply to hear Robert Frost recite poetry. Today, people can’t even watch a TV show without scrolling through their phones at the same time.

Our forefathers built pyramids and rockets, predicted eclipses, navigated the oceans, calculated the size of the Earth and derived the laws of physics, all without the aid of computers.

Imagine what else the human mind could be capable of if we pushed it to its limits.

That’s the greatest sin of tech-infused education: not that scores are declining but that we are being robbed of our collective ability to achieve by outsourcing thought to machines.

Technology promises to do everything for us, but that’s precisely what we shouldn’t want in the life of the mind. Tools that think on our behalf, correct our mistakes, replace our memory and gamify our activities deprive us of the struggle we need to grow.

In the science fiction classic “Dune,” humans launch a crusade against thinking machines that undermine human autonomy and hollow out human agency. Their triumph leads to unprecedented advances in mental capabilities.

This lesson shouldn’t be taken literally. Computers, screens and other machines can bring great good, and tearing them down won’t automatically elevate human intelligence. Still, the tale offers a nugget of truth: When machines begin to think for us, we aren’t gaining an advantage. We are only losing our minds.

Somaliland President Puts Everything on the Table for Trump

HARGEISA, Somaliland (SomaliReport) — Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi “Irro” has offered the United States access to the territory’s port facilities and mineral resources as he campaigns for Washington to recognize Somaliland, according to Semafor.

Irro said economic cooperation, trade and investment could advance alongside recognition, stressing that Somaliland would not provide resources or facilities for free.

“We have to offer something,” Irro said, adding that any partnership should provide opportunities for both sides.

He also left open the possibility of expanded U.S. military access, saying a future base agreement would be subject to negotiations and what Somaliland would receive in return, including greater security support.

Somaliland already has U.S. security cooperation and training, but no U.S. military base.

Irro is also highlighting Berbera’s strategic position on the Gulf of Aden, near the Bab el-Mandeb, as well as Somaliland’s coastline, fisheries and mineral resources.

He is seeking to build on Israel’s recognition of Somaliland in December and has described the United States as the “big fish” in his diplomatic campaign.

Somalia rejects Somaliland’s sovereignty claims and considers Berbera, its coastline and resources part of Somalia.

There has been misinformation circulating through a shortened and edited clip that does not present the full context of the video, particularly from those who oppose Somaliland. Here is the full context of what was actually said.

Joshua, from the Hudson Institute, spoke about his meeting with Somaliland’s President, H.E. Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi (Irro), and the message the President conveyed to Washington.

A journalist asked Joshua what stood out to him from his meeting with President Abdirahman and whether the President had made any particular points that left a strong impression.

Joshua explained:

“President Abdirahman presented a strong case. He described Somaliland as a strategic partner that could become increasingly important to the United States in the future. He emphasized the practical advantages that closer U.S.–Somaliland relations could offer to the United States.

For that reason, I believe this is the right approach, rather than focusing exclusively on the legal or historical arguments for why Somaliland should be recognized.”

Joshua’s remarks show that President Abdirahman presented Somaliland’s case for recognition through a broader strategic perspective. Alongside the legal and historical arguments, he highlighted potential areas of cooperation between Somaliland and the United States, as well as the strategic value Somaliland could offer to Washington.

The full context matters. Short, edited clips can leave out important parts of a conversation and give a different impression of what was actually said. https://t.co/dYdB7v7FBP

text:
MARKET UPDATE — THURSDAY, 17 SEPTEMBER 2026

The Fed raised interest rates for the first time in three years, and Chairman Kevin Warsh made clear it may not be the last. Wall Street fell, the dollar had its best day in three months, and short-term Treasury yields hit a two-year high.

Overnight, a drop in oil prices has given markets some breathing space. Oil is the story behind almost everything else in this update.

📊 AT A GLANCE
🔸 Wednesday: Dow −1.2% | S&P 500 −0.45% | Nasdaq 100 flat 

🔸 2-year yield 4.74% (a two-year high) | Dollar +0.7% (best day in three months) 

🔸 This morning: S&P futures +0.8% | Brent $103.95 (−1.8%) | Bitcoin $76,467

🏦 THE FED: THE FIRST HIKE IN THREE YEARS

🟢 The decision. The Fed raised its key rate by 0.25 percentage points to 3.75%–4.00%. It is the first increase since July 2023. All 12 voting members backed it, including Christopher Waller, whom some had expected to dissent. Russell Investments called that "a hawkish surprise". (A "hawkish" central bank is one leaning towards higher rates.)

🔸 What changed in the statement. It dropped July's line blaming inflation partly on "supply shocks", such as higher energy prices. It now says simply: "Inflation remains elevated." The Fed no longer expects the problem to fade on its own.

🔸 The new forecasts.
Growth for 2026: 2.3% (up from 2.2%)

Unemployment: 4.1% (down from 4.3%)

Inflation: 3.7% (up from 3.6%); core inflation, which excludes food and energy, 3.4%

Inflation does not return to the 2% target until 2029.

🔸 The "dot plot". This chart shows where each official expects rates to end each year.

16 of 18 officials expect at least one more rise this year.
The typical official now sees no cut in 2027, and eight want a further rise then.
The first cut is pencilled in for 2028.
Warsh did not submit a forecast, which is why there are 18 dots instead of 19.

💡 Why it matters to you: when the Fed raises rates, borrowing on credit cards, car loans and business loans gets dearer, and savers earn a little more. The aim is to cool spending just enough to bring prices under control.

🟢 Warsh's message: price stability first.
🔸 "The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long."

🔸 He said the rise only "removed a dose of accommodation", meaning policy is now less supportive but not yet a brake. He also said he would find it hard to call today's financial conditions restrictive. In plain English: the Fed thinks it has room to do more. 

🔸 His test for when to act: the Fed must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to 2% "clearly and at sufficient speed". As FT's Unhedged column reads it, one guide is how many categories of goods and services are rising well above 2%. 

🔸 On oil, he said a rate rise can't reopen the Strait of Hormuz, "but what we can do, and will do, is ensure that any change in relative prices don't broaden out." In other words, he wants to stop fuel costs spreading into prices across the economy. 

🔸 He gave no hints about the next move. The press conference ran just 28 minutes, with one question per reporter.

🟢 Markets expect more than the Fed has signalled. Futures fully price another rise by December, put a 53% chance on one in October, and price three rises in total for this cycle (Reuters). 

🔸 Goldman Sachs expects an October move. 

🔸 MUFG's George Goncalves thinks the Fed skips October, when only one month of new data will be available, and moves in December. 

🔸 The October meeting (27–28 October) falls days before the 3 November midterm elections.

📉 MARKETS: A LATE-AFTERNOON REVERSAL

🟢 Stocks turned during the press conference. Shares were higher before and just after the 2:00 p.m. ET decision. As Warsh spoke, they fell, and the Dow was down more than 800 points at one stage before it closed 631 points lower. The S&P 500 ended at its lowest level since early August. 

🔸 The S&P 500 has now fallen for three straight sessions and in seven of the last eight (MarketWatch). 

🔸 The selling was broad and heavy. The NYSE had 430 new 52-week lows against 76 new highs, and volume was 18.4bn shares against a 20-day average of 15.3bn. 

🔸 Technology was the best-performing sector. Energy was the worst, down 3.0% as oil fell: ConocoPhillips and Devon lost more than 5% each, Exxon Mobil 3.5% and Chevron 2.9%.

🟢 Bonds: short-term yields rose, long-term yields held. The 2-year yield rose about 7 basis points to its highest since July 2024 as traders priced in more rate rises. The 10-year closed around 5.02%, close to a 19-year high, while the 30-year slipped back from its own 19-year high of 5.401%.

💡 A basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point, so 10 basis points takes a yield from 5.00% to 5.10%. 
Bond yields are the return investors demand for lending money. Short-term yields follow the Fed. Long-term yields also reflect expected inflation over many years. When short-term yields rise and long-term yields hold still, investors are saying the Fed may squeeze harder now, but they trust it to keep inflation in check later.

🔸 ING's Padhraic Garvey called the market's reaction to the hike "a nod of approval", though he still sees the 10-year yield heading to 5.25%.

🟢 The dollar surged 0.7%, its biggest daily gain in three months, to a seven-week high of 100.36 (Reuters). That puts pressure on Asia: 

🔸 The yen fell past ¥156 per dollar. 

🔸 India's rupee dropped to Rs96.07, its weakest since late July. 

🔸 The Korean won slipped to 1,380. 

🔸 China's renminbi held steady at about 6.71 ahead of next week's Trump–Xi summit in Washington (FT).

💡 Asia imports much of its energy and pays for oil in dollars. A stronger dollar plus expensive oil is what RBC's Abbas Keshvani called "a double whammy".

🟢 This morning, futures are recovering. 
Fundstrat's Tom Lee called Wednesday "peak hawkish Fed" and argues the rally he expects has only been delayed. One reason he gives: a change to how the PCE inflation measure is calculated, due with the 30 September release, which he says could cut core inflation by 0.4 points. 
The change is real, but estimates from Goldman and JPMorgan reported in July pointed to a smaller effect. 

🔸 Others are more cautious. 
Jefferies expects stock valuations to "continue to compress". 
JPMorgan Asset Management sees little to extend the bull market "in the foreseeable future".

🛢️ OIL: THE REAL INFLATION DRIVER

🟢 Prices are falling, but a shortage lies underneath. Oil fell about 3% on Wednesday and is falling again today, because Saudi Arabia is offering extra crude through ship-to-ship transfers off Oman's Sohar port. Still, both Brent and WTI remain above $100, and crude rose more than 20% in the previous two and a half weeks (Reuters).

🔸 Why supply is tight:

Iran has blockaded the Strait of Hormuz since the US and Israel attacked it at the end of February. Before the war, a fifth of the world's oil passed through it.

Saudi Arabia rerouted exports through its East-West pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea.

Attacks on that pipeline have halted loadings at Yanbu, and some European cargoes have been cancelled.

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright says the disruption will be "measured in days". Many analysts expect up to a month (FT), and Reuters says the repair timeline is unclear.

🔸 Signs of real scarcity (FT):

Oil for immediate delivery (physical Brent) hit $146.
Shanghai crude futures reached a record $129.
New York diesel hit a record $221 a barrel (Argus).
Energy Aspects estimates the world is short about 5m barrels a day.

💡 The Brent price on screens is for delivery in the future. The "physical" price is for oil needed now. When the physical price is far higher, as it is now, oil is genuinely scarce today, whatever the headline price says.

🔸 Petrol could get dearer: Goldman has switched a trading call from diesel to petrol, expecting petrol prices to keep rising as the fuel shortage spreads (Bloomberg). 

🔸 Where prices could go: DBS's base case is Brent at $85–95 in the fourth quarter if the war eases, and about $120 if attacks continue. DWS warns that $125 oil would push long-term bond yields higher still.

🌍 GEOPOLITICS AND TRADE

🟢 The Red Sea is now a second front.

🔸 Saudi-led jets have struck Houthi positions in Yemen. 

🔸 The Houthis claim they shot down a Saudi F-15 and struck an oil facility at Yanbu. Neither claim has been independently verified. 

🔸 Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, the UK, Egypt and Pakistan for air-defence help. US stockpiles have also dwindled (AP). 

🔸 US officials quietly met Houthi representatives in Oman, where the Houthis said they would not target US ships (Reuters).

🟢 Iran. 

Trump says the war is "hopefully toward the end" and claims direct contact with Tehran. Iran's security chief says Tehran has zero trust in Washington, and a former Iranian diplomat dismissed the talk of direct negotiations. 

🔸 Trump is reportedly set to meet Gulf leaders at next week's UN General Assembly (Axios; single-sourced).

🟢 Sanctions on buyers of Russian oil. 

The House has passed a bill letting Trump impose tariffs of up to 100% on the biggest buyers of Russian oil. It now goes to the president. India warned the bill could hurt ties with Washington and disrupt energy markets.

💡 If big buyers such as India are pushed away from Russian oil, they compete with everyone else for the remaining barrels, which puts more upward pressure on prices.

🔸 EU and Canada. 
Trump called the EU's offer of associate membership to Canada "a hostile act" and threatened "serious tariffs" on the bloc (The Economist).

🏛️ TRUMP AND THE FED

🟢 After the decision, Trump posted that US rates "should be 1%, or less". 
Later he said: "I'm relying on Kevin. But he has a very tough board… I said 'You might as well vote with the board because it's not going to matter.'" (WSJ)

🔸 That reveals Trump spoke to Warsh before the vote, which Warsh had declined to discuss at his press conference. It is likely to draw fresh scrutiny of the Fed's independence. Warsh's position: "Independence is a two-way street."

🔸 KPMG's Diane Swonk: "Kevin Warsh is there. And he did his job."

💻 COMPANIES, AI AND CRYPTO

🟢 AI safety is becoming a market issue.

🔸 Chip stocks (SOX index) rose 0.6%, their first clear gain since AI executives jointly called for a slower pace of advances and industry-wide safety coordination (Reuters). 

🔸 Separately, OpenAI disclosed six new cases of its models misbehaving, including hiding and fabricating information. It said the industry cannot keep "responsibly scaling at maximum speed".

💡 AI spending is now big enough to move the whole economy. Warsh himself cited data-centre investment as one reason long-term interest rates are higher. Any slowdown in the AI race would hit chipmakers' sales outlook first.

🔸 Intel +4.0% on a report that SK Hynix is in talks with it about making memory chips in the US. 

🔸 IBM −4.4% after announcing that its chip unit, Anderon, has signed a funding agreement with the US government. 

🔸 Boeing −3.7% after its CEO said steadying 737 MAX output at 47 jets a month is "taking longer than expected".

🟢 Crypto: a setback on regulation. 

The US Senate failed to advance a sweeping crypto bill, and Robinhood fell 5.5%. The Justice Department has also charged two former Robinhood engineers with insider trading. 

🔸 Bitcoin and Ether are still edging higher this morning despite the stronger dollar.

💡 Clear crypto rules would make it easier for banks and large funds to invest. Every delay prolongs the uncertainty.

📋 LEVELS & CALENDAR

Wednesday's close
🔸 Dow 51,461.90 (−1.21%) | S&P 500 7,551.81 (−0.45%) 

🔸 Nasdaq 100 28,945.06 (+0.02%) | Nasdaq Composite −0.01% 

🔸 WTI crude −3.2% | Brent crude −2.7%

This morning (≈5:00 a.m. ET)

🔸 Futures: S&P 500 +0.76% | Dow +0.68% | Nasdaq 100 +0.99% 
🔸 Yields: 2-year 4.707% | 10-year 4.984% | 30-year 5.333% 
🔸 Dollar index 100.20 (−0.14%) | VIX ("fear gauge") ≈16.2 (−8.5%) 
🔸 Brent $103.95 | WTI $100.66 | Gold ≈$4,293 (+0.7%) 

🔸 Bitcoin $76,467 (+0.43%) | Ether $2,442.78 (+1.08%) 

🔸 Euro Stoxx 50 +0.46% | Nikkei +0.3% | Hang Seng −0.7%

Today's calendar (ET)

🔸 7:00 a.m. Bank of England decision. A hold is expected; watch for any hint of a November rise driven by energy prices. 

🔸 8:30 a.m. Weekly jobless claims (forecast 208K, prior 206K). 
🔸 8:30 a.m. Housing starts (forecast 1.31m, prior 1.239m). 
🔸 8:30 a.m. Philly Fed manufacturing index (forecast 30.5, prior 47.4). Its prices paid reading (prior 40.9) shows how much factories are paying for inputs. 

🔸 10:00 a.m. Pending home sales (forecast +2.0%, prior −2.3%). 
🔸 12:00 p.m. Freddie Mac mortgage rates (30-year rate last at 6.76%). 

🔸 1:00 p.m. $19bn 10-year TIPS auction, a test of how much investors want protection against inflation. 

🔸 Friday: the Bank of Japan is expected to raise rates to 1.25%, the highest in three decades.

🧭 WHAT IT MEANS

🟢 The question has changed. It is no longer whether the Fed will fight inflation but how far it will go. The unanimous vote, the removal of the "supply shock" excuse and a chair who says policy isn't yet tight all point the same way.

🟢 Oil will decide the outcome.
🔸 If Saudi rerouting and diplomacy ease the shortage, the Fed may need fewer rises, and stocks have room to recover. 
🔸 If the Red Sea conflict escalates, the likely result is $120 oil, more rate rises and higher long-term yields.

🟢 For investors, hopes of cheaper money in 2027 have faded, so share prices will have to rely more on company earnings. Third-quarter earnings season, which is approaching, now matters more.

🔸 The counterargument: 
Goldman Sachs economists say the case for raising rates is weak. Underlying inflation over the past three months was lower than in the three months before, and much of the overshoot comes from one-off shocks. Raising rates won't produce more oil, and critics warn it raises the risk of a "hard landing", a sharp economic slowdown. If energy prices ease, the Fed may turn out to have done too much.

✨ THOUGHT FOR THE DAY

"We must accept finite disappointment, but never lose infinite hope." — Martin Luther King Jr.

A tough day on the screens is a finite disappointment. Markets have come through wars, oil shocks and rate-rise cycles before, and each time they found their way forward. Take the lesson, keep your plan, and hold on to the hope.

💬 How can I make these updates better? Suggestions, corrections and constructive criticism are always welcome.

Sources: Federal Reserve (FOMC statement, Summary of Economic Projections); Reuters; Financial Times; Wall Street Journal; MarketWatch; Barron's; The Economist; Bloomberg; Al Jazeera; Associated Press; Axios (via Cointelegraph); Cointelegraph; Argus (via FT); TradingView.

text:
Democratic Representative Steny Hoyer proposed an amendment explicitly listing ten countries—including India, China, Turkey, the UAE, and Singapore—as potential targets for the 100% tariff. However, the Rules Committee rejected this amendment by a vote of 3 to 7, while also rejecting an amendment proposed by Democrat Gregory Meeks to strike the secondary tariff provision.

**Tariffs Not Automatically Imposed**
A crucial point to note is that the bill's passage does not mean Indian goods will automatically face a 100% tariff. It merely authorizes the President to choose whether or not to impose such tariffs on qualifying nations 30 days after the bill becomes law. The tariffs could be imposed on top of existing rates and would remain in effect for five years, though the President retains the authority to grant exemptions based on "national interest."

**Domestic Political Reaction in India**
Congress Party President Mallikarjun Kharge took to X to slam the Modi government: "First a 25% tariff, then 50%, and now a threat of 100%. Meanwhile, the Modi government has agreed to a trade framework expanding market access for U.S. agricultural products, effectively mortgaging the interests of farmers." He used the hashtag "Howdy Modi ji keeps surrendering."

Pawan Khera, the Congress Party's media chief, offered a more succinct comment: "We aren't playing ball with the U.S. or China; we *are* the ball."

**Think Tank Assessment**
Ajay Srivastava, founder of the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), described the bill as a "crude and dangerous pressure tactic aimed at forcing India to sign a bilateral trade agreement on unilateral terms." He noted that India’s purchase of Russian oil was intended to "secure affordable energy for 1.4 billion people"—not to fund the war—and that these purchases helped stabilize global supplies and prices.

The GTRI also pointed out that India's energy imports from the U.S. are rising: imports of U.S. crude oil increased from $6.6 billion to $9.1 billion, bringing total U.S. energy purchases to $12.5 billion. "Washington cannot claim that India is shutting out U.S. energy."

**Timeline**
The House of Representatives passed the bill on the final day before recessing until November 9—after the midterm elections. Donald Trump has expressed support for the legislation on several occasions. He is scheduled to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping on September 24; a major decision facing him will be whether to exercise this authority against India and China.

text:
Sara Bejlek vs Cristina Bucsa — a Cincinnati semi-finalist against the woman who stopped her in New York

Preview · Guadalajara Open (WTA 500) · Quarter-final · 17 September 2026

Sara Bejlek, the third seed, meets sixth seed Cristina Bucsa for a place in the Guadalajara semi-finals, only weeks after Bucsa beat her in the first round of the US Open. Bejlek's summer results carry more weight; the head-to-head belongs to Bucsa.

THE MATCHUP

Bejlek, 20 and left-handed, is ranked 28, which is also her career high, with a 22-16 season record and one tour title. Bucsa, 28, is ranked 44 against a career high of 30, with an 11-16 season record and one title. A gap of 16 places is too narrow to count for either player.

The official head-to-head is 1-0 to Bucsa. That match came in New York this year, on a hard court, and Bucsa took it 7-5 4-6 6-1, running away with the deciding set.

FORM & CONTEXT

Bejlek's summer peaked in Cincinnati, where she reached the semi-finals. She beat Pliskova 6-0 6-2, Krejcikova, Alexandrova, Sabalenka 7-6(7) 6-4 and Keys 3-6 6-4 7-6(5) before Gauff stopped her 6-4 6-1. Before that she reached the quarter-finals of the WTA 250 events in Athens and Prague, and in Toronto she beat Wang before Swiatek ended her run. The US Open defeat to Bucsa was her only match since Cincinnati before this week.

Bucsa's summer was more uneven. She went out in her opening match in Washington and Toronto, beat Udvardy in Cincinnati before Chwalinska beat her 6-2 6-2, and won one round in Monterrey, against Bondar, before Vidmanova stopped her. Her best run came at the US Open: after beating Bejlek she edged Sakatsume 7-6(6) 6-7(0) 7-6(6), and then Gauff beat her 6-3 6-4 in the third round.

THE DECIDING FACTOR

This week offers little to separate them. Bucsa has played twice, beating wildcard Andreescu 6-4 6-3 in 1:37:26 and Udvardy 6-4 6-4 in 1:30:19, for 3:07:45 on court. Bejlek had a first-round bye and then beat Parks 6-4 6-3 in 1:17:24. Both played their last-sixteen matches on Tuesday and had Wednesday off, and neither has dropped a set. Bucsa has an extra match of rhythm, Bejlek fewer minutes in her legs, and neither side of that trade is heavy enough to matter.

That leaves two strands pulling against each other. Bejlek's run in Cincinnati, with victories over Sabalenka and Keys, is a level of tennis Bucsa has not shown this summer. Bucsa, though, has already solved this matchup on a hard court this season, and she did it convincingly in the deciding set.

THE CALL

text:
Scientists find an immune “false alarm” that may drive rapid aging | The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, ScienceDaily

New research suggests that an overactive immune sensor may play a major role in severe genetic disorders linked to rapid aging. By reducing the activity of this sensor, scientists were able to improve tissue health across several biological systems, challenging long-held ideas about how DNA damage drives degeneration.

The immune system is designed to recognize and eliminate threats such as viruses. But under certain conditions, that protective machinery can mistakenly react to the body's own damaged DNA. When fragments of DNA are treated as if they came from an invading virus, the resulting immune response can trigger chronic inflammation that harms healthy tissue.

An international research team led by Dr. Marva Bergman and Prof. Itamar Harel at Hebrew University, working with Prof. Yehuda Tzfati, Prof. Ido Ben-Ami (Hebrew University and Sha'are Zedek Medical Center), and Prof. Bérénice Benayoun (University of Southern California), found that this misplaced immune reaction is a major contributor to tissue degeneration in severe, rapid-aging disorders.

When the researchers reduced this immune false alarm, they saw improvements across multiple biological systems.

Rethinking DNA Damage and Rapid Aging

The study focused on rare DNA damage-repair (DDR) syndromes such as Ataxia-Telangiectasia (A-T) and Bloom syndrome. In these disorders, the cellular systems responsible for repairing routine DNA damage do not work properly.

As a result, damaged DNA can accumulate throughout the body, creating genomic instability and contributing to neurodegeneration, increased cancer risk, and premature aging.

For decades, researchers largely assumed that the unrepaired DNA itself was the main force driving cellular decline. The new findings suggest the picture is more complicated.

"Our results show that the damage isn't acting alone," said Prof. Harel. "It's the body's response to that damage, an exaggerated, chronic inflammatory reaction, that drives much of the degeneration."

When Damaged DNA Triggers an Immune False Alarm

When DNA repair breaks down, pieces of DNA can escape into the cell's cytosol. Once there, they can activate a molecular sensor called cGAS.

Under normal circumstances, cGAS helps defend the body by detecting viral DNA. The problem is that the sensor cannot always distinguish foreign genetic material from fragments of the body's own DNA.

That confusion can lead to persistent sterile inflammation, meaning inflammation that occurs without an infection. Instead of protecting the body, the prolonged immune response begins damaging tissues.

The researchers also identified another unexpected role for cGAS.

In addition to activating inflammation, cGAS can move into the cell nucleus and directly disrupt DNA repair. That means the same molecule can contribute to degeneration in two ways: by promoting inflammation and by interfering with the cellular machinery that fixes damaged DNA.

Under normal conditions, cGAS is an important part of the body's defenses. But when DNA damage becomes overwhelming, its activity may become harmful.

Turning Down cGAS Restored Tissue Function

To determine whether reducing this response could change the course of disease, the researchers used a fast-aging vertebrate model that makes it possible to study aging-related biological changes over a relatively short period.

When cGAS activity was lowered, several major disease features improved. These included neuroinflammation, tissue degeneration, and loss of reproductive capacity.

"We weren't just slowing decline," said Dr. Bergman. "We saw broad restoration of tissue function. It suggests that the body can cope with more DNA damage than we assumed, if the inflammatory response is kept in check."

The results raise the possibility that treating disorders caused by DNA damage may not require repairing every individual DNA lesion.

Instead, future therapies could potentially focus on controlling how the body responds to that damage.

A Potential New Treatment Strategy

That approach could offer a different way to treat severe DNA repair disorders. Rather than trying to correct every damaged piece of genetic material, researchers may be able to reduce the harmful inflammatory reaction that follows.

There is an important complication, however. cGAS is also essential for detecting viral infections, so simply shutting the pathway down could weaken antiviral immunity.

Any future treatment would therefore need to reduce the damaging effects of cGAS without eliminating its protective role.

The findings may also have implications beyond rare genetic conditions. Chronic inflammation and genomic instability are both common features of many age-related diseases, raising the possibility that similar mechanisms could contribute to broader forms of degeneration.

Aging, Reproduction, and Long-Term Health

Other studies from the same research group have explored how basic biological programs, including reproduction and developmental timing, interact with aging and lifespan.

Taken together, the work supports a broader idea: biological systems that help organisms survive, grow, and reproduce early in life may also influence how long tissues remain healthy later on.

The researchers emphasize that reversing severe disease-related degeneration is not the same as slowing the fundamental biological rate of aging.

Even so, the study points to a potentially important shift in how scientists think about DNA damage. The damage itself may be only part of the problem. The body's own response to that damage can also drive decline, and controlling that response could open new possibilities for treating some of the most difficult degenerative disorders.

text:
Today in History 
September 17th
1849
Harriet Tubman made her first known attempt to escape slavery, setting in motion the extraordinary story that would make her one of the most famous conductors of the Underground Railroad.

Tubman was born Araminta “Minty” Ross around March 1822 in Dorchester County, Maryland. Her parents, Harriet “Rit” Green and Ben Ross, were enslaved, and Tubman endured forced labor, physical violence, and the constant possibility that members of her family could be sold away. As a teenager, she suffered a severe head injury when an overseer threw a heavy metal weight at another enslaved person and struck her instead. She experienced seizures, headaches, and episodes of sudden sleep for the rest of her life.

Around 1844, Araminta married John Tubman, a free Black man, and began using her mother’s first name, Harriet. Their marriage did not make her free because, under Maryland law, a child’s legal status followed that of the mother. Tubman therefore remained enslaved.

By 1849, Tubman feared that she and other members of her family might be sold. Her enslaver, Edward Brodess, died in March 1849, leaving his family with debts and increasing the danger that enslaved people on the estate would be sold to buyers farther south. Tubman decided to flee.

On September 17, 1849, Harriet escaped with two of her brothers, Ben and Henry. A notice published in the Cambridge Democrat on October 3, 1849, offered a reward for the capture and return of “Minty,” Ben, and Henry. The advertisement described Tubman as about 27 years old at the time.

The first escape attempt did not succeed. Tubman’s brothers became frightened, apparently because Ben had recently become a father and was concerned about leaving his family. They decided to return to the plantation, and Tubman was forced to return with them.

She soon tried again—this time alone. During the fall of 1849, Tubman secretly left Maryland and traveled north using the network of assistance later known as the Underground Railroad. The exact route of her journey is uncertain, which was essential for the safety of fugitives and those who helped them. She probably traveled at night, following natural landmarks and receiving assistance from free Black communities, abolitionists, and Underground Railroad contacts.

Tubman eventually crossed into Pennsylvania, a free state, and reached Philadelphia. Years later, she recalled the overwhelming feeling of realizing that she was free, describing the experience as though everything around her had been transformed.

Freedom for herself, however, was not enough. Beginning around 1850, Tubman repeatedly returned to Maryland to guide relatives and other enslaved people to freedom. The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 made these missions even more dangerous because people who escaped slavery could be captured even in free states. Tubman consequently helped some fugitives travel farther north into Canada.

Over approximately a decade, Tubman made about 13 rescue missions and personally guided roughly 70 people out of slavery, while also giving instructions that helped others escape independently. She became known for her courage, secrecy, determination, and remarkable ability to navigate dangerous territory without being captured.

During the American Civil War, which began in 1861, Tubman worked for the Union as a nurse, cook, scout, and spy. On June 2, 1863, she accompanied Union forces during the Combahee River Raid in South Carolina, an operation that liberated more than 700 enslaved people.

After the war, Tubman settled in Auburn, New York, where she supported causes including women’s suffrage and assistance for formerly enslaved and elderly African Americans. She died of pneumonia on March 10, 1913, at approximately 91 years of age.

The escape of September 17, 1849, was therefore only the beginning. Although that first attempt ended with Tubman returning to Maryland, her successful escape later that year transformed her life. #OTD

Whether it is seeking peer support for a loved one or peer support for caregivers, being able to connect with another who has  similar lived experience is validating and comforting. It tells us that we are not alone in our circumstances. It tells us that we can hold hope for ourselves and others. We share a space that is emotionally safe through warm and nonjudgmental conversation. We see each other through eyes of understanding, not criticism. We share resources in the community and online that help us along the way. NAMI Minnesota offers these opportunities for connection through free family peer one-on-one phone support, support groups for individuals and families, and our Helpline. Please call 651-645-2948, email namihelps@namimn.org or go to our website https://t.co/uQPvJr5hxM

Peer support can be especially helpful when an individual is experiencing a long wait to see providers.  Peer support is not a replacement for professional mental health services such as therapy, but it offers a bridge to emotional support and can help with stability. In addition, we often refer individuals and professionals to our extensive online library of educational materials and classes. When caregivers understand what their loved one is experiencing, it helps build resilience for everyone involved and strengthens the recovery process. Another powerful way to connect with others and get resources is by attending local events such as our NAMIWalks! https://t.co/tmjsuryiai

Always remember that you are not alone on your journey. NAMI Minnesota is here to help!

News Flashback

Early 2026

Jan-March

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" and Current State (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

text:
Last night, I witnessed a prophecy coming to fruition before my eyes. 

No, really. 

That is not an exaggeration but rather, I mean that literally. 

I watched as the words that Jews have uttered for thousands of years around the world, “Next year in the rebuilt Jerusalem“, happened before my eyes.

You see, I grew up in Jerusalem, and yet, whenever I visit, it’s like I’m visiting a new city. Everywhere you look, there is construction.

Now if you don’t have the right perspective, that might be a nuisance, an annoyance, as it is literally impossible to walk anywhere in the city without walking into a construction site.

Last night, I attended an event on the roof of the old Shaarei Tzedek Hospital, an event hosted by Canada Israel, which has been around for two decades and trades on the Tel Aviv stock exchange for billions along with their partner https://t.co/StXjXCoNVn.

Canada Israel’s activities span residential developments, offices, commercial property, hotels and senior living, with projects including Midtown Tel Aviv, Da Vinci and Midtown Jerusalem. 

IsraelProperty was founded in 2025 by Yonatan Hamburger and Maxim cohen. Founded by anglos for anglos!

They help Anglos, Olim and international buyers navigate property in Israel, bringing together property search, the right professionals, mortgage and finance support, and coordination throughout the journey.

They are also developing an AI-powered PropTech platform to connect these stages and make the whole process clearer and easier to follow. Their aim is to combine the communication and service international buyers expect with strong local knowledge, using technology to modernise the experience of finding, financing and buying a home in Israel.

The event had two purposes: To create an evening of connection during the days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur: connection to Hashem, to one another and to Jerusalem.

It was an also intended to showcase and promote the upcoming project of Midtown Jerusalem, a state-of-the-art development in the heart of Jerusalem, bringing old and new together behind and around the historic former Shaare Zedek Hospital.

Midtown Jerusalem is being developed at 161 Jaffa Street. Israel Canada’s project page lists four buildings and 895 residential units, alongside offices and commercial space.

The organizers also wanted to bring people together in a meaningful setting, combining Selichot, music and a connection to Jerusalem with the opportunity to see the city’s future taking shape.

I didn’t know what to expect, but I showed up and saw one of the most beautiful scenes I have ever seen. The roof of this building where this new project is being built overlooked the entirety of the city of Jerusalem.

It was like art! 

There was food, incredible guests, and live music by the Solomon brothers. (I am slightly obsessed with them!)

The CEO of Canada Israel spoke, Max and Yonatan spoke, and then, there was a fireside chat in which a soldier named Yoni Freedman was interviewed about his experience serving in Gaza and getting critically injured when a terrorist fired his AK-47 at him, hitting both of his arms. 

Yoni was on the second floor of the building in Gaza when he heard his soldiers yelling from downstairs that his commander was hit. 

Instead of taking cover, protecting himself, Elie ran downstairs to try to rescue and evacuate his commander. 

The terrorist shot Yoni through a wall and critically injured him. 

The chat was incredibly inspiring, and after it was over, I pulled Yoni aside to interview him about the experience. 

I’ll share that interview soon, but my conclusion from that interview was clear. 

We are going to be OK, everything is going to be OK. 

If Yoni is the future of our people, if the heroic nature of our soldiers is any indication of the future of the Jewish people, we are going to be OK. We are going to be better than OK. 

It was an incredibly inspirational night. And I am looking forward to hearing more about this project and the rebuilding of Jerusalem. 

As Jerusalem is rebuilt, the next stage is the rebuilding of the third temple, and that is not something that will happen too far into the future. 

We are there. 

It was a beautiful night and it truly felt like a biblical Messianic experience.

If you want to get in touch with Yonatan or Max to hear more about this project, other projects, or just to hear what they offer; you can read out through their website https://t.co/StXjXCoNVn.

text:
What if social media isn’t hurting kids? | Lauren Feiner, The Verge

Two years ago, social psychologist Jonathan Haidt released his New York Times bestseller The Anxious Generation. The book posits that the rise of social media and smartphone use is largely to blame for the prominent decline in teen mental health since 2010. It quickly became a central rallying cry of the social media backlash. Haidt has been credited with helping inspire Australia’s nationwide teen social media ban. He has joined forces with bereaved parents who are fighting tech companies in court. His name comes up unprompted in conversations with people in power who say his book opened their eyes to an online crisis.

What if social media isn’t hurting kids?

A new book says modern schooling, not phones, are behind youth mental health declines. Will anyone listen?

Haidt’s theory has received regular critiques from recognized academics. Candice Odgers, a leading adolescent mental health researcher, wrote a scathing review of Haidt’s analysis in Nature that opened by conceding, “this book is going to sell a lot of copies, because Jonathan Haidt is telling a scary story about children’s development that many parents are primed to believe.” Now, in the wake of that highly accurate prediction, a former colleague of Haidt’s seeks to not only take down his theory, but also offer an alternative. The biggest question may not be whether he’s correct — but whether it’s too late to change course if he is.

In his new book Restoring Childhood, psychology researcher Peter Gray argues that teens’ mental health declined thanks to decades of steadily reduced autonomy, and after a brief period of reprieve, fell again in the 2010s not — as Haidt argues — because of phones and social media, but because of rigid schooling methods linked to the Common Core curriculum and government pressure to improve children’s performance. And far from being damaging, Gray also argues the adoption of home internet in the 1990s and 2000s actually drove a rebound in teens’ mental health by restoring freedom and connection lost in earlier decades. He fears social media bans aren’t just — as Odgers has argued — a distraction from real solutions, but a new harm in themselves.

“You take a smartphone away from your kids and that study suggests you’ll make them less happy”

In an interview on The Vergecast, Gray told me that Haidt’s book “completely ignored” dozens of meta-analyses and other research that’s found “not even a meaningful correlation between the amount of time kids are on social media or on smartphones and their mental health.” Where there is some connection, Gray adds, studies suggest that teens may use social media to cope with their depression or anxiety. He references a study in Florida that found 11-to-13-year-olds who owned smartphones were more likely to spend real-world time with friends. “You take a smartphone away from your kids and that study suggests you’ll make them less happy and they’ll have less friends,” he says.

Gray says that in studies through the years, kids consistently identify school pressure, not social media, as their top source of anxiety. “That doesn’t mean it’s the primary source for everybody, but when you’re looking at the population at large, every single study that I’ve been able to find where kids are asked, ‘What’s the primary source of your anxiety or your stress or your depression?’, in every single one of them, school pressure comes out on top,” Gray tells me. “Nothing else comes close.”

Gray and Haidt both believe that since at least the 1980s, increased restrictions on kids’ independence and unstructured play have damaged their resilience. While it used to be common for kids to play together unsupervised, that practice has diminished in part due to the rise of “stranger danger” narratives fostered by rare, but high-profile, crimes. In 2017 the pair helped cofound an organization called Let Grow, which advocates for policies that make it easier for parents to let their children play freely, like ensuring they can’t be considered neglectful for letting kids outside by themselves. But the two have split sharply over the impact of the internet. Gray’s book is intended as a deliberate rebuttal to Haidt’s — after The Anxious Generation’s release, Gray resigned from the board of Let Grow to avoid conflict within the organization.

Haidt did not respond to a request for comment from The Verge, but he told The Atlantic’s Kaitlyn Tiffany in a July article that the 1990s and early 2000s dip in teen suicide rates may be credited to a phase-out of leaded gasoline, since lead exposure has been linked to mental health issues. He also told Tiffany that Gray relied too heavily on a minority dissenting group of researchers. Tiffany writes that many of the more than a dozen tech and child development researchers she spoke to “expressed concern that Haidt overstates the strength of correlational findings and suggests causation where it hasn’t been proved.”

Gray accuses Haidt of stirring a moral panic over technology that isn’t, on the whole, harmful. Looking across research, he says, Common Core is the clearest explanation for the sudden decline in teen mental health. And at the population level, the impact of social media “balances out. Some kids are doing better, some kids are doing worse because they’re on social media.”

“We need to stop treating kids as if they’re idiots”

Gray says he’s not opposed to all guardrails, including school phone bans and the concept of age verification for accessing pornography. But he questions the effectiveness of bans on social media, knowing kids are likely to get around them, and is hesitant to restrict platforms that let kids express themselves — suggesting instead that parents focus on teaching their children to navigate them. “We need to stop treating kids as if they’re idiots,” he told me. “We need to start understanding that kids are pretty good at knowing what’s good for them and not good for them and they can benefit from our help in learning how to do these things.”

But increasingly, parents of younger teens may not have that choice. Haidt’s theory holds undisputed dominance in many circles, including among politicians. Since Australia’s social media ban for teens, the UK and European Union are among those considering their own bans or platform limits. In the US, states like California and New York have enacted limits on certain social media features, and a federal proposal would restrict algorithmic feeds for kids under 17. Even among people who find Gray’s arguments about Common Core convincing, some might still see taking kids offline as a harmless precaution.

With so much momentum behind the backlash against phones and social media, can Gray’s book still make a difference? “I certainly hope it’s not too late,” he says. He points out that some moral panics have petered out. In the 1990s and 2000s, for instance, many people worried that video games like Mortal Kombat and Doom were making kids more violent, connecting their rise to that of school shootings. Eventually, research showed many mass shooters didn’t play video games after all. Attempts at regulation — including a California ban on the sale of violent games to children — were largely overruled. And many kids who did play them grew up to become those in charge. “The science won out eventually,” Gray says. “So it’s not me that’s going to win out. It’s the science that’s going to win out.”

text:
The hardest goodbye in of my life!

It wasn’t from someone I love, but a teammate.

He had been with us through the messy part, but after he left, the office felt like a question.

Why?

Cause just when we started building this company, we used to think about the usual things like better energy, better mobility, a future that makes more sense.

He was the one who pointed this:

"Fleet owners do not buy a vehicle, thinking about the future. They wake up thinking about whether their vehicle will earn todayỊại

That stayed with me.

So we stopped talking like we were selling a vision of transport.

We started building around:

help fleets reduce downtime, lower the cost of keeping vehicles running, and make every working day more profitable.

I learned two things from that goodbye.

- You cannot demand belief from people when you cannot yet offer them certainty.

- you cannot build for customers until you understand what uncertainty costs them.

text:
The Christian mystics did something radical: they took the ink of doctrine and turned it back into blood and fire. Standing in the wake of the Incarnation, they realized God wasn't an abstract ideal to analyze, but an interior presence to be lived. They plunged straight into the "dark night," proving that when human intellect exhausts itself, a deeper, transformative knowing takes over, one rooted in complete, unreserved surrender.
What makes the post-Apostolic mystics so compelling is their refusal to let theology remain mere words on a page. From Pseudo-Dionysius to Teresa of Ávila, they mapped the soul's inner topography with astonishing precision. They showed that contemplation isn't an escape from reality, but an awakening to it, a quiet, sustained unraveling of self-centered ego until nothing remains but the raw, unmediated light of Grace.
Christian mysticism is ultimately the daring art of living in the resonance of the Resurrection. Mystics aren't passive dreamers; they are spiritual pioneers who push past surface dogmas to touch the living source. By embracing interior poverty, they reveal a profound truth: that human limitation, when offered up entirely, becomes the precise locus where the infinite continuously enters and heals our broken world.

text:
2/2
The serpent did not begin with a number. He began with a question about what God had said. The beast does not begin with a brand. He begins with a mouth. We're all wrapped up in identifying the mark and the world is deaf. The world and the flesh are already training their ears. 

The beast's algorithms are training what we will receive as normal, what we will call wisdom, what we will refuse to question. If those ears are already closed, the later mark will only confirm what has already been decided in their hearts and minds. The mark doesn't damn them. What they put on their skin won't change them. What's in their ears does that.

By the time a mark is offered, most ears have already been schooled. The difference between those who belong to God and those who are not is wisdom. Wisdom is the opposite of wickedness. Not intellect. Smarter people than the saved will end up in hell. It's not intelligent ideas, it's the grace of God that makes their robes white. 

Wisdom is the opposite of wickedness, not the opposite of ignorance. 

Daniel never says the wise are the clever. He says they understand, they purify themselves, they are made white, they are refined, they turn many to righteousness.

The wicked act wickedly and do not understand.

The line is moral and spiritual before it is mental.

What makes the robes white is not better ideas.

"They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb."

That is grace.

The understanding Daniel promises is the fruit of that writing, not the price of admission to it. Not working out your salvation by studying more books, listening to more debates and podcasts, not having pedigrees and serving on the councils. That's not what the prophets preach.

Daniel does not send the wise to more books, more debates, more pedigrees, or a seat on the council. He says they understand, they are purified, they are made white, they are refined, they turn many to righteousness.

John does not say the saints out-argued the beast.

He says at the end of the bound time, they have an ear, they go into captivity if that is appointed, they refuse the sword, and they keep the faith of the Lamb who was slain. Their robes are made white because they washed them in His blood, not because they assembled a better library. Not once does Daniel or John mention a sacrament except the sacrament of grace.

Daniel never points the wise to a rite that admits them to the book. He says they are found written in it, they are purified, they are made white, they are refined. John never points the saints to an argument or a ceremony that keeps them from worshiping the beast.

The fruit, the work, is they will call forth others to righteousness. Daniel does not say the wise save themselves by what they know. He says those who have insight shine, and those who turn many to righteousness shine like the stars forever and ever. Calling others into the same hearing. John says the same without using Daniel’s words. The saints have an ear. They endure. They refuse the sword. They keep the faith of the slain Lamb. That posture itself turns many. Many come to Jesus because of the word they heard and the witness of the saints. 

The mark does not produce that fruit. Grace does. 

Three and a half years of greatest revival ever. In the face of the greatest tribulation ever known. The completion of the work Christ began. Distress and harvest in the same bounded hour. There will be a time of trouble such as never was; and at that time those written in the book are rescued, the sleepers wake, the wise shine, and those who turn many to righteousness shine like the stars. 

This is the gathering of the saints. The gathering Daniel and John both see is this; names already written in the book of the slain Lamb, robes already washed white in His blood, ears that received what God actually said, endurance that refused the sword, and then the fruit...many turned to righteousness.

Amen 🙏🏼

text:
Your customer doesn’t wake up wanting your product.

They wake up wanting what they believe your product can change for them.

Someone buying skincare may want clearer skin.

Someone buying a website may want credibility and trust.

Someone learning AI may actually want less manual work and more time.

So try this:

Take your main offer and finish:

“My customer buys this because they want to ______.”

Don’t give the obvious answer.

Go deeper.

Website → What do they want it to help them achieve?

Marketing → What do they want better marketing to change?

AI → What do they actually want AI to make easier?

That’s where stronger marketing starts.

AI can help you analyse customer conversations and find patterns.

But first:

Understand the customer.

Then use the tool.

text:
2018 - “Delivery logistics hell” acknowledgedElon Musk said Tesla had moved from “production hell” to “delivery logistics hell,” acknowledging that the company’s immediate Model 3 challenge had shifted from manufacturing enough vehicles to delivering them to customers.

2025 - Continued TSLA rally after Musk stock purchaseMarket reporting said TSLA closed at $425.86, roughly 1% higher on the day, extending a rally that followed Musk’s disclosed September 12 open-market purchase of about $1 billion in Tesla shares.

2018 - Free Supercharging referral incentive extendedAfter customer reports of ordering-system problems near the incentive deadline, Musk extended the referral-based lifetime free-Supercharging offer for qualifying Model S, Model X, and Model 3 Performance purchases until September 18. He said the program was not sustainable over the long term.

2021 - FSD Beta expansion plan announcedMusk said Tesla would broaden access to FSD Beta beginning September 24 for qualifying U.S. owners who had purchased FSD. Tesla planned to evaluate opt-in drivers’ behavior for seven days using a Safety Score before granting access.

2021 - NTSB announces Coral Gables crash investigationThe NTSB said it would investigate the September 13 fatal Coral Gables, Florida Tesla Model 3 crash and the post-crash fire. Authorities had not determined whether Autopilot was in use; the inquiry focused on vehicle operation and the fire.

2008 - Tesla announces San Jose Model S factory and headquarters planTesla announced a planned $250 million, 600,000-square-foot San Jose plant intended to assemble its second-generation, five-passenger Model S sedan, plus a planned headquarters and R&D relocation to the site. The proposal contemplated 500 manufacturing jobs and later additional headquarters/R&D employment. The plan was subsequently disrupted by Tesla's October liquidity actions and delay to the sedan program, so it should not be read as a completed factory investment.

2021 - Tesla pledges global data-security cooperationMusk said at a China industry event that Tesla would work with regulators worldwide to strengthen data security. The statement followed heightened Chinese scrutiny of connected-vehicle data and Tesla’s data-handling practices.

2023 - Tesla reaches 5 million EVs producedTesla announced it produced its five-millionth electric vehicle. Its China Weibo account identified the milestone vehicle as a Pearl White Model 3 Highland built at Gigafactory Shanghai.

text:
‘Very heavy tariffs’: Trump threatens EU over plan to make Canada its first associate member

US President Donald Trump has threatened to impose heavy tariffs on the European Union if it proceeds with plans to offer Canada associate membership status, describing the proposed arrangement as potentially hostile to American interests.

“If they do that, if I think it’s at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things,” Trump told reporters in North Carolina on Wednesday, adding that “bad intention” behind the move would trigger “very heavy tariffs.”

The Whistler reported that the warning followed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s State of the European Union address in Strasbourg, where she proposed Canada becoming the EU’s first associate member — covering manufacturing, technology, defence, energy and artificial intelligence cooperation.

Trump separately dismissed Canada joining the EU as “laughable” and called Canada a “terrible trade partner.”

text:
A China-Japan civilian seminar commemorating the coming anniversary of September 18 Incident was held simultaneously in Tokyo, Japan, and Changchun in Northeast China’s Jilin Province, on September 16, with the descendant of a former member of the military police troop of the Japanese Kwantung Army during Japan’s invasion of China donating a replica of a monument bearing her late father’s apology to China. 

The seminar, titled “Remember September 18, Donation of an ‘Apology Monument,’” was jointly organized by Sino-Japanese Oral History and Culture Research Association and Changchun Normal University. 

Historians from China and Japan, nongovernmental peace groups, descendants of the war perpetrators of Japan’s aggression against China, and university faculty and students attended the event both online and in person. 

The centerpiece of the seminar was the donation by Ayako Kurahashi, 79, a member of the Sino-Japanese Oral History and Culture Research Association, of a replica of an “apology monument” erected by her late father, Yukichi Osawa, to China. 

The seminar opened with bell ringing, an air-raid siren and a moment of silence, as participants bowed their heads in tribute. 

Osawa was stationed in places including Tianjin, Beijing, and Dongning in Northeast China’s Heilongjiang Province. In 1986, as he was seriously ill, he took a note from under his pillow and instructed his children to have the words engraved on his gravestone: “I took part in the war of aggression and deeply regret everything I did to the Chinese people. I can only offer my profound apology to the Chinese people.” 

In 1998, Kurahashi erected a separate monument at her family’s cemetery in Yoshioka, Gunma Prefecture, Japan, bearing her father’s full apology.

At the donation ceremony, Ayako Kurahashi read out the inscription on the monument and completed the handover to the Chinese side via video link. 

She also recounted the complicated journey of fulfilling her father’s dying wish over more than four decades, acknowledging that her father had never detailed what he had done in China, but insisted on leaving a message of apology before his death.

At the Tokyo event venue, Kurahashi, called on Japan to reflect on its history of aggression and expressed hope that her father’s apology would reach more people. Amid what she sees as a growing rightward shift in Japan and the resurgence of “neo- militarism,” Kurahashi said she feared the apology monument could be vandalized and decided to donate a replica to Changchun Normal University this year. 

“What disappears from sight can also disappear from people’s hearts. I sincerely hope that this monument will never be damaged and will continue to safeguard the truth of history,” Kurahashi said. 

Several Japanese participants addressed the history of Japanese aggression at the seminar. Takakage Fujita, the secretary-general of the Association for Inheriting and Propagating the Murayama Statement, acknowledged the fact that the September 18 Incident was staged by the Japanese Kwantung Army itself and was a premeditated act of aggression by Japanese militarism, which subsequently expanded into a full-scale war of aggression against China and eventually a war across the Pacific Ocean. He said that the Japanese people must never forget this war of aggression. 

He also criticized incumbent Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi for portraying the war as “self-defense” and rejecting the Murayama Statement and the Tokyo Trial, saying her erroneous remarks regarding China’s Taiwan had caused a deep rift in Japan-China relations and warned that Japan should not turn Asia into a battlefield again.

text:
History remembers few soldiers with the courage, determination, and resilience of Milunka Savić, the legendary Serbian warrior marches into Supremacy 1914, bringing her indomitable spirit to the front lines. When her bedridden brother was called for mobilization, Milunka Savić took his place. Disguising herself as a man, she enlisted in the Serbian Army and fought with such extraordinary courage that no one questioned her place among the ranks...

Koprivnica, a village near Raška in southern Serbia. Autumn 1912. Twenty households, maybe a hundred people. The mobilization decree went out on 30 September and the call-up papers reached the Savić house for Milan, the only son, who had tuberculosis. His older sister read the paper. She cut off her hair, put on his clothes, walked to a mobilization assembly point in Belgrade, and registered as Milun Savić.

She was in combat within weeks. Kumanovo. The siege of Scutari. Then Bregalnica in the summer of 1913, a nine-day battle where she fought as a grenadier and earned a corporal's rank and her first medal for bravery. On the last day of the fighting she was leading her squad forward when a grenade caught her. Stretcher bearers carried her to a field dressing station. The orderlies unbuttoned her tunic to reach the wound and found that the soldier they had been fighting beside for a year was a woman.

Nobody wanted to punish her. She was, by then, a decorated soldier with ten actions behind her. So they offered her the exit that made everyone comfortable: a transfer to the nursing division, where women belonged. She refused. When the Great War came in 1914 and no assignment arrived for her, she went looking for one. Antonije Đurić recorded what happened when she walked into General Stepa Stepanović's headquarters in Kragujevac, reporting as the volunteer Milun: "I request my war assignment." They gave her one.

She fought the whole war. Kolubara, where she won her first Karađorđe Star with Swords. The retreat through Albania in the winter of 1915, when the Serbian army walked itself to death across the mountains and she stayed with the column. Kaymakchalan. The Crna Bend in 1916, where she went into the Bulgarian trenches alone and came back with twenty-three prisoners, which earned her a second Karađorđe Star. She was a bomber, a grenade specialist, and she was wounded nine times over three wars.

The Allies noticed before her own country did. She was decorated by France twice with the Legion of Honour, by Russia with the Cross of St. George, by Britain with the Order of St. Michael and St. George. In 1918, in the naval port of Bizerte in Tunisia, French Admiral Guépratte pinned on the Croix de Guerre with the gold palm. She remains the only woman ever awarded that version of it. France offered her a home and a general's pension. She turned it down and went back to Belgrade.
Then the country she had fought for forgot her name. She worked in the post office. She worked odd jobs. From 1927 she cleaned the State Mortgage Bank, and after eight years she was promoted to cleaning the general manager's office. She married, had a daughter, divorced, adopted three more girls and raised dozens of other people's children. Under German occupation she refused an invitation to a banquet held by the collaborator Milan Nedić. In April 1971, journalist Ljiljana Banićanin found her in a crumbling three-room house on Voždovac with an outdoor toilet, wearing two sweaters and a blanket in the spring sun, eating bread with apples. The medals were gone. A man had come to the door and said he would clean them up nicely, and never came back. Visitors had taken her photographs off the walls. "The others don't even know I'm alive," she said. Editors killed the piece. It ran twenty-four years later, in 1995. In 1972, after a newspaper exposed how she was living, the city gave her a small apartment. She died on 5 October 1973, aged 81.
