text:
Today in History 
September 17th
1968
When Julia premiered on NBC on September 17, 1968, American television gained a leading character rarely seen in prime time: an educated, independent Black professional woman whose everyday life formed the center of the story. Diahann Carroll’s starring role made her the first Black woman since the end of Beulah in 1953 to headline a regularly scheduled network television series. More significantly, Julia Baker was conceived as a sharp departure from the stereotypes that had long limited the roles available to Black women on television.

Created by Hal Kanter, the comedy followed Julia Baker, a widowed mother living in Los Angeles with her young son, Corey. Her husband, an Army captain, had been killed while serving in Vietnam. Julia supported her family by working as a nurse for physician Dr. Morton Chegley, portrayed by Lloyd Nolan, while Marc Copage played Corey.

The character represented a striking change from earlier television portrayals. Black performers had often been confined to roles rooted in stereotypes inherited from radio, vaudeville, and Hollywood. Even Beulah, important as an earlier series built around a Black female star, featured its central character as a maid employed by a white family. Julia, arriving fifteen years later, instead showed its heroine with a career, a home of her own, and a family life in which her race mattered without becoming the subject of every storyline.

The series also appeared at an extraordinary moment in American history. Its debut came only months after the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr., as the country continued to struggle with segregation and racial inequality in employment, housing, and other areas of life. Against that turbulent background, Julia generally chose the familiar rhythms of a warm network sitcom rather than direct examinations of the era’s racial conflicts.

That choice became central to the debate surrounding the program. Many viewers valued seeing a capable and successful Black professional treated with dignity in prime time. Some Black critics, however, believed Julia Baker’s comfortable and largely integrated surroundings offered too polished a picture of American race relations. Carroll recognized the tension herself: she wanted television to depict Black people with sophistication and humanity while understanding that her character’s circumstances could not stand for the experiences of all Black Americans.

Carroll had already established a formidable career before television made her Julia Baker. Born Carol Diann Johnson in the Bronx in 1935, she became known as both a singer and actress, appearing in nightclubs, on television, and in such films as Carmen Jones (1954) and Porgy and Bess (1959). Broadway provided another milestone. In 1962 she won the Tony Award for Best Actress in a Musical for No Strings, becoming the first Black woman to receive the award in that category.

Her three seasons on Julia turned Carroll into one of television’s best-known stars. The show produced 86 episodes before concluding in 1971, and Carroll’s performance brought her a Golden Globe Award and an Emmy nomination. The series’ approach to racial issues may seem cautious from a later perspective, but its weekly image was itself consequential: millions of viewers saw a Black woman whose professional and personal life was unquestionably the focus of the program.

Julia neither resolved television’s problems with representation nor tried to encompass the full complexity of Black American life. Its historic contribution was simpler but profound: it made a Black woman the undisputed center of a major network series and allowed audiences to know her as a professional, mother, neighbor, and multidimensional individual. Carroll’s achievement helped expand what television considered possible for the Black actresses and characters who came afterward. #OTD

TOP 5 GROWTH LEN5 NAMES: FOUR OF THESE BANKS SELL THE SAME THING. BOK FINANCIAL $BOKF SELLS SOMETHING ELSE:

BOK Financial, ticker BOKF, at $132.82, -$2.95 / -2.17% on Wednesday, with no trade since the bell. Third of thirty on the Growth Len5. The Tulsa company is a bank that also runs a securities trading desk, a mortgage business and a wealth manager.

Cheap growth in this market is almost entirely a bank story - this Len5's list is lenders nearly all the way down. That matters, because a bank's growth is mostly a spread it does not set: what it earns on loans, minus what it pays depositors. BOK Financial largely sells something else.

The number that decides it is 40 cents - how much of every revenue dollar it booked in the June quarter came from fees, not lending. The other four run 18 to 23 cents.

The June quarter, reported July 20:

- Net profit $176.5M, or $2.92 a share, against $2.19 a year earlier - up 33%
- Fee revenue $237.6M, beside $351.8M of lending revenue
- Net interest margin 2.91% - the gap between what it earns on loans and what it pays savers - the narrowest of the five here
- Loans $27.1B, +11.5% over the year; running costs took 60.2 cents of each revenue dollar, from 65.4
- Credit: $500,000 written off all quarter, and no charge taken against profit for future bad loans

So the worst lending margin on this board sits under the second-largest profit jump on it. At about 12.5 times the last year of profit and 1.33 times book value - what owners would keep if everything were sold and every debt paid - that is a bank price for a business only 60% bank.

The strongest fact against sits in the same release. Fees are the swinging half: trading fees fell $12.7M on lower volumes as interest-rate markets moved around - and on Wednesday the Federal Reserve raised its target range, the rate banks charge each other overnight, a quarter point to 3.75%-4.00%. Its last four quarters earned $2.22, $2.89, $2.58 and $2.92 a share. Analysts carry $2.54 for September - 13% under the quarter just delivered, and 14% above the same quarter a year ago. Both are true, and that is the point.

CHANGE IT: fee revenue growing in a quarter when the trading desk is quiet, which would put the fiduciary and asset-management side, $71.0M last quarter, in charge. WHEN: October 19 after the close, company-confirmed. RISK: the shares are 9.6% under their August 17 high of $146.84. VERDICT: the growth here does not lean on the Fed, and the reason it does not is also the reason the next quarter is pencilled below the last.

What this Len5 hunts, in a line: profit growth the share price has not already charged for. The other four, from most fee income to least.

- Ameris Bancorp at $83.72, -$1.11 / -1.31% on Wednesday, no trade since. Ninth of thirty. The Atlanta bank lends across the Southeast and runs a large retail mortgage arm, which is why 23 cents of each revenue dollar is fees. The growth is the half that stalled: the June quarter, reported July 23, earned $1.60 a share with one-time items stripped out, against $1.59 a year earlier. Flat. The reported figure was $0.77, cut by an $82.5M charge: on July 27 a federal court entered a $79.5M judgment against Ameris Bank in a whistleblower-retaliation case brought by the founder of Balboa Capital, a lender Ameris owns. It will appeal. CHANGE IT: loan growth, running at 6.4% a year, reaching profit per share again. WHEN: October 26, tentative. VERDICT: near 13 times profit once the court case is set aside, on a year that has not grown.

- Popular at $160.96, -$3.94 / -2.39% on Wednesday, no trade since. Twelfth of thirty. Puerto Rico's largest bank, trading since 1893, with $70.2B of deposits. It is both the fastest grower here and the cheapest: the June quarter, reported July 23, earned $4.35 a share against $3.09, +41%, at about 11 times the last year of profit. Its margin widened to 3.66% from 3.49%, and on August 20 it lifted the quarterly dividend 20% to $0.90, paid October 1. CHANGE IT: bad loans, at 1.04% of its lending against 0.82% a year ago. WHEN: October 22, tentative. VERDICT: the largest profit jump here, and the only one whose credit is worsening while everything else improves.

- Trustmark at $47.17, -$0.35 / -0.74% on Wednesday, no trade since. Eleventh of thirty. The Jackson, Mississippi bank lends and runs a wealth-management arm, where revenue grew 13.3% over the year to $10.9M. Read its growth carefully: the June quarter, reported July 28, showed $1.08 a share, but $0.11 of that was two one-off gains - a sale of mortgage loans and a Visa stock exchange. Take those out and it is $0.97 against $0.92, up 5%, on revenue of $208.2M that landed under the $210.3M expected. CHANGE IT: fee income growing without a sale inside it. WHEN: October 27, tentative. VERDICT: the slowest grower here, and the one whose headline flatters it most.

- Home BancShares at $29.74, -$0.47 / -1.56% on Wednesday, no trade since. Sixth of thirty. The Conway, Arkansas bank is the purest lender of the five - 18 cents of each revenue dollar is fees - and has the widest spread to show for it, a 4.51% margin against BOK Financial's 2.91%. The June quarter, reported July 15, was a record: net revenue $295.1M, +8.9%, and $0.64 a share with one-time costs stripped out, against $0.58, after $12.7M of expenses from buying Mountain Commerce Bancorp and the $1.47B of loans it brought. CHANGE IT: whether 4.51% survives now that savers are offered more elsewhere. WHEN: October 14 after the close, company-confirmed. VERDICT: the widest margin on this board, and the most to lose if it narrows.

Four of these banks report the same number in late October: what they charged borrowers, minus what they paid savers. BOK Financial reports that one too, on October 19, and then reports the 40 cents that came from somewhere else. The second number is the one worth reading.

Below is a list of some national, international, global and local observances for September 17, 2026:

Constitution Day and Citizenship Day commemorates the September 17, 1787 signing of the U.S. Constitution by 39 of 55 Convention delegates in Philadelphia, an observance that also honors naturalized citizens and requires federally funded schools to provide Constitution-related education; three prominent holdouts—George Mason, Elbridge Gerry, and Edmund Randolph—refused to sign because the original document lacked a Bill of Rights, a omission that later amendments only partially addressed after intense public debate.

https://t.co/LJrRV9s2Uj

National Apple Dumpling Day celebrates the Colonial-era dessert of whole apples wrapped in pastry, baked with spices and often served with cream or sauce, a treat rooted in English and German immigrant baking that became a staple in early American households; George Washington reportedly favored apple dumplings, and the dish’s simple construction allowed it to travel well on long journeys when fresh fruit was scarce.

https://t.co/LJrRV9s2Uj

National Monte Cristo Day honors the deep-fried ham, turkey, and Swiss cheese sandwich dusted with powdered sugar and often served with jam, a mid-20th-century American diner adaptation of the French croque-monsieur that Bennigan’s popularized when it established the day in 2015; the sandwich’s theatrical presentation and sweet-savory contrast made it a signature item at Disneyland’s Blue Bayou restaurant, where it has been served since the park’s early years.

https://t.co/CKyrKMI0dN

International Country Music Day recognizes the genre’s Appalachian, blues, and cowboy roots and was created in 2003 to mark the birthday of Hank Williams, born September 17, 1923; Williams’ brief, turbulent career produced songs that still define the “high lonesome” sound, yet he died at 29, leaving an outsized influence that later artists from Nashville to Australia continue to reinterpret.

https://t.co/CKyrKMI0dN

World Patient Safety Day, proclaimed by the World Health Organization in 2019, focuses global attention on preventable harm in healthcare, which causes an estimated 2.6 million deaths annually in low- and middle-income countries alone; the day’s rotating annual themes underscore that even high-resource systems still struggle with communication failures and medication errors that account for a surprising share of avoidable injury.

https://t.co/LJrRV9s2Uj

National Professional House Cleaners Day, established in 2019 by the American House Cleaners Association, acknowledges the skilled labor that maintains healthier indoor environments in homes and businesses; professional cleaners routinely encounter hidden hazards—from outdated wiring to chemical residues—that homeowners rarely notice until they become problems.

https://t.co/CKyrKMI0dN

National Pet Bird Day, created in 2019 by the organization BEAK, encourages owners to enrich the lives of companion parrots, finches, and other avian pets through interaction and proper care; many commonly kept species can live 50–80 years, outlasting multiple human generations and creating long-term welfare responsibilities that few first-time owners anticipate.

https://t.co/CKyrKMI0dN

Time’s Up Day, originated by Thomas and Ruth Roy of Wellcat Holidays, urges people to end lingering grudges and repair strained relationships rather than let them fester; the Roys built a cottage industry of quirky observances after discovering they could submit new “holidays” to Chase’s Calendar of Events in the late 1980s.

https://t.co/LJrRV9s2Uj

World Manta Day, launched in 2020 by the Manta Trust, highlights the conservation of manta and devil rays, filter-feeding giants whose gill plates are sought in traditional medicine; a single female may produce only four to seven pups in her lifetime, making populations extremely slow to recover from overfishing.

https://t.co/vLF00zm9aZ

National Pawpaw Day (third Thursday in September) celebrates Asimina triloba, North America’s largest native fruit, whose banana-mango custard flavor was a staple for Indigenous peoples and later for Lewis and Clark when other provisions ran low; Kentucky State University created the day in 2019 and still runs the world’s only full-time pawpaw research program aimed at breeding better cultivars.

https://t.co/shdGK0kgZ4

International Day of Listening (third Thursday in September), established by the International Listening Association, promotes the under-practiced skill of attentive listening in an era of constant interruption; studies consistently show that most people overestimate their listening ability while simultaneously feeling unheard themselves.

https://t.co/CKyrKMI0dN

National Teach Ag Day (third Thursday in September) highlights the work of more than 11,000 agricultural educators who prepare students for careers in food and natural-resource systems; the National Association of Agricultural Educators notes a persistent teacher shortage even as global food demand continues to rise.

https://t.co/KXBwj5Ap8p

Free Queso Day (third Thursday in September), begun by Moe’s Southwest Grill in 2010, offers complimentary chile-con-queso at participating locations as a customer-appreciation promotion; the dip’s popularity has turned a single-day giveaway into an entire “queso season” for some chains.

https://t.co/aSOVwomC1d

National Table Shuffleboard Day, founded in 2017 by manufacturer Zieglerworld, honors the parlor game that evolved from 15th-century English “shove-groat”; King Henry VIII banned commoners from playing because they became too absorbed, even though he himself enjoyed the game.

https://t.co/LJrRV9s2Uj

Australian Citizenship Day, first observed in 2001, encourages reflection on the rights and responsibilities of Australian citizenship and often features community events and ceremonies; it was deliberately placed on September 17 because it is the anniversary of the renaming of the Nationality and Citizenship Act 1948 to the Australian Citizenship Act 1948, which occurred on September 17, 1973.

https://t.co/LJrRV9s2Uj

International Microorganism Day commemorates the September 17, 1683 letter in which Antonie van Leeuwenhoek first described single-celled organisms he observed with his handmade microscopes; the Portuguese Society of Microbiology launched the observance in 2017 to spotlight microbes’ beneficial roles in health, food, and ecosystems rather than only their pathogenic ones.

https://t.co/0ihNHJitHV

National Pet Carbon Monoxide Safety Day, established by Kidde in 2020, reminds owners that pets can suffer CO poisoning before humans notice symptoms because they often rest closer to the floor where the odorless gas concentrates; detectors placed at pet level can provide an earlier warning than those mounted higher on walls.

https://t.co/CKyrKMI0dN

National DEI Day aligns with Constitution Day to emphasize that diversity, equity, and inclusion efforts are part of the ongoing American project of forming “a more perfect union”; organizers chose the date because the original Constitution’s silences on who counted as fully included have been incrementally addressed through amendments and social movements.

https://t.co/UmDafHC4cT

text:
Why Worst Blacks, Jews and Socialist Democracies Since @BarackObama Emergency Management @JonesDay Is Clean Water A Constitutional Right? Erin Brockovich take. Remember Flint? I remember when the president drank the water on TV to show the water was “safe.” Officials dragged their feet. It took almost two years after residents reported that something was wrong with the water for Flint Mayor Karen Weaver to declare a state of emergency due to elevated lead levels.

The 6th Circuit’s approach in the Flint litigation, allowed a constitutional claim to clean water move forward. They found that city and state did violate people’s constitutional right to “bodily integrity” by knowingly poisoning them and covering it up. Unfortunately, none of the officials have been successfully charged or convicted in the Flint water crisis.

The Fifth Circuit didn’t rule on whether people deserve clean water; it ruled on whether the Constitution requires a city to give it to them.

This ruling is only binding on federal courts in Mississippi, Louisiana, and Texas. It doesn’t bar similar claims anywhere else in the country. That means two federal appeals courts now disagree with each other on the same basic question: whether people harmed by a government’s contaminated water have a constitutional claim.

The Supreme Court exists to resolve these kinds of disagreements between circuits, and it leaves the Jackson residents one option they didn’t have before this ruling. They could take their case up to the highest court in the land.

Plus, a separate case, brought by the NAACP and Jackson residents over how federal infrastructure money for water repairs was distributed, is still pending.

While the community members who brought this case didn’t win, I want to point out what they gained.

The dissent in this ruling puts on the record, in a federal court document, that the city introduced and worsened lead contamination under a former mayor, misled residents about it, and knew the risks while it kept quiet. This ruling is now citable by the next lawsuit and the next lawmaker who wants to point out what went wrong and who let it happen.

This case also went all the way to the full court, not just a three-judge panel. Courts don’t send cases to en banc review, and judges don’t write dissents like this one, in questions they consider settled.

Of course, none of these legal battles directly fix people’s water troubles. They don’t undo what families have had to live through, and they don’t force Jackson or any other city to act faster or with more transparency next time.

This ruling does offer the next fight something concrete to build on. A different court could have a different ruling, helping the next community. When people without power take on a system that isn’t built to hear them, you get mixed results. The good news is that they get a record that no one can erase.

Speaking of Dragging Our Feet… PFAS Is Here To Stay

text:
**ACVA — ACV Auctions Inc.**

ACVA is the NYSE ticker for **ACV Auctions**, a Buffalo-based digital marketplace for wholesale used vehicles. Dealers and commercial sellers list cars; other dealers bid online. The pitch is remote auctions with condition data, instead of standing in a physical lane.

Founded in 2014 and public since 2021, ACV wraps the auction with services around the sale: transportation quotes, short-term inventory financing (ACV Capital), post-sale assurance, remarketing/reconditioning centers, and data tools such as True360 condition reports and ACV MAX inventory software. In 2025 it reported about $10.4 billion of marketplace GMV. Revenue has been growing (TTM around $800 million); the company has still been reporting a GAAP net loss.

The live story now is M&A. On September 10, 2026, **Copart** agreed to buy ACV for **$10.50 per share in cash** — about $1.9 billion, a roughly 45% premium to the unaffected price. The deal is structured as a tender offer plus merger, targeted to close by year-end 2026, subject to antitrust clearance and other conditions. ACV is expected to keep operating as an independent subsidiary. Near-term, the stock has traded close to the offer price.

THE PAYPAH ☕📰 | 005
SEPTEMBER 17, 2026
Information cutoff: 6:12 a.m. Central (CDT, UTC−05:00).

The Fed raised the price of money. Oil is offering a little relief. Neither tells us the inflation fight is over.

FED: ONE HIKE, NOT NECESSARILY THE LAST

Yesterday’s unanimous decision lifted the federal-funds target by 0.25 percentage point to 3.75%–4.00%. Of 18 policymakers, two project no further increase by year-end, 12 another quarter-point and four another half-point.

Those are individual projections—not promised moves or market probabilities.

Our read: higher required returns make distant earnings worth less today. Softer inflation and falling yields would weaken that valuation headwind.

Fed: https://t.co/QAvyiPMUZf
Projections: https://t.co/mPf5Br2JHN

RETAIL: THE WALLET IS STILL OPEN

August retail and food-services sales rose 1.2% month over month, seasonally adjusted, after July’s revised 0.5% decline. These are dollars spent, not inflation-adjusted volumes.

Our read: that rebound gives the Fed less reason to fear an immediate demand collapse. It does not prove purchasing power improved; weakening real spending would challenge the resilience story.

Census: https://t.co/0h2djuwbLa

OIL: RELIEF HAS TO REACH THE DOCK

Brent futures were $104.33 a barrel, down 1.42%, at 5:00 a.m. Central (CDT, UTC−05:00). Reuters reports additional Saudi cargo offers via Oman are easing supply worries after pipeline attacks.

Our read: alternative shipments can soften the shortage premium. Offers are not completed deliveries or repaired infrastructure; renewed export losses would puncture the relief.

Reuters: https://t.co/ua1TFiEWKu

AI: TRUST IS PART OF THE PRODUCT

OpenAI yesterday introduced a framework for reporting model misalignment and published six case reports. It cautions that individual examples do not establish how frequently misalignment occurs.

Our read: enterprise adoption needs permission controls, monitoring and auditability—not just smarter demos. Transparency can help build trust; recurring failures despite safeguards would weaken the monetization case.

OpenAI: https://t.co/fd4adaNoHe

WATCH NEXT

7:30 a.m. Central: initial jobless claims, August housing starts and permits, and September Philadelphia Fed manufacturing. All are upcoming at this cutoff.

New York Fed calendar: https://t.co/A5BdyEeUqQ

At the open, watch whether softer yields lift Nasdaq-100 stocks broadly, not just a few megacaps. If tech cannot respond to cheaper money, look beyond the Fed for the explanation.

As a flagship global event for university communications and reputation management, THE World 100 Annual Conference 2026 recently took place in Vienna, Austria. Organised by @timeshighered and THE World 100 Reputation Network, the conference was hosted in partnership with the University of Vienna and TU Wien.

Centered on the theme "University reputation and trust in a time of change", this year’s conference brought together senior representatives and international education leaders from dozens of prestigious universities worldwide. As the only Hong Kong institution participating in this year's event, CityUHK was represented by Professor Shirley Chong, Chief Communications and Global Affairs Officer, who engaged in deep exchanges with global higher education leaders.

THE World 100 Reputation Network comprises reputation management strategists from top global institutions, including King's College London, the London School of Economics and Political Science, the University of Toronto, and University of New South Wales. Serving as a committee member of the network representing Asian universities, Professor Chong is dedicated to elevating the brand presence and influence of Asian higher education on the global stage.

The co-hosting institutions both enjoy prestigious academic standing in Europe: the University of Vienna is the oldest existing university in the German-speaking world with over 660 years of history, while TU Wien boasts over 200 years of heritage with renowned strengths in engineering and natural sciences.

At the panel session titled "Strategically leveraging university-industry relationships", Professor Chong shared how CityUHK drives global impact through its twin engines of Internationalisation and Innovation. She highlighted that CityUHK leverages its unique advantage as the world's " Most International University", combining robust research capability with its flagship innovation and entrepreneurship initiative, HK Tech 300—which has incubated over 1,000 start-ups—to actively accelerate the translation of research achievements into practical applications.

The conference featured interactive sessions where international experts offered valuable insights into the societal role of higher education, institutional reputation management, and global collaboration. Professor James Tang, Secretary-General of the University Grants Committee of the HKSAR Government, was also invited to attend the conference dinner.

Through this premier international platform, CityUHK gained valuable insights into building global reputation and public trust while further reinforcing strategic partnerships with leading universities worldwide. Moving forward, CityUHK will continue to collaborate with global higher education peers to navigate future challenges, drive educational transformation and innovation, and elevate Hong Kong’s academic and innovation impact worldwide.

GOOGLE PAID $2.4 BILLION TO HIRE ONE MAN AND NOT BUY THE COMPANY HE RAN

Friday July 11 2025. Windsurf, one of the hottest AI coding startups on earth, had spent months in exclusive talks with OpenAI for a $3 billion acquisition. The exclusivity expired that morning.

His name is Varun Mohan. Co-founder and CEO of Windsurf, 250 employees.

Hours after the OpenAI window closed, Google announced it was hiring Mohan, co-founder Douglas Chen, and a handful of top researchers. It paid $2.4 billion. It did not buy the company. It licensed some tech and walked away with the people.

Everyone else stayed at their desks.

Jeff Wang, head of business for two years, got the interim CEO title that morning and had to face the room the same day. He described the all-hands to Bloomberg in one sentence.

"Probably the worst day of 250 people's lives."

Of the $2.4 billion, roughly $1.2 billion was compensation for the ~40 people Google hired. Most of that went to the two founders. Investors got 4x. The rest of the team was expecting an OpenAI payout that never arrived. Cognition signed the leftovers Monday at 9:30 am and waived every vesting cliff.

Big tech figured out how to buy the team without buying the company, and antitrust has no answer. Microsoft/Inflection. Amazon/Adept. Character/Google. Now Windsurf. Same structure four times in eighteen months.

Take an offer at a hot AI startup and the number on the term sheet is not what you earn. What you earn depends on which side of the reverse-acquihire wall you sit on when the phone rings. Founders sit on one side. Common-stock engineers sit on the other.

Watch Wang say it on Bloomberg. He smiles.

text:
The capture of the Independence Palace in Saigon on April 30, 1975, concluded the Ho Chi Minh Campaign and marked the collapse of South Vietnam. Following the 1973 Paris Peace Accords and the withdrawal of United States combat units, North Vietnamese forces launched a rapid general offensive in early 1975, swiftly overrunning the Central Highlands and coastal redoubts. By late April, the People's Army of Vietnam (PAVN) had encircled Saigon, prompting Operation Frequent Wind—the emergency American helicopter evacuation—and leaving the southern capital militarily isolated. 

At midday on April 30, armored columns from the PAVN 203rd Tank Brigade reached the presidential compound. Soviet-built tanks, led by units 843 and 390, crashed through the perimeter gates without meeting armed resistance. Inside, General Duong Van Minh—who had assumed the presidency only two days earlier hoping to negotiate a settlement—waited with his cabinet to transfer authority. PAVN commissar Bui Van Tung dismissed the offer, stating that Minh held no power left to give, before taking custody of the government. 

Soldiers raised the National Liberation Front flag over the palace roof, and Minh was escorted to Saigon's central radio station to broadcast an unconditional surrender. His directive ordered all South Vietnamese forces to lay down their weapons and officially dissolved the Saigon administration. The seizure terminated thirty years of military conflict, transferring interim authority to the Provisional Revolutionary Government prior to formal national reunification in 1976.

text:
Hashtpar Hub
A Strategic Development for Western Gilan, Iran.
Transforming Talesh into an Ecological, Cultural, Industrial, Tourism, and Innovation Hub
By Raghu Kondori @RaghuKondori | Shahvand Think Tank.
Hashtpar, the administrative center of Talesh County in western Gilan, occupies one of the most unique geographical and cultural positions in northern Iran. Situated between the Caspian Sea and the Talesh mountain range, the region possesses an extraordinary concentration of natural and human assets: Hyrcanian forests, fertile agricultural plains, rivers, coastline, biodiversity, high rainfall, mountain landscapes, and a deeply rooted Tavalesh cultural identity.
Despite these advantages, the region continues to operate below its strategic potential. Much of the local economy remains dependent on low-value raw agriculture, fragmented tourism, seasonal income patterns, and migration toward larger urban centers. Educational specialization remains limited, industrial infrastructure underdeveloped, and many historical and cultural assets continue to deteriorate.
The Hashtpar Hub proposal presents a long-term transformation model for western Gilan. Rather than relying on isolated sectors, the project creates an interconnected regional ecosystem where tourism, agriculture, industry, education, culture, and ecological preservation reinforce one another.
The proposal is structured around six integrated development axes:
holistic tourism, advanced agro-processing industries, education and innovation,
urban-cultural infrastructure, bamboo value-chain industries, and ecological preservation.
Together, these pillars form a new model of regional modernization designed for a future Iran open to international tourism, foreign investment, cultural exchange, and advanced economic integration.
The objective is not uncontrolled urbanization or destructive coastal commercialization. The objective is intelligent modernization rooted in the ecological and cultural identity of Talesh itself.
Nature becomes the foundation of development rather than its victim.
Over a ten-year horizon, the project aims to increase regional GDP from approximately one billion dollars to more than five billion dollars while reducing unemployment, reversing brain drain, modernizing urban life, attracting investment, and preserving the Hyrcanian ecosystem.
Strategic Vision
The Hashtpar Hub functions as a circular regional economy rather than an extractive one.
Agriculture feeds industry.
Industry supports exports.
Tourism finances preservation.
Education drives innovation.
Culture strengthens civic identity.
Urban modernization attracts talent and investment.
Ecological preservation increases long-term economic value.
The regional development cycle can be summarized as:
Nature → Tourism → Industry → Education → Innovation → Export → Reinvestment into Nature
The project gradually transforms the region:
from raw production to value-added industry,
from seasonal tourism to year-round premium tourism,
from migration toward local opportunity,
and from fragmented development toward integrated strategic planning.
Axis 1 — Luxury Holistic Tourism
Hyrcan Holiday
The flagship tourism project of the Hashtpar Hub is the creation of an integrated ecological wellness destination called Hyrcan Holiday.
Located around the Gisum coastal corridor and surrounding forest zones, the project combines luxury tourism with environmental stewardship and ecological preservation.
The tourism ecosystem includes ecological four- and five-star hotels, sea-facing meditation halls, yoga and mindfulness retreat centers, forest therapy trails, eco-spas, artistic cafés, cultural-modern nightlife spaces, music festivals, eco-tourism programs, and carefully regulated water sports areas.
The development model remains intentionally low-density. Only approximately twenty to thirty percent of the designated coastal zone would be structurally developed. The majority remains protected ecological territory. High-rise construction and destructive forest clearing would not be permitted.
The objective is not mass tourism but premium ecological tourism aimed at affluent visitors from Europe, Gulf states, East Asia, Iranian diaspora communities, and upper-middle-class urban travelers seeking balance between nature, wellness, culture, and modern leisure.
During the daytime, visitors experience hiking, forest bathing, meditation, yoga, sea relaxation, ecological retreats, and cultural tourism. During the evening, the region offers refined nightlife, artistic cafés, music venues, social gathering spaces, festivals, and modern entertainment integrated into a controlled ecological environment.
The project positions Talesh as a destination defined by:
forest, sea, wellness, culture, and ecological sophistication.
The long-term target is approximately one million annual visitors generating between three hundred and five hundred million dollars in annual tourism revenue while creating tens of thousands of direct and indirect jobs.
Axis 2 — Advanced Agro-Processing Industries
The second pillar of the Hashtpar Hub is the creation of a modern agro-industrial and logistics ecosystem capable of transforming western Gilan from a raw agricultural supplier into a high-value export region.
The proposal establishes a five-hundred-hectare industrial park focused on processing kiwi, medlar, honey, hazelnuts, herbal products, fishery outputs, and caviar-related products into branded export-grade goods.
The industrial ecosystem includes modern processing lines, dried fruit production facilities, premium jam manufacturing, organic fertilizer systems, fishery and caviar packaging centers, smart cold-storage infrastructure, eco-packaging industries, food laboratories, logistics hubs, and export distribution platforms.
Rather than exporting raw products, the region begins exporting finished products with significantly higher value and stronger international market positioning.
The project is supported through public-private partnerships and strategic investment channels involving domestic investors, Iranian diaspora capital, and regional investment partners and Europe.
The industrial axis aims to generate more than two hundred million dollars in annual export revenue while creating approximately twenty thousand direct industrial jobs and stabilizing agricultural income across the region.
Environmental sustainability remains integrated into all industrial planning to ensure that economic growth does not damage the ecological foundations of western Gilan.
Axis 3 — Education and Innovation
Long-term transformation requires a local knowledge economy capable of producing expertise, innovation, and regional leadership.
The proposal therefore establishes Hashtpar University Campus as a regional center for applied ecological and technological education.
The university specializes in:
forestry sciences, sustainable agriculture, aquaculture, environmental engineering,
bamboo engineering, ecological architecture, tourism management, renewable energy systems, agro-technology, and smart regional planning.
Unlike isolated academic institutions disconnected from local economies, the university operates as a direct innovation engine connected to surrounding industries and tourism systems.
Research and startup activity focuses on ecological agriculture, bamboo composites, sustainable packaging, tourism systems, aquaculture technologies, smart irrigation, environmental monitoring, and agro-industrial innovation.
The university also serves as a mechanism to reverse migration patterns by allowing educated youth to remain in western Gilan while participating in a modern economic ecosystem.
The long-term outcome is the emergence of a regional managerial and entrepreneurial class rooted in the identity and ecology of Talesh itself.
Axis 4 — Urban-Cultural Infrastructure
Soroodi Cultural Center and Civic Transformation
Economic development without cultural continuity eventually creates socially hollow cities. The Hashtpar Hub therefore places major emphasis on urban and cultural transformation.
At the center of this vision stands the revitalization of Amjad Sardar Palace. Rather than remaining an abandoned historical structure, the palace would be transformed into a Museum of Talesh History and Culture dedicated to the language, architecture, anthropology, music, traditions, and historical memory of the Tavalesh people.
The palace becomes both a museum and a symbolic landmark of Talesh itself.
Another major cultural project concerns the complete redevelopment of the historic Soroodi Bookshop site.
For nearly eighty-five years, Soroodi Bookshop occupied a unique place within the intellectual and educational life of western Gilan. During a period when even larger northern cities such as Astara and Bandar Anzali still lacked bookstores, Soroodi had already become a center for books, newspapers, magazines, photography, stationery, and public culture.
For generations of students across Talesh, the bookstore functioned as one of the primary places for obtaining school textbooks and educational material. In practical terms, it operated as an unofficial educational distribution center for the region itself.
Soroodi was not only associated with bookselling. He was also active in journalism and occasionally published reports and news related to Hashtpar and Talesh in national newspapers, helping connect the region to the wider cultural and media landscape of Iran.
The bookstore also maintained a strong connection to photography and camera culture during an important historical period of the region. Over decades, large numbers of photographs documenting daily life, schools, streets, families, ceremonies, landscapes, agriculture, and social transformation in Talesh were produced and preserved.
Today the original structure stands in complete ruin and cannot realistically be restored. The project therefore proposes the demolition of the remaining building and the construction of a new four- to six-floor cultural institution on the existing urban plot together with its approximately five-hundred-square-meter rear land reserve.
The new institution would be called:
Soroodi Cultural Center
The center is envisioned not merely as a library, but as one of the principal civic and intellectual institutions of future Hashtpar.
The building would integrate:
public library spaces, modern reading halls, digital learning areas, historical archives,
photography and visual-memory collections, conference halls, theater spaces, artistic workshops, cultural exhibitions,public lecture facilities, and civic gathering areas.
The ground floor would remain socially open and integrated into urban life through bookstores, exhibition spaces, and public gathering zones.
One of the most important dimensions of the center is the preservation of the visual memory of Talesh itself. Historical photographs, newspapers, publications, printing culture, camera collections, and documentary archives would become part of a permanent historical and cultural archive dedicated to preserving the social memory of western Gilan.
The project could eventually establish one of the first major regional digital memory archives in northern Iran through the digitization of photographs, publications, and local historical records.
Architecturally, the Soroodi Cultural Center reflects the broader philosophy of the Hashtpar Hub:
modern yet rooted, contemporary yet connected to memory, urban yet human-centered.
The building can integrate natural light, ecological materials, internal courtyards, green rooftop spaces, reading terraces, and panoramic views connecting the city to the surrounding landscape.
Upper floors or rooftop spaces may include cultural cafés and public terraces overlooking Hashtpar and the surrounding ecology.
The proposal also includes the creation of riverside hilltop parks overlooking the Caspian landscape together with green public corridors, cafés, walking paths, ecological recreation zones, and urban public spaces designed to increase quality of life and tourism attractiveness.
Education infrastructure forms another major component of the urban-cultural axis. Following the educational architecture model previously developed in Shahvand Think Tank’s Kurdistan school proposal, Hashtpar can become one of the pilot regions for a new generation of educational campuses in Iran.
These schools integrate climate-adapted architecture, central courtyards, laboratories, libraries, sports facilities, cultural halls, artistic spaces, and intelligent transportation access systems.
Alongside educational modernization, the project supports the development of regional sports clubs and athletic infrastructure focused on football, wrestling, volleyball, swimming, martial arts, athletics, and youth development systems.
Finally, the proposal prioritizes pedestrian-oriented urbanism. Walkable districts, riverside pathways, interconnected cultural spaces, green corridors, and intelligent transportation systems gradually transform Hashtpar into a human-centered city attractive to investors, educators, entrepreneurs, returning diaspora communities, artists, and skilled professionals.
Amjad Sardar Palace Museum
At the symbolic center of Talesh stands Amjad Sardar Palace — one of the most recognizable historical landmarks and cultural icons of the region. For generations, the palace occupied a unique place in the collective memory of Hashtpar and western Gilan. More than a historical structure, it represented a visible connection between the social history of Talesh and its architectural identity.
The proposal transforms Amjad Sardar Palace into the Museum of Talesh History and Culture, establishing it as the principal heritage institution of the region and one of the central cultural pillars of the Hashtpar Hub.
The palace would preserve and present the historical memory of Talesh through exhibitions dedicated to language, music, traditional clothing, oral history, architecture, agriculture, mountain life, coastal culture, family histories, and the relationship between the Tavalesh people and the Hyrcanian environment.
Rather than functioning as a static museum, the palace would become a living cultural space capable of hosting exhibitions, festivals, lectures, artistic programs, educational visits, heritage events, and tourism activities throughout the year.
Architecturally, the palace would remain one of the visual anchors of Hashtpar itself — a recognizable landmark connecting the historical identity of Talesh to its future modernization.
In the broader structure of the Hashtpar Hub, Amjad Sardar Palace becomes the heritage and historical icon of Talesh, while the Soroodi Cultural Center becomes the intellectual and civic memory center of the city. Together, they form the cultural backbone of the entire regional transformation project.
Axis 5 — Talesh Bamboo Value-Chain Hub
One of the most distinctive components of the Hashtpar Hub is the creation of a complete bamboo economic ecosystem.
Western Gilan’s humid ecological conditions are highly suitable for bamboo cultivation and processing. Bamboo already exists within Gilan’s traditional craft culture but remains economically underdeveloped as a modern industrial and design sector.
The proposal establishes the Talesh Bamboo Value-Chain Hub as a regional center for bamboo processing, manufacturing, branding, tourism integration, and ecological material innovation.
The system purchases bamboo from local growers and transforms it into high-value products including handicrafts, decorative architecture, wall and ceiling panels, eco-furniture, balcony structures, garden systems, bamboo cafés, pergolas, tourism décor, composite boards, ecological packaging, and lightweight construction materials.
The bamboo ecosystem integrates directly into the tourism strategy itself. Bamboo architecture becomes part of Hyrcan Holiday, ecological cafés, meditation centers, wellness retreats, and eco-tourism villages.
This creates a distinctive regional identity built around:
forest, sea, bamboo, and wellness culture.
The bamboo sector also supports artisan entrepreneurship, women-led industries, rural employment, ecological exports, reduced plastic dependency, and low-carbon industrial growth.
Axis 6 — Ecological Preservation and Smart Growth
The Hashtpar Hub is built upon one central principle:
The Hyrcanian ecosystem is not an obstacle to development.
It is the foundation of development itself.
Forest preservation, coastline protection, ecological zoning, renewable energy integration, smart waste systems, sustainable water management, and controlled urban expansion become structural principles of the project.
Rather than repeating the uncontrolled coastal destruction visible in many tourism regions around the world, the Hashtpar Hub adopts a model of smart ecological urbanism balancing economic growth, tourism, environmental sustainability, and long-term livability.
The project transforms preservation itself into an economic asset through ecological tourism, wellness industries, bamboo innovation, forest therapy systems, and sustainable urban planning.
Funding and Implementation
The financing structure combines private-sector participation, public-private partnerships, banking and investment financing, and public infrastructure support.
Development occurs in three major phases.
The first phase focuses on infrastructure, utilities, industrial groundwork, ecological zoning, bamboo pilot systems, and transportation networks.
The second phase includes the construction of Hyrcan Holiday, university launch, industrial scaling, and major cultural projects including the Soroodi Cultural Center.

The third phase consolidates international tourism integration, export expansion, innovation ecosystems, ecological urban maturity, and global regional branding.
Strategic Outcome
The Hashtpar Hub transforms western Gilan into:
an ecological tourism destination,
a premium agro-industrial exporter,
a bamboo innovation ecosystem,
a cultural-modern urban center,
and a knowledge-based regional economy.
More importantly, the project demonstrates that modernization does not require the destruction of memory, identity, or nature.
Economic development and ecological preservation become mutually reinforcing forces rather than opposing ones.
In this vision, Talesh evolves into a region that is not only wealthier, but more coherent, more educated, more beautiful, more livable, and more resilient.
A regional model where prosperity, culture, memory, and preservation grow together.

𝗠𝗔𝗡𝗚𝗢 𝗚𝗥𝗢𝗪𝗘𝗥𝗦, 𝗣𝗔𝗬 𝗖𝗟𝗢𝗦𝗘 𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗗𝗨𝗥𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗙𝗟𝗢𝗪𝗘𝗥𝗜𝗡𝗚!

The flowering stage is one of the most important periods in mango production. It is also a stage when farmers need to pay close attention to irrigation, nutrition, pests and diseases, particularly powdery mildew, which can attack flowers and young developing fruits.

💧 𝗠𝗔𝗡𝗔𝗚𝗘 𝗜𝗥𝗥𝗜𝗚𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗖𝗔𝗥𝗘𝗙𝗨𝗟𝗟𝗬

During flowering, avoid treating irrigation as a fixed routine. Adjust the frequency and amount of water according to soil type, prevailing weather, tree age, canopy condition and growth stage.

Mangoes are relatively drought tolerant, but young grafted trees need regular watering. Excessive moisture and poor drainage can also create conditions favourable for disease problems.

💡 Drip irrigation can be useful where appropriate. The goal is to keep the soil adequately moist without causing waterlogging.

🌸 𝗪𝗔𝗧𝗖𝗛 𝗙𝗢𝗥 𝗣𝗢𝗪𝗗𝗘𝗥𝗬 𝗠𝗜𝗟𝗗𝗘𝗪

Powdery mildew can be particularly damaging around the flowering period because infection of flowers can interfere with fruit set.

Do not wait until the flowers are heavily affected before taking action. Scout your orchard regularly, especially when weather conditions favour disease development, and follow an appropriate crop-protection programme using locally registered products and label recommendations.

Some growers use potassium phosphite/phosphonate-based products as part of their crop-health programme. These products may have a role in plant defence and disease management, but they should not replace proper disease monitoring or an appropriately registered fungicide programme.

If powdery mildew is already present, use a fungicide registered for mango and the target disease in Kenya. Always follow the product label for application rate, timing, pre-harvest interval and permitted uses.

Products containing active ingredients such as tebuconazole or prochloraz may be included in some disease-management programmes. However, always confirm current registration and label directions before application.

⚠️ 𝗗𝗢 𝗡𝗢𝗧 𝗠𝗜𝗫 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗗𝗨𝗖𝗧𝗦 𝗖𝗔𝗥𝗘𝗟𝗘𝗦𝗦𝗟𝗬. Only combine products when the label or a qualified crop adviser specifically recommends it.

🥭 𝗗𝗢𝗡'𝗧 𝗙𝗢𝗥𝗚𝗘𝗧 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗥𝗘𝗦𝗧 𝗢𝗙 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗢𝗥𝗖𝗛𝗔𝗥𝗗

Good mango production is not only about spraying.

🌱 Proper nutrition
💧 Correct irrigation
✂️ Pruning
🌿 Weed control
🐛 Pest monitoring
🔎 Disease scouting
🥭 Fruit management
📦 Proper harvesting and post-harvest handling

All these practices contribute to better yields and improved fruit quality.

🐛 𝗞𝗘𝗘𝗣 𝗠𝗢𝗡𝗜𝗧𝗢𝗥𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗙𝗢𝗥 𝗣𝗘𝗦𝗧𝗦

Farmers should also monitor important mango pests, including fruit flies, mango seed weevil, scales, gall midge and flower beetles.

Early detection allows you to respond before pest pressure becomes difficult to manage and affects yield or market quality.

🌱 𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗥𝗧 𝗪𝗜𝗧𝗛 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗥𝗜𝗚𝗛𝗧 𝗦𝗘𝗘𝗗𝗟𝗜𝗡𝗚

The variety you plant matters.

We currently offer 𝗚𝗥𝗔𝗙𝗧𝗘𝗗 𝗠𝗔𝗡𝗚𝗢 𝗦𝗘𝗘𝗗𝗟𝗜𝗡𝗚𝗦 𝗙𝗥𝗢𝗠 𝗞𝗦𝗵 𝟭𝟱𝟬–𝟱𝟬𝟬, depending on the variety.

Available varieties include:

🥭 𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗠𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗼 – valued for its sweet flavour and attractive fruit.

🥭 𝗧𝗼𝗺𝗺𝘆 𝗔𝘁𝗸𝗶𝗻𝘀 – known for firm flesh, good handling characteristics and relatively long shelf life.

🥭 𝗞𝗲𝗻𝘁 – produces large, sweet, relatively fibreless fruits and is widely grown for commercial markets.

🥭 𝗩𝗮𝗻𝗱𝘆𝗸, 𝗡𝗴𝗼𝘄𝗲, 𝗔𝗹𝗽𝗵𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗼 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗦𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗻 – additional options depending on your location, target market and production objectives.

📏 𝗣𝗟𝗔𝗡𝗧𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗔𝗡𝗗 𝗢𝗥𝗖𝗛𝗔𝗥𝗗 𝗘𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗕𝗟𝗜𝗦𝗛𝗠𝗘𝗡𝗧

Recommended spacing can range from approximately 𝟱 × 𝟱 𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝟴 × 𝟭𝟬 𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗲𝘀, depending on the production system, variety and available growing conditions.

At 𝟱 × 𝟱 𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗲𝘀, you can establish approximately 𝟭𝟱𝟬–𝟭𝟲𝟬 𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗲𝘀 𝗽𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝗰𝗿𝗲.

Planting holes of about 𝟲𝟬 × 𝟲𝟬 × 𝟲𝟬 𝗰𝗺 can be prepared and filled with well-decomposed manure and appropriate fertilizer based on soil-test results.

🌍 𝗖𝗛𝗢𝗢𝗦𝗘 𝗔 𝗩𝗔𝗥𝗜𝗘𝗧𝗬 𝗧𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗠𝗔𝗧𝗖𝗛𝗘𝗦 𝗬𝗢𝗨𝗥 𝗠𝗔𝗥𝗞𝗘𝗧

Kenya has diverse mango-growing environments, from lowland areas to higher elevations.

Before planting, consider your location, climate, soil, water availability, target market and the characteristics of the variety you intend to grow.

🥭 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗚𝗢𝗔𝗟 𝗜𝗦 𝗡𝗢𝗧 𝗝𝗨𝗦𝗧 𝗧𝗢 𝗚𝗥𝗢𝗪 𝗠𝗔𝗡𝗚𝗢𝗘𝗦 — 𝗜𝗧'𝗦 𝗧𝗢 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗗𝗨𝗖𝗘 𝗤𝗨𝗔𝗟𝗜𝗧𝗬 𝗙𝗥𝗨𝗜𝗧

Whether you are planting for the local fresh market, processors or exploring export opportunities, start with a suitable variety, establish healthy grafted seedlings and maintain your orchard consistently throughout the season.

🌱 𝗚𝗘𝗧 𝗚𝗥𝗔𝗙𝗧𝗘𝗗 𝗠𝗔𝗡𝗚𝗢 𝗦𝗘𝗘𝗗𝗟𝗜𝗡𝗚𝗦 𝗙𝗥𝗢𝗠 𝗙𝗔𝗥𝗠𝗘𝗥𝗦 𝗧𝗥𝗘𝗡𝗗

𝗟𝗢𝗖𝗔𝗟 𝗪𝗢𝗠𝗔𝗡 𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗣𝗟𝗘𝗧𝗘𝗟𝗬 𝗕𝗥𝗢𝗞𝗘𝗡 𝗔𝗙𝗧𝗘𝗥 𝗙𝗢𝗨𝗥 𝗗𝗔𝗬𝗦 𝗢𝗙 𝗦𝗘𝗟𝗟𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗖𝗢𝗙𝗙𝗘𝗘 𝗧𝗔𝗕𝗟𝗘 𝗢𝗡 𝗙𝗔𝗖𝗘𝗕𝗢𝗢𝗞 𝗠𝗔𝗥𝗞𝗘𝗧𝗣𝗟𝗔𝗖𝗘
𝗦𝗛𝗔𝗪𝗡𝗘𝗘, 𝗢𝗞 — Local woman 𝗥𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗹 𝗪𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 was reportedly admitted to Red Rock’s Shawnee Crisis Unit Tuesday after a four-day attempt to sell a $40 coffee table on Facebook Marketplace.
According to family members, Whitmore began the ordeal Friday afternoon simply wanting to declutter her home and get rid of an old coffee table taking up space in her garage.
“I’ve never used Facebook Marketplace,” Whitmore reportedly told her boyfriend beforehand, “but how hard could it be?”
“𝙊𝙖𝙠 𝙘𝙤𝙛𝙛𝙚𝙚 𝙩𝙖𝙗𝙡𝙚. 𝙎𝙩𝙞𝙡𝙡 𝙞𝙣 𝙜𝙧𝙚𝙖𝙩 𝙨𝙝𝙖𝙥𝙚, 𝙣𝙤 𝙙𝙖𝙢𝙖𝙜𝙚,” Whitmore wrote in the original listing. “$𝟰𝟬. 𝙋𝙞𝙘𝙠𝙪𝙥 𝙞𝙣 𝙎𝙝𝙖𝙬𝙣𝙚𝙚.”
Three minutes later, her phone dinged.
A Brooklyn Holmes responded to the ad, “Is this still available?”
“Yes!”
Brooklyn was never heard from again.
Seven minutes later:
“Is this still available?” from Antonio Montez.
“Yes, it is!”
No further contact was made by Antonio.
“Is this still available?” from Anonymous Participant GoatTurd28.
“Yes!”
Nothing.
By the 16th identical message, witnesses said the exclamation points had disappeared from Whitmore’s responses.
Her fortunes appeared to improve Saturday afternoon when a woman offered her $30 for the coffee table.
Whitmore agreed.
“Awesome!” the woman replied. “Can you deliver?”
“Where?”
“Tulsa.”
Whitmore explained that the table was listed as pickup only.
“Oh. Can you do $10 then?”
Whitmore reportedly stared at the message for several minutes, trying to understand how the price of her coffee table had somehow decreased because the person who wanted it had to pick it up.
Whitmore declined the offer. 
Later that evening, another buyer offered the full $40 and promised to pick it up at 6 p.m.
“I will absolutely be there,” said Gabriel Davenport.
Whitmore called her boyfriend, Alex Ford, to let him know she might be a little late to their dinner plans. Whitmore then cleaned the table, moved it near the front door and waited.
6:00 came.
Then 6:30.
Then 7:15.
At 8:04, Whitmore finally messaged him.
“Are you still coming?”
The buyer responded the following morning.
“Where are you located?”
“Shawnee.”
“That’s kinda far.”
Investigators believe this was the moment Whitmore first began exhibiting signs of psychological collapse.
By Sunday, Whitmore was willing to negotiate.
“Would you take $25?” another woman asked.
“Yeah.”
“Can you hold it until Friday?”
“Sure.”
“Actually I don’t get paid until next Friday.”
Whitmore agreed to hold the table until then, ignoring the steady stream of messages that continued pouring into her phone about it.
Two hours later, the woman messaged again.
“My husband says no. Sorry.”
Whitmore sent a thumbs-up.
Family members said Whitmore stared at the thumbs-up for nearly 20 minutes.
Sunday evening, Whitmore lowered the coffee table to $20.
A man immediately messaged.
“What’s the lowest you’ll take?”
“$20.”
“10 cash?”
Whitmore reluctantly agreed.
“Yea.”
“Can you meet me halfway?”
“Halfway between where?”
“Ardmore.”
Neighbors reported hearing a woman scream shortly afterward.
By Monday night, after four days of negotiations, no-shows, lowball offers and approximately 60 people apparently needing confirmation that the coffee table continued to exist, Whitmore changed the listing to:
𝗙𝗥𝗘𝗘 — 𝗣𝗜𝗖𝗞𝗨𝗣 𝗢𝗡𝗟𝗬 — 𝗙𝗜𝗥𝗦𝗧 𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗘, 𝗙𝗜𝗥𝗦𝗧 𝗦𝗘𝗥𝗩𝗘𝗗 — 𝗜 𝗪𝗜𝗟𝗟 𝗡𝗢𝗧 𝗗𝗘𝗟𝗜𝗩𝗘𝗥 — 𝗜 𝗪𝗜𝗟𝗟 𝗡𝗢𝗧 𝗛𝗢𝗟𝗗 𝗜𝗧.
Within seconds, her phone dinged.
“Is this still available?”
“Ya.”
“Does it have any scratches?”
Whitmore sent him the eight photographs already included in the listing.
“What are the dimensions?”
Whitmore copied and pasted the dimensions from the listing.
“Where are you located?”
“SHAWNEE.”
“Can you bring it to Moore?”

East Asia faces escalating regional militarization driven by US strategy, with Japan expanding military capabilities to levels unseen since World War II. The Republic of Korea, commonly known as South Korea, hosts approximately 30,000 US troops.

DPRK strategists are closely watching Iran's experience. Tehran complied with the 2015 JCPOA, accepted intrusive inspections, and mothballed its program. Iran's lesson: agreements without security guarantees are worthless.

The DPRK's nuclear development accelerated following the 2019 collapse of negotiations with the US, when Washington declined to offer security guarantees in exchange for disarmament steps.

text:
"Iran’s next move is unlikely to be a clean surrender or a dramatic new offensive. The more probable path is a dual track.

Hard public line (standing tall, showing no signs of weakness) + quieter bargaining: Security officials (Mohsen Rezaei and others) have just restated that there will be “no talks until Iran’s conditions are met.” Those conditions usually include lifting the port blockade, sanctions relief, compensation, and a recognized role in managing the Strait of Hormuz.

At the same time, President Pezeshkian has said Tehran is ready for dialogue if the U.S. drops military pressure and sanctions. That split is typical: the security state protects the narrative of resistance while the government tests whether economic relief is available. 

Hormuz and the Gulf states first: Iran’s strongest remaining lever is the strait. Recent diplomacy has focused on Oman and a possible GCC meeting to lock in a temporary shipping arrangement that gives Tehran some say over traffic without looking like it folded to Washington.

If that channel produces even limited oil-export relief, it eases the inflation crisis without a full U.S. deal. If it fails, Tehran can keep intermittent pressure on shipping rather than reopen a full-scale fight it cannot easily win.

Wait on the U.S. calendar: Trump has repeatedly tied an end to the war and falling oil prices to the period after the November midterms. Iranian officials appear to be calculating that holding out a few more weeks may produce a better offer than accepting today’s terms. That is a high-risk bet given how fast living standards are deteriorating.

The least likely near-term outcomes are regime collapse or an all-out new war.

The most likely is messy delay: public defiance, private Gulf talks, and small economic concessions if they can be framed as Iranian conditions being met rather than American victory. Whether that works depends less on speeches than on whether China, India, and the Gulf states keep or cut the remaining trade lifelines."

text:
TRUMP JUST TURNED CANADA’S EU MOVE INTO A TRANSATLANTIC TRADE QUESTION
A new trade confrontation is emerging between Washington and Brussels after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed making Canada the European Union’s first associate member.
President Donald Trump responded by calling the idea “laughable” and warned that, if he considers the move hostile, the United States could impose very serious tariffs on Europe or restrict trade in certain areas.
The significance goes far beyond the political rhetoric.
Canada and the European Union already have a comprehensive trade relationship through CETA. The new proposal would go considerably further, potentially expanding cooperation across trade, defense, energy, critical minerals, artificial intelligence, technology and economic security. The exact legal structure of associate membership has not yet been defined and would require further agreement among EU governments.
For Canada, this represents an attempt to diversify its economic and strategic relationships.
For Europe, it offers access to a major energy producer, critical minerals, advanced industrial capacity and a significant geopolitical partner.
For Washington, however, deeper Canada-EU integration could alter the economic architecture of North America and the Atlantic.
That is where the trade implications become important.
Canada remains deeply integrated with the United States, particularly through energy, manufacturing and cross-border supply chains. At the same time, Ottawa has been seeking to reduce its dependence on the American market as trade tensions have intensified.
If Canada succeeds in building substantially deeper economic links with Europe, the long-term consequence could be greater diversification of trade flows, investment and supply chains.
That does not necessarily mean an immediate economic rupture.
But it could mean that companies and governments begin preparing for a world in which North American and European supply chains are less dependent on a single bilateral relationship.
And that is where tariffs become economically significant.
Tariffs do not simply affect the country being targeted.
They can increase the cost of imported inputs, alter supply chains, reduce trade volumes and force companies to reconsider where they manufacture, source and invest.
The potential escalation therefore creates a much larger question:
Will the global economy continue moving toward deeper integration, or toward increasingly regional economic blocs?
Canada’s proposed relationship with Europe is one example of that broader transformation.
Energy security, critical minerals, defense production, technology and supply-chain resilience are increasingly becoming intertwined with trade policy.
The European Commission has emphasized that the proposed partnership with Canada is intended to strengthen cooperation rather than act against another country, while Prime Minister Mark Carney has similarly described closer Canada-EU ties as a way to increase resilience rather than create a rival power bloc.
For markets, the immediate question is whether Trump's tariff threat remains rhetoric or develops into concrete trade measures.
The longer-term question is potentially more consequential:
Does Canada’s pivot toward Europe accelerate the fragmentation of the Western trading system?
Because trade policy is no longer only about tariffs.
It is increasingly about who controls energy, minerals, technology, capital and strategic supply chains.
Canada brings resources.
Europe brings market scale.
The United States remains Canada’s dominant trading partner.
And the next phase of this relationship could reshape how those economic interests are connected.

For Bulgaria, this would be a logical step, as it would mean transitioning from the old L-39ZA to the new L-39NG. Government has urged farmers and small businesses to take advantage of affordable financing facilities aimed at expanding production, value addition and enterprise growth.

Speaking during the FY2027/28 Local Government Budget Consultative Workshops, Sarah Nantongo of the Bank of Uganda explained that the Agricultural Credit Facility (ACF) supports projects across the agricultural value chain through participating financial institutions.

The ACF provides loans of up to UShs5 billion, with interest capped at 12% per annum, a fixed rate throughout the loan period, and an arrangement fee of up to 0.5%. 

Government contributes 50% of the financing through commercial banks and 70% through credit institutions, microfinance deposit-taking institutions and regulated SACCOs, with the Government contribution attracting 0% interest.

Applicants access the facility through participating financial institutions, which appraise, disburse and recover the loans. Eligible activities include farm development, irrigation, livestock and other biological assets, agro-processing and post-harvest handling. The facility does not finance land purchases, forestry/tree planting or refinancing of existing loans.

Nantongo said the ACF has received more than 23,000 applications worth over UShs2.1 trillion, with more than 15,000 applications worth about UShs1.5 trillion already disbursed.

She also highlighted the Grain Trade Facility, which provides financing of up to UShs10 billion for purchasing and storing surplus grain, with a tenure of six months to two years and interest capped at 15% per annum.

The Small Business Fund, which evolved from the COVID-19 Small Business Recovery Fund, now supports viable businesses beyond agriculture, including retail, tailoring, carpentry, schools and hardware businesses. 

It offers loans of up to UShs500 million, for up to four years, at a maximum interest rate of 10% per annum on a reducing balance, with an arrangement fee capped at 0.5%.

By the end of June 2026, the Fund had received more than 4,000 applications worth UShs96.06 billion and disbursed nearly 4,000 loans worth UShs75.56 billion, including UShs37.78 billion in Government contribution.

Local governments were encouraged to help businesses formalise, maintain proper records and meet local requirements, while SACCOs were urged to seek Bank of Uganda regulation to access Government-supported financing directly.

The facilities are part of Government’s broader effort to expand access to affordable credit, commercialise agriculture, strengthen businesses and create jobs and household incomes.

Canada is a sovereign country. We will decide who we trade with and how we build our future.

It’s of no surprise that President Trump is now lashing out at the prospect of Canada increasing our trade ties with Europe.

His response is next level fear of missing out. 

He has an option: stop being a bully and maybe you’ll get invited back to the party.

I am proud that Canada is spreading our wings. 

Nova Scotia has a long history of trade with the world.  Two major Canadian banks - Scotiabank and RBC - were founded in our province to help our entrepreneurs, traders and explorers do business with the world.

We have a long history of trade and travel with Europe specifically. Expanding access for Canadian goods to European markets is a good thing, as is strengthening our defence ties with the region. 

Nova Scotia will always value our friendship with the American people. We value our historic ties to New England in particular. But this friendship cannot mean dependence on a country whose administration has become increasingly unpredictable towards its allies.

We’re ready to work with Europe and every reliable partner who wants what Nova Scotia has to offer.

We will not be bullied by those who look to oppress us.

My focus will continue to be on protecting our future and building Nova Scotia.

text:
Early conclusion: The key facts are confirmed. Palm Beach County is the world's largest local government investor in Israeli bonds, with a total investment reaching $1 billion in January 2026, representing approximately 16-18% of its overall portfolio. Resident protests are real and well-documented, with a budget hearing on September 15, 2026, disrupted by protesters and the arrest of prominent lawyer Noura Erakat. However, the picture is more complex than the post suggests: county officials defend the investment as a purely financial choice, based on yields higher than U.S. Treasuries, and a lawsuit filed by residents was dismissed at first instance in August 2026, with an appeal pending.

THE NUMBERS AND CONTEXT
Palm Beach County reached the $1 billion milestone in Israeli bonds in January 2026, following a $350.5 million purchase authorized by Clerk of the Circuit Court & Comptroller Mike Caruso. This amount represents approximately 16-18% of the county's investment portfolio, which stands at approximately $6 billion. The county is the world's largest municipal investor in these bonds, with the State of Florida being the second largest investor, holding approximately $350 million.

THE FINANCIAL REASONS GIVEN BY THE AUTHORITIES
Caruso has repeatedly defended the choice as a purely financial, not political, decision. He stated that Israeli bonds offer higher yields than U.S. Treasuries, generating over $23 million more in interest than comparable investments. The total investment is expected to generate approximately $136 million in interest over two to three years. The county increased the investment limit in Israeli bonds from 5% in 2021 to 15%, then temporarily raised it to 18% by a unanimous vote of the Commission in October 2025.

text:
Shares of SK Hynix surged 5.6% to €1,125 on September 17 after Reuters reported the South Korean memory giant is in early talks to produce chips at Intel's Ohio fabrication complex — a move that would mark SK Hynix's first-ever U.S. manufacturing footprint. The stock had been sliding from €1,220 just a week earlier, making the bounce as much about sentiment relief as substance.
SK Hynix Talks U.S. Memory Production With Intel at Its Stalled Ohio Campus — But Is a Deal Without Details Worth a 5.6% Rally?

Shares of SK Hynix jumped 5.6% to €1,125 on September 17 after Reuters reported the South Korean memory leader is in early-stage discussions to manufacture chips on American soil for the first time. The stock had slid from €1,220 over the prior week, making this bounce as much about sentiment as substance. For shareholders, the question is whether exploratory talks with no signed agreement can sustain a move that added billions in market value overnight.

• Two Paths on the Table, Neither Finalized. 
Under one scenario, SK Hynix could lease part of Intel's planned Ohio facility; another involves a joint venture with Intel and major cloud companies seeking to secure memory supplies.
 Yet 
SK Hynix clarified that "nothing has been finalized regarding cooperation with any specific companies."
 Investors are pricing in strategic possibility, not contractual reality.

• Intel's Ohio Site Is Years Behind Schedule. 
Construction on Intel's first Ohio factory is now expected to be completed in 2030, with operations beginning by end of 2031 — half a decade later than originally planned.
 
Intel once estimated the full site could cost around $100 billion; the first phase alone was budgeted at $28 billion.
 For SK Hynix, leasing idle or underused space could mean lower upfront capital than building from scratch — but it also ties them to a partner whose execution track record at this site is poor.

• Washington's Push and Seoul's Pushback Create a Political Tug-of-War. 
The White House has signaled it could impose broader tariffs on semiconductor imports while offering tariff relief to companies investing in domestic manufacturing.
 That gives SK Hynix a strong incentive to plant a flag on U.S. soil. However, 
Seoul could review any deal involving national core technology,
 meaning South Korean regulators might block the transfer of SK Hynix's most advanced production techniques — particularly its dominance in high-bandwidth memory chips used in AI processors.

• SK Hynix Already Has a U.S. Footprint — But Only for Packaging. 
The Commerce Department awarded SK Hynix up to $458 million under the CHIPS Act to build an advanced packaging and R&D facility, supporting the company's $3.87 billion investment in West Lafayette, Indiana.
 Actual wafer fabrication in the U.S. — the far more capital-intensive step — would be a major escalation. The cost gap between manufacturing memory in Korea versus Ohio remains wide, and SK Hynix has offered no projections on how it would close it.

The rally reflects a real strategic logic — U.S. production would insulate SK Hynix from tariffs and deepen ties with cloud giants. But nothing is signed, the factory won't exist until at least 2030, and regulatory risks span two governments. Shareholders got a headline; they haven't yet gotten a deal.
