text:
Podcast Summary | The Mel Robbins Podcast: Oprah Winfrey: How to Find Your Unique Purpose, Authentic Power, and Calling In Life

Overview
Oprah Winfrey treats purpose not as a grand achievement but as an internal call expressed through service, daily conduct, and the effect you have on others. Her central claim is that everyone carries an inner guidance system, and her difference is obedience to it. She defines success by who you become rather than what you acquire, reframes forgiveness as giving up the hope that the past could be different, and recasts legacy as the heart print you leave in everyday interactions. The throughline across her life story, from a Mississippi outhouse to a media empire and a new immersive project, is that hardship becomes fuel, intention shapes outcomes, and the dream you hold is usually smaller than the one life has for you.

Key Themes
- Everyone has an internal GPS, and the decisive variable is obedience to it rather than talent or circumstance.
- Purpose is relational: it is not what you do, but what happens in others when you do it.
- Legacy is built through daily behavior and how you treat your immediate circle, not a single big achievement.
- Every interaction leaves a heart print, so being responsible for the energy you bring is the practical work of a calling.
- Forgiveness means giving up the hope that the past could be any different, which releases a person from being stuck.
- Intention governs cause and effect; people feel the why behind your yes or no, so clarifying intention transforms work and boundaries.
- You always have the right to change your mind, and breaking a commitment to please others rather than honor yourself creates collapse.
- Gratitude is a repeatable practice that shifts energy, and small acts of connection demonstrate real personal power.
- What you did not receive in life can become exactly what you are able to give others.

Detailed Summary
Oprah frames the conversation itself as a purpose: to be used as a light so listeners can see themselves through her stories and Mel's, and ignite that light in themselves. Mel says she has been Oprah's student for 44 years. Oprah says she came to Boston to be with Mel rather than having Mel come to her, and describes Mel as the voice of our time in leading people home to themselves.

The measure of a life, in Oprah's framing, is not what you acquired but who you became, and the work of becoming is available to everyone. She describes an internal GPS, a light, a call inside every person. Her difference, she says, is that she is obedient to hers. People miss out because they are not obedient to the call, which is within rather than external or on social media. She says she was successful because she saw no difference between herself and her audience and acted as the audience's surrogate voice. People often tell her they or their mothers and grandmothers watched her show, which ran as number one for 25 years, and she thinks of them as part of the children she raised.

A childhood memory anchors her sense of direction. Between ages four and five, while churning butter on her grandmother's back porch and watching her grandmother hang clothes through the screen door, she heard an internal voice say, "No, you won't. This will not be your life. But don't tell her." Early responsibilities included emptying a slop jar and sorting clothes pins. Her grandmother was a domestic worker who boiled sheets brought home from white people's houses.

Mel reframes the question of what you want by also asking what you do not want, and Oprah agrees that knowing what you do not want is vital information. Purpose does not have to be big or Instagrammable. It is internal and expressed through how you serve where you are. Every person has a platform: family, community, church, job, work. Legacy is not only the big picture but what you do today and how you treat people in your immediate circle. Oprah introduces the heart print, what you leave or do not leave with people, crediting the term to Mattie Stepanek.

That legacy theme runs through how she talks about feeling and memory. People do not remember what you said or did, but how you made them feel, so being responsible for the energy you bring matters. Recognizing a deeper reason for being here, beyond survival, creates room to breathe amid overwhelming daily pressures such as costs of living. Being stuck is framed as an inability to see the bigger picture, on the premise that the source of being did not bring you here to stay stuck. Reframing everything happens for a reason does not mean the bad thing should have happened or that you are responsible for it. It means finding a reason to move forward so you do not stay stuck and debilitated.

Mattie Stepanek, a boy in a wheelchair who died at 13, spoke of leaving a heart print whenever you touch someone's heart. Oprah describes her past as chaos, fear, anxiety, self-destruction, people-pleasing, and addiction. Hearing a certain voice silenced everything, and she began practicing what she learned. She was raped at nine, again at 10 and 14, grew up poor in Mississippi on a red dirt road with no running water or electricity, and had an outhouse for her first six years. She expresses gratitude for that upbringing, saying it makes everyday things like flushing a toilet feel like a wow experience.

She grew up lonely and did not feel loved by her mother or grandmother, though she now believes they loved her in the best way they knew how. She attributes her drive to become a talker, speaker, and orator, and to do well in school, to getting validation and love from teachers and strangers rather than at home. She recalls her mother saying, we didn't have much, but we sure had love, and Oprah says she almost wrecked the car because she never felt or was shown that love and does not remember her mother complimenting her or saying she was proud of her. She remembers being punished for wanting to read, told to go outside with the other kids and accused of thinking she was better than everyone.

TD Jakes taught the ten-gallon person idea in a Life Class: ten-gallon people try to get ten gallons of love, responses, reception, and acceptance from pint-sized people who lack the capacity to give it. The lesson is to stop expecting love and attention from people who do not have the capacity, and to accept them exactly where they are with what they do have. Her mother could cook incredible collard greens and cornbread like nobody else, and that was how she offered love. Many parents of her generation or earlier believed providing food, shelter, and keeping kids off the streets was love. Her mother and grandmother were maids and domestic workers giving all their energy to other people's children and had nothing left when they came home. Oprah says she recognizes this now and forgives it.

Her definition of forgiveness is giving up the hope that the past could be any different. Holding onto wishes for a different past keeps a person stuck, while acceptance leads to freedom. She references Elisabeth Kubler-Ross's five stages of grief, noting denial, anger, bargaining, and acceptance, with acceptance leading to freedom.

An on-air humiliation incident became a turning point. Producers were proud of getting a man, his wife, and his mistress on national television. The man told his wife on air that the mistress was pregnant, and the audience gasped. Oprah apologized to both the wife and the man afterward, but says she has still never gotten over it and vowed never again.

Around the late 1980s she was reading Gary Zukav's Seat of the Soul, which she calls one of the best books of her life. Its chapters on intention changed her approach. She links intention to cause and effect, calling cause and effect the law of karma: what you put out comes back. People feel your intention when you say yes to please them; they feel your acquiescence, not hidden resentment. She cites examples like loaning money, giving something, or being the person always asked to carpool because people know you will say yes. Learning to say no clarified her boundaries and transformed her work.

After that, she sat down with producers and said they would no longer do a show unless it came from a point of view of intention. Every show idea had to be presented with its intention. From 1989 onward, shows were designed around enlightening and uplifting people and creating aha moments. She generalizes the principle: any job or platform can become a force for good by shifting the why, such as doing a boring job for the love of family. She describes a conversation with a man with a dull job who ended up crying after she asked why he does the work and what he is doing it for. He said he pays bills so his family can eat. She tells people to shift the paradigm: this I do for the love of my family, offering safety and comfort.

She tells the Chevy Chevette story. She used to do her hair on the way to work, throw rollers in the back, and change clothes at stop signs. One day she looked at the wrecked car and saw it represented her life. She cleaned the car one roller at a time, finding 25 cents under the seat. Resistance keeps people stuck: if something is not going the way you want, ask what you are resisting. Being out of flow, off-center, or not listening to her inner GPS causes disruption in all areas of life. She references the question, what do I really want?

Many people cannot answer that question beyond surface answers like being happy or their children. People often pursue a dream defined by the world or social media rather than the dream they hold in their heart. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, audiences said they had done everything, degree, marriage, house, possessions, yet felt there must be more. Oprah identified the missing element as connection to one's spiritual core, not religion, and launched Remembering Your Spirit segments. In 1992, when Carolyn Mays appeared with Anatomy of the Spirit, the audience was confused about the word spirit, asking if it meant Jesus or Moses. Oprah explained it as the soul and spirit deeper than the mind.

Not listening to her inner voice when ending her show is, she says, one of the biggest mistakes of her life and led to 2012 being one of her worst years. Headlines read Oprah and the Struggling Own Network, which she calls painful because they were true. She says she knew not to end the show, woke up unable to breathe at night, but went ahead because she had already signed and wanted to keep her word. She reframes keeping your word as asking to whom you are keeping it, the outside world or yourself. The real reason was trying to please people and fearing what they would think if she changed her mind. Her out-of-alignment state felt sick, behind a wall, numb to receiving and giving. She compares ignoring inner warnings to waking up unable to breathe, dreading a job, or recoiling at a text from someone.

From What I Know For Sure, tenth anniversary edition, page 39: when facing a difficult decision, ask what you would do if you were not afraid of making a mistake, feeling rejected, looking foolish, or being alone. Removing fear brings the answer into focus. She recounts moving from Baltimore to Chicago, when people around her, including her father, warned the move would destroy her and that she would never find a job like her Baltimore anchor role.

Deepest struggles can produce the greatest strength if a person is willing and open. A core anchoring belief: your life belongs to something greater than yourself, and your reason for being is bigger than a job or what you can currently see. Fear is temporary, trouble don't last always. Even while sad, numb, depressed, and angry with herself early in building her network, she knew the trouble would pass, though she did not know how. Surrendering your personal dream to the life force or source that brought you here is presented as the key to receiving a bigger life than you can imagine.

Purpose is defined not as the thing you do but as the thing that happens in others when you do the thing you do. Gratitude is described as a practice and religion that can shift your life, energy, vibration, and what you attract. Her origin story: her parents were together only one time, and she was born colored in Mississippi, where the dream for a colored girl did not exist, which she frames as a miracle. Her producer Arlene Weiner, at 28 or 29, had a home where Oprah saw six trees out the window and dreamed of having six trees someday. Years later, sitting in her own kitchen making tea, she saw six trees out her window, then walked to the porch and saw hundreds more beyond them. She lives in a forest. The lesson: I had a dream for six trees. The life force that I call God had a bigger dream for me. The force is not jealous about the name you call it.

People get stuck because they cannot see their connection to something greater than themselves. Life is framed as belonging to the world, with the purpose of giving to the world. Hardship becomes fuel: being raped so she could help other women who were raped, not being seen so she could see other people, and what she did not get becoming what she can now give to others. A small experiment in personal power: at 5:55 a.m. outside a hotel, she smiled and said good morning to a frowning woman looking at the ground. The woman perked up and they had a positive energy exchange. That tiny exchange is proof you have enormous power through your energy and attitude to flip a switch inside someone else. It does not pay the bills, but it shifts something in you.

Everyone has a platform: family, roommate, coworkers, strangers you pass. Gratitude practice can start with five things, three things, or just your breath. Breathe. You are still breathing. Purpose thread is the idea that what people would say at your funeral or memorial connects the dots of your life and reveals your purpose. Her thread is inspiration and encouragement, traced back to speaking in church as a child, oratory contests in school, radio, television, and reaching the Mel Robbins podcast. Encouragement is helping people borrow someone else's belief in themselves when they cannot believe in themselves.

Social media bombardment pushes people to compare their lives to others, and the answers are not out there. Stillness and silence are required to hear inner direction. Oprah describes a 2023 post-Bono concert experience at the Sphere in Las Vegas as a felt calling: to use the venue not as a show but as an immersive experience connecting people to themselves, each other, and the universe. The project is an immersive musical light experience meant to be felt rather than just seen, now being scored by Max Richter, with the initial vision coming almost three years before this conversation. Others first thought of it as a show. She says she is 72 and consciously treating her remaining time as one solid good decade to deliver the message she came to give, with clarity, love, and without ego. Mel reframes that mindset as universally useful: live as if you have a decade to do what you came here to do, which shifts focus and intention.

She recounts a childhood feeling at age 5 on a back porch and says the Sphere moment felt identical. She reads from What I Know For Sure, page 79: loving others means the legacy continues, one person lends light to another, and lasting value is whether we have loved and been loved. Her closing message: you were born to fulfill the dream of your life here on Earth, so get about the business of doing that. Mel encourages listeners to share the episode generously to spread the power of good, framing it as an offering to the world and to people listeners love, and pointing to a follow-up episode as the next watch.

text:
HUMANITY: An Act Of Kindness

There was this man in my former compound who had one very annoying generator.

My people, this generator was not an ordinary generator.

Once he started it, the whole compound would know.

The sound was so loud that sometimes I would be inside my room watching television, and I would have to increase the volume.

At first, I ignored it.

But this man could run that generator for hours.

Sometimes he would start it in the afternoon.

Sometimes at night.

And sometimes, when everybody was already sleeping, we would suddenly hear:

Grrrrrrrrrrrrrr! 

The whole compound would wake up.

One evening, one of the tenants finally confronted him.

Please, can't you reduce the noise? Some of us have children sleeping.

The man simply said,

I'm sorry. I need the generator.

That was all.

No explanation.

After that, people started complaining about him.

Some said he was stubborn.

Some said he didn't care about other people.

I didn't say anything because, as usual, my own business was to greet my neighbours and face my front.

But one night, something happened.

Around 11 p.m., the generator suddenly went off.

The whole compound became quiet.

I was happy.

I said,

Thank God. At least tonight we will sleep.”

But about 20 minutes later, I heard the generator start again.

I was annoyed.

I came outside to complain.

As I got closer to his room, I noticed something strange.

His door was open.

And there was a small child inside.

The child was lying on a mattress.

There was a machine beside the child.

I stopped.

The man saw me and quickly came outside.

He looked embarrassed.

I asked,

Please, what is happening?

He didn't answer immediately.

Then he said quietly,

My daughter is sick.

I looked inside again.

The little girl was sleeping.

He explained that she needed a medical machine that depended on electricity.

Whenever there was no light, he had to put on the generator.

That was why he couldn't stop it, even when everyone complained.

I felt terrible.

All this time, we thought he was simply being inconsiderate.

Nobody knew what was happening inside his room.

I asked him,

Why didn't you tell us?

He smiled sadly.

He said,

I don't like people knowing my problems.

My people, that statement touched me.

The next day, the tenants held a meeting.

This time, nobody went there to complain about the generator.

Everybody went there to ask how we could help.

Some contributed money.

Some brought food.

Another tenant offered to help with fuel whenever there was no electricity.

And the man who everybody thought was the most annoying person in the compound became someone everybody was trying to support.

That experience taught me something.

Sometimes, we are very quick to judge people because we only see their behaviour.

We don't always know the reason behind it.

The generator we were complaining about was actually keeping a little girl alive.

Till today, whenever I hear that generator start, I don't get angry anymore.

I just say a little prayer for that child......

May God heal her.

text:
The Empty Yard and the Five Shots....

A rare photograph from inside Portlaoise Prison reveals the compound from which republican prisoners witnessed an attempted escape on 18 May 1988.

The precise date on which this photograph was taken is unknown. 

Yet, like many old prison photographs, it reveals rather more than might first appear.

This is the front compound of Portlaoise Prison, where republican prisoners took their daily exercise. It is a severe and enclosed place: high stone walls, barred windows and an expanse of ground over which every movement could be observed.

I am told that Paddy McVeigh regularly ran around this exercise yard, sometimes for an hour at a time. The @IrishPrisons came to believe that these daily runs were not merely exercise but preparation—an attempt to build the stamina that would later be required during his escape.

At the far end of the compound stands what was known as the “North Wall.” To the right is E Block. The upper row of windows belonged to E4 Landing, which housed republican prisoners associated with the Provisional IRA. Immediately below was E3 Landing, another Provisional IRA landing.

From the windows on the opposite side of E Block—the side known as “the fours”—prisoners had an unobstructed view across the compound. On 18 May 1988, those windows became grandstand seats to an extraordinary and deeply troubling event.

From there, the prisoners could see the attempted escape unfolding below. They could also see Prison Officer O’Brien pursuing Paddy McVeigh and Irish soldiers of the @defenceforces firing in their direction.

E Block was overlooked by the Irish Army’s Military Post 6. It was, I understand, the firing position from which the shots rang out, sending a hail of bullets in the direction of Officer O’Brien on that fateful day, 18 May 1988.

What had begun as an escape from custody became, within moments, a scene of gunfire inside one of the most heavily guarded prisons in Ireland and Europe at the time.

The building on the left formed part of the prison complex. Directly behind it stood the handball alley, an apparently ordinary feature of prison life that had acquired its own small ritual.

When a ball went out of reach, a prison officer was required to retrieve it and return it to the republican prisoners. Their code words were “handball chapel alley.” It was, one might say, the most expensive handball-retrieval service ever maintained by an Irish government: a prison officer employed to recover a ball inside a maximum-security institution.

Even this simple exercise carried security implications. 

At night, two prison officers were assigned to duty in the area because of the possibility that prisoners might escape through the windows under cover of darkness.

That is the curious thing about this photograph. At first sight, it shows very little: an empty yard, a stone wall and rows of barred windows. 

But prisons are places in which architecture becomes evidence. Every window offers a line of sight; every wall marks both a boundary and a possible route; every ordinary routine may conceal a purpose understood only afterwards.

The yard is empty now, at least in the moment captured by the camera. Yet it remains populated by memory: McVeigh running his daily circuits, prison officers watching from below, and republican prisoners looking out from E Block.

And then, on 18 May 1988, the running ceased to be exercise. 

The windows filled with witnesses, the soldiers raised their weapons, and a familiar prison compound became the scene of an extraordinary incident: five live rounds were fired, not at the escaping prisoner, but in the direction of the prison officers pursuing him—among them Officer Sean O’Brien, whose recollections of what happened that day have yet to be satisfactorily told.

Personally I think that the Spencer family is sadly marred with mental health issues to include Charles, Diana and Harry. I think this is why they look for attention from people and the media. 

Also Charles and Diana were not close as siblings and he had no part of her life, so I believe much of it will be untrue just like Spare.

That singular quote is completely made moot by the actual policies and actions of Israel.

1937 Peel Commission: British proposal for a small Jewish state and a larger Arab state (linked to Transjordan). The Jewish Agency accepted it in principle as a basis for negotiation; Arab leadership rejected it

1947 UN Partition Plan (Resolution 181): Proposed a Jewish state (~55% of the Mandate, much of it Negev desert), an Arab state (~45%), and internationalized Jerusalem. The Jewish Agency accepted it; Arab states and the Arab Higher Committee rejected it, followed by war after Israel’s 1948 declaration of independence.

1967 (post-Six-Day War): Israel indicated willingness to exchange captured territory for peace and recognition under UN Security Council Resolution 242 (“land for peace”). Arab states responded with the Khartoum “Three No’s” (no peace, no recognition, no negotiation).

1978–1979 Camp David Accords (with Egypt): Included a framework for Palestinian autonomy in the West Bank and Gaza leading to further negotiations. The PLO rejected the Palestinian component. Israel later returned the entire Sinai to Egypt in exchange for peace

1993 Oslo Accords: Israel and the PLO mutually recognized each other and agreed to a process of phased Israeli withdrawals and Palestinian self-rule, widely understood as a pathway to a two-state solution

2000 Camp David Summit + Clinton Parameters + 2001 Taba talks: Prime Minister Ehud Barak offered a Palestinian state on Gaza plus the large majority of the West Bank (commonly cited figures 91–97% depending on the exact proposal and land swaps), with arrangements for Jerusalem and limited refugee return. Yasser Arafat did not accept; talks continued at Taba but ended without agreement as Barak’s government lost power and the Second Intifada intensified
Bill Clinton:  "“I killed myself to give the Palestinians a state. I had a deal they turned down that would have given them all of Gaza."

2008 Olmert offer: Prime Minister Ehud Olmert presented Mahmoud Abbas a map for a Palestinian state on roughly 93–94% of the West Bank plus equivalent land swaps from Israel proper, Gaza, shared/divided Jerusalem arrangements, and a symbolic number of refugee returns to Israel. Abbas later said he did not respond in time or needed more details

2005 Gaza disengagement: Israel unilaterally withdrew all settlers and troops from Gaza (and four small West Bank settlements). This was not a negotiated two-state peace deal with the Palestinian Authority. Hamas later took control of Gaza

Israel also concluded full peace treaties with Egypt (1979) and Jordan (1994), returning territory in those cases.   

So the evidence is overwhelming that actual Israeli policy has been to seek peace as it has with other adversaries.  The evidence is clear that the Palestinians will not have peace with Israel under any circumstance.

It also shows that pursuing a resolution through violence as  the Palestinians have chosen over the decades has only left them weaker and with less than they would have had if they negotiated earlier.  

Losing territory after starting wars is a consequence of starting wars.

text:
Podcast Summary | Candace: BIG NEWS! Erika To File A Wrongful Death Lawsuit. For Charlie Or For PR? | Ep 388

Overview
Candace Owens argues the wrongful death notice of claim filed over Charlie Kirk’s death is less a genuine pursuit of justice than a preemptive public relations move by Turning Point USA and Erica Kirk. The filing blames Utah Valley University for security failures, but Owens contends the timing, the rushed eight-page notice, and the omissions inside it reveal an attempt to shift responsibility away from TPUSA’s own security decisions. She frames the case as larger than one filing, raising unresolved questions about the independent review, first responders, body camera footage, and who really bore responsibility for protecting Charlie Kirk.

Key Themes
- The wrongful death notice against Utah and UVU lands shortly before an independent security review that Owens says will be devastating to Turning Point USA.
- Owens argues TPUSA demanded the outdoor amphitheater despite being told traffic control was impossible, then blamed UVU for the consequences of that request.
- The claim that UVU should have secured rooftops ignores that TPUSA traveled with a large, elite security team including SEALs, Marines, Army snipers, and SWAT commanders.
- The filing’s use of the Dan Flood and Chief Jeffrey Long text exchange is portrayed as misleading because it allegedly omits the specific line tying the concern to a walkway above Kirk.
- Questions about why no ambulance was on standby, why TPUSA security arrived only at 9 a.m., and why TPUSA is not suing its own security remain central.
- The release of Tyler Robinson’s 2022 body camera footage years after a routine fender bender raises suspicion about deliberate narrative shaping.
- Owens sees the filing as a possible opening to learn what Erica and TPUSA told Charlie’s parents about responsibility and mistakes.
- A settlement with Utah is framed as a likely payday that would let the state avoid accountability rather than wait for the independent review.
- The case is described as much bigger than initially imagined, with unresolved threads around Israel, donor networks, and satanic abuse claims in Utah.

Detailed Summary
The notice of claim is directed at the state of Utah, Utah Valley University Police Department, UVU police chief Jeffrey Long, former UVU president Astrid Tuminez, and others presently unknown. A notice of claim is a mandatory prerequisite before suing a government entity, giving the government a chance to settle before litigation. Owens stresses this is an eight-page notice, not a full lawsuit, and calls it rushed and lackluster after more than a year.

Owens says Charlie Kirk’s parents had encouraged Erica to file a wrongful death lawsuit since around December, but that Erica was previously not keen to do so. The filing arrives shortly before a UVU-commissioned independent external review was due for release. According to an Associated Press article dated September 22, 2025, UVU commissioned that review in September, twelve days after Charlie Kirk’s death. Owens says the findings were expected to be released on Friday and would be devastating to Turning Point USA’s security apparatus, making the timing of the filing suspicious.

The filing alleges negligence by UVU and frames the university as responsible for exposing Kirk to a rooftop shooter. It invokes a state-created danger claim under the Due Process Clause and a wrongful death claim under Utah law. Owens pushes back hard on the premise. She argues the event was planned in weeks rather than the usual months, and that a Microsoft Teams events committee meeting on August 25, 2025, led by TPUSA employee Macy Crofts, included Crofts insisting the event be held in the amphitheater. UVU allegedly told TPUSA the amphitheater had no traffic control and could not be shut down. TPUSA still demanded it.

Owens argues this creates a core contradiction: TPUSA demanded the outdoor venue despite being told about the traffic control problem, then sues UVU for granting the request. She says UVU’s police allocation was reasonable given the size of the force and campus population. The filing claims only six UVU campus police officers were assigned, about twenty-five percent of the force, and that Chief Jeff Long requested more but was denied by then-president Astrid Tuminez. The event reportedly drew approximately three thousand attendees. UVU has fifty thousand students and twenty-four police officers total. Granting more officers, Owens argues, would have put other students at risk.

The filing also alleges UVU police did not conduct a meaningful risk assessment and did not hold a security briefing on unsecured rooftops identified to Chief Long. It cites prior threats including the Trump rooftop sniper and the attack on Nancy Pelosi’s husband as known risks. Owens counters that Charlie Kirk traveled with twelve security members to the UVU event, an unusually large detail for a college event. That team included former Navy SEALs, Marines, Army snipers, and SWAT commanders. She cites a clip of Brian Harpole on Shawn Ryan’s show describing the team’s experience, including a combat-proven Marine, SEALs, a twenty-two-year SWAT veteran, and a twenty-two-year Navy SEAL.

Owens says she worked for Turning Point USA and brought her own security to events. She describes private security liaising with local police, requesting bomb dogs, drones, rooftop snipers, and pulling events if security cannot be ensured. She argues Charlie Kirk’s private security team was large and highly qualified, making it unreasonable to blame the campus alone for security lapses. She questions why TPUSA’s security did not request a security brief, did not cancel despite Kirk reportedly fearing for his life, and showed up only at 9 a.m. on event day.

A central dispute is the Dan Flood and Chief Jeffrey Long text exchange. The filing allegedly omits the line “I was told students have access above us,” which tied the concern to a specific walkway above Charlie Kirk, not rooftops generally. The original text message quoted a student group saying there was roof access near where Kirk would be set up, with staircases to walkways on the Sorenson Student Center roof. The specific concern was students accessing the walkway or roof of the Hall of Flags above Kirk, potentially throwing water bottles or water. Owens says Richard Bracie was on the rooftop and moved after the explosion.

Chief Long’s “got you covered” response is disputed. Owens claims Long met both of Flood’s requests by sending Officer Baggley for rooftop traffic control and allowing Charlie’s security up there. She argues the filing misrepresents the text thread and that Brian Harpole earlier presented it as his own on Shawn Ryan despite not being on the thread. Owens contends TPUSA’s stated position is contradictory: it brought trained snipers and Navy SEALs but claims shock at being expected to use their expertise. She says they are trying to read between the lines of a text message to assert a discussion about rooftops occurred when it did not.

The filing says Kirk was transported to Panogos Regional Hospital in a private vehicle, not an ambulance. The speaker notes there was no ambulance on standby and says TPUSA events typically had one. Owens says TPUSA distributed security protocols to speakers, including the nearest hospital and ambulance standby information. The filing claims none were available, but Owens says UVU state-certified EMS were present beside the car with medical bags. She maintains that questions remain about why no ambulance was on standby and calls for fuller communications with the team.

The filing cites UVU could have created secure perimeters, limited ingress and egress, and restricted attendees. Owens says UVU told Macy Crofts on a Microsoft Teams call it could not do traffic control if the event was held in the amphitheater. The filing says TPUSA controlled the tickets. The summation says UVU’s omissions, actions, and misconduct led to Kirk’s death, exposing him to a rooftop shooter. Owens rejects the claim that security failures were only UVU’s fault and asks why TPUSA is not suing its own security, which arrived at 9 a.m. that morning.

Owens frames the filing as a preemptive PR strike aimed at distracting from expected damaging revelations about Turning Point USA’s shortcomings. She compares the filing’s initial shock value to Blake Lively’s filing, suggesting later receipts may reveal an incomplete story. She says the filing may offer unique insight into what Erica and Turning Point USA told Charlie’s parents about responsibility and mistakes. She says it is possible the state settles for a payday because Utah seems a little corrupt and the state may want the situation to go away. She hopes a settlement does not happen and instead holds out for the independent review. The filing is said to have been delivered to the Utah attorney general’s office.

Beyond the filing, Owens raises the release of Tyler Robinson’s 2022 body camera footage. Robinson’s footage was released seven days after the public learned he was the suspect. The footage is dated May 31, 2022, about three and a half years before release, and was released by Scripps Media. In that 2022 incident, no citations were issued, nobody was arrested, the body cam did not capture the accident, no ambulance or paramedics were present, and both drivers exchanged insurance. Robinson spoke to an officer and received an instant report number. The officer who recorded it was with the St. George Police Department.

Owens argues routine body cam footage should have been automatically deleted: in Tennessee about thirty days later; in Utah typically between sixty and ninety days for routine footage without arrest, citation, use of force, or citizen complaint. She asks who ordered the footage held for three years when Robinson was unknown and nineteen years old at the time. She alleges the footage release was deliberate narrative-shaping. The released clip shows Robinson in a hat and sunglasses described as similar to what he allegedly wore after Charlie Kirk’s killing. The New York Post described the 2022 footage as showing Robinson in a hat and sunglasses eerily similar to what he was seen wearing after the shooting. Owens draws a parallel to earlier media coverage of Robinson in a maroon shirt, claiming the public was imprinted with a specific image of him. She calls for information about who requested, stored, and submitted the footage. She notes Scripps News began in 2022, formerly known as Newsy, and that Scripps News founder Jim Spencer teaches digital media and journalism at UT Austin and has done so since 2018. Turning Point USA’s number one donor, Nell DeBockman, donated a 2,300-square-foot building to UT Austin in 2022 for mixed media and artists, called the Buckman Center. Owens argues TPUSA or its donors could use resources to investigate the footage’s release as a side inquiry unrelated to the courtroom hearing.

Owens also discusses the interim hosting arrangement for her show. Baron Coleman will take over the principal show during her maternity leave, with a joint episode planned beforehand. She praises his careful, methodical approach and legal background. A clause will prohibit him from discussing sandwiches on the show. The joint episode before maternity leave will go back to the beginning of the case, unpack what happened, and look through the state’s evidence. The interim show will run Monday through Wednesday. She says a full walkthrough of the Charlie Kirk case and the state’s evidence is needed, criticizing Andrew Wilson as insincere and disingenuous for missing that opportunity.

On Erica, Owens says Tucker Carlson reportedly praised her fearlessness and intensity and how Charlie valued her, but questions her loyalty, saying she lied about Charlie’s Iran and Israel views and handed Turning Point USA to the Daily Wire. Owens claims Erica was anti-Israel in May 2025 but is now pro-Israel and partnered with the International Fellowship of Christians and Jews, a contract revealed by Max Blumenthal. She says she was at Tucker Carlson’s in May 2025 and Erica was there the night before ranting about Israel and pushing Charlie in an anti-Israel direction. She expresses interest in David Levitt or Ovit as a thread worth pulling, while adding allegedly to a commenter’s claim about David and his wife taking a child to Scotland and buying a castle. She notes a steep history of satanic abuse claims in Utah and says it feels like the Charlie Kirk case is arriving at similar claims despite making no sense.

Owens describes John Mappen as a quintessential Englishman who would help without expecting anything in return, and says he and Arena have been loyal friends, especially in ensuring Charlie Kirk’s death is not treated as something to ignore and that questions about who was behind it are explored. She argues the Charlie Kirk case is much bigger than initially imagined. A Turning Point USA filing is framed as bratty and evasive, compared to a child blaming parents after ordering what the child asked for. She says Dan Flood provided security to Erica in the immediate aftermath and was with her at the White House when Charlie was there or Trump did something. She also says Anna Kay Casparian was not the interim host, though she covers multiple topics and had Owens on her show to explain problems with the case. Baron Coleman will keep track of Tricky Terrell, who bothers people and seems to get away with things.

Rodney Stark is cited as an author whose book was recommended by Charlie Kirk as required reading. The book Bearing False Witness is the current book club selection, and How the West Was Won was the first book Charlie told her she had to read. Merchandise mentioned as back in stock includes a stop anti-cannism mug and a Stanis cup, with shirts offered only in maroon. A personal anecdote references speeding through six states in a Mustang to the University of Rhode Island and a threatened driver’s license suspension. She states there is no footage of the incident.

BBC Investigation Confirms What Syrians Said From the Start: Assad Ordered Austin Tice’s Abduction

A new BBC investigation has produced the clearest evidence yet that Bashar al-Assad personally authorised the 2012 abduction of American journalist Austin Tice—confirming what Syrians maintained from the beginning, while Assad’s regime and its supporters internationally attempted to blame opposition or jihadist groups.

As was revealed in the BBC podcast Where Is Austin Tice?, based on hundreds of secret documents and testimony from regime insiders, Assad responded to information about the journalist’s movements with the instruction: “Bring him to us.”

Tice, a former US Marine reporting independently from Syria, disappeared near Darayya, outside Damascus, on August 14, 2012. The investigation says his trusted driver, Hamid Abu Obeid, had been passing information about him to a nephew of Bassam al-Hassan, a senior Assad confidant and head of the regime’s National Defence Forces militia network.

When Abu Obeid produced a gun, Tice reportedly initially laughed, believing his driver was joking. He then offered him his chequebook, but was handed to National Defence Forces personnel and taken into regime custody.

Seven weeks later, a video appeared showing Tice blindfolded and bound, being led by armed men dressed to resemble jihadists. No credible group claimed responsibility. The footage was used to create a convenient alternative story: that Tice had been captured by Islamist militants rather than Assad’s forces.

The BBC’s findings confirm that the scene was a fabrication intended to conceal the regime’s responsibility.

This was not an isolated use of the tactic. Assad’s regime repeatedly labelled journalists, peaceful activists, humanitarian workers and revolutionaries as “terrorists,” while presenting its own security forces—and their Russian, Iranian and Hezbollah backers—as supposedly moderate defenders of stability.

The regime’s records showed how broadly that classification was applied. Independent reporting, peaceful dissent, treating injured demonstrators or providing humanitarian assistance could all be treated as terrorist activity. This supplied political cover for detention, torture, forced disappearance and attacks on civilians.

The narrative was eagerly repeated abroad. Western far-right figures and organisations affiliated with Putin and Assad portrayed the Syrian dictator as a protector of Christians who was fighting Islamist terrorism. British white supremacist party Britain First circulated propaganda declaring, “I stand with Assad”;  far-right provocateur Katie Hopkins described him as “the best we have”; and Italian leader Giorgia Meloni praised Assad, Vladimir Putin, Iran and Hezbollah for supposedly protecting Syrian Christians.

Sections of the self-described anti-imperialist left promoted the same message. British politician George Galloway declared himself “proud” to have supported Assad, portraying the Syrian revolution largely through the imagery of ISIS.

This convergence was driven by overlapping prejudices and political interests. The far right’s racism and Islamophobia and the authoritarian left’s support for a nominally anti-imperialist regime, coupled with both extremes' blind support for Russia led both to erase Syria’s democratic opposition and conflate revolutionaries, civil-society activists and independent journalists with jihadists.

ISIS was not publicly established under that name until 2013—the year after Tice was seized—yet the label was subsequently applied retroactively to virtually every opponent of Assad.

The reality was almost precisely the reverse of the propaganda. Assad’s government was a state terrorist entity operated an extensive machinery of state terror, killing, torturing and forcibly disappearing civilians on an industrial scale. It also manipulated the jihadist threat for political purposes, releasing extremists while peaceful activists remained imprisoned, then presenting every alternative to dictatorship as terrorism.

US officials had reportedly assessed by October 2012 that Tice was in Assad regime custody. A secret regime security notice issued after his reported escape instructed agencies to search for him, further undermining Damascus’s repeated denials.

The new investigation therefore does not suddenly reveal that Assad’s forces held Tice. Rather, it establishes in unprecedented detail how he was betrayed, abducted and delivered to them—and points directly to Assad’s personal authorisation.

Tice’s fate remains unknown. An allegation by Bassam al-Hassan that Assad subsequently ordered his execution has not been independently corroborated and is disputed by Tice’s family, who continue to believe he may be alive.

For Syrians, however, the central revelation is painfully familiar. They described the method from the beginning: abduct the victim, manufacture a jihadist trail, deny responsibility and rely on foreign propagandists and journalists, accustomed by the War on Terror to not question leaders' claims on the issue,  to dismiss  millions of Syrian witnesses  and surviving victims as liars.

Fourteen years later, the documentary record is again confirming what Syrians said all along.

text:
a series of blatant lies and exaggerations designed to justify the indefensible.

Let us be direct about what happened on that radio program. Abdullateef did not make an innocent mistake. He did not stumble over his words or misremember a figure. He went on a public platform, faced with the task of defending an increasingly scandalous project cost, and chose to fabricate details to mislead Kwarans. He knew he could not defend the government's reckless decision on merit, so he resorted to telling lies.

He claimed that the renovated Kwara Hotel now has ten lifts and that each of those lifts cost between N600 million and N1 billion. Let us sit with that claim for a moment. A single lift, he told Kwarans on a public radio program, cost N600 million and N1 billion. That is not a slip of the tongue. That is a deliberate and calculated lie, constructed on the spot to make a N27 billion hotel renovation appear somehow reasonable and justifiable to an unsuspecting public.

When Kwarans on different platforms called out his falsehood and confronted it with evidence, pointing out that elevator costs of that magnitude are not consistent with any known market reality, Abdullateef retreated to a WhatsApp group to offer a belated clarification, claiming that what he meant to say was that all 10 lifts and their installation cost N1 billion, not that each lift cost N1 billion. This belated retreat, offered not on the radio platform where the lie was told but in a private messaging group, is not a clarification. It is damage control, and it is grossly inadequate damage control at that.

But there is another question his clarification conspicuously failed to address. Was his claim that the hotel has 10 lifts also a slip of the tongue? What does a 178-room hotel facility spread across five floors need 10 lifts for? What conceivable operational logic justifies the installation of 10 lifts in such an environment? The answer is none. The lift figures, like the cost justifications that accompanied them, appear to have been fabricated for a single purpose to defend a reckless government spending and to mislead Kwarans.

What makes this episode even more damning is the behaviour of APC supporters in its immediate aftermath. Before Abdullateef had even issued his belated clarification on the WhatsApp group, loyalists and apologists of the administration were already on social media vigorously defending his N1billion-per-lift claim as accurate. They were not defending the truth. They were defending a lie, because defending the government's narrative, however false, is what they are programmed to do. Their willingness to argue for something that sounds so ridiculous and that they could not possibly have verified speaks volumes about the intellectual dishonesty that has become endemic within the administration's support base.

Abdullateef Ibrahim owes Kwarans more than a WhatsApp clarification. He must return to the same radio program where he misled the public and correct the record openly, honestly, and without equivocation. Anything less is an insult to the intelligence of Kwarans.

Beyond the lies of a governor's spokesman, the fundamental questions surrounding this project remain unanswered, and they grow more pressing with every passing day. How did a project for which bids were submitted in the range of N3billion to N3.5billion end up costing N27billion? What specific elements of the renovation work account for this huge difference in cost?

More than N30 billion public funds have been channeled into the renovation of a hotel. Meanwhile, several critical roads across the state remain in a state of disrepair that makes daily commuting a hazard for ordinary citizens. The state's healthcare system continues to deteriorate, understaffed, and under-resourced. Kwara State still lacks basic, critical medical equipment like CT scan and MRI machines, forcing patients requiring these services to travel outside the state to access diagnostic services

text:
📺 THE FED SELLOFF IS REVERSING — CAN BULLS TAKE CONTROL? + $SPCX TECHNICAL REVERSAL + $TSLA IS BACK IN THE GAME + $AAPL REMAINS A POWER PLAY

The post-Fed reversal is underway, but now we need to see whether buyers can actually take control.

Yesterday’s strength offered a good opportunity for short-term $SPY and $QQQ puts ahead of the Fed volatility. $SPY $756 puts paid 2X–4X for some traders, while $QQQ puts bought around $0.60–$0.70 expanded sharply as the market unraveled. But those were intraday trades, not positions to marry overnight.

Remember the last Fed day: the market closed on the lows, bears thought they had control, and within days the breakdown was reversed and a new move toward the highs began.

Could we see something similar again?

*

$SPY is already rebounding roughly six points, essentially returning to where it was yesterday. The next 1–2 sessions are important. If today’s move can match and negate yesterday’s decline, the setup gets more interesting. A move through roughly $761 could break the short-term downtrend and potentially start a new active upside sequence.

$QQQ is also testing yesterday’s high around $711.85. Holding above it would be constructive, with roughly $717 the next area to watch. 

But this is still mid-September, historically a difficult period, so the key is to react rather than predict.

*

The macro backdrop is also providing some relief: $TLT is higher after the Fed delivered the quarter-point hike markets had largely priced in, while $USO is lower. 

Rates down + oil down is a better combination for growth and tech.

*

$SPCX may be the best lesson in tactical flexibility. Earlier this week, the break below $146 looked capable of opening the door toward $138 or even $130. But yesterday it gapped higher and reclaimed $148.46, effectively showing that the bearish candle had no follow-through.

If you sold Tuesday, Wednesday gave you a reason to get back in. Now a move above $155 could potentially turn the structure into a more meaningful cup-with-handle breakout setup.

*

$TSLA is also back in the game. It’s not perfect, but as long as it can hold around $354, the tactical setup remains alive. I’m long some stock and sold $350 puts. For real upside traction, $TSLA needs to clear approximately $365.

*

And $AAPL continues to act well. It remains one of the cleaner power plays, maintaining an active upside sequence despite all the broader market chop.

*

So, the biggest lesson: don’t stay married to yesterday’s trade.

The Fed selloff paid the bears. Today is a new setup. If buyers can erase yesterday’s damage and reclaim key resistance, the market could start a better upside sequence. If the rebound lacks power and volume, don’t force it.

Keep your mind clear, move your feet and adjust to what the market is actually doing.

*

Scott was a standout high school football player in South Carolina, moving up the ranks toward college scholarships, when he fell asleep at the wheel one morning after dropping his mother off at work. He jerked the steering wheel on gravel, sending the car across traffic into the median. The car flipped. Scott was thrown through the windshield.

He survived with a broken ankle and back injuries. Most scholarship offers disappeared. But Scott says the wreck set him on the path that ultimately led him to faith — and eventually to national politics.

text:
THIS IS A STORY OF TWO SILENCES THAT LEARNED HOW TO MEET EACH OTHER IN NORTH CAROLINA.

Brutus was a 110-pound Cane Corso, black as wet earth, his body mapped by an old violence. Strangers saw only the cropped ears, the scarred muzzle, the size of him, and stepped back. What they missed was the fear. He never snapped. When someone came close he dropped to the floor, pressed his belly to the concrete, and turned his face to the wall as if he could vanish if he made himself small enough. Volunteers tried the usual things—hands reaching, treats offered, voices too bright. He waited until they left before he ate. Kindness that arrived unasked still felt like a trap.
Then Nora saw the photograph. She did not see a dangerous breed. She saw a dog already flinching from a disappointment that had not happened yet. The staff warned her he might never accept a human hand. She said, “Then I won’t start by touching him.”
She brought a camping chair and a ball of dark green yarn. She sat fifteen feet from his kennel and knitted. She did not call his name. She did not look for his eyes. She simply occupied the same air, day after day, sun or rain, a still point in a world that had only ever moved toward him too fast.
One night the rain did not stop. Nora stayed. At first light the cameras showed Brutus asleep with his head against the iron bars, exactly where her lap had been on the other side. No one had crossed the distance. He had.
Two more months of the same quiet ritual passed before he followed her to a house at the edge of the woods. First he slept by the back door. Then the hallway. Then the living-room rug at her feet. Thunder still unravels him, but the dark is no longer empty.
A year later the picture is simple: Nora on the porch with her needles, Brutus stretched in the sun, the finished green scarf looped loosely around his neck. She wrote underneath it: “I stayed close enough that he could find me, and far enough that he could believe no one was coming to take anything from him again. Some hearts do not need to be forced open. They need to discover that the door can stay shut and still be safe.”

text:
They threw Black soldiers in prison for the dap, then turned around and begged them to teach it. Late in the Vietnam War, Black GIs were coming home inside their own minds, and they would not trust a white doctor to touch them. So the same military that banned the handshake brought in men fluent in it to dap with the wounded until they would accept help.

The thing they called a threat became the only bridge left to their own broken men, and that should sit with you for a long minute.

Two young men stand close in the heat, and for a moment their hands do something private. Fingers hook into fingers, knuckles meet knuckles, an open palm lands flat against a chest, and the whole exchange is over before a third man could follow it.

From any distance it looks like nothing at all. A greeting between friends, the kind of small motion you stop noticing by the second week in country.

But this was Vietnam, and these were Black soldiers, and what passed between their hands was not nothing. It was a promise, and on some bases it was treated as a crime.

The Black soldiers of that war had a name for themselves. They were the Bloods, and the dap was theirs.

The word is short and percussive, and it sounds a little like the thing it names. It could be plain, a bump and a clasp and done, or it could run long, dozens of moves strung in sequence, finished with a hand pressed over the other man's heart.

No two daps were exactly the same. The order of the moves shifted from one unit to the next, so that the way a man dapped could tell you who he had served beside.

That was the thing the men above them missed. The dap was never only hello.

It was a language, and it carried real weight. A run of movements could pass along what was waiting at the front, or what had gone wrong on the last patrol, moving hand to hand in plain sight where no officer could read a word of it.

Underneath all of it sat one sentence, repeated every time two of them met. I see you, I have you, we go home together or we do not go home.

That sentence existed because it had to. Black men were being funneled into the hardest corners of the war, and early on they were dying at rates well beyond their share of the men sent over.

And there were stories that moved quietly between them, of Black soldiers losing their lives not to the enemy but to white Americans in the same uniform. Whether every account held up or not, the fear behind them was real, and a man learned to count the people he could trust on the fingers of one hand.

So they made a pact. Not on paper, where it could be taken from them, but in their hands, where no one could.

There is a translation of the dap that survived into the museums, set down by the men themselves. The movements, they said, meant something close to this.

I am not above you. You are not above me, we stand side by side, we are together.

You will hear it said that the word stands for dignity and pride. The honest answer is plainer and a little lost to time, because no one is certain where the word truly came from, and that meaning may have been laid over it years later.

Some trace the snap and the clasp all the way back across the ocean to West Africa, to greetings that were old before any of these men were born. Whether the line runs that deep or not, what these soldiers built with it was new and entirely their own.

You do not need the dictionary to feel what it did. In a war that counted them as expendable, two Black men could reach out and hand each other their full human worth in under ten seconds.

To see the world that grew this thing, look at a place the soldiers called LBJ. The letters stood for Long Binh Jail, an Army stockade on the edge of Saigon, and the men inside lived under the bitter joke of a President's initials hanging over their cages.

It was built to hold four hundred. By August of 1968 it was packed with seven hundred and nineteen.

Black soldiers were about one in nine of the troops in Vietnam. Inside that jail, they were more than half of everyone there.

The worst cells were old steel shipping containers baking in the sun. A man could be locked inside one stripped to the skin, in heat well past a hundred degrees, a bare light left burning over him around the clock.

The summer of 1968 was already a wound that would not close. Word had reached the prison that Dr. King had been killed back home, and something in the men hardened that never fully softened again.

Into that place, the year before, had come an eighteen-year-old named Jimmie Childress. A judge had offered him a choice between prison and the Army, and he chose the Army, which is how a teenager ends up jumping out of airplanes with the 101st Airborne.

He fought, and then he stopped believing in the fight, and slipped away into a Saigon neighborhood where Black GIs gathered off duty. When they caught him and dropped him into LBJ, the thing that gnawed at him was not the cell itself.

It was the math of his own life. Long after, he still carried the question that would not leave him, why he should lay his body down for a country that would not let him sit at a lunch counter when he came home.

He was one man. The handshake belonged to thousands like him, and historians point to jails like this one, where the unfairness was stacked the highest, as one of the places the dap took its shape.

Here is where the story turns, and where it should make you stop scrolling.

That same year, the raised fist of Black Power had gone up on a podium at the Mexico City Olympics for the whole world to see. The military had already grown afraid of that fist, and had moved to ban its symbols wherever Black and white troops were packed in close.

Officers looked at the closed fist that ended the dap, and the long coded runs they could not crack, and they did not see men greeting each other. They decided they were watching the first moves of a Black uprising inside their own ranks.

So they banned a handshake. They wrote it up as a threat to good order and discipline.

And then they punished men for it. On bases from Vietnam to Germany to Hawaii, across the late sixties and into the seventies, Black soldiers were charged, court-martialed, jailed, and some were pushed out of the service with the kind of discharge that trails a man for the rest of his life.

Sit with the full shape of that. A young Black man could be handed a weapon, shipped to the other side of the planet, and ordered to die for the United States, and that same country would punish him for the way he said hello to the only people who had his back.

They did it anyway. Out in the open, daring the write-up, because every order against the dap only proved the one thing the dap was built to say.

The ban did not end it. It made it matter more.

And then comes the part almost no one was ever told, the part that turns the whole thing over in your hands.

Later in the war, the military that had been jailing men for the dap found that it suddenly needed it. There were Black soldiers coming apart from what they had carried, men who would not let a white doctor or nurse near them, because they no longer trusted anyone in that uniform to mean them any good.

So the Army went and found Black GIs who were fluent in the dap, and sat them down with these men, hand to hand, until enough trust was built for the wounded to accept treatment. The gesture they had branded a threat became the only bridge left to their own broken soldiers.

They could ban it. They could never replace it.

The dap should have died in a stockade outside Saigon. Instead it caught a flight home.

It came back in the hands of every man who made it out, and it spread the way only a true thing spreads. It traveled through blocks and barbershops and schoolyards and locker rooms, until a clasp of hands born as a survival code in a war zone became the ordinary, daily, almost unconscious way that Black America says I see you.

Now it lives everywhere. It is on the hardwood before tipoff, in the doorway when family arrives, between two strangers who catch something familiar in each other on a crowded street.

Decades later, a photographer named LaMont Hamilton went looking for what the record had let slip. He sat with old Black veterans and asked them to show him their daps, and he found the handshakes still changed from one former unit to the next, each one a small living museum of men who had been there.

And this is the last hard truth in it. The handshake conquered the world, and the men who built it mostly did not.

Their names were never written down. There is no wall anywhere carved with the list of who first hooked his fingers into another man's and decided that the gesture was a vow.

But the vow is still sitting in your hands. Every time you reach out and someone reaches back, knuckles to knuckles, you are finishing a sentence that frightened, furious, faithful young men began in a place that wanted them gone.

They were not allowed to keep their names. They kept their promise instead, and they handed it forward to you.

The next time someone daps you up, hold on a half second longer. Know exactly what it is you are holding.

text:
This gunner bought back the exact Chieftain he served in

In 2023, former British Army gunner Rob Dove found and bought Chieftain 05EB53 — the exact tank he had crewed with the 15th/19th The King’s Royal Hussars in Detmold, West Germany, during the Cold War.

Dove had joined the Army at 17 and spent two years as 05EB53’s gunner. The 56-tonne Chieftain carried call sign 20, and Dove trained on it with the same commander, loader and driver — the sort of familiarity a four-man tank crew depended on.

Decades later, he discovered 05EB53 was for sale. His first offer was rejected, but after the owners learned that he had actually served in the tank, a deal was agreed. Dove bought it and spent the next two years restoring it.

It now carries the markings it wore during his service in 1986 and sits at Eden Camp Modern History Museum in North Yorkshire. Preserving it keeps more than a 120mm-gunned Cold War machine alive; it preserves the working relationship between one crew and the tank they learned inside out.

Quite a reunion after nearly four decades.

OWNING / FLEET (from Owning Robotaxi Fleet dump)

- Fleet / Teslaconomics (Mar 2026): ~$30k/yr net profit per Robotaxi to owner is a base-case assumption from analyst models + Tesla long-term vision — after platform fee, charging, tires, maintenance, insurance, cleaning. No official real-world owner earnings in this dump. Profit/mile chatter ~$0.25–$0.50 after costs at 50k–100k+ miles/yr in high-demand areas.
- Fleet / Teslaconomics: Cybercab cost chatter ~$25k–$30k; Elon told that tester production was starting in ~1 month (Mar 2026 context — treat as dated tester claim). Rough capital for a ~$1M/yr fleet ~$850k–$1M in vehicles (tester arithmetic).

SAFETY

text:
White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles announced good news on the 16th: she has successfully beaten breast cancer following treatment.

According to reports from Politico, CBS News, and other outlets, the 69-year-old Wiles publicly announced her diagnosis of early-stage breast cancer in March of this year. She subsequently underwent treatment at the Mayo Clinic; following a follow-up examination earlier this week, the latest pathology report showed everything to be normal. On the 16th, Wiles posted on X to announce that she is "cancer-free."

In her post, she thanked "family, friends, doctors, and everyone who prayed for, cared about, and supported me." She added, "I am deeply grateful for President Trump's unwavering support and will continue to work hard to advance his 'America First' agenda."

The White House declined to comment on Wiles's statement.

Wiles is one of Trump's closest aides and continued to serve as White House Chief of Staff while undergoing cancer treatment. Reports indicate that she resumed White House duties—including chairing meetings—shortly after surgery. In July, she made a rare trip to Capitol Hill to meet privately with senior Senate Republicans and attempt to break the deadlock over passing Trump's controversial "SAVE America Act."

Last week, she also accompanied Trump to Dallas for a Republican midterm election event. According to the Air Force One passenger manifest provided by the White House, Wiles traveled with the President as usual.

A veteran political consultant from Florida, Wiles served as the campaign manager for Trump's 2024 presidential bid. Upon Trump's return to the White House, he appointed her as Chief of Staff, making her the first woman to hold the position.

Following her announcement of a successful recovery, numerous lawmakers and political figures took to social media to offer congratulations. Texas Republican Senator Ted Cruz stated, "Susie has shown amazing strength in this battle against cancer." Shortly after Welsh publicly revealed her cancer diagnosis, Trump posted on Truth Social on March 16, describing her as "one of the toughest people I know" and noting that she had an excellent medical team.

"Saudi Arabia suspends Yanbu loading, offers more crude via Oman
Two pumping stations along Saudi East-West Pipeline damaged in recent attack, sources say
Ukraine drone attack damages oil refinery in Russia's Yaroslavl, governor says.

 Oil prices ​eased on Thursday, extending losses as reports of additional Saudi crude cargoes through Oman eased supply concerns, though ‌prices stayed above $100 a barrel on fears the Middle East conflict could widen.

Brent crude futures were down $1.50, or 1.42%, to $104.33 a barrel at 1000 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate futures were down $1.09, or 1.06%, at $101.34 a barrel. Both contracts fell about $3 on Wednesday.

Crude retreated from weekly highs ​after US Energy Secretary Chris Wright signalled a quicker return to service for Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, while ​Saudi efforts to maintain shipments via additional loadings off Oman eased supply worries, said Tim Waterer, ⁠chief market analyst at KCM Trade.

Saudi Arabia is offering more crude cargoes to Asian refiners through ship-to-ship transfers off Oman's Sohar ​port, people familiar with the matter said, helping offset some of the disruption caused by attacks on the East-West pipeline to ​the Red Sea.

Oil prices climbed to around four-month highs earlier this week after shipping industry sources said crude loadings at Saudi Arabia's Red Sea export hub of Yanbu had been suspended and Riyadh had cancelled some cargo deliveries to European customers. The suspension followed attacks on the East-West pipeline, which supplies ​Yanbu.

SUPPLY ‌RISKS ⁠PERSIST
Despite Thursday's decline in oil prices, concerns about the escalating Middle East conflict remain.
Two pumping stations serving the East-West pipeline were damaged in an attack last week, and the repair timeline remains unclear, according to assessments from three oil and security sources.

DIESEL MARKET FEELS THE ⁠SQUEEZE
While crude supply disruptions remain the market's main concern, tightening diesel supplies have emerged as another source of pressure as disruptions to energy infrastructure in the Middle East and Russia constrain ​fuel availability.
European gasoil futures , a benchmark for diesel prices, settled at a record high on ​Tuesday. US ultra-low ⁠sulfur diesel futures also settled at a record high.

A Ukrainian drone attack damaged a refinery in the Russian city of ⁠Yaroslavl, causing ​a fire that was later extinguished, regional Governor Mikhail Yevrayev said on ​Thursday.

Goldman Sachs said in a note that concerns over diesel shortages and the resulting price rally had encouraged refiners to prioritise diesel production over gasoline."

You need to Do these important steps:
1.  Hire your own independent licensed structural engineer (not one chosen by Lennar) right away. Get a formal written report that documents the cause, whether the damage is structural, the extent of the problems, and recommended repairs. This report is critical evidence.
2.  Continue documenting everything: date-stamped photos and videos of all cracks (interior and exterior), doors/windows that no longer operate properly, floor slopes, any new or worsening damage, and every communication with Lennar.
3.  Contact a Texas attorney who specializes in residential construction defects / builder warranty claims (many work on contingency, meaning they only get paid if you recover money). Have them handle it. In Texas you generally must follow the Residential Construction Liability Act (RCLA) process before suing: send a detailed formal notice by certified mail describing the defects and including your evidence/engineer report. The builder then has a limited window to inspect and make a settlement offer. An experienced attorney will manage the notice, negotiations, and any lawsuit or arbitration.
4.  Also notify your local city/county building department or code enforcement office and request an inspection. They can sometimes force the builder to address structural or safety issues and may even revoke the certificate of occupancy if the problems are severe enough.
Because the home is still under the structural warranty window, keep pressing Lennar in writing while you pursue the independent engineer and attorney. Do not accept cosmetic patch jobs that ignore the underlying foundation/soil issues.

Two days, two giant elephant translocations. 

On Tuesday, we moved one truant bull who had developed a dangerous habit of breaking onto community land. On Wednesday, we moved his partner-in-crime.

After the SWT helicopter positioned him, KWS vet Dr Limo darted him from the air. The bull succumbed to the anaesthesia near the road, making for a relatively seamless loading operation – before the long journey to his new home.

Now both bulls are back together, with abundant food and water and space to roam safely.

text:
The Paul is Dead urban legend erupted into an international media sensation in the autumn of 1969, fueled by an article published on September 17, 1969, in the Drake Times-Delphic, the student newspaper of Drake University in Des Moines, Iowa. Written by Tim Harper, the article, titled Is Beatle Paul McCartney Dead?, brought together campus rumors and alleged clues hidden inside Beatles songs and album covers, quickly jumping from college radio stations to mainstream American and British broadcasts.

According to the theory, McCartney had supposedly stormed out of an Abbey Road recording session on November 9, 1966, suffered a fatal car crash, and was replaced by a lookalike named William Campbell (or Billy Shears), an orphan from Scotland who had allegedly won a McCartney lookalike contest.

Beatles fans began scouring album art and playing records backwards to find supposed clues:

Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band (1967): Fans pointed to the bass drum reading Lonely Hearts, claiming that holding a mirror across the text revealed the phrase 1 ONE 1 X HE DIE. Above McCartney’s head on the cover, a hand is held high, which theorists claimed was a symbol of death, while Paul stands facing backward on the rear sleeve with lyric text covering him.

Magical Mystery Tour (1967): On the cover, four figures wear animal costumes, with the black walrus singled out as a Scandinavian sign of death. Fans claimed John Lennon was singing cranberry sauce at the fade of Strawberry Fields Forever, mishearing it as I buried Paul.

Abbey Road (1969): The zebra-crossing cover became the cornerstone of the rumor, interpreted as a funeral procession: John Lennon in all white as the clergyman or preacher, Ringo Starr in black as the undertaker, Paul McCartney walking out of step and barefoot with his eyes closed as the corpse, and George Harrison trailing in denim as the gravedigger. Furthermore, McCartney held a cigarette in his right hand—despite being famously left-handed—and a Volkswagen Beetle parked along the street bore the license plate 28IF, which fans claimed meant Paul would have been 28 years old if he had lived.

Revolution 9 Backwards: When the repeating spoken-word loop of number nine, number nine on the White Album was spun backwards on turntables, listeners insisted they could hear the phrase turn me on, dead man.

The rumors grew so loud that a camera crew and reporters from Life magazine tracked McCartney down to his remote High Park Farm in Campbeltown, Scotland, where he was living quietly with his wife Linda and family.

After initially chasing the reporters off his land with a bucket of water, McCartney agreed to sit for an interview and photograph to put the nonsense to rest once and for all. On November 7, 1969, Life featured McCartney, Linda, and their daughters on the cover alongside the headline: Paul Is Still With Us. Inside, Paul offered his famous, deadpan verdict:

Perhaps the rumour started because I haven't been much in the press lately. I have done enough press for a lifetime, and I don't have anything to say these days. I am happy to be with my family and I will work when I work. I was on for ten years and I have never taken off. Now I take off whenever I can. I would rather be a little less famous than I am. The Beatle thing is over. It has been exploded, partly by what we have done, and partly by other people. If I were dead, I'm sure I'd be the last to know.
