Thought for 43s

The photo and caption 
are a compact self-portrait. 

The shirt motto
—“Live Slow, Die Whenever”
—is stoic 
and slightly dark-humored, 
paired with orchids 
whose last flower on the first plant 
still hangs on 
while the newer ones drop. 

You explicitly say 
the shirt
 fits “everything in the picture.” 

That is a man noticing 
persistence and loss 
at the same time, 
using plants and clothing 
as quiet metaphors 
while standing 
in an ordinary bathroom
 after a high-stakes job change.

The comments add the family layer. 
Sophia Annika
 (close enough to post with you and offer gifts) 
mentions Rocco’s travel hockey team, 
Bauer gear with his name and number, 
and “good luck 
when you go to your second job.” 

You answer with the extra-large size 
because your mother 
always bought clothes too big 
so you could grow into them, 
that you like them loose, 
and that hoodies 
are “always loose and big to conceal the gun.” 

The exchange is affectionate, 
practical, 
and unsentimental. 

It shows a mother or daughter-in-law
 who tracks a child’s sports 
and a child’s allergies, 
a grandfather who still accepts family gifts, 
and a man 
whose childhood clothing habit
 and adult security habit 
sit in the same sentence. 

Later memories confirm grandchildren
 (Rocco, Lucas, and others), 
sports 
(hockey, baseball), 
and relatives such as 
Jeanne Yee McLellan 
who stay in the comment threads. 

The circle is small, loyal, 
and ordinary 
in the best sense.

What it says about you: 
a dual-credentialed physician-lawyer 
who chose the forensic and correctional road 
for most of a 50-plus-year career, 
absorbed the violence and moral wear 
without claiming he suffered the most
 (you explicitly credit the nurses), 
and still pauses 
to photograph orchids 
and joke about shirt size. 

The “This Old Chinaman” moniker 
is self-chosen, 
wry, 
and consistent 
with a Chinese-American man 
who never hid the heritage 
while practicing in American institutions. 

You collect friends and stories, 
travel light, 
and keep posting the receipts 
years later.

What it says about friends and family: 
they show up with hockey hoodies, 
allergy-management labor, 
birthday comments, and sports photos. 

They treat the high-risk job 
as something 
that can still use a little luck 
and a little warmth. 

The relationships are intergenerational 
and durable even as you moved f
rom hospital to hospital.

The trajectory
from that bathroom mirror 
is continuity 
rather than rupture: 
more contracts, 
more books, 
more licenses, 
more memories posted, 
still licensed 
and still reflecting in 2026. 
The last orchid hanging on is the through-line.

All our times have come
Here but now they’re gone
Orchids don’t fear the falling
Nor does the last bloom hanging on
We can be like they are  
Come on, old doctor, 
don’t fear the reaper
Baby take my hand, 
don’t fear the reaper
We’ll still live slow, 
don’t fear the reaper
Baby I’m your man  
Wards of violence have come
Here but now they’re gone
Nurses took the heavier blows
You moved from Atascadero on
We can be like they are  
Come on, old Chinaman, 
don’t fear the reaper
Hoodie loose to hide the gun, 
don’t fear the reaper
Mom bought the clothes too big, 
don’t fear the reaper
Grow into them still  
Rocco’s team is on the ice
Sophia sends the Bauer luck
Petals drop and petals stay
Second job, first light of day
We can be like they are  
Come on family, 
don’t fear the reaper
Live slow, die whenever
The last flower’s still hanging on.

The post is a genuine
 September 17, 2017 Facebook memory. 
It was made a few months 
after you left Atascadero State Hospital 
(contract psychiatrist, February 2015–May 2017) 
and started at Patton State Hospital 
(May 2017–January 2018). 

Both are California Department of State Hospitals forensic facilities 
that house patients 
committed by the courts
—NGRI, incompetent to stand trial,
 and other high-risk populations. 

Those settings 
have long records of patient-on-staff
 and patient-on-patient violence;
 your description
 of being “marinated in violence,” 
burnout, and moral injury, 
with nurses taking the worst of the assaults, 
matches the documented environment.

You were in your late 60s, 
still taking contract work 
in one of the harder corners of psychiatry 
after decades of the same:

psychiatry training,

ER moonlight,

medical-director roles, 
then prisons and forensic hospitals
 across Michigan, California, and other states (
Pelican Bay, San Quentin, I-Max, Kalamazoo, and more). 

The 2017 snapshot 
sits in the middle of a long, 
mobile career 
that continued afterward 
with further contracts, 
a series of self-published 
“Psychiatric Consultation” books, 
multi-state licenses 
that remain active 
into the mid-2020s, 
and prolific posting under 
Kai Chiu /

text:
Ethical alternatives to Google. Here are 8 of their apps people use every day, and what to use instead.

Instead of Gmail, use Tuta Mail.
Gmail shows ads and isn't end-to-end encrypted. Tuta has no ads and encrypts your emails, contacts, and subject lines so even Tuta can't read them. The German company says it has no outside shareholders.

Instead of Google Drive, use Proton Drive.
Google Drive isn't end-to-end encrypted for regular users. Proton Drive encrypts files before they leave your device, so Proton can't see them, and a nonprofit foundation controls the Swiss company and can block any takeover.

Instead of Google Docs, use CryptPad.
Unlike Google Docs, CryptPad encrypts documents so its servers can't read them, and you can still write with others in real time. Its code is public, and it's made by XWiki, a French open-source company.

Instead of Google Meet, use Signal.
Google Meet isn't end-to-end encrypted by default. Signal encrypts group calls for up to 75 people, with screen sharing, and it's run by a nonprofit that says it can never be acquired by Big Tech.

Instead of Google Photos, use Proton Drive.
Google Photos doesn't offer end-to-end encryption, but the Proton Drive app from earlier backs up and encrypts your iPhone or Android camera roll automatically. Proton says no one can use your photos to train AI.

Instead of Google Calendar, use Tuta Calendar.
Unlike Google Calendar, it comes with the same Tuta account as your email and encrypts your events and reminders so Tuta can't see your plans. Tuta built its own Android notifications to avoid using Google.

Instead of Google Forms, use CryptPad Forms.
Like its document editor, CryptPad Forms is free and gives surveys and signup sheets end-to-end encryption Google Forms doesn't offer. Its public finances show it's funded mostly by grants and subscriptions.

Instead of Google Sheets, use Proton Sheets.
Proton gets a third spot because Sheets comes free with Proton Drive. Unlike Google Sheets, it encrypts your spreadsheets, even file names, and still lets you edit live with others and import Excel files.

Google runs so many of your apps that leaving feels impossible, but it isn't. Check the Conscious Spend app to find ethical alternatives to big brands.

text:
A UCF business professor caught 200 students cheating using stolen exam answers - and made them sit through a 14-minute statistical autopsy of exactly how he found them.

He didn't call the dean first. He called up a probability distribution on the projector.

Professor Richard Quinn had taught 21 years. Delivered course content to tens of thousands of students. And the one lecture he always hoped he'd never give - he gave it to 600 people sitting in stunned silence.

He ran the grade distribution after the midterm. It came back bimodal.

A bimodal distribution means an external force corrupted the data set. He didn't know what it was on Sunday. On Monday, a student anonymously slipped the stolen answer key under his office door.

Someone had sold the complete test bank to a third of the class.

Watch the moment at 2:42 when he puts both grade curves on the projector - the clean bell curve from the previous semester, then the bimodal spike from this one - and tells 600 students: "This is what cheating looks like in the data."

Then he offers a deal.

Turn yourself in by 7 a.m. Monday. Take a 4-hour ethics course. No permanent record. The matter disappears.

Don't - and academic affairs takes over. Publishers handed the case to their legal teams. He briefed faculty at 20 universities. The final exam test bank has already been replaced.

"Look at the person on your left. Look at the person on your right. Statistically, one of them cheated."

Nobody in the room moved.

He ends by telling the cheaters: "Don't call me. Don't ask me to do anything for you. Ever again."

The video is on YouTube. 7 million views.

🚨CEDAR CITY, Utah 

 A southern Utah couple is grieving after a routine veterinary visit ended in tragedy when their dog, Lilly, was accidentally euthanized.

​Cody and Amy Zylks were already mourning their 16-year-old dog, Remy, whom Cody had brought to Southern Utah Animal Hospital for cremation. While scheduling that service, Cody also requested an allergy shot appointment for their other dog, Lilly. 

Upon arrival, Cody confirmed Lilly’s name and the reason for the visit with the receptionist before being brought to an exam room.

​While Cody was distracted reflecting on Remy’s passing, the veterinarian administered a injection. 

When Lilly suddenly went limp, Cody questioned the vet, only to discover she had been given a lethal dose meant for euthanasia. Devastated, Cody broke down in the clinic. 

He alleged that the vet initially reacted with indifference, offering only to buy them a replacement dog an offer Cody firmly rejected, stating Lilly could never be replaced.

​The clinic staff later explained that a mix-up occurred because a cat scheduled for euthanasia at the same time had failed to show up, leading to confusion over the injections.

​Dr. Zachary Francisco later released a public statement expressing his condolences and taking responsibility for the error. According to Francisco, he had been in surgery when a technician informed him a euthanasia was waiting. 

Upon entering the room, he asked Cody if he was ready to proceed and invited him to stand by Lilly. Assuming Cody’s lack of response meant consent, Francisco administered the injection.

​Acknowledging that a grave error was committed, Dr. Francisco offered his sincere apologies to the Zylks family and pledged to update clinic protocols to ensure such a tragedy never occurs again.

text:
The story of the first Alor people adapting to climate change 43,000 years ago reveals a fascinating tale of human resilience and innovation in the face of environmental challenges. Through meticulous archaeological research, supported by funding from the Australian Research Council and the Indonesian government, and with the invaluable assistance of local communities and experts, we have unearthed compelling evidence of early human habitation on the island of Alor.

Our exploration centered on Makpan Cave, nestled along Alor's southwest coast, where we uncovered a treasure trove of artifacts and remains shedding light on the lives of our ancient ancestors. The excavation team, comprising Australian and Indonesian archaeologists, meticulously cataloged stone tools, shell implements, and remnants of marine life, indicating human occupation dating back an astounding 43,000 years.

This groundbreaking discovery not only extends the timeline of human presence on Alor but also underscores its pivotal role as a stepping stone for migration between neighboring islands. As sea levels fluctuated during the last ice age, Alor's inhabitants navigated a dynamic landscape, adapting their lifestyles to suit changing environmental conditions.

During the early habitation phase, spanning from 43,000 to 14,000 years ago, lower sea levels facilitated easier access to coastal resources, fostering a marine-centric diet supplemented by terrestrial flora and fauna. The connectivity between Alor and Pantar Island expanded, transforming the region into a sprawling mega-island and reshaping marine currents.

With the onset of the Pleistocene-Holocene transition around 14,000 years ago, rising sea levels brought Makpan closer to the coast, prompting a resurgence in marine resource utilization. The sheltered bay and surrounding waters teemed with an abundance of seafood, evidenced by dense midden deposits and sophisticated fishing technologies, including shell fishhooks and coral sinkers.

However, as sea levels continued to rise in the Early-Middle Holocene, the landscape underwent further transformation, leading to the eventual abandonment of Makpan approximately 7,000 years ago. The reasons behind this exodus remain shrouded in mystery, but it likely coincided with shifts in settlement patterns driven by environmental changes.

Despite, temporary abandonment, Makpan experienced a resurgence in the Neolithic era, around 3,500 years ago, marked by the introduction of pottery and domestic animals. This resurgence reflects the adaptability and ingenuity of early human communities, as they navigated the complexities of climate change and forged new paths forward.

In essence, the story of the first Alor people offers profound insights into our shared human journey, highlighting our capacity to thrive in the face of adversity through innovation, adaptation, and community resilience. As we continue to unravel the mysteries of our past, let us draw inspiration from the resilience of our ancestors, forging a path towards a more sustainable and harmonious future.

text:
The Baby Bear That Learned to Fish Before It Learned to Roar

The tide has only just pulled back, leaving a wide, glistening sheet of mud and sand stretching toward the water. A small brown shape sits hunched in the middle of it, shoulders rounded, head bowed low over something pink and wriggling. It is a bear cub, no more than a few months old, and it is eating a fish it caught entirely on its own. Its fur is soaked and matted, sand clings to its paws, and it pauses every few seconds to glance up and check the world around it. Then, almost comically, it rises onto its back legs, fish clamped between its front paws like a trophy, and takes a few wobbling steps before dropping back down to finish the job. A second cub shuffles into the frame moments later, equally soaked, equally focused, working on a catch of its own.

Nothing about this scene looks rehearsed, because it isn't. What you are watching is one of the most demanding lessons in the entire animal kingdom, playing out in real time on a strip of open mudflat: a baby bear teaching itself how to stay alive.

The First Weeks Outside the Den

To appreciate how remarkable this moment is, it helps to rewind a few months. When a mother bear finally leads her cubs out of the den after winter, the cubs she brings with her are still uncertain on their legs, easily startled, and almost comically uncoordinated. They stumble over rocks, tumble down small slopes, and stick close to her flank the way a toddler clings to a parent's hand in a crowded room. At this stage, the idea of one of them independently pinning down a live fish would seem almost impossible.

But bear development moves fast. Within a matter of weeks, wobbly steps become confident trotting. Within a couple of months, cubs that once needed constant supervision are wandering several body-lengths away from their mother to investigate a rock, a log, or a puddle on their own. This expanding radius of independence is not accidental; it is exactly how curiosity gets converted into competence. Every short solo excursion is a rehearsal for the much bigger solo excursions that will eventually define their adult lives.

A Nursery Built on Tide Charts

Brown bear cubs are born in the depth of winter, inside a den, weighing barely a pound — smaller than a loaf of bread, blind, nearly hairless, and utterly dependent on their mother's body heat and milk. By the time spring arrives they have grown into round, clumsy balls of fur, but they are still functionally helpless. Everything they know about surviving in the wild has to be built from scratch over the following two or three years, and much of that education happens on beaches exactly like the one in this footage.

Coastal tidal flats are not a random backdrop. They are a calendar. Twice a day the water retreats and exposes a temporary buffet: small fish that were swimming happily in shallow channels suddenly find themselves stranded in receding pools, trapped in ankle-deep water or squirming across wet sand with nowhere to go. For an adult bear with decades of experience, this is easy pickings. For a cub who has never done this before, it is closer to a final exam with no notes allowed.

Reading a Landscape That Keeps Changing

One of the hardest parts of this particular skill is that the classroom itself never stays the same. A stretch of mudflat that was thick with stranded fish yesterday might be nearly empty today, depending on the size of the tide, the direction of the wind, or the timing of a fish run further upstream. Adult bears carry years of accumulated knowledge about which channels tend to trap prey, which sandbars form productive pools, and which times of day are worth the effort. A cub has none of that history yet. All it has is trial, error, and a mother who already knows the answers but rarely gives them away for free.

This is part of why the same stretch of coastline can produce such different behavior from one individual to the next. A cub that spends its first season on a slow, shallow inlet will develop very different instincts than one raised along a fast-moving channel where fish move quickly and disappear just as fast. By the time these animals reach adulthood, their fishing style often reflects the specific classroom where they served their apprenticeship.

Learning by Doing, Not by Being Told

Bears do not train their young the way a sheepdog is trained, with commands and rewards. Almost everything a cub learns comes from two sources: watching its mother, and simply doing the thing badly, over and over, until it stops being bad. A mother bear will lead her cubs to a productive stretch of shoreline and let them tag along while she forages, but she rarely intervenes directly in their fumbling attempts. She is a walking demonstration, not a coach. The cubs absorb her posture, her timing, the way she angles her head and freezes before a lunge, and then they go try it themselves, usually with far less grace.

The footage captures this perfectly. The cub does not stalk its prey with any of the calculated patience an adult would show. It splashes, it pounces at the wrong moment, it loses its balance in the shallow water more than once. And yet it succeeds anyway, because at low tide the odds are stacked heavily in its favor — the fish have nowhere to run, and a cub does not need finesse when its target is trapped in three inches of water. This is precisely why tidal flats function as a training ground: the margin for error is enormous, which means a clumsy student can still walk away with a full stomach and a small, priceless dose of confidence.

When the Attempt Fails

Not every lunge in this kind of footage ends with a fish in the mouth, even if the version that gets shared online is naturally the success story. For every clip of a triumphant cub trotting along the sand with its prize, there are dozens of unfilmed moments where the same animal comes up with nothing but a mouthful of mud, or watches helplessly as its target flicks away into deeper water at the last second. These failures rarely carry any real cost beyond wasted energy and a bruised sense of dignity. There is no punishment, no scolding from a watching mother, no lasting setback. The cub simply resets, scans the shallows again, and tries once more a few steps further down the flat.

This tolerance for repeated failure is, in its own way, a luxury. It exists only because the environment happens to be forgiving during this particular window: fish are plentiful, predators are relatively scarce compared to open water, and a mother is close enough to intervene if real danger appears. Later in life, on a fast river packed with adult bears competing for the same fish, the cost of a clumsy miss will be much higher. Right now, on a quiet tidal flat, a cub gets to be bad at something important without paying a steep price for it.

The Toolkit of a Very Small Predator

A cub this young does not yet have the crushing bite force or the raw strength of an adult, but it already carries a surprisingly capable set of tools. Its claws, though small, are sharp and slightly curved, ideal for pinning a slippery body against the sand rather than slicing through it. Its paws are broad and sensitive, able to feel the vibration of a fish thrashing beneath the surface even when it cannot be seen clearly through churned-up water. Its sense of smell, already remarkably refined even at this age, lets it detect the presence of fish long before its eyes would ever pick them out among the ripples and glare.

What it lacks in technique, it makes up for in sheer physical commitment. Watch closely and you can see the cub throw its whole body into the chase, sand flying from its back paws as it scrambles forward, front legs plunging into the shallows almost simultaneously with its snout. There is no elegance in it. There does not need to be. Survival rarely rewards style points; it rewards results, and a wriggling fish clamped firmly in the jaws counts as a result no matter how it got there.

Standing Tall for a Better Look

That brief moment when the cub rises onto its back legs, fish still clutched tightly in its front paws, is one of the most striking parts of the entire clip, and it is worth pausing on. Bears do not stand upright to threaten or attack; that posture is almost entirely about gathering information. Rising up lifts the nose and eyes higher, giving a clearer view across the flat ground, a better read on scent carried by the breeze, and a quick check for anything approaching from a distance. For a cub, still learning which parts of its surroundings deserve attention and which can be ignored, that upright pause is a small but meaningful habit taking shape.

There is likely something else going on as well. Holding a hard-won catch up off the wet ground, even briefly, keeps it out of the shallow water and away from the scavenging attention of nearby gulls, which are often quick to snatch an unattended meal the moment a bear looks away. A few seconds of balancing on two legs, awkward as it looks, may simply be the most efficient way to keep a prize secure while deciding what to do next.

Why a Fish Is Worth So Much

To understand why this moment matters so much, it helps to think in calories rather than sentiment. A growing cub burns an extraordinary amount of energy simply existing — playing, exploring, keeping warm, growing bone and muscle at a startling rate. Fish, especially the fatty, protein-dense species that congregate near coastlines and river mouths during spawning season, are about as efficient a food source as nature offers a young bear. A single successful catch can provide more usable energy than hours of digging for roots or stripping berries from low shrubs.

This matters even more heading into autumn, when bears of every age enter a physiological frenzy scientists sometimes describe as an eating binge, gorging to build up the fat reserves that will carry them through months of winter sleep without eating or drinking at all. A cub that has already spent its first spring and summer mastering the art of catching its own food enters that critical season with a real advantage. It is not relying entirely on its mother's ability to provide; it is contributing to its own survival, one thrashing catch at a time.

Counting the Cost of Growing Up

Wildlife researchers who track individual bear families across multiple seasons consistently find that the first two years of life are by far the most dangerous stretch in a bear's entire existence. A significant share of cubs never make it to independence, and the causes are varied: disease, accidents, harsh winters that deplete a mother's fat reserves before spring, conflict with other bears, and simple bad luck in a landscape full of hazards. Against that backdrop, something as small as successfully catching one fish on one afternoon might sound trivial, but it is not. It is one data point in a running tally that, added up over hundreds of similar moments, determines whether a particular cub survives long enough to become an experienced adult, or becomes one of the many that do not.

This is also why patience from a mother matters so much. A mother who rushed in to finish every difficult task for her cubs would be protecting them from short-term frustration while quietly setting them up for long-term failure. The animals that tend to do best later in life are consistently the ones that were given room, early on, to struggle through exactly these kinds of small, low-stakes challenges.

The Long Shadow of the Mother

None of this happens in isolation. Even as the cub triumphantly parades its prize across the sand, standing briefly on its hind legs the way you might raise a flag, its mother is almost certainly nearby, watching, tolerating, occasionally intervening if a larger, more dangerous bear wanders too close. Cub mortality in the wild is brutally high, and the greatest threats rarely come from starvation alone. Adult male bears, unrelated to the cubs, will sometimes kill young animals, and a mother's presence, along with her willingness to defend her offspring fiercely, is often the single biggest factor determining whether a cub survives its first two years.

That protective shadow is part of why this kind of independent foraging is allowed to happen at all. The mother is not merely feeding her young directly; she is giving them the safety and the opportunity to fail safely, to flounder in shallow water and come up empty-handed a dozen times before finally closing their jaws around something solid. Each failed attempt costs almost nothing under her watch. Each success builds the exact skill set that will, eventually, let the cub survive entirely without her.

Siblings, Rivals, and Practice Partners

The presence of a second cub in the frame adds another layer to the story. Littermates spend an enormous amount of time play-fighting, wrestling, chasing one another across open ground, and this rough play is not simply entertainment. It builds the same muscles, reflexes, and balance that a young bear will later rely on when lunging for a fish or defending a carcass from a rival. Two cubs foraging side by side on the same stretch of mud are, in a sense, still training together, each one's success or failure a small data point the other absorbs simply by being present.

There can also be quiet competition folded into this cooperation. A fish caught by one cub is a fish the other did not get, and siblings do occasionally squabble over a catch, especially when food is scarce. But in a setting as generous as a tidal flat at low water, where multiple stranded fish might be available within a few dozen steps of each other, there is rarely a need for real conflict. Instead what you see is closer to parallel practice: two young animals working the same patch of ground, learning the same lessons, at their own individual pace.

The Sound and Motion of a First Catch

Watch the footage again with attention to the small details rather than the overall action, and the texture of the moment becomes even richer. The spray kicked up with each lunging step. The way wet fur clumps into dark, heavy strands along the cub's back and flanks. The tiny stumble as a hind paw sinks slightly into softer mud. The brief, almost theatrical pause after the catch, as if the cub itself needs a second to register what just happened before continuing. None of this is staged for an audience; it is simply what genuine effort looks like when there is no script and no guarantee of success.

This is also, in large part, why footage like this resonates so widely with people who will never set foot near a tidal flat or a bear of any kind. There is something instantly recognizable in watching a young animal struggle, fail, adjust, and eventually succeed at a task that matters to its survival. It maps, however loosely, onto something almost universal about learning anything difficult: the early attempts are clumsy, the failures outnumber the successes, and the eventual competence arrives quietly, built from repetition rather than a single flash of insight.

A Quiet Kind of Confidence

There is one more detail worth noticing in this footage, easy to miss amid the splashing and the proud little march across the sand: the cub never once looks back toward its mother for help mid-attempt. It stumbles, it adjusts, it finishes the job on its own terms, and only afterward does it seem to check its surroundings again. That small sequence, struggle followed by self-reliance followed by awareness, is arguably the real lesson hiding inside an otherwise simple thirteen seconds of video, and it is one this cub will keep relearning, in slightly harder forms, for the rest of its life.

From Clumsy Splashing to Practiced Precision

The techniques on display here are only the first chapter. Over the following months and years, a cub's fishing style will change dramatically. What begins as frantic, whole-body lunging into shallow tide pools eventually matures into something far more deliberate: standing motionless at the edge of a channel, reading the water for the telltale ripple of an approaching fish, timing a single precise strike instead of a flailing chase. Adult bears in fish-rich habitats can become remarkably specialized hunters, some developing individual preferences for particular stretches of water or particular techniques, passed down not through instruction but through years of trial, observation, and repetition.

The cub in this footage is nowhere near that level yet, and it does not need to be. Its job right now is simpler: get wet, get frustrated, get lucky, and repeat the process enough times that its body starts to understand, almost without conscious thought, exactly how much force a paw needs and exactly when a lunge will land instead of missing. Every clumsy splash recorded in this clip is quietly rewriting the cub's instincts for the rest of its life.

Different Coastlines, Same Lesson

Coastal brown bear populations around the world face a version of this same challenge, even though the details of geography vary considerably. Some grow up along fast rivers where fish arrive in dense, predictable pulses during a short spawning season. Others, like the cub in this footage, learn their craft on broad, gently sloping tidal flats where the timing depends less on a single dramatic run of fish and more on the steady rhythm of the tide itself, rising and falling twice a day regardless of season. The specific techniques these young bears develop differ accordingly: a cub raised on a churning river learns to time a leap against fast current, while a cub raised on a flat estuary learns to read the subtle signs of a shrinking pool of trapped water.

What stays constant across all of these settings is the underlying process. Regardless of geography, a young bear cannot simply inherit fishing competence the way it inherits the shape of its skull or the color of its coat. It has to build that competence through direct, repeated, often unglamorous experience, guided loosely by a mother's example and shaped heavily by whatever particular stretch of coastline it happens to call home during its first uncertain seasons of life.

Watching the Weather Change Everything

Anyone who has spent real time observing bears on a coastline will tell you that conditions can transform an easy feeding ground into a frustrating one almost overnight. A sudden storm can churn the water and scatter fish that would otherwise be trapped in shallow, calm pools. An unusually high tide might submerge a productive flat for longer than usual, shrinking the window of opportunity. Even something as simple as an overcast sky versus bright sunlight can change how easily a cub can spot movement beneath the surface. Learning to fish, in other words, is never just about mastering a fixed set of movements. It is about learning to adapt those movements to whatever the day happens to offer, which is a far more demanding kind of intelligence than simple repetition alone could produce.

This adaptability is precisely what separates a truly experienced adult bear from a merely practiced one. Two bears might both know, in principle, how to pin a fish against the sand, but only the one that has weathered dozens of different tides, storms, and lighting conditions will know how to adjust that basic technique on the fly when circumstances refuse to cooperate. The cub in this clip is, quite literally, at the very beginning of accumulating that kind of hard-earned flexibility.

A Bigger Story Written in Small Footprints

There is a reason wildlife photographers and researchers return again and again to scenes exactly like this one. A bear cub fumbling its way through a first fishing season is, in miniature, a portrait of how an entire ecosystem stays balanced. Bears that fish are not just feeding themselves; they drag caught fish up onto land, leave partial carcasses behind, and in doing so transport nutrients from the water into the surrounding soil and vegetation, fertilizing forests far from any riverbank. The humble spectacle of a cub learning to catch its own dinner is, quietly, part of a much larger cycle that keeps entire coastal habitats alive.

It is also, increasingly, a fragile cycle. Shifts in water temperature, changes in the timing of fish runs, and disruption to coastal habitats all have the potential to throw off the delicate synchronization between when fish arrive and when hungry bears, especially inexperienced cubs, are ready to exploit them. A late season, a poor run, a degraded stretch of shoreline — any of these can turn what should be a routine training ground into a much harder test, with real consequences for cubs already living on the edge of survival.

The Weight of a Single Afternoon

It is tempting to watch thirteen seconds of a cub trotting proudly along a beach and treat it as a light, purely charming moment, and on the surface, that is exactly what it is. But zoom out even slightly and the same clip becomes something closer to a progress report on an ongoing, high-stakes project: a young animal's slow, unglamorous transformation from a helpless newborn into a self-sufficient predator capable of surviving on its own terms. Every wet, sandy step captured on camera represents hours of unfilmed practice that came before it and hints at the countless more hours of practice still to come.

None of that undermines the charm of the scene. If anything, understanding the stakes behind it makes the small triumph land harder. A cub standing briefly on its hind legs with a fish in its mouth is not simply an adorable accident caught by a lucky camera angle. It is a genuine milestone, earned through repeated failure and built, quite literally, one clumsy lunge at a time.

What the Footage Really Shows

Strip away the charm of a small, dripping cub standing proudly with a fish held in its front paws, and what remains is one of the oldest stories in nature: an animal with almost no experience, thrown into a demanding world, figuring things out through repetition, risk, and the quiet, constant presence of a parent willing to let it try and occasionally fail. There is no shortcut here, no moment where instinct alone hands the cub a finished skill. It has to be built, splash by splash, one soaked and sandy afternoon at a time.

By the time this same animal reaches adulthood, the frantic scrambling will be gone, replaced by something closer to calm expertise. It will read tides the way its mother does now, choose its spots with the same quiet confidence, and, if it survives long enough to raise cubs of its own, it will stand nearby one day on a similar stretch of mud, watching a new generation splash clumsily after fish they have not yet learned to catch. The cycle will repeat, exactly as it has for this cub, exactly as it did for its mother before her.

For now, though, it is simply a small, soaked animal on an open beach, fish in its mouth, front paws still dripping, taking a few proud, wobbling steps across the sand before sitting back down to finish its meal. It does not know yet how good it will eventually become. It only knows that today, for the first of what will be countless times, the effort finally paid off.

33 Key Voices First 1,600 yrs of Christendom whose theological metaphysics opposed Westminster’s Guaranteed Fall of “Not By Bare Permission” 
→
1. Justin Martyr (c. 100–165) — Angels and men created free. Foreknowledge is not causal determination.
2. Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 130–202) — No coercion with God. Man is cause to himself of becoming wheat or chaff.
3. Tertullian (c. 155–220) — Adam willed the sin he committed. The Fall is not a necessity God imposed.
4. Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–215) — Virtue and vice require real choice. Fate does not author the first sin.
5. Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253) — Autexousion against Valentinian determinism. God does not create anyone wicked.
6. Methodius of Olympus (d. c. 311) — God is not the author of evil. Evil begins in a will that could have kept the command.
7. Archelaus (c. 320) — Anti-Manichaean: devil and man fall by refusing the commandment, not by nature or fate.
8. Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373) — Creatures are mutable by nature, not predetermined to sin. Defilement is from turning, not from God’s making.
9. Cyril of Jerusalem (c. 313–386) — The soul is inherently autexousios (self-governed) as the image of its Creator. Humans do not sin by necessity, cosmic fate, or biological drive, but entirely by the exercise of real-time choice.
10. Cyril of Alexandria (c. 376–444) — God’s eternal foreknowledge neither restricts nor compels the human will; human nature “fell ill” in Adam with mortality, but individual destiny is determined by real-time choice, not an arbitrary divine blueprint.
11. Basil the Great (c. 330–379) — Evil is a voluntary choice. It originates entirely inside the creature’s defect.
12. Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335–395) — Image of God includes being without a master. Ruin and return hang on deliberate choice.
13. John Cassian (c. 360–435) — Free will actively cooperates with grace. God does not force salvation or damnation. Not Bañezian but Western resistance to extreme predestination.
14. Vincent of Lérins (d. c. 445) — Opposed extreme predestinarian views. Preserved the baseline consensus of moral accountability. Not Bañezian. Western resistance to extreme predestination.
15. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407) — The call is not forced. Not all who were called obeyed.
16. Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662) — Created will is a real power of self-determination. God does not necessitate the gnomic turn to evil.
17. John of Damascus (c. 675–749) — God foreknows what is in our power; He does not predetermine it. He neither wills wickedness nor compels virtue.
18. Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109) — The will is the cause of its own falling. God does not make the creature fall.
19. Peter John Olivi (1248–1298) — The will retains power for opposites. First sin is from the created will, not from divine or intellectual necessitation.
20. John Duns Scotus (1266–1308) — Synchronic contingency: at the instant of choice the will can do otherwise. God co-causes the act as being, not the deformity of sin.
21. Gregory Palamas (1296–1359) — God foreknows but does not predetermine. His plan reflects what we freely choose.
22. William of Ockham (1287–1347) — God is not the author of sin. Created freedom is not a necessitated effect of the divine will.
23. Gabriel Biel (1420–1495) — The will is not determined ad unum to evil. The Fall is not the output of a necessitating premotion.
24. Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536) — Defended the power of human choice. Explicitly opposed early Protestant deterministic bondage.
25. Balthasar Hubmaier (1480–1528) — Radical Reformer who argued human choice was restored by the Word; if God necessitated the Fall, subsequent cosmic punishment would be fundamentally unjust.
26. Philip Melanchthon (1497–1560) — Luther’s right-hand man who later rejected absolute predestination, developing synergism to protect the universal offer of grace against divine determinism. Caveat is that he is only here by his later synergist phase.
27. Sebastian Castellio (1515–1563) — Early Swiss reformer who openly fought Calvin’s predestinarian system, arguing that a guaranteed blueprint turns God into a hypocrite and the true author of evil.
28. Luis de Molina (1535–1600) — God knows what Adam would freely do. He does not physically predetermine the choice.
29. Francisco Suárez (1548–1617) — Rejects physical premotion that makes the free act inevitable apart from the will.
30. Jacobus Arminius (1560–1609) — No absolute decree necessitating Adam’s fall. Adam could have stood.
31. Benjamin Whichcote (1609–1683) — Moral evil is not necessitated by God. Divine government does not cancel created liberty.
32. Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688) — Attacks “neoteric” divine fatalism: decrees that make all actions necessary are contrary to the ancient church.
33. John Wesley (1703–1791) — Championed universal prevenient grace. Fiercely resisted the Westminster model of unconditional election.

What unfolded yesterday in the European Parliament marks a historic turning point in the relationship between Austria’s Freedom Party, the State of Israel and the Jewish people.

More than a turning point, this was a crossing of the Rubicon, following a long process of building trust, deepening cooperation, and creating a genuine political bridge between Israel and Austria’s Freedom Party. 

The speech delivered yesterday by Herbert Kickl, Federal Chairman of the Freedom Party of Austria, in the European Parliament in Strasbourg, was one of the most significant speeches ever delivered by an Austrian politician regarding Israel and the Jewish people.

I had the privilege of being part of this process and of helping advance it over the past two years, together with my friend Harald @vilimsky, Member of the European Parliament for the Freedom Party of Austria, and Yossi Dagan, Chairman of the Samaria Regional Council.

Here are the key passages from his speech:

“Ladies and gentlemen,
It has been nearly three years since Hamas carried out the most severe attack on Israel from Gaza since the state’s founding, and the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust.

Thousands of rockets. Terrorists breached the border fence. Well over a thousand dead, mostly civilians: children, women and the elderly. 251 hostages were abducted to Gaza.

That was not so called ‘resistance’. It was a crime against humanity. 
The deliberate killing of civilians and the taking of hostages are clearly war crimes.

I do not wish to pass blanket judgment on Muslims here. Millions of people of the Muslim faith reject violence and want to live in peace. But Islamism is not a private matter of faith. It is a politically extremist ideology.

Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis, Boko Haram, they all preach the same hatred toward who we are, what we believe in and what we stand for...

Across Europe, antisemitism is on the rise. Experts warn that Europe could experience many small ‘October 7ths’. 

That must not happen. 
And it will not happen if patriotic forces take responsibility.

This must be stated honestly and without hesitation. Islamism is a politically extremist ideology. It threatens our states, our legal systems, Christians and Jews, as well as our Western values.

In many European cities, synagogues and Jewish schools require heavy security. Students hide their Star of David. Families wonder whether Europe still offers them a future.

Jewish citizens must be able to study, work, pray, assemble and participate in public life without fear, no ifs, ands or buts. Their safety is the benchmark for the freedom of the entire republic.

As chairman of the FPÖ, 
I also stand here in the tradition of my country and my party. 

I take responsibility for today and tomorrow. Combating antisemitism and protecting Jewish life will be part of the agenda of a federal government that I intend to lead, if the Austrian people grant us the mandate and cast their votes for us.

Antisemitism must be rejected, no matter where it comes from: from the far right, from the radical left, from conspiracy movements and from Islamist networks that have gained influence through illegal migration.

A credible commitment also requires confronting one’s own history. As an Austrian, I in particular wish to reaffirm this.

The unprecedented crime against humanity that was the Holocaust must not be forgotten.

As chairman of the Freedom Party of Austria, I express my deep regret before this international audience and sincerely apologize to the Jewish citizens of Austria, to the victims and survivors of National Socialism, to their descendants and to the Jewish people.

There must be no relativization of the Holocaust and no tolerance for those who glorify that regime.

We cannot undo the past. Unfortunately. But we can actively shape the future together.

And we want to do this in concrete terms and without interpretation... >>>

text:
The Apple of Discord

Paris, a Trojan prince, was living as a shepherd because a prophecy warned his father, King Priam, that the boy would one day bring down Troy. 

The drama began at a divine wedding feast when Eris, the goddess of discord, was left off the guest list. 

In revenge, she crashed the party and threw a golden apple onto the table inscribed with the words, "To the fairest."

Three powerful goddesses claimed the prize, and Zeus appointed Paris to judge their beauty. 

To win his favor, each goddess offered him a monumental bribe:

Hera (Juno) promised to make him the king of all Europe and Asia.

Athena (Minerva) offered him supreme wisdom and unmatched military prowess.

Aphrodite (Venus) promised him the love of Helen of Sparta, the most beautiful mortal woman alive.

Paris chose Aphrodite and awarded her the golden apple. 

To claim his prize, he traveled to Sparta and abducted Helen from her husband, King Menelaus. 

In response, an alliance of Greek city-states launched a fleet of a thousand ships to wage war on Troy. 

Ultimately, a divine beauty contest triggered the catastrophic, 10-year Trojan War.

text:
Good morning, friends.

This is precisely the underlying logic behind our decision to go long yesterday: when the market prices in every conceivable piece of bad news, yet prices demonstrate resilient elasticity after a thorough washout of "chase-the-short" liquidity, a market bottom is often quietly established amidst this extreme cognitive bias. Looking back at the past two weeks, retail and macro traders endured a near-dystopian "bearish stress test"—ranging from the September seasonal curse and geopolitical escalations (blockades of key Middle East straits) to the specter of secondary inflation driven by surging crude-to-diesel crack spreads; from tech stock valuation corrections sparked by AI safety concerns, hotter-than-expected CPI data, and the stalling of the Clarity Act, to the Federal Reserve finally dropping the "rate hike shoe" that was already more than 90% priced in. If one wanted to find reasons to be bearish, the market offered a dozen excuses for a crash at any given moment. Yet, yesterday’s price action perfectly illustrated a classic "bad news fully priced in" buying scenario: following a vertical, indiscriminate 2% plunge, the index saw strong support from institutional TWAP algorithmic buying at 3:30 PM, subsequently erasing all intraday losses during overnight trading. When every bearish argument is laid bare and the market has been thoroughly cleansed of weak hands, this classic "Sell the News" event is by no means the start of a trend collapse; rather, it is a ruthless shakeout driven by a rebound in institutional liquidity.

The deeper rationale for buying lies precisely within the Federal Reserve’s seemingly "confident" Summary of Economic Projections (SEP). When the SEP showed a historic shift—with the number of committee members seeing downside risks to GDP dropping to zero—the market’s reaction was not one of reassurance, but rather a display of extremely dangerous "collective blindness." As General Patton famously said, "If everyone is thinking alike, then somebody isn't thinking." Looking back at late 2017 and late 2021—moments when the Federal Reserve was most dismissive of downside risks—we see that these were precisely the starting points for subsequent market volatility and abrupt policy pivots. As an institution typically driven by "looking in the rearview mirror," when policymakers effectively assign zero probability to downside growth risks, it signals that latent tail risks—such as a sudden liquidity crunch or a resurgence of inflation—have entered their policy blind spot. When consensus expectations hit a dead end, even the slightest divergence in perception can trigger a valuation reset. Yesterday’s sharp market sell-off represented an immediate repricing of this "perfect illusion," while the subsequent strong rebound validated a shift in capital’s understanding of the fundamental economic bottom. This is precisely why we unhesitatingly bet against the trend yesterday: we do not trade the "rearview mirror" narratives so neatly packaged by the Fed; instead, we trade the purest buying opportunities born of expectation gaps following a liquidity washout.

🎭 Nigel Farage: There is indeed a clear chain woven from money, ideology, and political opportunism, connecting British far-right agitators like Farage, Robinson, and Hopkins with Israeli interest groups. Their anti-Muslim rhetoric is not an expression of "patriotic outrage," but rather a well-funded political strategy designed to divert attention from domestic tensions in the UK and serve foreign geopolitical agendas.

From "Antisemitic Bullying Thug" to "Defender of Israel"

Nigel Farage is not of "Portuguese Sephardic Jewish descent," as you described. Public records indicate that his father was a stockbroker and his family is of British and German heritage. Yet, a distinct trajectory runs through Farage’s political career. He began as an openly antisemitic bully and later transformed into a staunch defender of Israel.

· Student Days: Multiple classmates accused him of subjecting a Jewish student to persistent, vicious antisemitic bullying, using Nazi slogans such as "Hitler was right," "gas them," and "stupid Jews."

· Political Transformation: In adulthood, Farage underwent a remarkable "metamorphosis." The Reform UK party, which he leads, accepted a lobbying trip worth over £50,000 funded by the Israeli Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Even more direct evidence lies in the establishment of "Reform Friends of Israel" (RFI), which was formed with the direct assistance of Jason Pearlman, the international media advisor to the Israeli President. Pearlman was raising "seed funding" for this pro-Israel lobbying group while still employed by the Israeli President's office. Farage himself has never concealed his stance. He once publicly warned British politicians: "If you don't support Israel, you cannot survive in British politics today."

💰 Tommy Robinson and Katie Hopkins: "Anti-Jihad" Agitators Directly Funded by Israeli Backers

If Farage is a political opportunist, then Tommy Robinson, real name Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, and Katie Hopkins are propagandists and agitators directly employed by Israeli interest groups.

· Tommy Robinson: He was officially invited to visit Israel by Amichai Chikli, Israel’s Minister of Diaspora Affairs, and publicly declared, "I am here to express solidarity with the Jewish people and the people of Israel." His legal fees and campaign funds have come from various pro-Israel American donors, including the Middle East Forum (MEF), a Philadelphia-based think tank known for its anti-Muslim and staunchly pro-Israel stance. The forum once provided him with $32,000 to organize a rally. Israeli media itself has acknowledged that Robinson is "a Machiavellian figure attempting to use a pro-Israel stance to launder his extremist image and legitimize his anti-Muslim agenda."

· Katie Hopkins: Like Robinson, she is a "fellow" funded by American tech billionaire Robert Shillman. Shillman provided funding to Hopkins, Robinson, and American conspiracy theorist Laura Loomer, among others, through the right-wing media outlet "Rebel News," enabling them to operate as "citizen journalists." Shillman also directly donated $100,000 to a rally organized by Robinson.

🔗 The core of the strategy: replacing "antisemitism" with "anti-Muslim sentiment" to serve Israel's geopolitical interests.

This chain of funding reveals a tacit political division of labor between the British far-right and Israel:

· Israel and its supporters provide "ideological products" and funding: they steer the focus of British far-right hatred away from traditional antisemitism and toward anti-Muslim sentiment. By bankrolling figures like Robinson and Hopkins, they have manufactured a "common enemy" called Muslims.

· The British far-right handles "localized marketing": figures like Farage and Robinson employ domestic rhetoric, such as "patriotism," "protecting British culture," and "anti-immigration stances," to package anti-Muslim sentiment as a seemingly legitimate nationalist cause, thereby gaining broader resonance within British society.

The ultimate goal of this strategy, as summarized by one analyst, is "to bring to power a Reform Party government that is even more anti-Muslim than the current Labour administration." A British government more hostile toward Muslims would offer unreserved support for Israel in international affairs, such as the Palestinian issue, while suppressing any pro-Palestinian or anti-Israel voices domestically.

Therefore, the agitation displayed by British far-right provocateurs does not stem from spontaneous "racism" or an organic "fear of Muslims." This is a political war, meticulously orchestrated through foreign funding and geopolitical interests, designed to tear British society apart, scapegoat ethnic minorities, and advance a specific agenda. The hatred and violence endured by the British Muslim community are the direct consequences of this war.

text:
Clarification on Joshua Meservey’s i24NEWS Interview

A short clip from Joshua Meservey’s i24NEWS interview, “Why Somaliland Wants US Recognition” (17 September 2026), has been taken out of context to give the impression that Meservey described President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdillahi (Irro) as “inconsistent.” That is not what he said in the full interview.

Meservey spoke positively about the President’s recent approach, particularly his Washington visit. He noted that the President took the right strategic approach by focusing on the practical benefits and strategic value Somaliland can offer the United States, rather than relying solely on Somaliland’s legal and historical case for recognition (1:17–1:45).

When Meservey later used the words “consistent enough” and “strategic enough,” he was discussing Hargeisa’s broader outreach strategy, not describing the President personally as inconsistent (4:24–4:41).

His wider point was that Somaliland has a strong national-interest argument for recognition, but that this case needs to be communicated strategically, persistently and consistently to policymakers around the world. He emphasized that the President’s current arguments are sound and that this approach needs to be sustained over time (5:47–6:07).

text:
PART 2 OF 2

CONTEXT MATTERS

The answer now being widely circulated came from a different question.

Meservey was asked why the United States and other countries had not followed Israel in recognizing Somaliland.

His answer addressed Somaliland’s long term diplomatic approach over many years, saying in substance that Somaliland had not always pursued its case consistently and continuously enough.

That is a point Somaliland should take seriously.

But it was not his assessment of President Cirro’s current Washington visit.

Those two answers should not be mixed together.

One concerns decades of Somaliland diplomacy and the work that remains to be done.

The other concerns how President Cirro is presenting Somaliland in Washington today.

When Meservey was specifically asked about President Cirro’s argument, his description was clear:

“The right argument.”

The larger message of the full interview is therefore important.

Somaliland has made progress in Washington. It has influential friends, growing strategic relevance and greater access to American policymakers.

President Cirro arrived in Washington at a moment when these factors are increasingly converging, presenting Somaliland not merely as a country seeking something from America, but as a potential strategic partner with something meaningful to offer America in return.

There is still considerable work ahead. Meservey made that clear.

But that should be understood as a call to build on the progress already made, not as evidence that no progress has been made.

The opportunity is there. The challenge now is to turn access, strategic relevance and political support into sustained diplomatic results.

That, in my understanding, is the real message of Joshua Meservey’s full interview.

text:
Charles de Gaulle vetoes the proposal for Canadian, Australian and New Zealand associate membership in the European Union:

The trade strategist laid the tablet on the table, displaying the digital image published by the Spanish prime minister. A red maple leaf sat embedded within the circle of yellow stars on the European flag. The European Commission president had just offered Canada associate membership of the European Union, with Australia and New Zealand slated to follow.

"It isn't full integration," the strategist explained, noting that the status grants no voting rights or free movement. "It's a practical alliance to secure critical minerals and defence technology while protecting our industries from American tariffs."

Charles de Gaulle looked down at the screen, his expression unchanged. "You believe you've invented a clever contract," he said, his voice quiet and firm. "You tell yourself that because you don't grant them seats in your parliament, you've preserved your sovereignty. But you haven't understood what a nation or a continent is."

He gestured towards the red leaf on the blue field. "You're offering a European identity to a country whose security, trade, and strategic allegiance belong irrevocably to Washington. You think you're expanding Europe. In reality, you're completing its dilution."

The strategist pushed back, pointing out that global supply chains require pragmatic partnerships beyond continental borders. "If we don't bind Canada, Australia, and New Zealand to our regulatory orbit, we leave our supply chains vulnerable," she argued. "This doesn't create a superstate. It creates a commercial shield."

"A shield made of paper," de Gaulle countered, leaning forward.

"When I vetoed British entry twice in the 1960s, it wasn't out of malice towards London. It was because Britain was bound to the maritime empire across the Atlantic. If you open your regulatory perimeter to Ottawa, Canberra, and Wellington, whose standards will prevail when American policy shifts? These states will always choose the American security umbrella over European preferences. You're not acquiring raw materials. You're institutionalising your role as an administrative suburb of the Anglo-Saxon world."

The strategist hesitated as the underlying mechanism became clear. Associate membership attempts to solve a resource deficit by sacrificing political definition. Once a union defines its perimeter by shared trade agreements rather than a common geographic and political destiny, it ceases to be a potential sovereign power. It reclassifies itself as a global regulatory authority whose real boundaries are drawn in Washington.

"So the choice isn't between isolation and expansion," the strategist admitted. "It's between remaining a European power or becoming a manager for an Atlantic market."

De Gaulle stood up quietly. "Europe exists only if it is European," he said. "The rest is just commerce."

***
Charles de Gaulle (1890-1970) was a French general and statesman. He's best known for leading the Free French resistance during World War II and founding the Fifth Republic, serving as president from 1959 to 1969 to rebuild France as an independent global power.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez shared an EU flag featuring a Canadian maple leaf amid proposals for Canada to become the first associate member of the bloc, followed by Australia and New Zealand.

THE PRINCE AT NIAGARA; SHOCKING RAILROAD ACCIDENT; Interesting from Arizona; AFFAIRS IN SYRIA

The Prince at Niagara – 2

“Special Dispatch to the New-York Times. CLIFTON HOUSE, NIAGARA FALLS, Sunday, Sept. 16 -- 11:20 P.M. Since the arrival of the Royal party, the Prince has enjoyed himself in an unaccustomed round of pleasurable excitements. At sunrise on Saturday the Royal standard was saluted by a Hamilton artillery company. At 10 o'clock a large yacht was set adrift in the rapids above the Falls, the Prince having expressed a desire to see something go over. The image of a man was placed at the helm, besides which no other passenger was allowed on board. A ride on horseback, a frolic with the little ZIMMERMAN children and a tour of the park comprised the doings of the morning. BLONDIN having invited the Prince to witness his perilous undertakings, announced an exhibition at 4 o'clock. The Prince and suite went on horseback to see him, and occupied a rustic lodge, surrounded by the French flag. There were present several thousand spectators, who thronged both sides of the river, and entirely blocked the passage of the bridge. Having gone through his usual performances, standing on his head, carrying a man across on his back, making believe stumble, turning sommersaults and scaring almost every one, BLONDIN announced to the Prince that in his honor he would do what had never before been done in public -- cross on stilts. The Prince remonstrated, and said he was entirely satisfied and did not wish him to endanger himself on his account, but BLONDIN re-assured him, and finally offered in the most gentlemanly way to carry the Prince over, and had it not been for the Duke there is no telling what might have been the result of the interview. . . .”

He had once mentioned, in passing, that some of his real estate deals involved “creative financing” and “under-the-table arrangements” that allowed him to move money quickly without triggering federal reporting requirements.

Michael, the federal prosecutor, began making phone calls to colleagues in the FBI and the IRS. He explained that he suspected his brother-in-law of money laundering, tax evasion, and possibly involvement with organized crime. He provided them with my account of Ricardo’s suspicious activities and offered to have me testify if needed.

He also explained that Ricardo had just committed what could be considered fraud by inducing me to marry him under false pretenses—that he had never intended to be faithful, that he had hidden his criminal activities from me, and that he had used our marriage as a cover for his illegal operations.

Within two weeks, federal agents showed up at my brothers’ office with a search warrant for Ricardo’s financial records. What they found was staggering: over $50 million in unexplained transfers, shell companies registered in offshore locations in the Cayman Islands and Panama, fake invoices for non-existent business transactions, and direct evidence of money laundering through his real estate developments.

The investigation revealed that Ricardo had been laundering money for a Mexican drug cartel for over eight years. His luxury real estate developments weren’t just businesses—they were fronts for moving illegal cash. His restaurants were used to process payments from drug trafficking operations. His hotel chains had hidden accounts that tracked drug proceeds and facilitated international transfers.

The federal prosecutors estimated that Ricardo had moved over $500 million in drug money through his various businesses over the past eight years. This wasn’t a small-time operation. This was a major money laundering enterprise that had been operating right under the noses of federal authorities. And I had been married to the man running it, completely unaware of the crimes I was unknowingly facilitating simply by being his wife, by attending his business dinners, by allowing my name to be on some of his property deeds.

My brothers worked with the federal authorities to build an airtight case against Ricardo. They obtained warrants for his phone records, email communications, and financial accounts. They interviewed business associates who were willing to cooperate in exchange for reduced sentences.

They traced the money through multiple jurisdictions—California, Nevada, Arizona, Texas, Mexico—and documented every transaction, every wire transfer, every deposit and withdrawal. They created a timeline showing how the money moved from drug trafficking organizations in Mexico, through Ricardo’s various businesses, and into offshore accounts.

They also made sure that I was protected throughout the process. My identity was kept confidential in all federal documents. My location was secure, and I was never identified as a witness in any public filings. My brothers ensured that I would not be charged with any crimes, despite having been married to a major money launderer and despite having unknowingly benefited from the proceeds of drug trafficking. The federal prosecutors understood that I was a victim, not a criminal, and they treated me accordingly.

I wrote articles for legal journals about the intersection of family law and criminal law, about how marriages can be used as covers for criminal activity, and about how women can protect themselves.

Lucas is now five years old. He’s a smart, kind, curious boy who loves dinosaurs and asking questions about everything. He has never met his father—Ricardo is serving his sentence at a federal penitentiary in Northern California, and I have made the decision to keep Lucas away from him. I don’t know if that will change when Lucas is older and can make his own decisions, but for now, I’m protecting him from the trauma of knowing that his father is a criminal and a coward who abandoned him before he was even born.

My brothers became my heroes in ways I never could have anticipated. Michael continued his work as a federal prosecutor, and he has since prosecuted over thirty major money laundering cases, many of them inspired by what he learned from Ricardo’s case. He has become one of the most respected prosecutors in the Department of Justice, known for his meticulous attention to detail and his ability to untangle complex financial crimes.

Daniel became one of the most respected family law attorneys in Los Angeles, and he now offers free legal consultations to women who are going through divorces or custody battles. He has established a foundation that provides legal assistance to women who are victims of financial abuse or fraud.

We have a saying in our family: “The Valdés case changed everything.” It changed our careers, our lives, and our understanding of justice. It showed us that the legal system can work, that criminals can be caught and punished, and that family loyalty and determination can overcome even the most devastating betrayals.

I have also become an advocate for women’s financial literacy and legal protection. I speak at universities and community centers about the importance of understanding prenuptial agreements, protecting your assets, and knowing the warning signs of financial abuse and criminal activity.

I tell women that they don’t have to accept betrayal, that they don’t have to accept being thrown out of their homes, and that they have rights—legal rights, financial rights, and human rights that cannot be taken away by a prenup or a powerful man. I tell them that the legal system, while imperfect, can be a powerful tool for justice if you have the right people fighting for you. I tell them that family matters, that loyalty matters, and that sometimes the most important thing you can do is reach out for help.

To anyone reading this who is going through a similar situation—who has been betrayed by someone they trusted, who has been abandoned, who feels alone and afraid—I want you to know that you are not alone. There are people who will fight for you. There are lawyers who will help you. There are family members who will stand by your side. And there is a life waiting for you on the other side of the pain. My son and I are proof of that. We survived Ricardo Valdés, and we thrived. And so can you.

The prenuptial agreement that was supposed to leave me with nothing? It became the least important document in my life. What mattered was the love of my family, the strength of my character, and the determination to build a better life for myself and my son. Ricardo Valdés is serving twenty-two years in federal prison, and I am free—free from his control, free from his lies, and free to build the life I always wanted. Justice was served, and I got my life back.

🔚
