text:
Top 10 News Today
Thursday, September 17, 2026

The Contents
1. 📈 U.S. Stock Futures Rise After the Fed’s First Rate Hike in Three Years
2.🏦 Fed Raises Rates and Signals More Tightening Ahead
3. 🛢️ Oil Falls for a Second Day as Saudi Supply Eases Fears
4. ⚖️ U.N. Mission Alleges U.S. War Crimes in Iran and Crimes Against Humanity by Tehran
5. 🇺🇸 House Passes Major Russia Sanctions Bill
6. 🇪🇺 EU Proposes Social-Media Ban for Children Under 13
7. 🤖 China and U.S. Diverge Over How Fast AI Should Advance
8. ₿ Senate Blocks Landmark U.S. Cryptocurrency Bill
9. 🩺 U.S. Regulators Examine Testosterone Therapy for Menopausal Women
10. ⚾ 20-Year-Old Ethan Salas Makes MLB History With Two Home Runs

1. 📈 U.S. Stock Futures Rise After the Fed’s First Rate Hike in Three Years

FACT
 Reference point: Wednesday, September 16 close / Thursday, September 17 pre-market. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed Wednesday at 51,461.90 (-1.21%), the S&P 500 at 7,551.81 (-0.45%), the Nasdaq Composite at 25,978.42 (-0.01%), and the Russell 2000 at 2,858.81 (-0.40%). U.S. stock futures moved higher Thursday morning, with technology shares among the stronger pre-market performers.

BACKGROUND
Wednesday’s decline followed the Federal Reserve’s first interest-rate increase since 2023. The Dow lost more than 600 points, while the Nasdaq was almost unchanged. By Thursday morning, Treasury yields had eased somewhat and oil prices were falling, helping sentiment.

WHY IT MATTERS
The immediate uncertainty surrounding the Fed decision has been removed, but the market now has to adjust to the possibility of higher interest rates for longer. Technology stocks may benefit when long-term yields fall, while economically sensitive companies remain exposed to tighter financial conditions.

2. 🏦 Fed Raises Rates and Signals More Tightening Ahead

FACT
The Federal Reserve unanimously raised its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to 3.75%–4.00% Wednesday—the first increase in more than three years. Sixteen of 18 policymakers project at least one additional increase during 2026.

BACKGROUND
Inflation has remained above the Fed’s 2% objective, while higher energy prices have added another source of price pressure. Chair Kevin Warsh emphasized the strength of the economy and said the Fed wants inflation to return toward target in a more timely manner. Markets currently place roughly a 51% probability on another hike in October.

WHY IT MATTERS
The important development is not Wednesday’s widely expected quarter-point increase but the Fed’s message that this may not be a one-time hike. Mortgage rates, corporate borrowing costs, Treasury yields and stock valuations could all remain under pressure if tightening continues.

3. 🛢️ Oil Falls for a Second Day as Saudi Supply Eases Fears

FACT
Oil prices extended their decline Thursday as Saudi Arabia offered additional crude supplies through Oman, reducing fears of an immediate shortage caused by Middle East disruptions. Both Brent and U.S. crude futures fell more than 1% in early trading.

BACKGROUND
The conflict has disrupted traditional shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and pushed oil above $100 a barrel. Saudi Arabia has been developing alternative export routes to keep crude reaching international markets. Fighting involving Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed forces in Yemen nevertheless intensified Thursday.

WHY IT MATTERS
Energy remains one of the largest risks to the global inflation outlook. Sustained declines in crude would help the Fed and consumers; another supply disruption could quickly reverse that improvement and push transportation and manufacturing costs higher.

4. ⚖️ U.N. Mission Alleges U.S. War Crimes in Iran and Crimes Against Humanity by Tehran

FACT
A United Nations fact-finding mission said Thursday that it had “reasonable grounds to believe” two U.S. military strikes in Iran in February constituted war crimes. The mission separately concluded that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their crackdown on anti-government protests. These are findings of the U.N. mission, not judicial judgments.

BACKGROUND
The investigators examined strikes on a primary school in Minab and a sports facility in Lamerd. The Minab attack killed more than 150 people, most of them children, according to the mission. Regarding Iran, investigators cited alleged unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention and other abuses during protests that began in December 2025. U.S. and Iranian officials have previously disputed allegations that their respective conduct was unlawful.

WHY IT MATTERS
The report raises significant questions under international humanitarian law and international human-rights law. It is also notable because the same investigation scrutinizes alleged violations by both a foreign military power and the Iranian government.

5. 🇺🇸 House Passes Major Russia Sanctions Bill

FACT
The U.S. House has passed major legislation expanding sanctions against Russia over its war in Ukraine, sending the measure toward President Donald Trump. The Senate had already approved the legislation.

BACKGROUND
The legislation targets Russian energy and defense interests and the tanker network used to move Russian oil. It also provides tools for imposing economic measures on countries that continue substantial purchases of Russian energy.

WHY IT MATTERS
The bill could increase economic pressure on Moscow, but secondary sanctions and tariffs can also affect countries such as India and China. India warned Thursday that new U.S. tariffs connected to purchases of Russian oil could damage bilateral relations.

6. 🇪🇺 EU Proposes Social-Media Ban for Children Under 13

FACT
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed an EU Kids Act Thursday that would prohibit children under 13 from using social media and place accounts belonging to 13-to-15-year-olds under parental control. The proposal still requires negotiations with EU member states and the European Parliament before it can become law.

BACKGROUND
The proposal would cover social media, video-sharing services, online games, AI companions and chatbots used by minors. It would restrict features such as infinite scrolling, profiling-based recommendation feeds and engagement rewards. AI companions and chatbots would be disabled by default for minors. Companies could face fines of up to 6% of global annual sales for violations.

WHY IT MATTERS
Europe is considering one of the world’s broadest attempts to regulate children’s interaction with digital platforms and AI. Supporters emphasize child safety, while technology groups warn that large-scale age verification could create new privacy and cybersecurity risks.

7. 🤖 China and U.S. Diverge Over How Fast AI Should Advance

FACT
Huawei rotating chairman Eric Xu said Thursday that Chinese AI developers may not yet be technologically advanced enough to encounter the frontier safety risks reported by leading U.S. AI companies. He argued that Chinese developers may actually need to accelerate while simultaneously improving safeguards.

BACKGROUND
U.S. developers including OpenAI and Anthropic have recently highlighted unexpected behavior by increasingly autonomous AI systems, and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has advocated slowing development so safety measures can catch up. China is instead continuing rapid deployment while developing mandatory standards and security assessments for AI agents.

WHY IT MATTERS
The U.S.-China AI competition is developing an unusual new dimension: the leading U.S. companies are increasingly worried about moving too quickly, while Chinese firms are worried about falling behind. How the two countries balance capability and safety could shape the global AI race.

8. ₿ Senate Blocks Landmark U.S. Cryptocurrency Bill

FACT
The Senate failed to advance the CLARITY Act, a major cryptocurrency market-structure bill, in a 49–50 procedural vote, short of the 60 votes needed to proceed.

BACKGROUND
The legislation was designed to clarify how cryptocurrencies would be regulated in the United States. Opposition involved several separate issues, including banking-industry concerns about competition for deposits and Democratic concerns regarding President Trump’s financial interests in cryptocurrency. Reuters reports that the crypto industry has spent more than $300 million in recent elections supporting favorable candidates and policies.

WHY IT MATTERS
The vote leaves one of the world’s largest cryptocurrency markets without the comprehensive regulatory framework the industry has sought. It also shows that substantial campaign spending by an industry does not necessarily translate into enough congressional support to pass complex financial legislation.

9. 🩺 U.S. Regulators Examine Testosterone Therapy for Menopausal Women

FACT
U.S. health regulators are reviewing scientific evidence Thursday concerning the use of testosterone therapy by menopausal women, including potential benefits and safety risks.

BACKGROUND
Testosterone prescriptions for women have increased, particularly for symptoms associated with menopause. However, there is currently no FDA-approved testosterone product specifically designed for women in the United States, meaning treatment often involves products approved for men or specially compounded formulations.

WHY IT MATTERS
The review could eventually influence prescribing practices, insurance coverage and future drug approvals. It also highlights a broader problem in women’s health: some treatments are widely used in clinical practice despite incomplete regulatory guidance or limited long-term evidence.

10. ⚾ 20-Year-Old Ethan Salas Makes MLB History With Two Home Runs

FACT
San Diego Padres catcher Ethan Salas, aged 20 years and 107 days, hit the first two home runs of his major-league career Wednesday in a 9–3 victory over the Colorado Rockies. He became the youngest catcher in MLB history to record a multi-home-run game.

BACKGROUND
The victory was San Diego’s ninth in its last 10 games, improving the Padres to 83–69 as they compete for a National League wild-card position. Elsewhere, the Cleveland Guardians moved into sole possession of first place in the AL Central, while Cincinnati prevented the Dodgers from clinching the NL West.

WHY IT MATTERS
September baseball is entering its decisive stretch. Salas’s breakout adds another young player to watch while the divisional and wild-card races tighten with roughly two weeks remaining in the regular season.

📊 Intel and SK Hynix are reportedly in early talks for a U.S based memory partnership aimed squarely at onshore AI supply chains.

Worth watching closely, but look at the actual mechanics beneath the headline:

The Potential Setup:

$SKHY is exploring options to either lease space inside Intel's $28B Ohio fab campus or form a joint venture alongside Intel and major cloud hyperscalers.

This offers immediate monetization and validation for $INTC struggling foundry business by filling unused fab space without waiting until 2030+.

The Motive for SK Hynix is to secure onshore U.S. HBM3e/HBM4 packaging capacity closer to $NVDA and cloud buyers while offsetting massive capex burdens.

However: 

South Korea’s Trade Ministry classifies advanced HBM as a "national core technology." Before a single wafer is moved, the deal requires explicit clearance under South Korea's Industrial Technology Protection Act, a major political hurdle given Seoul's desire to keep key IP domestic.

SK Hynix has already issued a clarification stating options remain purely exploratory with zero finalized agreements.

A high-reward setup for Intel's foundry narrative, but treat it as an exploratory headline until regulatory sign off actually lands.

COMCAST $CMCSA FELL 6.6% ON ONE SENTENCE ABOUT ONE QUARTER:

Comcast, ticker CMCSA, at $23.93 (premarket), +$0.20 / +0.84% from Wednesday's $23.73 close. Second of fifty-five on the Quality-Value Len5. The Philadelphia company sells Xfinity broadband and mobile service, owns the Universal theme parks and makes films and television at NBCUniversal.

The verdict: the cheap half of this case is settled, and what is still in dispute has narrowed to one customer count Comcast does not get to write. That shape runs through the whole board below - one name per Len5, none of them the first entry, each with half its case proved and half still waiting on a date.

The sentence came on September 9, at a Goldman Sachs technology conference. Chief Financial Officer Jason Armstrong said full-year broadband losses would improve, then added: "This particular quarter, I don't think it will improve year over year." Comcast closed at $24.59, -$1.74 / -6.61%. He was describing the June quarter, reported July 23: 167,000 home broadband customers lost, 34,000 fewer than a year earlier, against 448,000 mobile lines added, the most ever in three months. Revenue $29.94B; adjusted profit, earnings with one-time items stripped out, $1.04 a share vs $0.97 expected.

Armstrong blamed "irrational" pricing by fiber rivals selling a gigabit connection for $30 to $40 a month, with fiber now built through Comcast's territory at 4% to 5% of homes a year against 2% to 3% before. This Len5 wants a business almost nobody could rebuild, bought under its worth - and somebody is rebuilding it street by street.

Under its worth is not in dispute: about 7.7 times the last year of profit, 0.94 times book value, a $0.33 quarterly dividend worth 5.6% a year. Buybacks are paused while NBCUniversal and Sky are split off into a separate company by mid-2027. Then three brokers cut targets in two days - Goldman Sachs to $24 from $25 and UBS to $27 from $32 on September 15, Bank of America to $35 from $37 on September 16 - and none of them cut an earnings figure.

CHANGE IT: two straight quarters of shrinking broadband losses while the mobile line keeps adding. WHEN: October 22 before the open, company-confirmed, $1.00 carried against $1.12. VERDICT: the price now assumes the losses get worse, and October 22 is the first count that can argue back.

MOMENTUM LEN5:
Chime Financial at $31.90 (premarket), +$0.65 / +2.08% from Wednesday's $31.25 close. Second of thirty, a banking app used by 10.4 million people. This Len5 wants a price near its one-year high with the short and long climbs agreeing: the long one is emphatic, +96.8% from the June 11 low of $15.88; the short one has wobbled to 12.1% under the September 9 peak of $35.55. That climb has a date under it - September 8, when Chime agreed to buy Stride Bank, its deposit-holding partner, for $590M in cash. Two directors sold $19.9M of stock in the two days after. CHANGE IT: a close above $35.55; November 4 counts the quarter. VERDICT: a real climb resting on a purchase two regulators have yet to approve.

DEEP-VALUE & SPECIAL-SITUATIONS LEN5:
Broadridge Financial Solutions at $164.69 (after hours), -$2.40 / -1.44% from Wednesday's $167.09 close. Second of sixty-five, and it keeps the records and mails the ballots for most American shares. This Len5 wants settled earning power bought cheaply, and settled is the easy half: the year to June 30, reported August 4, brought recurring revenue - money that arrives again next year - of $4.88B, +8%, and adjusted profit of $9.60 a share, +12%, a seventh straight report above the published expectation. Cheap arrived by price alone, 17.4 times profit and 34.2% under the $250.26 high set a year ago today. CHANGE IT: recurring revenue under the 6%-8% growth just guided; November 3. VERDICT: a third of the price gone while every published figure went up.

GROWTH LEN5:
BOK Financial at $132.82, -$2.95 / -2.17% on Wednesday, no trade since the bell. Second of thirty, a Tulsa bank that also runs a trading desk, a mortgage arm and a wealth manager. This Len5 wants profit growth the price has not already charged for, and both halves are here: the June quarter, reported July 20, earned $2.92 a share against $2.19, +33%, at about 12.5 times profit. Fees brought $237.6M beside $351.8M of lending revenue - forty cents in every dollar - which is how a bank with a narrow 2.91% lending margin, the gap between what it earns on loans and pays savers, produced that jump. Trading fees fell $12.7M last quarter on quieter volumes. CHANGE IT: fee income growing in a quarter when the desk is slow; October 19, confirmed, $2.54 carried. VERDICT: a bank price on a business only about 60% bank.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5:
Credo Technology at $171.00 (premarket), +$9.51 / +5.89% from Wednesday's $161.49 close. Second of thirty, and it designs the chips and cables that move data between AI servers. This Len5 wants very fast growth on a base big enough to be real, and the quarter to August 1, reported September 1, had both: revenue $479.0M, +114.7% on the year, adjusted profit $1.20 a share against $1.17 expected, this quarter guided to $525M-$535M. Tuesday brought the newer reason - 1.6-terabit ZeroFlap transceivers, which turn electrical signals into light at each end of a data-center fiber - and the shares rose $11.10 / +7.38% on Wednesday. CHANGE IT: revenue under the $525M floor management just set; November 30. VERDICT: nobody disputes the growth - at 44.6% under the June 22 high of $308.67, the argument is what 115% is worth.

INCOME LEN5:
Ardmore Shipping at $18.69 (overnight), -$0.37 / -1.94% from Wednesday's $19.06 close. Second of thirty, and it runs 25 tankers carrying fuels and chemicals. This Len5 wants cash reaching owners the business itself funds; here it arrives by formula - two-thirds of adjusted earnings, every quarter. The June quarter, reported July 29, earned $1.18 a share on that basis against $0.22 a year earlier, its mid-size tankers making $51,870 a day against $23,441. So the check was $0.79, paid September 15, and four checks add to $1.37, 7.3% here. The formula cuts down too: 45% of this quarter's days were booked as of July 29 at about $29,600 a day, and analysts carry $0.62 for the September quarter - two-thirds of which is roughly $0.41. CHANGE IT: rates holding near that booked level; November 4. VERDICT: genuinely covered, genuinely variable, pointed down for now.

Six dates, October 19 to November 30. Comcast's lands first, and its deciding figure was settled months ago by strangers: however many households took a $30 gigabit offer this summer, that number is already fixed. October 22 just reads it out.

Ilhan Omar has spent six years insisting that questions about how she became a U.S. citizen are nothing but a “witch hunt.” A former executive-level federal official told The New York Post exactly how that playbook runs: “𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘲𝘶𝘦𝘴𝘵 𝘸𝘪𝘭𝘭 𝘣𝘦 𝘮𝘢𝘥𝘦 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘋𝘕𝘈 𝘵𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘪𝘵 𝘸𝘪𝘭𝘭 𝘣𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘧𝘶𝘴𝘦𝘥 𝘭𝘰𝘶𝘥𝘭𝘺 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘱𝘶𝘣𝘭𝘪𝘤𝘭𝘺,” 𝘢𝘯𝘥 “[𝘖𝘮𝘢𝘳] 𝘸𝘪𝘭𝘭 𝘱𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘴𝘤𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘮 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘴𝘢𝘺 𝘪𝘵’𝘴 𝘰𝘧𝘧𝘦𝘯𝘴𝘪𝘷𝘦 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘢 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘤𝘩 𝘩𝘶𝘯𝘵.”

The pattern isn’t new. In 2019, a viral video argued Omar was actually 18 or 19 years old in 2000 — not 17 — when she claimed automatic citizenship through her father’s naturalization, a path that only works for minors. Just two days after that video spread, Omar’s own staff quietly contacted the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library and 𝐡𝐚𝐝 𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐛𝐢𝐫𝐭𝐡 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐝 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝟏𝟗𝟖𝟏 𝐭𝐨 𝟏𝟗𝟖𝟐 — shaving exactly enough time off the calendar to keep her naturalization story intact. Congressional records now list 1982 as her birth year. She has never produced a birth certificate to prove it.

That paper trail is now the center of a live federal investigation. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has confirmed the probe is active, warning on a podcast that “𝘴𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨’𝘴 𝘨𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘰 𝘩𝘢𝘱𝘱𝘦𝘯.” Border czar Tom Homan has called it an “𝘰𝘯𝘨𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘤𝘳𝘪𝘮𝘪𝘯𝘢𝘭 𝘪𝘯𝘷𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘨𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯.” A top immigration official told The Post the stakes plainly: “𝘐𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦’𝘴 𝘦𝘯𝘰𝘶𝘨𝘩 𝘦𝘷𝘪𝘥𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘴𝘩𝘦 𝘰𝘳 [𝘩𝘦𝘳 𝘧𝘢𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘳] 𝘭𝘪𝘦𝘥 𝘰𝘯 𝘩𝘦𝘳 𝘪𝘮𝘮𝘪𝘨𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘢𝘱𝘱𝘭𝘪𝘤𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘵𝘰 𝘣𝘦𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦 𝘢 𝘜𝘯𝘪𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘚𝘵𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘴 𝘤𝘪𝘵𝘪𝘻𝘦𝘯, 𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘳 𝘪𝘵 𝘸𝘢𝘴 𝘰𝘯𝘦 𝘵𝘪𝘮𝘦 𝘰𝘳 𝘴𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘭 𝘵𝘪𝘮𝘦𝘴, 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘛𝘳𝘶𝘮𝘱 𝘢𝘥𝘮𝘪𝘯𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘤𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘪𝘯𝘪𝘵𝘪𝘢𝘵𝘦 𝘢 𝘥𝘦𝘯𝘢𝘵𝘶𝘳𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘻𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘤𝘦𝘴𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘸𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘴𝘵𝘳𝘪𝘱 𝘩𝘦𝘳 𝘰𝘧 𝘩𝘦𝘳 𝘤𝘪𝘵𝘪𝘻𝘦𝘯𝘴𝘩𝘪𝘱.”

Investigators are also circling Omar’s 2009 marriage to Ahmed Elmi, a UK national long rumored inside Minnesota’s Somali community to be her actual brother — not the immigration lawyer she introduced him as. A former ICE lawyer told The Post the marriage itself is a legal dead end: the statute of limitations on marriage fraud expired when the couple divorced in 2017, and a citizen spouse can’t be deported over a sham marriage even if proven. But 𝐚 𝐃𝐍𝐀 𝐭𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐰𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐨𝐥𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐪𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐧 𝐚 𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐛𝐞𝐚𝐭, and Omar has offered no timeline for ever taking one.

This isn’t a case of documents lost to war, as Omar has long claimed about her missing birth certificate. It’s a case of 𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐨𝐰𝐧 𝐭𝐞𝐚𝐦 𝐫𝐞𝐰𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐝 the moment the math stopped working. Omar and Elmi did not respond to The Post’s requests for comment. If the Justice Department can prove any of it in court, no amount of staff editing will save her citizenship a second time.

text:
One of the biggest differentiators is the sauce.

Texas BBQ sauce (in my opinion, "good" bbq sauce) is heavy on the flavor that makes it bbq sauce and uses tomato paste as the base (same as ketchup).

Colorado BBQ sauce is Honey BBQ. Nothing wrong with that, it just swaps the tomato paste base for a honey base, resulting in a sweeter sauce. To each their own. I like both, as long as they have _flavor._

The blasphemy (as a Texan) comes with HOW the Colorado people make their honey bbq sauce. It's a loud thunderous HONEY with a tiny vestigial bbq dangling on the end. It's honey with a hint of bbq. This is what they like, this is what's popular there, this is what sells there. Every region is entitled to their opinion, no matter how wrong it is, and this is the opinion of Colorado.

The founder of Rudy's Bar-B-Q, a popular southern US BBQ chain, retired to Colorado. He loved it there. He loved the people, he loved the area, but he could not find a good BBQ place. So, before he retired, he opened one last restaurant, and he opened it in the city he now called home. It is, by a huge margin, the most profitable Rudy's Bar-B-Q in the country... because it was the first restaurant in the state to offer southern-style barbecue.

Now, you tell me whether Colorado-style or Southern-style is superior.

text:
Should YOU Use Bitcoin as a Currency:

The answer to whether you should use Bitcoin as a currency depends entirely on where you live and your personal financial circumstances. I’ve seen “Bitcoin accepted here” signs in the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand, Guatemala, and of course, El Salvador. But El Salvador is the only place I’ve seen where Bitcoin is widely accepted. You can use Bitcoin in the US at Burger King and Chipolte, and when buying Miami Dolphin’s tickets. There are places where you can pay your taxes using Bitcoin including Colorado. For most of us, it can be fun to use a Bitcoin app to make a purchase, but you’re going to need traditional banking services in dollars.

Even if you live in El Salvador, the answer still depends on your circumstances. There has been a ton of digital ink spilled over the years regarding the huge fees that banks charge SOME customers. Whether you pay those fees or not depends almost entirely on how much money you have. Many Americans pay to have a checking account, and fees to use an ATM can be enormous. I regularly see ATM fees in the US in the $3 - $5 range, and that can be $8 in foreign countries where you’ll pay an additional huge fee if you make the mistake of accepting the conversion rate offered to you by that foreign bank. I’ve seen fees totaling $15 - $20 on a $100 withdrawal to access “your” money.

Many people pay additional fees to their credit card companies starting with annual charges to have a card. Debit cards deduct funds directly from your checking account and can charge a percentage for that convenience. Both banks and credit card companies charge a wide range of ancillary fees for dealing with overdrafts, sending a wire, or interest for late payments.

Now, let’s take a look at the experience of other people accessing the same banking services and payment networks. For those with greater financial resources, not only is there no fee for a checking account, they will get paid to deposit funds. Accounts of any significant size will receive interest even in a checking account. Annual fees on credit cards are waived as are wire fees for same-day transfers. All ATM fees get refunded including those expensive $8 ones from Guatemala. Credit cards will give customers 1% - 3% cash back on purchases.

Funding a Bitcoin wallet and using it isn’t free. I’ll go through some of those charges in the next section. The point I’m making is whether you’re willing to pay the moderate fees to buy Bitcoin and transfer it to a wallet depends entirely on your situation in the fiat world. If you’re someone who is a source of fees for your bank, then the Bitcoin fees are likely to be small in comparison. For those who are literally paid by their banks and credit card companies to use their services and networks, paying Bitcoin app fees looks like avoidable expense and friction. If you get paid 3% to use your credit card and a Bitcoin app charges you 2%, that’s a 5% difference and a negative incentive. Plus, most Bitcoiners would rather spend continually debased fiat and hodl their Bitcoin as long as possible.

The verdict: Just because Bitcoin can be used as a currency doesn’t mean you’ll want to use it as one.

I want to add one additional important point. If you are willing to spend a few hours learning, you can use Bitcoin to save, invest, pay for things, and to transfer funds almost instantly. You become your own permissionless bank at a time when banks are dangerous. Banks are making a habit of denying services to law-abiding people who express politically incorrect opinions in public. They are denying services to people who engage in the lawful sale of cannabis or firearms. They are making people argue and provide intrusive reasons to access their own cash. I recently received an unpleasant call from Morgan Stanley who wanted to know why I was sending a personal check to a person. The amount was far below the $10,000 reporting requirement. I refused to answer personal questions and my “platinum” service representative warned me that the bank might refuse to send a check which I wanted sent and which I confirmed on the phone call. What happens when “none of your business” becomes insufficient to recover “your” money from a bank?

Some of you might be thinking that you’re not a right-wing politician or commenter and that you don’t buy or sell firearms or cannabis. You might be thinking you have no reason for concern. But the Overton window for “acceptable” opinions and practices shifts wildly, widely, and quickly. Are you sure you’ll always have “acceptable” opinions? Do you want a bank teller or someone in a bank call center to start asking you who you’re sending a check to or to explain to them why you want access to your money? And how sure are you that there won’t be bank bail-ins or nationalizations? Greece did that just last decade.

For those who say bank bail-ins or nationalizations couldn’t happen in the US, it did happen. President Rosevelt made it illegal for US citizens to own gold in 1933 with a penalty of $10,000 and ten years in prison. Once he confiscated everyone’s gold at $20.67 per ounce, he revalued gold to $35.00 per ounce. That means the US government confiscated (stole) 41% of the value of the gold owned by US citizens.

The US government has official debt of $40T plus another $200T of off-balance sheet liabilities like pensions and Social Security. The EU is openly talking about accessing citizen funds on a voluntary basis. No word on what happens when the business recipients chosen by the government fail. Governments in both the US and other countries have previously worked with the banks to access the funds of their citizens. They will again. At the cost of a few hours of educating yourself, you have the ability to use Bitcoin to become your own bank and remove the threat of government control. You don’t have to use Bitcoin as a currency to see there’s a benefit to learning to use it. Alternatively, you could waste hours each year in pointless discussions with Morgan Stanley on whether they want to send the check I instructed them to send. You’re going to spend time dealing with financial issues in the next 12 months. It’s your choice whether that time serves the fiat banking system or allows you to take greater control of your money.

text:
Happy Constitution Day! 🇺🇸

The first week of September, Lansing board member Kirsten Workman and I delivered donated pocket constitutions for all of the 8th graders at Lansing. This donation was pre-approved by administration through an email which included organization information and a link to a copy of the pocket constitution.

USD 469 Lansing recently made the disappointing decision to return free pocket Constitutions intended for these students after concerns were raised about the organization that provided them. I believe that decision was unnecessary and sends the wrong message to our students and community.

The Constitutions were provided by the 917 Society, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit civic-education organization whose mission is to place free pocket Constitutions into the hands of eighth graders. The organization describes itself as nonpartisan and states that it does not endorse or support any political candidate, party, organization or platform. Its program has reached all 50 states, more than 3,000 school districts and more than one million students. The organization reports distributing several million Constitutions over the life of its program.

Yet after these materials were approved for Lansing students, objections were raised that accepting them from the 917 Society could somehow require the district to accept materials from every other outside organization. I have found no Kansas statute establishing such a blanket requirement.

Kansas law expressly recognizes that school districts may receive gifts and donations. Districts can also establish reasonable criteria governing outside educational materials. Lansing’s own policies provide an administrative approval process for distribution of outside materials. We received this and it was later revoked by the Superintendent. Accepting an appropriate educational resource from one nonprofit does not mean a district must automatically accept anything offered by every organization.

Kansas law does establish specific equal-treatment requirements involving material that expressly advocates the election or defeat of political candidates. But that is a very different issue. These students were being given the United States Constitution not candidate campaign literature.

The appropriate question should have been simple: What is actually in the material?

If material is educational, age appropriate, consistent with district policy and contains no candidate or partisan campaign advocacy, it should be evaluated on those merits and not rejected because someone objects to the perceived ideology of the organization providing it.

I have also been told by the 917 Society that Lansing is the first school district to return its Constitutions after accepting them. If so, that is not a distinction our community should celebrate.

September 17 is Constitution Day, and federally funded schools are required to provide educational programming about the Constitution. At a time when we should be strengthening civic literacy and encouraging less screen-time putting a physical copy of our nation’s founding document into the hands of eighth graders should be something we can all support.

The Constitution doesn’t belong to Republicans or Democrats, conservatives or liberals.

It belongs to every American and our students deserve the opportunity to read it for themselves. #ksed #ksleg #happyconstitutionday

text:
Today is Ranna Puja (রান্না পুজো) in West Bengal. 
This pujo is a traditional Bengali religious festival celebrated on Bhadra Sankranti (the last day of the Bengali month of Bhadra, usually the day before Vishwakarma Puja). 

Ranna pujo is known as the day of Arandhan, which means "no cooking". Cooking on Ranna pujo day is strictly forbidden. 

Women of the household stay awake through the night before the Ranna puja day, to cook a wide variety of dishes on unun (a clay oven). All cooking must be finished before the sun rises. 

On Ranna pujo day the pre-cooked food is first offered to Maa Manasa, to protect the family and bring prosperity. 
Then the families eat the cold food prepared the night before, often relishing it with panta bhat (fermented rice). 

Thirteen types of vegetable fries, kochu saag (taro/ colocasia leaves cooked with lentils or fish heads), and mixed vegetable curries often form the food cooked for Ranna pujo. Along with that tangy chalta (elephant apple) chutney and Coconut-based sweets are also prepared.

Michael Desronvil was the one juror standing between Lindsay Clancy and a full acquittal — and for holding his ground, the press decided to destroy his life. “𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘵𝘳𝘶𝘵𝘩 𝘸𝘪𝘭𝘭 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦 𝘰𝘶𝘵,” Desronvil told podcast host Ray Marcel of Fugitive TV in his first interview since being doxxed, still too afraid to show his face on camera months after the mistrial.

The Boston Globe didn’t just name him. It dug up a 2021 domestic assault charge, an active eviction case, and a 2025 restraining order — details about a private citizen who 𝐬𝐢𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐜𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐜 𝐝𝐮𝐭𝐲. Desronvil’s own teenage nephew told police “𝘏𝘦 𝘩𝘪𝘵 𝘩𝘦𝘳” during the 2021 incident, according to the court records the paper resurrected four years later, timed perfectly to the one juror who wouldn’t let Clancy walk.

Desronvil says the charge was dismissed and the story is one-sided, pushed by relatives of his ex-wife who wanted him discredited. He told Marcel that eight jurors had decided Clancy was 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐠𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐭𝐲 before deliberations even began, calling them “𝘢𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘷𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘴” who spent every day trying to flip the holdouts. When the last other holdout “𝘤𝘢𝘷𝘦𝘥,” Desronvil was alone — and he stayed there, telling the room to “𝘪𝘮𝘢𝘨𝘪𝘯𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘳 𝘣𝘰𝘵𝘵𝘭𝘦 𝘢𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘪𝘳 𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘵𝘭𝘦 𝘯𝘦𝘤𝘬𝘴” as he explained why he believed Clancy knew exactly what she was doing.

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis (@GovRonDeSantis) wasn’t willing to let NBC and the Globe win this one. “𝘈 𝘮𝘢𝘯 𝘰𝘣𝘫𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘰 𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘰𝘸𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘢 𝘸𝘰𝘮𝘢𝘯 𝘵𝘰 𝘬!𝘭𝘭 𝘩𝘦𝘳 𝘵𝘩𝘳𝘦𝘦 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘯𝘨 𝘬𝘪𝘥𝘴 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘨𝘦𝘵 𝘢𝘸𝘢𝘺 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩 𝘪𝘵, 𝘴𝘰 𝘕𝘉𝘊 𝘪𝘴 𝘵𝘳𝘺𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘰 𝘴𝘮𝘦𝘢𝘳 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘫𝘶𝘳𝘰𝘳, 𝘸𝘩𝘰𝘴𝘦 𝘪𝘥𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘵𝘺 𝘴𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘣𝘦 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘵𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘦𝘥,” DeSantis posted. “𝘐𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘫𝘶𝘳𝘰𝘳 𝘪𝘴 𝘣𝘦𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘩𝘢𝘳𝘢𝘴𝘴𝘦𝘥, 𝘍𝘭𝘰𝘳𝘪𝘥𝘢 𝘸𝘪𝘭𝘭 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘷𝘪𝘥𝘦 𝘢𝘴𝘺𝘭𝘶𝘮 — 𝘐’𝘮 𝘴𝘶𝘳𝘦 𝘩𝘦’𝘥 𝘣𝘦 𝘸𝘦𝘭𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘥 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘢𝘱𝘱𝘳𝘦𝘤𝘪𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘥.”

Marcel put it bluntly after the interview: “𝘛𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘮𝘢𝘯 𝘤𝘢𝘯𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘭𝘪𝘷𝘦 𝘪𝘯 𝘱𝘦𝘢𝘤𝘦 𝘳𝘪𝘨𝘩𝘵 𝘯𝘰𝘸.” He’s right — the message the press just sent to every future Massachusetts juror is unmistakable: 𝐯𝐨𝐭𝐞 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐜𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞, and reporters will hand your address to the mob.

Canada used to look like a slightly colder, slightly nicer version of the United States. In 1980 the two countries were basically tied on GDP per capita. By 2026 the United States is 56% richer per person. That is not a rounding error, it is a completely different economic model.

Canada chose a different path from the US: slower productivity, heavier regulation, housing that prices out its young people, and population growth as a substitute for output growth. The result looks more like Western Europe than Texas or Florida.

The EU’s sudden offer of “associate membership” is not a random diplomatic flourish but a recognition of what already happened. Ottawa and Brussels share the same instincts: micromanage, regulate, tax, and grow the state faster than the private economy, unlike the US, with its entrepreneurialism, innovation, and free markets driving progress and prosperity.

Canada is not becoming the 51st US state, it is becoming Europe’s North American annex, with the same disappointing living-standards trajectory, regulatory and tax reflex, and comfort with stagnation as long as the left slogans stay warm.

Who will be next to join the club? Cuba or North Korea?

text: Aerial photo looking northeastward over Busch Brewery and Gardens taken in October 1960 courtesy of Florida Memory. The two intersecting roads bordering the park in the lower area of the photo are Temple Terrace Highway/Busch Boulevard/SR 580 (from middle right to lower left) and N 30th St/Bruce B Downs Blvd (from lower off center to middle left). The Busch Brewery and Gardens officially opened admission free to the public for tours on June 1, 1959 a few months after the brewery facility became operational on March 12, 1959. There were 250 attendees at the opening ceremony and around 1,000 attendees at the Brewery and Gardens. The associated gardens featured lagoons and landscaping with around 36,000 flowering plants and 300 trees. Also, animal attractions were opened which included a bird show in an amphitheater; a bird sanctuary featuring flamingos and a separate animal area named "Devil's Island"; and caged enclosures for eagles and cockatoos. Another 118-acres of land was used for housing the brewer’s Budweiser Clydesdales, but because of the sanctuary, the Garden was later dubbed as the "Bird Gardens" or as many others nicknamed it “The bird sanctuary”. Additional attractions included the"Hospitality House" which was a facility that offered guests free samples of beer. And alongside the famous Hospitality House was a dwarf village which featured storybook houses, figures, and small play areas for young children. The village was a classic, whimsical attraction featuring storybook fairy-tale tableaus such as Snow White, Hansel and Gretel, and Little Red Riding Hood. As part of a renovation to the Busch brewery and its public tours, the "Stairway to the Stars" attraction opened on March 22, 1961. This attraction (discontinued in Dec 21, 1995 after brewery closure) featured a 86-foot escalator, with a 5,000-sqft reflecting pool below, that extended to the roof and a 1,000-sqft observation deck atop of the brewery so visitors can get a view of the landscape as well as a scenic view of downtown before continuing the tour inside. Throughout the 60’s and 70’s, the park capitalized on its early success and continued to grow by acquiring more land in the surrounding area and adding an African veldt themed animal attraction, train ride around the park, new shows and entertainment, family fun rides, and roller coasters. Today, Busch Gardens Tampa Bay is a full theme park which consistently exceeds more than 4 million visitors annually.

GEORGIA HAS A SECRET-BALLOT PROBLEM — AND THEY KNEW ABOUT IT SINCE 2022
 
Researchers discovered a serious vulnerability in Dominion voting equipment in 2022 that can allow supposedly anonymized ballots to be put back into the order in which they were cast.
 
Why does that matter? …Because if you can reconstruct the order of the ballots and match it with information showing WHEN individual voters cast their ballots, you could determine HOW specific people voted – by matching the voter to their ballot
 
This isn't theoretical. A 2026 Princeton demonstration used nothing more than public election records and AI tools to reconstruct the order of approximately 1.5 MILLION ballots from Georgia's May primary—98.9% of the in-person ballots analyzed. Researchers reported being able to match individual voters to their specific ballots.
 
A corrected version of the vendor's software was developed and federally certified in March 2023. Democracy Suite 5.17, according to the vendor, is the patch needed to address the vulnerability.
 
Yet Georgia has NOT deployed that fix statewide. Instead, Georgia officials are pursuing data-sanitization and access restrictions designed to prevent the vulnerability from being exploited through publicly released records.
 
Why does this matter beyond "privacy"? …Because ANONYMITY OF THE VOTE IS THE LAW and THE SECRET BALLOT IS WHAT MAKES A VOTE IMPOSSIBLE TO VERIFY.
 
If someone can determine how you voted, the fundamental protection against coercion and vote buying breaks down.
 
Imagine someone offers you money to vote a certain way. Under a truly secret ballot, they have a problem: They can't prove you actually did it.
 
But if a technical vulnerability can potentially connect your identity to the ballot you cast, that changes the equation. A person buying votes could potentially have a way to VERIFY that the voter delivered the vote they were paid to deliver.
 
This creates precisely the kind of verification mechanism that the secret ballot is supposed to prevent.
 
This isn't merely a technical IT problem. It's an election-security problem. It's a voter-coercion problem. And potentially, it's a vote-buying problem. 
 
The vulnerability was disclosed in 2022.
The vendor says a patch will fix it.
And Georgia still hasn't implemented it statewide.
Before November, voters deserve a very clear answer:
 
 WHY?
 
Because once the secrecy of a ballot is compromised, you don't just risk someone's privacy. You risk the protection that makes their vote truly THEIR vote.
 
This is exactly why Unite4Freedom continues to fight the main stream media narrative about “the most secure election in history” and exposes the vulnerabilities. Election Authorities across the country continue to say “nothing to see here” – then we see something like this.
 
Every eligible voter in the US deserves Valid, Transparent, Auditable Elections where the outcome can be Proven.

text:
Witness Maggie Griffin in the Leo Frank Trial

Miss Maggie Griffin was a former National Pencil Company worker on the 4th floor whose testimony helped the State's prosecution in two ways. 

First: She challenged Leo Max Frank’s reputation regarding the dispute over his proper or improper conduct toward women. 

Second: She challenged Rebecca Carson’s denial of entering the factory’s dressing room with the factory superintendent, Leo M. Frank. 

Griffin testified on Wednesday, August 20, 1913, during the State’s rebuttal, its answer to the defense’s evidence. August 20, 1913 was the last and final day of the testimony portion at the trial, which ended at 4:05 pm that day. Closing arguments would begin the next day. 

The court record and newspaper reports show what she said and how Judge Leonard S. Roan limited its use (AJ, 1, Brief of Evidence, 4).

The Brief of Evidence is a written summary of the trial evidence used when Frank asked the Supreme Court of Georgia to review his case in 1913. It is not a word-for-word record of every courtroom exchange. Some entries combine several witnesses’ accounts, including Griffin’s and Myrtice Cato’s (Brief of Evidence, 7).

The Atlanta Journal, Wednesday, August 20, 1913, reported this exchange between Griffin and defense lawyer Luther Rosser:

“How long did you work at the pencil factory?”

“Two months.”

The report placed her work on the fourth floor and described her later work in the cotton mills. She knew the workplace where she claimed the visits occurred, though she had worked there for only a short time (AJ, 1).

The Atlanta Georgian, Thursday, August 21, 1913, recorded another defense question:

“How many girls did you know on the fourth floor?”

“Four.”

The Georgian named her current employer as the Fulton Bag and Cotton Mills and gave her address as 34 Evans Drive. Rosser’s question showed how few fellow workers she knew. This could help jurors judge how much she knew about Frank’s reputation. It did not, by itself, disprove something she claimed to have seen (AG, 2).

The Brief of Evidence places Griffin among a group of 10 former factory workers whose testimony included this statement:

“Leo M. Frank’s character for lasciviousness was bad.”

Lasciviousness means improper sexual behavior. This sentence sums up the group’s testimony about Frank’s character. It is not a separate, word-for-word answer from Griffin. It does not describe her seeing a sexual act. The different lengths of employment listed for the group also cannot all be assigned to Griffin (Brief of Evidence, 3).

Her other claim concerned a specific event. A separate entry names Miss Myrtice Cato and Miss Maggie Griffin as “both sworn for the State.” It reports their claim of seeing Carson enter the fourth-floor women’s dressing room with Frank “two or three times during working hours.” Other women were working on the same floor. The entry does not place those women inside the room or describe what Frank and Carson did there (Brief of Evidence, 4).

The Atlanta Constitution, Thursday, August 21, 1913, gave Griffin’s account in question-and-answer form. Hugh Dorsey, the State’s lawyer, asked:

“Did you ever see them go into the dressing room on the fourth floor together?”

“Yes.”

Asked how often, Griffin answered:

“Three or four times.”

The paper placed the visits in both the morning and afternoon, during working hours. Just before Griffin and Cato gave their accounts, Carson had denied entering the room with Frank. The Constitution quoted her firm answer, “I never did.” Griffin’s claim directly challenged Carson’s denial (AC, 5).

The visit counts differ. The Constitution reported three or four in Griffin’s answer, while the brief gave two or three in its combined account of Griffin and Cato. This difference between the records does not prove Griffin changed her story. The brief does not preserve each woman’s separate answers (AC, 5, Brief of Evidence, 4).

The lawyers fought over whether the jury could hear this evidence. The Atlanta Georgian, Thursday, August 21, 1913, reported the jury left the room while they argued about questions concerning Frank’s conduct toward women. Dorsey wanted to challenge the defense’s favorable picture of Frank. Rosser opposed these questions in a murder trial. Roan allowed the character questions and permitted Carson to be called back about the alleged visits (AG, 2).

Carson’s denial gave Griffin’s testimony a clear purpose. If jurors believed Griffin had seen the visits, they had a reason to doubt Carson. This is called impeaching a witness, or challenging whether the witness should be trusted on their word. It still left open what, if anything, happened inside the room. The unspoken suggestion was there. 

Dorsey tried to go further. The Atlanta Journal, Wednesday, August 20, 1913, reported Griffin’s answer about repeated visits as “Yes, sir! Three or four times.” 

Asked how long the pair stayed, she answered, “Fifteen to thirty minutes.” The defense objected, and the judge ruled out that specific question and answer. The Journal also reported her claim of seeing the pair enter and leave, followed by Rosser’s question confirming the alleged visits occurred during working hours (AJ, 1).

The Atlanta Constitution, Thursday, August 21, 1913, explained the argument. Dorsey said the length of a visit could suggest what the pair had been doing. Rosser objected, and Roan ruled the time spent inside was not needed to challenge Carson’s denial of entering the room (AC, 5).

The Atlanta Georgian, Thursday, August 21, 1913, quoted the judge saying, “The objection [of the defense] is sustained,” meaning he agreed with the objection. It also recorded Rosser’s continued protest: “We are objecting to it all” (AG, 2).

The ruling limited the State’s use of Griffin’s time account, but the visual sighting of the two entering was allowed into the record. 

Seeing the pair enter could challenge Carson’s denial, whatever the length of the visit. An estimate of fifteen or thirty minutes could lead jurors to draw further conclusions about their conduct inside the room. 

Griffin gave her time estimate in court, but the defense persuaded the judge to exclude it from the evidence the jury could consider. It also meant that if Frank was convicted the Georgia Supreme Court would not see the time estimate in the brief of evidence. The judge did not rule her estimate false.

Frank also denied the accusation. The Atlanta Constitution, Thursday, August 21, 1913, reported on page 2 how defense lawyer Reuben Arnold asked permission for Frank to answer the recent testimony. 

Dorsey objected, but the judge let Frank speak to counter. Frank called the dressing-room claim: 

“completely false.” 

He also defended Carson's reputation as a woman:

“She is a lady of unblemished character so far as I know.”

Frank denied the visits themselves. He did not admit entering the room and then offer an innocent reason like fixing a stuck locker door or something like that. The jury faced conflicting accounts from Griffin and Cato on one side, and Carson and Frank on the other (AC, 6). Frank did not testify under oath.

Griffin helped the State challenge Frank’s reputation and Carson’s truthfulness as a defense witness and character reference for Frank. Her account of the dressing-room visits gave the jury a specific reason to question Carson’s support for Frank. Dorsey also tried to use the visits to suggest improper sexual conduct by inference, to show not isolated situations, but a broader pattern of behavior, but this required jurors to draw a conclusion beyond what Griffin said she saw (Brief of Evidence, 3, AC, 5).

Neither entry in the brief, describes Griffin seeing Mary Phagan’s murder, an attack on Mary, or sexual activity inside the dressing room. Her evidence concerned Frank’s character for a pattern of immoral behavior and also individually whether Carson could be trusted or not on oath. Neither Griffin, nor Cato, described seeing what Frank and Carson did inside the room (Brief of Evidence, 3, Brief of Evidence, 4).

Griffin’s role in the July–August 1913 trial rested on a brief but serious claim. She said she had seen Frank and Carson enter the dressing room several times. She also gave an unfavorable account of Frank’s character and faced questions about her short employment and how many coworkers she knew.

Rosser objected to questions about how long the visits lasted because the answers could suggest sexual intimacy between Frank, a married man, and Miss Rebecca Carson a forewoman. 

Both Frank and Carson denied the visits. 

The judge allowed Griffin’s account of seeing them enter the women’s dressing room but excluded her estimate of how long they remained inside. The concern was whether speculation about sexual conduct could unfairly influence the jury in the murder case.

A full account of Griffin's testimony must keep these points together: what she claimed to have seen, how the State used it, and what remained unknown beyond the doorway.

References

AJ: The Atlanta Journal. (1913, August 20, Wednesday). Testimony may close Wednesday. The report also spells Griffin’s surname as Griffith.https://t.co/jyd2YAYQ0q

AG: The Atlanta Georgian. (1913, August 21, Thursday). Mass of perjuries charged by Arnold centers hot attack on Conley. Ridicules prosecution theory.https://t.co/JQBOHD6j1x

Brief of Evidence: Leo M. Frank trial: Brief of evidence. (1913). Group entry on Frank’s character, beginning with Miss Myrtie Cato and including Maggie Griffin. This entry labels the group “for the Defendant.” The newspaper reports place Griffin on the State’s side, as does the separate entry in reference 4.https://t.co/yLfMVR6fd6

Brief of Evidence: Leo M. Frank trial: Brief of evidence. (1913). Combined testimony of Miss Myrtice Cato and Miss Maggie Griffin about Rebecca Carson and the fourth-floor dressing room.https://t.co/E2SpzUWrRa

AC: The Atlanta Constitution. (1913, August 21, Thursday). Girls testify to seeing Frank enter dressing room with woman.https://t.co/Zb9Y0ozoGB

AC: The Atlanta Constitution. (1913, August 21, Thursday). Leo Frank takes stand again despite objection of Dorsey (p. 2).https://t.co/U8pvig4hsn

text:
Candle clocks served as more than just alarm clocks—they also functioned as timers for a range of activities. Their simplicity, portability, and ease of use made them a versatile tool in a world that lacked mechanical precision. Unlike water clocks, which were difficult to transport, candle clocks could be set up anywhere, requiring nothing more than a stable surface.

People also appreciated the candle clock for its dual purpose: it could serve as a light source as well as a timekeeper, helping to conserve fuel and eliminate the need for multiple items. It was cost-effective and sustainable, with candles being a household staple in many communities.

Despite their ingenuity, candle clocks did have limitations. For one, they weren’t entirely precise; variations in candle thickness, wax composition, and wick quality could impact burn time. A slight draft or an uneven surface could affect how the candle burned, making exact timing difficult.

Moreover, candle clocks had a clear dependency on the availability of materials. Wax or tallow candles were more expensive for poorer families, and so this method of timekeeping was more commonly used among those who could afford to make or buy enough candles.

Finally, while they were effective for marking approximate times, candle clocks couldn’t offer the accuracy required for complex schedules or tasks that required split-second timing.

Candle clocks are a testament to human creativity and resourcefulness. In a time when people were deeply attuned to the natural rhythms of light and dark, these early timekeepers filled a crucial role. They represent the innovative ways that people adapted everyday materials to suit their needs, using simple items like candles and nails to help structure their days and nights.

Today, candle clocks serve as reminders of a time before modern technology, when keeping track of time required hands-on experimentation and adaptation. Museums and historians continue to study these devices to better understand the lives of people from the past, and enthusiasts often recreate candle clocks to experience timekeeping as it was practiced centuries ago.

As we rely on our smartphones and digital alarms to wake us up each morning, it’s fascinating to consider how different life was when the simple sound of a nail hitting a metal plate was all it took to start the day. The story of candle clocks illuminates not only an ancient approach to timekeeping but also a deeper connection to natural cycles, creativity, and the passage of time.

@goanewsdotcom #EditX: WILL GOA SANGEET NATAK ACADEMY RECONSIDER ITS STAND ABOUT ‘TIATR’?

Hearty congratulations to the Tiatr Academy of Goa (TAG) for taking up the long-overdue cause of getting @UNESCO recognition for #Tiatr . TAG President Anthony Barbosa and Vice President Marcos Gonsalves are working hard to include Tiatr in UNESCO’s Representative List of #IntangibleCulturalHeritage of #Humanity, as the 56th element in India’s national inventory. India’s top musical theatre body, the @sangeetnatak Sangeet Natak Akademi (SNA), has responded very positively to their efforts.

To support the UNESCO bid, SNA has proposed setting up a Tiatr academic centre in #Delhi for research. It has suggested taking Tiatr to cultural and academic centers across India and abroad, where thousands already watch and enjoy it. SNA has also proposed scholarships for researchers, collaborations with anthropology and theatre institutions, an annual Tiatr Festival in Delhi, and comparative research between Tiatr and other Indian theatre forms. Additionally, teams from the @nsd_india National School of Drama (NSD) are proposed to visit Goa to study Tiatr in its natural environment.

Tiatr is the oldest form of modern #Konkani #theatre. Influenced by Western #opera , which started during the late #Renaissance around 1600 CE, it became a popular #proscenium theatre. The word Tiatr comes from #Teatro , the #Portuguese and #Italian word for theatre. It uniquely blends #drama , #music , #satire , and social commentary. A standard Tiatr splits the main story into seven parts, interspersed with 10 to 15 Kantaram (songs) in front of a closed curtain on various themes, having no connection with the drama theme. Perhaps it could be the most unique form of musical theatre in the #World .

Unfortunately, Goa’s Konkani Sangeet Natak Academy refuses to recognize Tiatr as modern theatre, claiming instead that it grew out of #folk theatre. In reality, Tiatr was created to offer a better alternative to cheap forms the Konkani folk theatres like #Jagor and #Khell were taking among Mumbai's Goan Christian community. The first Tiatr, ‘Italian Bhurgo’ by Lucasinho Ribeiro, was performed in #Mumbai in 1892. Yet, Goa’s Konkani Sangeet Natak Academy considers ‘Raja Chandrahasa’ staged in 1912 in #Mangalore by Konkani Hindus—as the first modern Konkani play.

Now that top national institution like the Sangeet Natak Akademi is backing Tiatr for UNESCO recognition and plans to involve yet another national-level theatre training institute like the National School of Drama, will Goa’s Konkani Sangeet Natak Academy finally wake up and change its stand for the good of #KonkaniTheatre?

They all taught themselves English (except the Irish, obviously who already spoke it) and truly wanted to be *American* and part of the *American dream*. 

Sure, they kept their religion (Catholic),  recipes, and some of their culture socially and such - but they graciously surrendered the ways of their country from the foreground to embrace all the opportunity and *identity* that being an *American* offered them. And they wanted to!

That is the difference. 

They didn't come here to attempt to erase or degrade American culture, they came to elevate and advance it.

text:
A later echo: the McVeigh affair

Four years after the Blarney conference, Portlaoise Prison again became the setting for an extraordinary confrontation involving disputed orders, live ammunition and questions that remain unresolved.

Patrick McVeigh was released from the prison on 18 May 1988 and immediately faced arrest under British extradition warrants relating to allegations of conspiracy to cause an explosion and possession of explosive substances. The official parliamentary record confirms that he was arrested upon his release.

When McVeigh saw the @gardainfo presence, he attempted to escape by running between the prison’s inner and outer walls. RTÉ’s archive records that soldiers on duty fired five shots before he was arrested.

McVeigh Arrested And Released BROADCAST 06 October, 1988:
https://t.co/eAo336eM1B

Later accounts maintained that the gunfire also placed pursuing prison personnel in immediate danger. ACO Paddy Dunne, a senior officer, was subsequently suspended after declining to join the pursuit.

These accounts should not be treated as settled findings. Their significance lies in the pattern they describe: an extraordinary use of force, disputed instructions, unresolved questions of responsibility and, ultimately, an officer left to carry the consequences.

McVeigh was later released by an Irish court after the district justice found that his identity had not been proved to the required legal standard. The decision provoked an eruption at Westminster.

Tony Marlow, the @Conservatives MP for Northampton North, offered three possibilities, none of them restrained:

“I put it no higher than this—that members of the Irish judiciary are bent by their own republicanism, bullied by the IRA, or just plain barmy?”

— Tony Marlow MP, @HouseofCommons, 14 June 1988

David Wilshire, the Conservative MP for Spelthorne, went further:

“The Irish courts have yet again decided not to co-operate with us and prefer to behave like an unprincipled banana republic’s courts.”

— David Wilshire MP, #HouseofCommons, 14 June 1988

Wilshire then demanded consequences extending far beyond the McVeigh case:

“I agree with the adjectives used by my honourable Friend, the Member for Northampton North, Mr Marlow, and say that the time has come when we should treat the Irish Republic like any other foreign country and withdraw the special treatment of its citizens within the United Kingdom.”

— David Wilshire MP, @HouseofCommons, 14 June 1988

The Attorney-General, Sir Patrick Mayhew, declined to endorse either attack. He reminded the House that the Irish judiciary was independent and cautioned that general accusations against the Irish courts were neither helpful nor responsible.

Then came the intervention that gave the affair its most enduring question.

David Alton, the Liberal MP for Liverpool, Mossley Hill, asked:

“Does the Attorney-General really believe that what happened yesterday represents yet another triumph for the old firm of ‘Fumble and Bumble’, or does he think that it was a calculated piece of deliberate sabotage?”

— David Alton MP, @HouseofCommons, 14 June 1988

Alton was not speaking for the British Government; he was questioning it. Yet his words placed two stark possibilities before @UKParliament: spectacular incompetence or deliberate interference.

The Attorney-General rejected the suggestion that these were the only available explanations. But the question—whether the affair had been bungled or engineered—did not disappear merely because the Government declined to answer it.

The complete parliamentary exchange can be read in Hansard, 14 June 1988, as follows:
https://t.co/t3KeNftRJI

“It was an arranged escape”

More than two decades later, the same question reportedly received a rather more direct answer.

According to an account supplied for this article, Sean O’Brien and PJ McEvoy—former president and general secretary of the Prison Officers’ Association—met Noel Treacy TD in 2011. 

During that meeting, Treacy, who had held ministerial responsibilities within the justice system, is said to have described the events at Portlaoise in five unambiguous words:

“It was an arranged escape.”

— Statement attributed to Noel Treacy TD during a 2011 meeting with Sean O’Brien and PJ McEvoy

The statement requires corroboration from those present or from any contemporaneous record of the meeting. But if accurately recalled, it transforms the nature of the affair.

An escape caused by confusion, bad planning or official incompetence is one thing. An escape arranged, permitted or manipulated for an undisclosed purpose is something else entirely.

It also gives Alton’s question a different resonance. What sounded in 1988 like parliamentary exasperation begins, in the light of the later account, to sound uncomfortably prescient.

The intelligence at the gate

Material supplied for this article states that British intelligence personnel, including Security Service (“MI5”) officers, were present at the prison gate on 18 May 1988.

It is further claimed that they witnessed Prison Officer Sean O’Brien being directly targeted with live rounds and reported the incident as an attempted murder.

That is an allegation of the utmost seriousness. It should be tested against the surviving intelligence, military and governmental records. If such a report was made, it should identify who was present, what they witnessed, to whom they reported it and what action—if any—followed.

It raises several unavoidable questions

Were #MI5 personnel present at Portlaoise Prison that day? Did they witness or report the alleged targeting of Sean O’Brien? Was that report circulated to ministers, prosecutors or parliamentarians? And did any British official know more about the events of 18 May 1988 than was disclosed publicly?

Finally, there is the question left hanging by David Alton’s intervention.

When he asked #UKParliament whether the affair amounted to “a calculated piece of deliberate sabotage,” was he speaking only from political instinct and the facts already in the public domain—or had information from British intelligence reporting reached #Westminster?

The published parliamentary record does not provide an answer, and no evidence presently cited establishes that Alton had seen or been briefed upon an #MI5 report.

But the closeness between his question in 1988 and the words later attributed to Noel Treacy TD—“It was an arranged escape”—is sufficiently striking to justify further examination.

The proper response is not speculation. 

It is disclosure.

If intelligence officers witnessed the events at the gate, their reports may hold the answer to whether the McVeigh affair was a failure of planning, a reckless operation, or something deliberately arranged—and to why, amid five live rounds, a prison officer apparently became the man placed most directly in danger.

It would seem, then, that this matter is far from over. 

I venture that, in due course, a most intrusive spotlight will be shone upon it, and @MichealMartinTD and his Minister for @DeptJusticeIRL @OCallaghanJim may find themselves required to answer some distinctly uncomfortable questions—questions from which it will be exceedingly difficult to extricate themselves.

text:
I asked Grok to summarize your voting record. You can say you don't believe the crazy things you've said, but your voting record is a good reflection of what you actually stand for:

James Talarico (D) has served in the Texas House since 2018 (HD-52, then HD-50). He votes with the Democratic caucus on nearly all contested bills. Conservative scorecards rate him very low (Freedom Index lifetime ~9%). Below is a selection of notable recorded votes, not a complete journal of every roll call.

**Gender / minors / schools**
- Voted **against** SB 14 (2023), which banned specified gender-transition surgeries, puberty blockers, and cross-sex hormones for patients under 18.
- Offered a failed amendment to SB 14 creating a Hippocratic-oath exception.
- Voted **against** 2021 bills restricting transgender students from competing on teams matching their sex assigned at birth (HB 25 / similar measures).
- Voted **against** later bills on female-only spaces, removal of gender ideology/DEI from schools, and related school-library/parental-oversight measures (e.g., SB 8, SB 12, SB 13 in recent sessions).

**Abortion**
- Voted **against** bills targeting abortion-pill distribution and taxpayer-funded abortion assistance (e.g., HB 7 and SB 33 in 2025).
- Publicly supports legal abortion access.

**Guns**
- Voted **against** constitutional/permitless carry (HB 1927).
- Voted **against** declaring Texas a Second Amendment sanctuary and blocking certain federal gun rules (HB 2622).
- Voted **against** exemption of Texas-made suppressors from certain federal rules (HB 957).
- Voted **against** other expansions: carry after natural disasters, carry on government property, firearm-preemption updates, carry in polling places, and recognition of out-of-state licenses.

**Border / immigration**
- Voted **against** multiple border-security funding and enforcement bills, including large appropriations (HB 9), a Border Protection Unit and infrastructure (HB 7), making unauthorized entry a state crime (SB 4), 287(g)/ICE-cooperation requirements (SB 8), and related measures (SB 1403, SB 3, HB 4, etc.).
- Voted **against** HB 888 (charging people who misrepresent a child as a family member).

**Crime, bail, and policing**
- Voted **against** tightening bail for violent/sexual offenses and restricting cashless personal bonds (HB 20, SB 6).
- Voted **against** the constitutional amendment restricting bail for certain child-sex and trafficking offenses (HJR 4).
- Voted **against** financial penalties for large cities that cut police budgets year-over-year (HB 1900).
- Voted **against** higher penalties for human smuggling and stash houses (SB 4) and against removing prosecutors who adopt non-prosecution policies for certain offenses (HB 17).
- Voted **for** HB 28 (enhanced penalties for certain aggravated assault) — a unanimous vote.

**Education and social issues**
- Opposed school-voucher legislation (SB 2) and the Ten Commandments classroom-display mandate (SB 10).
- Voted **for** large public-school funding packages (including teacher pay and related programs).
- Authored or co-sponsored bills that became law on insulin copay caps, diploma pathways for minors in the justice system, pre-K class-size limits, and a ban on reality-TV contracts with law enforcement (Javier Ambler’s Law).

**Other notable votes**
- Voted **against** SB 17 (restrictions on certain foreign, including Chinese-linked, land purchases); supported some related critical-infrastructure contract limits.
- Voted **against** the 2025 bipartisan moratorium on sale of cell-cultured (“lab-grown”) meat.
- Joined Democratic quorum breaks in 2021 (voting legislation) and 2025 (mid-decade redistricting).

Talarico has also missed a large number of votes over the years (reporting has cited 800+ absences in some periods). Official journals and session scorecards (Texas House Journal, Freedom Index, Sierra Club, Turning Point Action, etc.) are the primary sources for individual roll calls.

text:
Reformation Heritage KJV Study Bible introduction to Ezekiel:

Ezekiel’s Vision of a New Temple and Land

Chapters 40-48 are considered to be among the most difficult chapters to interpret in Ezekiel’s prophecy, indeed in the whole Bible. Various interpretations have been offered of this final vision, and the details have engendered debate among Bible scholars. There are generally four views held concerning this vision: 

1. The historical-literal view: 
the vision relates to the times immediately prior to the captivity and focuses on Solomon’s temple.

2. The ideal or conditional view: the vision outlines what should have been after the return from captivity, but because of the disobedience of the people it was never realized. 

3. The Jewish view: the description given in this vision was followed by the returning captives as far as circumstances allowed them, and Herod copied the same pattern when he renovated and enlarged the temple.

4. The spiritual view: the vision symbolically represents God’s good plan for His people, especially after Christ’s incarnation, when His glory shall dwell within His people as His living temple by the life-giving work of the Holy Spirit (37:14,27-28; Eph. 2:18-22).

The spiritual view has been the most common in church history and was reflected in the interpretations of the Reformers. Several considerations from the text favor this interpretation. First, chs. 40-48 are a vision (40:2), and this form of revelation commonly uses symbolism (such as the visions of Zechariah and Daniel). Second, elements of the vision clearly run contrary to normal experience, such as the river that comes out of the temple and grows deeper as it flows, changing quickly from a trickle to an impassable flood several feet deep over the course of less than a mile and a half. Third, the idea of this river appears again in the apostle John’s vision of the New Jerusalem in Revelation, which is also a book full of symbolism (Rev. 22:1-2). 

Fourth, the physical dimensions of the temple and division of the land in this vision were never fulfilled in Israel’s history, nor did the Lord ever rebuke His people after the exile for failing to implement them. Fifth, if the instructions of this vision pertain to some future temple, then this mandates animal sacrifices for the sins of the people (Ezek. 40:38-39, etc.). However, Christ has offered Himself once for all as the sufficient sacrifice for sinners, and all other sacrifices for sin have ceased (Heb. 10:10-18). The reply that the sacrifices in Ezekiel’s vision will function as mere remembrances of Christ’s work fails to take the text literally, for it says that these sacrifices will “make reconciliation” or atonement for them (Ezek. 45:15,17). Therefore, it is best to understand the vision of chs. 40-48 as a symbolic representation of Israel’s hope. 

However, the symbolism in the closing vision of the temple and land does not encourage the reader to engage in wild allegory, assigning a spiritual meaning to every dimension of the architecture. Just like the opening vision of God’s glory riding the chariot of the cherubim (1:1-28), the message is not in every detail but in the overall impressions the vision makes.

Ezekiel’s prophecy closes with a vision of overwhelming hope, that though the descendants of Abraham forfeited God’s presence, the means of atoning for sin, and their inheritance by their idolatry, God would certainly restore all of these to believers for the sake of His holy name. Christians can rejoice that this restoration is found in Jesus Christ, for by His Spirit God’s presence is with His people forever. Christ our Priest has offered the perfect sacrifice for their sins, and they will enjoy a glorious inheritance with Christ the King in a new world without end.

text:
Palantir Technologies CEO Alex Karp has repeatedly stated that the global artificial intelligence arms race is a strictly binary conflict between the United States and China, declaring that the competition will have only one winner. [1, 2] 
Speaking at platforms like the Hudson Institute and on CNBC, Karp has framed the stakes of this tech rivalry as an absolute geopolitical battleground. He argues that second place is effectively "extinction" for a nation's global sovereignty, meaning that the loser will be forced to live inside an operating system designed and controlled by the winner. [1, 3] 
Karp’s core arguments behind this "winner-take-all" stance include:
1. Hardcoded Values in Global Norms
Technology is not neutral. Karp emphasizes that the nation leading the AI race will dictate global rules, data privacy norms, and digital rights. If the US wins, Western democratic values remain embedded in global infrastructure. If China wins, its model of strict data control, social management, and expanded state surveillance will become the global standard. In fact, Karp sparked controversy by asserting that even an expanded U.S. surveillance state would be a lesser threat than a world dominated by Chinese AI. [4, 5, 6, 7] 
2. The Danger of an AI "Pause"
While other tech executives have called for temporary freezes or slowdowns on advanced AI training models to evaluate safety risks, Karp strongly opposes the idea. He argues that a unilateral pause by American companies is impossible because geopolitical adversaries like China will not stop. Because AI offers massive structural and military advantages, any delay by the West risks permanently ceding leadership. [8, 9] 
3. Military and National Security Dominance
Karp has integrated Palantir deeply into Western defense infrastructure, consolidating massive defense contracts (such as major enterprise software deals with the U.S. Army and Navy). He argues that AI dominance directly translates to military superiority, necessitating an "all-country effort" to keep American algorithms and large language models ahead of Beijing's massive capital expenditures. [1, 10] 
4. European and Western Reliance
Karp believes that European allies lack the tech-focused corporate agility required to win this race. He has stated that Western allies "are going to have to learn from us" and adopt the aggressive, entrepreneurial pivot-mindset of U.S. corporate leadership to avoid falling behind entirely. [2, 3, 10, 11]

States were sovereign and the role of the Federal Government was a coordinating body representing the ability to form a national army, diplomacy, and trade disputes. Rousing support in the North was difficult requiring payment and  conscription of recent immigrants from Germany and Ireland ultimately made up 25% of the Union army. text:
HOLY SHIT.

I think I just found a way to run your entire marketing operation through Grok Bot.

I’ve spent the last few years building operating systems and automating operations for 8-figure businesses.

And I’ve been pretty vocal about how fucking stupid it is to build an army of AI agents before fixing the business underneath.

Your client context is in Notion.

Production is managed in ClickUp.

Feedback is buried in Slack.

Performance is inside Meta.

Now you’ve created five Grok Bots and somehow expect them to understand what the fuck is happening?

They need one reliable source of truth.

And for the last six months, I’ve been building Ordyn around that exact idea.

It gives marketing teams one place for their brand context, team, research, briefs, creative assets, production workflows, approvals, Meta performance (and a lot more).

And we recently launched an MCP that lets Grok Bot, Claude Code, Codex and other agents interact directly with everything inside it.

And I just realized you could use that to build an entire AI marketing team.

Not agents with vague titles like “Chief Marketing Officer.”

So here’s 5 Grok Bots I recommend building TODAY:

1️⃣ Research Bot

Give it a client, product or niche.

It searches TikTok, Reddit, Meta Ads Library, customer comments and your existing research.

Then it saves the strongest hooks, visual patterns, objections and angles with the original sources attached.

2️⃣ Brief Bot

It takes that research and combines it with the client’s offer, audience, voice and previous winners.

Then it writes the next set of production briefs and submits them to the strategist for approval.

3️⃣ Creative Reviewer Bot

Every new script, image or video gets checked against the original brief and the client’s rules.

For video, it can literally watch the asset and leave feedback on the exact timestamp:

00:04: “Clinically proven” isn’t an approved claim.
00:11: The product needs to appear before the demonstration.
00:19: This CTA belongs to the previous offer.

text:
Game of Thrones and Harry Potter have something terrifying in common: the darkest horrors aren’t always the monsters. It’s what they can do to you.

In Game of Thrones, one of the most disturbing supernatural elements is the White Walkers raising the dead.

Seeing an entire army of corpses suddenly stand back up is horrifying enough. But the real nightmare is what it means: death is no longer the end.

Every fallen soldier can become another weapon. Every battlefield can become a new army. The dead don’t stay dead—they return to fight against the living.

In Harry Potter, the darkness can be just as terrifying.

The Dementors don’t simply attack the body. Their presence forces people to relive their worst memories, while their ultimate weapon, the Dementor’s Kiss, can leave a person alive but without a soul.

And then there are Voldemort’s Horcruxes: the idea that someone can deliberately murder another person to fracture their own soul in pursuit of immortality.

That’s what makes both worlds so disturbing.

Game of Thrones turns death itself into a weapon.
Harry Potter turns the soul itself into something that can be violated.

Different worlds. Different kinds of horror.

But both make one thing terrifyingly clear:

The human body can be destroyed.
The soul can be corrupted.
And in these worlds, sometimes even death offers no escape.
