text:
Technical rebuttal, which I am making by running your comments through a Grok evaluation in order to be unbiased toward your points:

"I’ll check the Lusitania cargo, prize-law rules on munitions at sea, and the exact terms of the Zimmermann Telegram so the three claims can be weighed against the record.The three claims mix things that are true, things that are half-true, and a conclusion the 1917 United States did not accept.1. “We were selling munitions to England, so the ships were legitimate targets.”True that the United States sold a great deal of war material to Britain and France. False that this made every ship carrying it a free-fire target under the rules Washington recognized.Under traditional prize law a belligerent could stop a merchantman, search it, and seize contraband. An enemy merchant ship (British flag) was also subject to capture. Sinking it without warning, without visit and search, and without giving passengers a chance to leave was the dispute. That is what unrestricted U-boat war did. The United States treated that practice—not the existence of Allied munitions contracts—as the casus belli in 1917.Also: most of the ships Americans cared about were not U.S. Navy vessels. Lusitania was a British liner. Neutral American ships carrying contraband could be stopped; they were not, in U.S. legal doctrine, to be torpedoed on sight because Britain had bought Du Pont powder.2. “Munitions [shouldn’t] be placed on passenger liners but the British knew this would likely draw us into the war.”Two separate points.Cargo: Lusitania was carrying war material. The New York collector’s report and the supplementary manifest listed about 4,200 cases of Remington .303 cartridges (on the order of four million rounds) and 1,250 cases of shrapnel shells from Bethlehem, plus fuses. U.S. rules at the time allowed small-arms ammunition on passenger ships. Whether the shells were “live” in a way that explains the second explosion is still argued; that they were military cargo is not. Later British internal papers and dives on the wreck confirm ammunition in the holds. London’s long public denial was false. 

https://t.co/gx37Ri4zQG

Bait: That Britain put those goods on a liner in order to get America into the war is a much weaker claim. The sinking was May 1915. The United States did not declare war until April 1917. Wilson sent sharp notes; Germany pulled back from unrestricted attacks for a time (Sussex pledge). If the Admiralty’s aim in 1915 was an immediate U.S. entry, it failed for almost two years. Using passenger routes for small-arms cargo was sloppy and useful to German propaganda. Calling it a successful trap overstates both British control of U.S. politics and the timeline.3. “The deal was offered to Mexico but contingent on us entering the war.”This one is right. The Zimmermann Telegram of January 1917 is explicit:Germany would resume unrestricted submarine war and still try to keep the United States neutral. “In the event of this not succeeding” it proposed an alliance with Mexico: war together, peace together, money, and German “understanding” that Mexico might recover Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. Eckhardt was to tell Carranza “as soon as the outbreak of war with the United States of America is certain.” Japan was to be invited in as well. 

https://t.co/775FxeTzh6

So the Mexican offer was a contingent wartime alliance, not an invitation to start a war while the United States was still neutral. Mexico declined. Publication of the telegram, on top of the U-boat campaign, helped Wilson take the country into the https://t.co/kODKHE77PT this sits with April 1917Wilson’s war message put the weight on unrestricted submarine warfare against commerce, including neutrals, and on the Zimmermann intrigue. Allied munitions purchases were already two years old and were not the legal hook he used. A fair scorecard:Claim
Verdict
U.S. sold munitions to Britain:
True

That made passenger ships shoot-on-sight targets under U.S.-accepted law:
Not how Washington defined it

Lusitania carried munitions:
True

Britain loaded them as a plan to force U.S. entry in 1915:
Speculative; the lag to 1917 cuts against it

Zimmermann deal was contingent on U.S. entry:
True"

text:
List by Ken Blackwell
This is a long post. Read it anyway, and then send it to the friend who keeps telling you nothing has changed in Washington.
I have been in and around politics for a long time, and I have never seen a gap this wide between what a President has done and what his own voters can recite. Ask ten Republicans to name three things President Trump has accomplished since January 2025. Most of them will stall after one. That is not because the record is thin. The record is the deepest of any first two years in modern memory. The problem is that the press buries the wins, and too many conservatives have stopped telling the story themselves.
So here is the story. These are laws signed, court cases won, policies in force, deals closed, and numbers on the board. None of them are promises. Pick five, learn them cold, and use them the next time someone tells you this President has done nothing.
Start with the border, because that is where the change is easiest to see.
1. The border is under control for the first time in a generation. Illegal crossings fell to their lowest point in roughly 50 years within months of the inauguration. Catch-and-release ended. Wall construction restarted and grew. Remain in Mexico came back. Releases of illegal aliens into the interior fell by more than 99 percent.
2. Migration reversed. In 2025, more people left the country than came in, something America had not recorded in at least half a century. Close to three million illegal aliens are gone, with more than 675,000 removed by force and the rest leaving on their own. The administration offered plane tickets and a cash bonus to anyone who chose to self-deport, which saved taxpayers a fortune compared to the cost of a forced removal.
3. The Laken Riley Act is law. Federal authorities must now detain illegal aliens arrested for theft, burglary, shoplifting, assault on a police officer, or any crime that kills or seriously injures someone. States can sue federal officials who refuse to enforce it. This law exists because a young woman was murdered by a man who should have been in custody. It will keep other families from living her parents' nightmare.
4. Violent crime fell faster in 2025 than in any year on record. FBI data shows a 9.7 percent drop, with murder down 18.1 percent and robbery down 18.5 percent. The national violent crime rate is now the lowest since 1900. Putting the National Guard on the streets of the most dangerous cities in the country produced fewer victims and safer neighborhoods for the poorest Americans.
Now look at the economy, because this is where the next decade is being built.
5. The 2017 tax cuts are permanent and bigger. The One Big Beautiful Bill locked in the doubled standard deduction, the larger Child Tax Credit, and full expensing for factories and equipment. It added no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, relief on Social Security benefits, and a larger deduction for seniors. Every Democrat in Congress voted no. Had they won, the largest tax increase in American history would have hit in January.
6. Regulations are coming off the books at a rate of 129 to 1. In fiscal 2025, federal agencies finalized 646 deregulatory actions against five new rules, and most of those five were written to undo old ones. The White House regulatory office says the savings already exceed the whole of the first Trump term. The largest single item was the repeal of the 2009 Endangerment Finding, the legal foundation for the electric vehicle mandate. EPA calls it the biggest deregulatory action in American history and estimates it will save Americans more than $1.3 trillion. The federal EV mandate is dead, and Americans can once again buy the cars and trucks they actually want.
7. Companies have committed $18 trillion in new American investment. That figure is nearly two thirds of the entire U.S. economy. It is paying for chip plants, data centers, steel mills, shipyards, energy projects, and supply chains staffed by American workers. Apple, Meta, NVIDIA, Micron, Hyundai, U.S. Steel, Ford, and Taiwan Semiconductor are all on the list, alongside sovereign wealth funds from around the world. No President has attracted anything close to it.
8. Reshoring is happening in real factories, with real payrolls. Ford is moving Lincoln production out of China. Toyota is bringing Tacoma production from Mexico to Texas. General Motors, Honda, Mercedes-Benz, and Stellantis are all expanding American plants. The machinery being installed today is the foundation of the boom you will read about next year.
9. Trade deals are balanced again. The President used tariffs as leverage to reopen agreements that had tilted against American workers for 80 years. The result is new or improved deals with trading partners representing more than half of the world's economy. Those deals open foreign markets, tear down hidden barriers, protect strategic industries, and make it more profitable to build here than to ship jobs abroad.
10. American energy leads the world. A country that once sent $700 billion a year overseas for oil now produces more than Saudi Arabia and Russia combined. Exports of oil, natural gas, and LNG are setting records, and the United States became the first nation ever to ship more than 100 million metric tons of LNG in a single year. The administration opened federal land, sped up permits, and approved pipelines and export terminals to make it possible.
11. Five new nuclear reactors reached criticality in one year. For more than four decades, not one new privately developed advanced reactor had gone live in America. The President set a target of three by July 4, 2026. The Energy Department delivered four by that date and a fifth a month later. That is a real nuclear revival after 40 years of nothing.
12. Prescription drug prices are coming down. The President signed the most favored nation order requiring drug makers to charge Americans no more than they charge patients in other wealthy countries. Major manufacturers signed agreements to cut prices, and the administration launched a direct-purchase channel so patients can buy at those lower prices without a middleman.
The next group is about who actually runs the government. This is the part the press understands least and fears most.
13. The Supreme Court restored the President's power over the executive branch. In Trump v. Slaughter, decided this June, the Court overruled a 1935 precedent that had shielded so-called independent agencies from the elected President for 90 years. Ask yourself why elections so often change nothing. The answer is one President and about 5,000 appointees against roughly 2.8 million career employees who could not be fired. The administration then made the ruling real by putting policy-making bureaucrats on notice that they can be removed for misconduct, incompetence, or defying lawful orders.
14. Nationwide injunctions are no longer a veto for a single judge. In Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court sharply limited the power of one district judge to block a national policy for the whole country. That tactic had been used against this President on a near-daily basis since 2017. The Court took the weapon away.
15. USAID is closed. The agency had grown into a taxpayer-funded engine for abortion promotion, gender ideology, censorship programs, and political meddling abroad, with a budget larger than the CIA and State Department combined and almost no oversight. The President shut it down and moved real humanitarian work under the State Department. In the months that followed, seven socialist governments in Latin America lost elections.
16. The federal workforce is the smallest it has been since 1966. Reductions in force, agency closures, and canceled spending cut the headcount from its Biden-era peak to a 60-year low. When Biden left office, more than nine in ten federal employees were working from home. The administration ended that. If you want a federal paycheck, you show up.
17. DEI is out of the federal government. The President eliminated DEI offices across the executive branch and barred race and sex preferences in hiring and contracting. Merit and equal treatment under the law are the standard again.
18. Public broadcasting no longer gets a federal check. Congress passed the President's rescissions package, which clawed back more than $9 billion in previously approved spending, including every dollar earmarked for NPR and PBS. Taxpayers are no longer required to fund a news operation that treats half the country with contempt.
19. The Department of Education is being wound down. The President signed the order to close it and return authority over schools to the states. Its workforce has been cut roughly in half, and its programs are being moved to other agencies where they can be run without a federal bureaucracy sitting on top of every local school board.
Then there is the fight for faith, family, and common sense.
20. Life is protected at every level the executive branch can reach. In his first term, the President appointed the justices who overturned Roe v. Wade. Since returning, he has enforced the Hyde Amendment, restored and expanded the Mexico City Policy, ended federal fetal tissue research, strengthened conscience protections, blocked Medicaid dollars from flowing to large abortion providers, and pardoned 23 pro-life Americans prosecuted by the Biden Justice Department. He has done everything within the executive branch's power to cut off Planned Parenthood. Congress should finish the job.
21. Men are out of women's sports. The federal government once again recognizes two sexes, male and female. The President ended federal support for the chemical and surgical transition of minors, cut off taxpayer funding for it, and pressured more than three dozen hospital systems to end or suspend those programs. Title IX is being enforced as written. Girls have their own teams, their own trophies, and their own locker rooms again, and the NCAA rewrote its rules to comply.
22. America has its first nationwide school choice program. The One Big Beautiful Bill created the Education Freedom Tax Credit, which funds scholarships for tuition, books, and other costs for families who want out of a failing school. On top of that, the new Trump Accounts give every eligible newborn a $1,000 seed in a tax-advantaged account. Parents gain leverage. Bureaucracies lose it.
23. Anti-Christian bias is being investigated instead of ignored. The President created the White House Faith Office, the Religious Liberty Commission, and a task force dedicated to rooting out discrimination against Christians inside the federal government. Conscience protections are back. No American forfeits the First Amendment by taking a job or entering public life.
24. English is the official language of the United States. For the first time in the nation's history, a President signed an order making it official. A shared language is part of what makes a nation, and the federal government now says so.
Finally, peace through strength. This is the part that keeps our adversaries up at night.
25. NATO allies are finally paying their share. For decades, wealthy European governments underfunded their militaries and let American taxpayers cover the difference. The President forced the alliance to scrap its old two percent of GDP target and adopt five percent by 2035. Allied defense spending is climbing, orders for American-made equipment are surging, and Europe is becoming a partner rather than a dependent.
26. Iran's nuclear program was hit where it lived. In June 2025, American bombers struck Iran's fortified enrichment sites at Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan in a single night, with no American casualties. The regime that chanted death to America for 40 years learned what an American President with resolve looks like.
27. China's foothold in our hemisphere collapsed. Beijing had spent years building positions at both ends of the Panama Canal, in Cuba, and in Venezuela. The President forced Panama out of the Belt and Road Initiative, expanded American security access around the Canal, and ordered the operation that captured Nicolás Maduro, who is now in a federal jail in New York awaiting trial on narco-terrorism charges. The Monroe Doctrine is back in force.
28. Eight peace agreements in eight months. The President brokered settlements in eight conflicts across four continents, including wars that had dragged on for decades and the deal that brought the Israeli hostages home from Gaza. No President has a record like it.
29. Golden Dome is funded and under construction. Ronald Reagan dreamed of a shield that would make nuclear missiles obsolete. This President is building it, a layered defense with space-based sensors and interceptors, conventional systems, microwave weapons to defeat drone swarms, and directed-energy systems that can replace an $11 million interceptor with a few dollars of electricity. Congress has approved the first $25 billion, with more coming in this fall's defense bill.
30. The military is recruiting again. After years of missed targets under Biden, every active-duty branch met or beat its 2025 recruiting goal. The President and Secretary Hegseth refocused the Department of War on winning wars and poured resources into shipbuilding, munitions, drones, and missile defense. Young Americans are signing up because they believe the man at the top has their back.
That is 30, and I could keep going. Every item on this list is a change in law, power, money, or the structure of the government itself. None of it came from a press release.
Midterm elections are decided by turnout. We do not need to persuade a single Democrat to admire this President. We need Republicans and friendly independents to understand what has been won, what is at stake, and to show up in November.

"I hear from people every week who say the Republicans are doing a poor job telling this story. Understand something. You are the Republicans. The other side does not wait for its elected officials to make its case. Its supporters carry the message every day, in every conversation, whether or not the facts hold up. Our side has more information at its fingertips than any group of people in history, and half of us cannot name three of these wins.
Sulking over what has not happened yet is a losing habit, and losers do not get to complain about the results. This President is delivering. Learn five of these, share this list with someone who needs it, and vote like the most consequential presidency of our lifetime depends on you... because it does!"
(Karla Jean Horn)

No doubt Watson displayed arrogance when confronted with the lawsuits initially. His original attorneys did him no favors. Retaining Rusty Hardin was the right move for him. At that point due to Watson’s arrogance he had created a PR nightmare for the NFL. Watson appealed the NFL determination that he had violated the PCP. An arbitrator that the NFL and NFLPA had agreed to serve per the CBA heard the appeal. As Mike Florio pointed out the arbitrator was likely to “split the baby” IE satisfy both sides since either side could fire her on their own volition . That’s exactly what she did. Found Watson to have violated the PCP but limited the suspension to 6 games since the NFLPA was not given proper notice of changes to the PCP.

The NFL wasn’t having a 6 game suspension and the CBA allowed the Commissioner to review the arbitrator’s finding and overrule the length of the suspension. The narrative was that the NFL wanted an indefinite suspension. A legal battle in the form of a lawsuit was brewing between the NFL and NFLPA. The NFL and NFLPA arrived at a SETTLEMENT in lieu of a drawn out and expensive legal process Daryl. 

The idea that settling a lawsuit equates to zero accountability is absurd and quite frankly disingenuous. Both sides recognize the other side’s case has merit and thus arrive at a compromise. Clearly paying a party in a settlement is taking accountability.  NDAs and privacy concerns being what they are almost certainly limits what Watson can say about his settlements.  

I understand the frustration that Browns fans have with this situation and feeling that the disaster this trade has been can’t be over soon enough. I am almost certain Watson feels likewise. Come next March it will be.

From Watson’s perspective he was 16-22, had 205 yards passing, 1 TD, 1 INT a 97+ rating, 39 yards rushing being the Browns leading runner and the media lays that loss on him when the Browns pass defense was terrible such that the Jaguars could have scored 50+. Browns RBs had 34 yards in 13 carries. From Watson’s point of view the media was being completely unfair. Watson isn’t wrong.

text:
COUNTDOWN60 — Day 5
The Inflation Illusion — Why Washington's Numbers Say "Better" While Your Bank Account Says "Worse"
Daily Countdown to November 3rd — 47 days remaining
(2/2)
EFFECT: CREDIT, AUTO & SENTIMENT
Part 1 was the locked house. This is the unlocked debt: the car, the card, and the savings rate that just fell to 3.0%.
A $44,000 car now takes seven years to "afford." The average new-car payment is $777. Negative equity on the trade-in just set a record at $6,884. That is not a consumer preference. That is the financing system stretching the loan because the paycheck did not stretch with the price.
The average amount financed for a new vehicle hit $44,156 in Q2 2026. A record 36.5% of new-vehicle buyers took loan terms of 73 months or longer in Q2 2026, and 23.9% went to 84 months (seven years) or longer. Despite those stretched terms, the average monthly new-car payment hit a record $777, with 20.3% of buyers paying over $1,000/month. Down payments fell to just 11.6% of the average purchase price, the lowest share since late 2020. Average negative equity rolled into a new trade-in hit an all-time record $6,884 in 2026.
The standard auto loan term in 1980 was 48 months at an average APR of 14.30%; that rate spiked to 16.54% during the 1981 Volcker shock, compressing the spread over the federal funds rate to a razor-thin 16 basis points. The Tax Reform Act of 1986 eliminated the personal tax deductibility of consumer interest, including auto loan interest, which had previously been fully deductible — so even as headline auto loan APRs drifted down through the late 1980s and 1990s, the after-tax cost of financing a vehicle became significantly more burdensome. The "One Big Beautiful Bill" (OBBBA), signed July 2025, temporarily reintroduced an above-the-line deduction for up to $10,000 in interest on qualifying passenger vehicle loans through 2028 — but the relief is structurally narrow: it applies only to new vehicles with final assembly in the U.S., excludes vehicles over 14,000 pounds, and carries income phase-outs for higher earners. Seven-year car loans aren't a financing preference — they're the only way lenders can keep a $44,000 vehicle "affordable" on a stagnant paycheck, and it's trapping a large share of buyers underwater on a depreciating asset for most of the loan's life.
In 1980, the average credit card rate was about 17.30% — not free-market pricing, but an artificial ceiling from state usury caps, which put banks in a position of losing money on card lending as their wholesale funding costs exceeded what they could legally charge. The 1978 Supreme Court decision in Marquette National Bank of Minneapolis v. First of Omaha Service Corp. let nationally chartered banks export their home state's interest rate limits nationwide, prompting major issuers to relocate card operations to states with no usury caps — South Dakota and Delaware among them — deregulating revolving credit nationally. Rate history since: 15.70% in 1994, 16.00% in 2000, 13.40% in 2010, 12.20% in 2015, 14.50% in 2021, and 20.94% by May 2026 (with accounts actually carrying a balance averaging 22.15%). The spread between credit card rates and the federal funds rate was under 400 basis points in 1980; with the effective funds rate now at 3.75–4.00% following yesterday's hike, that spread has widened to roughly 1,700 basis points. Total revolving consumer credit topped $1.35 trillion in mid-2026, and the credit card delinquency rate climbed to 2.92% in Q1 2026, reversing the artificially low delinquency levels from 2020–2021 stimulus and forbearance programs. That spread didn't widen because default risk went up 4x since 1980 — usury caps were deregulated 48 years ago, and issuers have had that whole span to find out how much margin the market will bear, aided by algorithmic pricing and rewards programs subsidized by what revolvers pay.
In 1980, despite stagflation, the personal saving rate held in the 9–11% range. COVID-era stimulus and lockdowns pushed the saving rate to an artificial 15.1% annual average in 2020, peaking over 30% in specific lockdown months. By July 2026, the U.S. personal saving rate had collapsed to 3.0%, close to the all-time low of 2.3% set in 2005 just before the housing crash. Families aren't saving less because they've gotten worse with money — they're liquidating the cushion they built during COVID stimulus because the cost of food, shelter, and financing has outrun their paychecks. The Household Debt Service Ratio currently shows acute stress on the non-mortgage (credit card, auto) side, while the overall ratio is still partially buffered by homeowners holding sub-4% mortgages locked in before 2022.
The University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment Index registered 51.7 in August 2026 and a preliminary 47.8 in September 2026 — statistically as low as the 2008 financial crisis and comparable to 1980 stagflation-era gloom — even though unemployment sits at only 4.1% and the Misery Index (7.5) says this should be a calm, stable economy. Three specific factors explain the disconnect. First, Cumulative Price Level Exhaustion: the inflation rate measures velocity year-over-year, but consumers feel the absolute, compounded price level, which is why cooling from 8.0% to 3.4% doesn't feel like relief. Second, the Shadow Cost of Capital: the Misery Index captures unemployment and headline inflation but nothing about the cost of financing life — a $777 monthly car payment for seven years, or 22% revolving credit. Third, the Generational Housing Divide: the affordability collapse has created a dual-tier economy where owners of pre-2022 assets are insulated and new entrants are mathematically locked out of the traditional path to wealth — a structural pessimism no unemployment statistic captures. In short: the bill didn't go back down — the rate cooled, the level didn't. The Misery Index ignores the loan — it counts jobless plus CPI, not 22% revolving credit or a seven-year car note. And owners and buyers no longer live in the same country — sub-4% mortgages on one side, 5x income and lock-in on the other.
SOLUTIONS
None of this gets fixed by manipulating how it's measured — it gets fixed by addressing what's actually driving it, and the deficit sits at the top of that list. A federal deficit near $2.0–2.1 trillion for FY2026, with net interest alone running around $1.0 trillion, keeps upward pressure on the 10-year yield, which sets the floor under every mortgage, auto loan, and business borrowing rate discussed above. The deficit is a spending-versus-revenue problem inside this country's own budget, and both parties have voted for the spending and the tax policy that produced it.
A candidate or officeholder worth voting for on this issue should be able to answer specific questions, not slogans: What will you actually cut or reform to bring the deficit down, by name, not by category? Will you touch entitlement growth, defense spending, or both, since those are where the real money is? What will you do to unlock housing supply without wrecking the equity of people who already own? And do you support restoring meaningful usury limits on unsecured consumer credit, or does the 1978 deregulation stand as-is under your watch? That last question isn't a free shot — restoring caps is a real policy choice with tradeoffs, since it can also ration credit for higher-risk borrowers and push them toward payday lenders and fintech products with even less oversight. A serious candidate should be able to name that tradeoff, not just promise a cap.
"Failure is not an option" doesn't work as an excuse-generator either — a candidate blaming the other party for the deficit while proposing more deficit-financed spending of their own is not offering a solution, regardless of which party they belong to. Blaming the other party while adding to the same deficit is not a plan.
On the growth side: reshoring critical industries, and advancing AI research and the data centers that support it under real safety and security controls, plus nuclear expansion and maximizing domestic oil production, together form a credible growth argument — the country needs the added generating capacity regardless of AI demand, given decades of underinvestment in generation and transmission. New York's residential electricity prices have ranked as high as third in the nation earlier in 2026 and sat fifth at 29.5 cents per kilowatt-hour in June — about 61% above the national average. That's the direct result of emissions mandates written on a timeline the physical grid can't meet, and it's a preview of what other states risk if they follow the same path instead of pursuing energy abundance as a growth lever.
ENERGY AND INFRASTRUCTURE POLICY
Nuclear reactor safety and licensing already sits with the federal government — the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, not individual states, governs whether and how a reactor operates. That argues for a national nuclear buildout program run at the federal level with state input, not fifty separate state fights over whether to allow it — paired with a federal directive that ties data center approvals to the operators actually funding and building out the added generation and grid infrastructure their own demand requires, rather than leaving ratepayers to absorb it.
New York banned high-volume hydraulic fracturing statewide in December 2014. Pennsylvania, sitting on the same Marcellus Shale formation, allowed regulated fracking to proceed. Multiple economic studies comparing Marcellus counties on each side of that border have found real income and investment gaps favoring the Pennsylvania side — this isn't a hypothetical, it's a same-resource, same-geology natural experiment with two different regulatory outcomes. A governor who won't permit fracking or keep a working nuclear plant running, while mandating an electric grid conversion the state's own generation can't support, is making a choice — it isn't an accident that the bill lands on ratepayers.
Meanwhile, plenty of state and local governments still find public money for stadium subsidies benefiting billionaire team owners who could finance their own construction — which makes the claim that there's "no money" for energy infrastructure or permitting reform a matter of priorities, not actual capacity.
NYSEG and RG&E — utilities serving a large share of upstate New York — are owned by Avangrid, which is majority-controlled by Iberdrola, a Spanish multinational. This is not a hypothetical concern: a federal bill introduced in 2025 specifically targets blocking foreign ownership of U.S. utilities like NYSEG and National Grid, and a sitting member of Congress is actively pressing the Department of Energy to review foreign-owned utilities serving their district as of mid-2026. Handing control of the wires and pipes that keep the lights on to foreign-owned companies — even friendly, private ones — is a live national security and reliability question, not a settled one.
The federal government has the authority and the standing to revisit those ownership arrangements and, where warranted, unwind them — energy infrastructure is a national security asset, and treating its ownership as a purely private commercial matter is a policy choice that can be reversed, not a law of nature. This belongs at the federal level for the same reason nuclear oversight does: individual states have shown themselves either unwilling or unable to manage energy policy competently on their own, whether that's New York's fracking ban, its premature nuclear shutdown, its stalled all-electric mandate, or its dependence on foreign-owned utilities to keep the lights on in the meantime.
OUTCOMES
If nothing changes: the lock-in effect keeps suppressing housing turnover, auto loan terms keep stretching, credit card balances and delinquencies keep climbing as the savings cushion runs out, and Treasury yields stay elevated because the deficit keeps growing regardless of which party holds the gavel. None of that shows up as "high inflation" in the headline number — which is why this will keep polling as "the economy is bad" even in years the government calls it fine. That is why the government can call it fine and the country still votes like it isn't.
The 2022–2026 Fed cycle is history rhyming with 1980, not repeating it. Volcker deployed brute monetary force and accepted the Sacrifice Ratio's collateral damage up front — deep recession, mass unemployment, crushed asset prices. The 2020s Fed instead attempted what's been called an "immaculate disinflation": guiding inflation from 8.0% back toward 2.0% without triggering that same severe contraction. It partially worked — sub-4% inflation without a 1980-style recession — but it also left the structural mechanics of consumer credit permanently reshaped: mortgage lock-in instead of a price crash, 84-month auto loans instead of cheaper cars, and 22% revolving credit instead of usury caps.
If the reshoring/energy growth path is pursued seriously alongside real named spending cuts and a federal nuclear/energy-security program, it offers a route to outgrowing the debt without waiting on a deficit deal neither party has shown the will to make on its own. This is not the worst position this country has ever been in — 1980 and the WWII debt peak both prove worse is survivable and fixable. But it is a real, self-inflicted, bipartisan problem, and it will be on the ballot November 3rd — 47 days from today — whether or not either party wants to talk about it in these terms.
1980 was worse. That is not permission to leave this one unfixed. It is on the ballot November 3rd whether either party wants the argument in these terms.

Palantir co-founder Joe Lonsdale discusses efforts by the left to regulate artificial intelligence on 'The Will Cain Show:'

WILL CAIN: Palantir co-founder Joe Lonsdale joins me now. Joe, good to see you. Thanks for being with us here today. Are the woke wizards somebody we can count on to save us from AI doomsday?
 
JOE LONSDALE, PALANTIR CO-FOUNDER: Man, the woke ones are the worst, but you got Steve Bannon appearing with Bernie at that same conference. I call it the BBC. It's Bannon, Bernie, and the CCP. It's crazy guys on both sides. And you got Josh Hawley proposing regulation here. This is a really interesting time, Will, because you have dozens of NGOs that are trying to astroturf this AI panic. We had lots of people call me and my friends this weekend.
 
There's a panic going on because they're trying to scare people, because they want people scared, because they want to put new rules in place to capture things. And the same way they want to scare us with climate change or scare us with God knows what killer bees in the past, they're now trying to scare us with this. And they're trying to use it to push communism, push globalism, and push a lot of regulatory capture. And we're not going to allow it. We shouldn't let them do it.
 
CAIN: OK, well, we're offered two sets of superheroes to save us from this doomsday. You mentioned the politicians. We'll come back in a moment to the politicians.
 
But sticking with these group of Silicon Valley effective altruists, why do we suppose they have some vision of the future that saves humanity?
 
LONSDALE: Well, listen, a lot of the people who live in San Francisco, they are very much lacking spiritual lives. They've given up Christianity and everything else. And so for a lot of them, this is like a masonic complex, where this is their religion, that the end of the world may be coming.
 
And they're obsessed with it. And they have very strong opinions about it. And you go, it's a very weird time now in the Valley, where people think the world's about to change dramatically.
 
And it really is somewhat non-rational to them. It's like it's a religion. And yes, like this meter thing, the model evaluation thing you're talking about, it's obviously funded by the same people who are saying it should regulate them.
 
They are globalists. They are very left, very weird group. And giving that any sort of official power is crazy to me.
 
Of course, that's what they want. They want their own co-religionists to be looking into them.
 
CAIN: As you mentioned, this isn't strictly partisan. Senator Josh Hawley, Republican of Missouri today, has joined with Senator Richard Blumenthal to propose legislation that instead of meter and the effect of altruists, our superheroes should be government politicians. What's going on?
 
Why would Josh Hawley join with the likes of Bernie Sanders?
 
LONSDALE: Josh has been attacking tech for a long time. He thinks it's his ticket to be popular on the right. Listen, we should hold big tech accountable, but we should do it in a way that's American based on how the American founders wanted things.
 
Woodrow Wilson, when he created this massive regulatory state, he was recreating the star chamber that we fought against in England. If you go back in our civilization, we don't need star chambers. We don't need cronies.
 
We don't need these regulators harassing people. What you need is you need liability. These companies should be held extremely liable for any damage they do.
 
It's going to be a $2 trillion IPO. They should lose all of that if they cause hundreds of billions of dollars of damage because they'll be liable for the damage. We should pass laws.
 
We should do our gosh darn job passing laws, making sure it's even more clear what they're liable for, making it easier for them to be liable. We shouldn't be putting regulators in. They're just going to get captured.
 
They're just going to be unaccountable. That's not how America works. The right should be against regulation, but for liability to hold companies accountable.
 
CAIN: That sounds rational. I don't trust big tech. I also don't trust politicians.
 
I'll do respect to you, Joe, coming from the world of big tech. I only trust the concept of competition. The idea is that if somebody out there is creating something so nefarious, then somebody else should come along and be able to create something better.
 
LONSDALE: That's worked. That's worked for the railroads.
 
CAIN: It's worked for cars. It's worked for phones. It's worked for communication. That's pretty much worked throughout the history of America.
 
LONSDALE: There's an important point here because there's big tech and there's little tech. When you're trying to start companies, I'm involved in hundreds of new companies we're building. The big tech tries to smash us.
 
Big tech tries to capture government to smash the new innovators because there's always new innovators. America wins because of new innovations. What you have to do is you have to stop the big guys from smashing little guys by keeping things free, but then hold them accountable the right way, not the way that lets them capture it.
 
CAIN: All right. Joe Lonsdale, good to see you. Thanks, Joe.

text:
An Amsterdam company paid me $12,500 to sit in their studio for two hours.

That was actually the friends-and-family discount.

My normal rate for an in-person appearance is $25,000 to $30,000. But we had worked together for two and a half years, and factoring in the 8-hour flight from Dubai and two lost filming days back home, $12,500 made sense for both of us.

A lot of creators assume companies will only cover a flight and a hotel room for an in-person recording.

The reality is that serious marketing teams expect to pay talent fees. They aren't just buying the views. They are paying because they know you will show up on time, know the tech stack, and nail the recording without needing seven check-in emails beforehand.

The same thing applies when speaking fees climb into the $50,000 to $100,000 range.

If you charge $70,000 just to stand on stage for 45 minutes, people look at the invoice funny.

So you package it up. You include the talk, two short-form clips, some behind-the-scenes footage, and a dedicated post reviewing the event. Now the company gets a full campaign for their marketing budget, and you aren't stuck arguing over an hourly rate.

Companies almost never tell you their maximum budget upfront. The worst thing that happens when you quote a real number is a polite counter-offer.

I still remember the first tech conference that flew me out years ago. They handed me a plastic lanyard and a branded water bottle, and I walked through the airport thinking I had made it.

text:
The smallest list I ever built booked more meetings than the massive one I spent weeks perfecting. 

The big list had the right titles, the right company sizes, the right filters. The small list had one thing the big one didn't: a reason for each person to care this quarter.  

A buying signal tells you when someone is ready to talk. That's the piece I was missing for years. Four rules came out of it:  

1️⃣ Find the trigger before you find the person.  

A job title tells you who has an email address. A trigger event tells you who has urgency. New product launches, expansions, leadership changes, policy shifts. 

Find the signal first, then find the person behind it. No trigger means no reason to send. 
 
2️⃣ Split the ICP before you build a single list.  "Marketing agencies" is too broad to build one useful campaign around. 

A construction company owner and a law firm partner don't share pain points or vocabulary. Break the ICP into sub-niches first. One list per niche, one offer angle per niche.  

3️⃣ Keep the list small on purpose.  A massive list creates fake confidence. 

Start with the tightest band that can plausibly buy: employee count, geography, tech stack. Expand only after you see traction on the small list. The tight list forces precision. The big list hides the fact that you don't know who actually buys.  

4️⃣ Read replies like product feedback every Friday.  → Which niches pulled "yes, interested" → Which ones asked the same question → Which ones went dark after the first reply  Feed the winners more data and cut everything else.  → What's one signal you've started tracking recently? Drop it below.

text:
If you're in North America, leave the non-native daffodil and tulip bulbs on the shelf. Plant these native early spring flowers instead, and plant them now.

Daffodils and tulips are from Europe and Asia, and the heavily hybridized ones sold in bins offer little to no usable pollen or nectar for most native bees. They bloom, they look great, and nothing local participates.

Native spring ephemerals do the opposite. They come up in the narrow window after the ground thaws and before the trees leaf out, which is exactly when native bees are emerging and starving. The timing isn't a coincidence, it's a relationship.

1. Trout lily. Mottled leaves, small yellow nodding flower. It has its own specialist bee, Andrena erythronii, that feeds on almost nothing else. Colonies of this flower can be over 100 years old, sometimes older than the trees above them.

2. Virginia bluebells. Pink buds opening to true blue. Works for bumblebees, long-tongued bees, butterflies, hummingbird moths and hummingbirds.

3. Dutchman's breeches. Weird little white flowers shaped like pants on a line. A critical early food source for bumblebee queens coming out of hibernation.

Honorable Mentions: Bloodroot, trillium, bellwort, spring beauty, shooting star. All the same high impact on native wildlife.

Fall is the window for planting them. These ship bare-root while dormant and this is when they want to go in the ground. Plant them in shade or part shade with decent organic soil, then mulch with four to six inches of clean straw.

They go dormant by midsummer and vanish, so mark where they are and interplant with ferns or woodland asters to fill the gap.

Then leave them alone to do their thing. They'll still be there in fifty years.

text:
Parents often find it hard to believe their precious boy can do something evil.

Core govt evidence against Brian Cole Jr. (written by grok):

•  Purchase records: Bank and credit-card data show Cole bought components matching the devices (1-inch-by-8-inch galvanized pipes from a specific manufacturer, matching end caps, 14-gauge red/black wire, 9-volt batteries and connectors, white kitchen timers, steel wool, plus tools like safety glasses and wire strippers) at Home Depot, Lowe’s, Walmart, and Micro Center in Northern Virginia across 2019–2020. He allegedly continued buying similar items after January 6. A November 16, 2020 Home Depot receipt and matching parts were later found.

•  Location data: Historical cell-site records placed his phone interacting with towers covering the DNC/RNC area between roughly 7:39 p.m. and 8:24 p.m. on January 5, aligning with surveillance of the suspect (7:34–8:18 p.m.) and the alleged drop times (DNC ~7:54 p.m., RNC ~8:16 p.m.). A license-plate reader captured his vehicle exiting I-395 South at South Capitol Street around 7:10 p.m., near the sites.

•  Surveillance video: Footage showed one person in dark pants, a gray hoodie, dark gloves, a medical mask, and Nike Air Max Speed Turf shoes planting both devices. Cole is described as 5’6” and wearing glasses. Prosecutors say the path of the figure matches his phone data.

•  Search of home and vehicle: After the arrest, agents recovered matching pipes, iron/galvanized end caps, wire, and a 9-volt battery in a closet accessible from Cole’s bedroom and in his car.

•  Confession: In a multi-hour videotaped FBI interview after Miranda waiver, Cole initially denied involvement and said he was heading to a protest. After being shown a surveillance still and warned that lying was a crime, he paused, put his head down, and said “yes.” He then described assembling the devices that day (black powder from charcoal, Lilly Miller sulfur dust, and potassium nitrate bought at Lowe’s; learned from a video game and YouTube), cleaning them with disinfectant wipes, setting 60-minute timers, carrying one at a time in a backpack, and placing them (one under a bench near the DNC, one by a trash can at the RNC). He said “something just snapped” amid election-related grievances, targeted “the parties” because “they were in charge,” and “I really don’t like either party at this point.” He denied targeting Congress or the January 6 certification, said he planted at night because he did not want to kill people, and was “pretty relieved” they did not explode. Prosecutors say he first offered a cover story. Defense has demanded the recording and related materials. 
￼
•  Digital activity: Forensic review found 943 factory resets/wipes on his phone from December 2020 through December 2025, including one about three hours before arrest. He also used computer-cleaning software. Prosecutors treat this as concealment; the defense attributes it to OCD. ￼

text:
Someone Reached Into the Water—Then an Octopus Came Out in a Way That Changes How You See These Animals

The first few seconds look almost ordinary. A person leans over the edge of a waterfront, peering into clear, shallow water where rocks, algae, and patches of shadow break up the bottom. Then a shape moves near the concrete.

It is easy to miss.

The animal is not large. It is not charging toward the camera. There is no dramatic splash. Instead, an octopus is pulled from the water, and its arms immediately begin doing something that makes the scene unforgettable: they keep moving, curling, reaching, gripping, and searching for surfaces even while the animal is suspended above the water.

That small detail is the real story.

An octopus does not have a skeleton like ours. Its body is soft, flexible, and extraordinarily responsive to its surroundings. Each of its eight arms is packed with muscles and sensory structures, and the thousands of suction cups along those arms are not passive pieces of equipment. They help the animal touch, grip, manipulate, and explore the world around it.

In the video, that ability is visible almost frame by frame.

The animal twists its arms around themselves and around the hand holding it. One arm reaches downward. Another curls upward. Others cling to the body. The movements do not resemble the simple reflex of a rope being pulled through the air. They look coordinated, purposeful, and remarkably independent.

This is one reason octopuses seem so strange to us. We are used to animals whose bodies are organized around a rigid skeleton. Our arms move because bones provide a framework and muscles pull against them. An octopus has no such internal scaffold. Its arms can bend, shorten, lengthen, curl, flatten, and change direction without a fixed set of joints.

The result is an animal that can turn its entire body into a collection of flexible tools.

And the creature in this video appears to be perfectly adapted to a world where flexibility can mean survival.

### A body built without bones

Octopuses belong to the cephalopods, a group of marine mollusks that also includes squid, cuttlefish, and nautiluses. They may look nothing like a garden snail, but they are distant relatives. Their evolutionary history took the soft molluscan body in a very different direction.

Instead of carrying a large external shell, most modern octopuses have a soft body with only tiny internal remnants of shell. That absence gives them an extraordinary advantage: they can squeeze through openings that seem absurdly small compared with the size of their body.

Their most obvious features are the eight arms surrounding the mouth. In everyday language they are often called tentacles, but zoologically there is an important distinction. Octopuses have arms rather than the two longer tentacles characteristic of squid and cuttlefish.

Those arms are not identical to human limbs, yet the comparison is useful in one respect. They are used for an astonishing range of jobs.

An octopus can use an arm to crawl along the seafloor, another to investigate a crevice, and several others to hold prey or stabilize the body. The animal does not need to reposition its entire body every time it wants to interact with something.

Its mouth sits in the center of the arms, and beneath the body is a muscular structure called the siphon. By forcing water through the mantle cavity and out through the siphon, an octopus can produce jet propulsion. The same system also helps move water across the gills.

The video does not show this underwater machinery directly. What it does show is the other side of the animal's design: a body whose flexibility remains obvious even when it is out of the water for a moment.

### The suction cups are more than tiny anchors

Look closely at an octopus arm and one of its most remarkable features becomes impossible to ignore.

Rows of suction cups cover the underside.

To a human observer, they can look like hundreds of small rubber plungers. But their function is much more sophisticated. Each sucker can create attachment against a surface, allowing the animal to hold on with extraordinary precision.

Research has shown that octopus suckers are also sensory organs. They can detect chemical and mechanical information, meaning that an octopus can effectively taste and feel with its arms.

That changes the way we should interpret the constant movement seen in footage like this.

When an octopus touches something, it is not simply asking, “Can I grab this?” Its nervous system is receiving information from the contact. The arm is participating in exploration. The sucker is part grip, part sensor.

Imagine walking through a completely unfamiliar room while being able to feel and chemically sample almost everything you touched with your hands. That gives a rough sense of how different an octopus's relationship with its environment can be.

The animal in the video repeatedly curls its arms against the hand and the concrete edge. Those motions are not enough to tell us exactly what it is sensing or thinking, but they demonstrate why an octopus is so difficult to handle like an ordinary fish.

There is simply much more going on at the surface of its body.

### Eight arms, but not eight simple limbs

The nervous system of an octopus is famous for another reason: a large amount of its nervous tissue is distributed throughout its arms.

This does not mean that each arm is an independent creature. The central brain remains essential for coordinating the animal as a whole. But the arrangement allows an octopus to process and control movement in a highly distributed way.

That architecture helps explain an observation that often surprises people watching octopus behavior. An arm can continue to make complex movements even when it is not being consciously directed in the way a human might consciously move a finger.

For the octopus, movement is not simply a command traveling from a central control room to eight obedient cables. Its arms contain neural circuits capable of handling substantial local processing.

The practical benefit is obvious.

The seafloor is a chaotic environment filled with rocks, holes, shells, plants, currents, prey, and potential predators. A flexible arm needs to respond quickly to contact without waiting for every tiny adjustment to be planned centrally.

The video gives a brief, almost accidental demonstration of this principle. Suspended above the water, the octopus keeps trying to establish contact. Its arms curl, extend, and wrap around available surfaces.

The animal has lost the support of the seafloor, but the movement system that evolved for constant contact is still there.

### The color in the video tells a story—but not the whole story

The octopus appears reddish to orange-brown in the footage, with darker and lighter areas across its body and arms. That coloration is striking, but identifying an octopus species from a short video is unreliable.

Many octopus species can change their appearance. They possess specialized skin cells known as chromatophores, along with other structures that help alter the way light is reflected from the skin. Depending on the species, situation, and physiological state, an octopus can change color and pattern with remarkable speed.

Some changes are used for camouflage. Others can be involved in communication, warning, courtship, or responses to disturbance.

This is why the animal should not be treated as a simple “red octopus” merely because it looks red in one moment.

Lighting matters. Water depth matters. The animal's physiological state matters. The camera itself can alter the apparent color. Even the background can influence how our eyes interpret the pattern.

The safest identification from this video is therefore an octopus, not a confidently named species.

The shallow rocky habitat and the animal's appearance could fit several coastal octopus species depending on where the footage was recorded. Without the location, close views of diagnostic features, and ideally expert examination, a species-level identification would be guesswork.

That uncertainty is important because nature rarely fits neatly into a thumbnail.

### Why does it look almost like it is climbing?

One of the most fascinating parts of the footage is the way the octopus's arms interact with the edge.

To us, the concrete wall is a hard, simple surface. To an octopus, it is a landscape of microscopic textures and irregularities.

The animal can press suckers against a surface, establish attachment, release them, and attach again. It can use several arms simultaneously, shifting its weight and changing its point of contact.

On the seafloor, this is a normal way of moving.

An octopus does not need legs arranged in a neat sequence. It can crawl, pull, push, and flow across surfaces. It can anchor part of its body while another arm explores ahead.

That is why the motion can look strangely reminiscent of climbing.

But there is an important difference. The octopus is not using a fixed climbing technique comparable to a human's hand-over-hand movement. Its arms are constantly adapting to whatever surface happens to be available.

This is one of the central themes of octopus biology: instead of forcing the environment to match a rigid body plan, the animal has a body plan capable of adapting to the environment.

A rock is a foothold.

A narrow crack is a shelter.

A shell can become a shield.

A patch of sand can become camouflage.

A gap in a wall can become an escape route.

For an animal with such a flexible body, the physical world offers possibilities almost everywhere.

### The animal's softness is a weapon

Softness sounds like a weakness until you consider what it allows.

An octopus can disappear into spaces that would be inaccessible to many predators. It can flatten its body, change its shape, and move through complex terrain. Its lack of a rigid external shell makes it vulnerable in some situations, but it also gives the animal an extraordinary range of movement.

This trade-off is fundamental.

A crab has armor. A turtle has a shell. Many fish have scales and rigid skeletal structures that provide support and protection. An octopus relies heavily on behavior, camouflage, flexibility, intelligence, and speed.

When threatened, an octopus may release ink, change color and pattern, rapidly move away using jet propulsion, or squeeze into a hiding place.

Ink is not simply a cloud that makes the water dark. It can interfere with a predator's sensory systems and create an opportunity for escape. In some species and circumstances, the released material may also contribute to a deceptive visual target.

Again, the video does not show every one of these defenses. What it shows is the physical foundation beneath them: the octopus is built to manipulate its environment with a soft, muscular body.

### The beak is the part most people never see

At the center of the arms is the mouth, and inside it is one of the few hard structures of the animal: a powerful beak.

It is made primarily of chitin and is shaped somewhat like the beak of a bird, although the resemblance is superficial. The beak allows an octopus to bite and tear prey.

This is especially important because the animal's arms do much of the work of capture and manipulation, while the beak handles the final mechanical task.

Octopuses eat a variety of prey depending on species and habitat. Crabs, shrimp, mollusks, fish, and other marine animals can all appear in the diets of different octopuses.

Some species are active hunters. Others spend substantial time concealed and strike when prey comes within reach.

The contrast is remarkable: the same animal that can appear almost delicate when its arms are moving through the water possesses a compact feeding apparatus capable of breaking through hard material.

There is another unusual feature too. Octopus saliva contains substances that help subdue and process prey, and many octopuses use venom delivered through their bite. The chemistry varies among species.

That does not mean an octopus encountered near a dock is automatically dangerous to people. Most interactions are far more mundane. But it is a useful reminder that this animal is not merely a soft, curious ornament of the sea. It is an active predator with a highly specialized body.

### Intelligence without a familiar face

Octopuses have become symbols of animal intelligence because their behavior can be surprisingly flexible.

They have been studied for learning, problem-solving, exploration, memory, and manipulation of objects. Some can open containers, navigate complex spaces, distinguish between individuals, and learn from experience.

But the most interesting thing about octopus intelligence may be that it evolved in a body so unlike our own.

Humans tend to associate intelligence with a familiar combination of a large central brain, eyes, hands, and a vertebrate skeleton. Octopuses challenge that template.

Their ancestors followed a completely different evolutionary path. Their nervous systems developed in mollusks, not mammals. Their arms can perform sophisticated movements without bones. Their skin can change appearance. Their environment is dominated by water rather than air.

And yet the result is an animal capable of flexible behavior.

Watching the octopus in the video, it is tempting to assign a human story to every movement: it looks as though the animal is trying to escape, reach for safety, or grab the person.

Some of those interpretations may be reasonable possibilities, but the video alone cannot reveal the animal's internal state.

What we can say is more interesting.

The octopus is responding to physical contact and an unfamiliar situation with a body designed to explore, grip, and maneuver. Its arms are constantly testing the available environment.

That is enough to make the scene remarkable without turning the animal into a character from a cartoon.

### A short life can contain an extraordinary amount of complexity

Many octopus species do not live for decades. Depending on the species, life spans can range from less than a year to several years, with some larger species living longer.

Their life histories are often intense. Growth can be rapid, reproduction is central to the final stage of life, and in many species adults die after reproducing.

Females of many octopus species show extraordinary parental behavior. After laying eggs, a female may guard and clean them, keep water moving over them, and protect them from predators. In species where the female stops feeding during brooding, the period can place an enormous physiological cost on her.

Eventually the eggs hatch, and the female's life usually ends around that reproductive cycle.

This means the animal seen in a few seconds of social-media footage may belong to a species whose entire existence is measured in a surprisingly short span.

That perspective changes the image.

It is no longer simply a strange creature pulled from the water.

It is an animal near the surface of a marine ecosystem, carrying millions of years of evolutionary history in a body that can change shape in an instant.

### What the habitat tells us

The water in the video is shallow enough to reveal the rocky bottom. The animal is close to a hard waterfront edge, apparently in an area influenced by human infrastructure.

Places like docks, marinas, seawalls, and rocky shorelines can become habitats for marine life. Structures built for people do not automatically become biological deserts. Crevices, submerged surfaces, shade, algae, and accumulated debris can create shelter and feeding opportunities.

For an octopus, a complex shoreline can offer many places to hide.

The exact location of the video is unknown from the footage alone, so it would be wrong to assign the animal to a particular coast or ecosystem without additional evidence. But the scene illustrates a broader truth about coastal wildlife: some of the most interesting animals are living within meters of places people walk every day.

Clear water can make this especially deceptive.

A person may see a few rocks and patches of algae.

An octopus sees cover.

A crab sees shelter.

A small fish sees structure.

A predator sees an opportunity.

The same landscape can have completely different meanings depending on the animal looking at it.

### What happens when an octopus meets a human hand?

The most visually striking moment in the video is also the one that deserves the most restraint.

A human hand is holding the octopus above the water. The animal's arms are wrapped around the body and the fingers, with suckers contacting the skin.

An octopus sucker can adhere strongly, especially to smooth surfaces. That is normal biology, not evidence that the animal is deliberately trying to attack or “grab” the person.

For the animal, a moving object has appeared in an unfamiliar environment. Its arms are the main instruments through which it interacts with that environment.

There is also a welfare issue whenever wild marine animals are handled.

An octopus is adapted to water. Its gills require water flow for gas exchange, and prolonged exposure to air can be stressful and potentially harmful. Handling can also damage delicate tissues or interfere with the animal's normal behavior.

For viewers, the safest lesson is not that octopuses should be picked up whenever they are found near shore. It is the opposite: a fascinating encounter is usually best observed without unnecessary handling.

The animal's ability to survive in a difficult environment does not make it indestructible.

Its softness is exactly what makes careful treatment important.

### A creature that can taste with its arms

Perhaps the strangest fact about an octopus is not its color-changing skin or its ability to squeeze through gaps.

It is the way its body interacts with information.

The suckers contain chemical and mechanical receptors. In simple terms, contact can provide information about both what something feels like and what chemical properties it has.

That means the animal's arms are not merely appendages attached to a central body. They are active sensory surfaces.

This makes an octopus's world fundamentally different from ours.

When a human wants to inspect an object, we generally look at it, then reach out with a hand. The sensory systems are separated in a familiar sequence.

An octopus can bring sensing and manipulation together.

An arm can explore a crevice.

A sucker can attach to a surface.

The animal can receive chemical information from contact.

The same arm can then change position and continue exploring.

It is a form of embodied intelligence that scientists continue to study because it does not fit neatly into the usual human-centered picture of how a smart animal should work.

### What we can actually conclude from the video

The footage shows a small octopus in shallow, clear water near a hard shoreline or waterfront structure. A person reaches into the water and lifts the animal. The octopus's arms curl and attach around the hand and body, displaying the flexibility and gripping ability characteristic of cephalopods.

The animal appears reddish to orange-brown in the recorded light.

Beyond that, caution is necessary.

The exact species cannot be established confidently from this short footage alone. The geographic location is not visible. The video does not provide enough diagnostic detail to determine age, sex, or health. It also cannot tell us why the animal was in that precise location.

Those unknowns are not a problem.

They are part of the story.

A good wildlife observation does not become more valuable by pretending to know what cannot be known.

In fact, the uncertainty makes the visible biology more interesting. Even without a species name, we can recognize an animal using a body plan that has evolved for exploration, camouflage, manipulation, and survival in a three-dimensional world.

### The shoreline suddenly looks different

After seeing the video, it becomes difficult to look at shallow coastal water in quite the same way.

A quiet patch beside a seawall may seem empty.

But beneath the surface there can be a network of cracks, stones, algae, shells, and shadows.

A small octopus can disappear into that landscape.

Its body can match the background.

Its arms can reach into spaces that a rigid animal cannot enter.

Its suckers can investigate surfaces one contact at a time.

Its eyes can monitor the surroundings while the rest of the body remains hidden.

The animal does not need a dramatic reef or remote expedition to demonstrate its abilities.

Sometimes a few feet of shallow water are enough.

That is the quiet lesson hidden inside the footage.

Wildlife does not always announce itself.

Sometimes it is waiting under the surface, inches from a place where people are standing, using a body so flexible and specialized that the human eye barely knows what it is looking at.

And when the animal finally appears, even for a few seconds, the familiar waterfront can suddenly become an entirely different world.

### A final look at those moving arms

Return to the moment when the octopus is suspended above the water.

The arms keep curling.

One bends around another.

A sucker contacts the person's hand.

Another arm hangs downward, twisting under its own weight.

The body shifts.

Nothing about the movement is wasted. The animal's anatomy is built around flexibility.

There is no rigid limb waiting to be placed in a single position.

There is a living network of muscles, nerves, and sensory structures constantly adjusting to the conditions around it.

That is the feature worth remembering.

Not the color alone.

Not the shock of seeing an unusual animal.

Not the assumption that it is trying to do something human.

The remarkable fact is simpler.

This animal has evolved a body that can turn touch into information and information into movement, while remaining soft enough to flow through an environment full of spaces, surfaces, predators, and prey.

For humans, the ocean often looks like a flat surface hiding darkness underneath.

For an octopus, it is a world of textures.

Every rock can be explored.

Every crack can be entered.

Every surface can be tested.

Every movement can produce new information.

And that is why the creature in this short video feels so much larger than it really is.

It is not large in size.

It is large in possibility.

An octopus does not need to roar, chase a camera, or display enormous teeth to be extraordinary.

It only needs to move its arms.

Once you understand what those arms can do, the scene at the edge of the water stops looking like a strange encounter and starts looking like a brief window into one of evolution's most unusual experiments.

A soft-bodied predator.

Eight flexible arms.

Hundreds of sensory suckers.

A brain unlike ours.

A body that can change shape.

And an entire underwater world that it can explore almost entirely by touch.

The next time a calm patch of coastal water looks empty, remember what the video reveals.

Empty does not always mean empty.

Sometimes, something is already there.

It is simply better at disappearing than you are at looking.
 And that is the real magic.

Along the lonely coast south of San Francisco, small towns and isolated buildings punctuate the journey. text:
America does have a culture into which immigrants are asked to assimilate, but I don't mean “culture” in the shallow sense of food, music, clothing, or even ethnicity,

America is a people, not a race.

An immigrant does not need to abandon his ancestry/genetic history (as if one could), his native cuisine, certain family traditions, or every custom he brought with him. Nor has American citizenship historically required everyone to belong to the same Christian denomination or even to be Christian.

What matters far more is civic assimilation.

The United States inherited and developed a particular constitutional order: representative government, the rule of law, individual liberty, freedom of conscience and religion, due process, peaceful transfers of political power, constitutional limitations upon government, and the principle that political disputes are settled through lawful institutions rather than violence.

That is part of American culture in the deepest sense of the word.

Our Constitution makes it possible for Americans who can sometimes profoundly disagree with one another about religion, morality, economics, and politics nevertheless to remain fellow citizens. A progressive and a conservative need not agree about economics. Neighbors do not have to eat the same food, listen to the same music, attend the same church—or attend a church at all.

But they do need some common civic ground upon which to live together peacefully.

That is why I think the modern discussion about assimilation frequently goes wrong. Assimilation need not mean erasing someone's ethnicity or demanding some dramatic cultural uniformity, you don't need to enjoy baseball or apple pie. It means joining an existing political community and accepting the basic constitutional compact that allows a very large population to remain one united people in common cause. 

Immigration therefore cannot be discussed solely in terms of what an immigrant wants from America. A sovereign nation is also entitled to ask what immigration means for the citizens already living here and for the constitutional order their children will inherit.

That principle is not peculiar to America. Every functioning political community has institutions, laws, expectations, and public norms that immigrants must learn to navigate.

The American version is unusual because so much of our common identity is political rather than ethnic. There is no single American race. Americans descend from peoples all over the world. Precisely because that ethnic bond does not define us, our common civic inheritance becomes especially important.

I think this also explains why some Americans react so strongly when they hear someone say, “I came here, but I have no obligation to assimilate.”

What exactly does not assimilating mean?

If it means, “I will continue cooking the food I grew up with, speaking my native language at home, and celebrating my family's traditions,” then I see no threat to American citizenship in that at all. That is ordinary American thought.

But if it means, “I reject the legitimacy of your constitutional system; I do not regard its laws as binding upon me; I want different political institutions and systems substituted for yours; and I have no obligation to become part of the civic community that received me,” then we are talking about something fundamentally different.

That is not diversity in food, faith, or folklore. It is disagreement over the political compact itself.

And no society can remain peaceful indefinitely if its inhabitants cease to share enough common ground to recognize one another as members of the same political community.

None of this requires pretending that an earlier America was a utopia. It wasn't. Americans have always sinned, committed crimes, fought bitter political battles, and sometimes failed spectacularly to live according to our own professed principles. Nor have Americans ever completely agreed about what those principles require.

But the constitutional structure has displayed remarkable durability. Governments change. Presidents leave office. Congressional majorities disappear. Political movements rise and fall. Yet the government itself does not ordinarily have to be rebuilt every time political power changes hands. 

That distinction matters.

I therefore don't believe the important immigration question is whether immigrants look like my ancestors, worship as I do, speak with my accent, or reproduce every social custom of the place where I grew up.

The important question is whether people arriving from a hundred different nations can say with those already here:

This is our country now. These are our neighbors. These laws bind us alike. These liberties belong to all of us. Our political disagreements will be fought through constitutional and lawful means, and the future of this republic and its children is now our responsibility too.

That is the assimilation people speak about. 

It asks something of the immigrant, certainly.

But becoming a citizen has always meant becoming part of something larger than oneself. And in return, America offers something extraordinary: the possibility that people whose ancestors came from opposite sides of the earth can inherit the same country, enjoy the same liberties, live under the same Constitution, and call one another fellow Americans.

That isn't the destruction of someone's identity.

It is the creation of a common civic one. We only ask that immigrants truly seek to understand these principles and come because they want to be a part of what we have here, not because they want to force us to abandon our very way of life to accommodate our enemies who don't hold these truths to be self evident.

text:
Honoring the Constitution. Honoring Those Who Defended It.

From Sept. 17–23, we observe Constitution Week — a time to reflect on the document that established the framework of our government and the freedoms it represents. For Veterans, the Constitution carries a deep personal meaning. They raised their right hands to swear an oath to support and defend it, answering a call to service rooted in duty, liberty and responsibility.

As our nation celebrates its 250th anniversary of independence, Constitution Week offers an opportunity for all of us — especially those who have worn the uniform — to reflect on the freedoms we enjoy, share the stories of service and participate in the civic life of our communities. The Constitution is more than history. It is a living promise — and protecting its principles is a responsibility we all share.
