33 Key Voices First 1,600 yrs of Christendom whose theological metaphysics opposed Westminster’s Guaranteed Fall of “Not By Bare Permission” 
→
1. Justin Martyr (c. 100–165) — Angels and men created free. Foreknowledge is not causal determination.
2. Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 130–202) — No coercion with God. Man is cause to himself of becoming wheat or chaff.
3. Tertullian (c. 155–220) — Adam willed the sin he committed. The Fall is not a necessity God imposed.
4. Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–215) — Virtue and vice require real choice. Fate does not author the first sin.
5. Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253) — Autexousion against Valentinian determinism. God does not create anyone wicked.
6. Methodius of Olympus (d. c. 311) — God is not the author of evil. Evil begins in a will that could have kept the command.
7. Archelaus (c. 320) — Anti-Manichaean: devil and man fall by refusing the commandment, not by nature or fate.
8. Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373) — Creatures are mutable by nature, not predetermined to sin. Defilement is from turning, not from God’s making.
9. Cyril of Jerusalem (c. 313–386) — The soul is inherently autexousios (self-governed) as the image of its Creator. Humans do not sin by necessity, cosmic fate, or biological drive, but entirely by the exercise of real-time choice.
10. Cyril of Alexandria (c. 376–444) — God’s eternal foreknowledge neither restricts nor compels the human will; human nature “fell ill” in Adam with mortality, but individual destiny is determined by real-time choice, not an arbitrary divine blueprint.
11. Basil the Great (c. 330–379) — Evil is a voluntary choice. It originates entirely inside the creature’s defect.
12. Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335–395) — Image of God includes being without a master. Ruin and return hang on deliberate choice.
13. John Cassian (c. 360–435) — Free will actively cooperates with grace. God does not force salvation or damnation. Not Bañezian but Western resistance to extreme predestination.
14. Vincent of Lérins (d. c. 445) — Opposed extreme predestinarian views. Preserved the baseline consensus of moral accountability. Not Bañezian. Western resistance to extreme predestination.
15. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407) — The call is not forced. Not all who were called obeyed.
16. Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662) — Created will is a real power of self-determination. God does not necessitate the gnomic turn to evil.
17. John of Damascus (c. 675–749) — God foreknows what is in our power; He does not predetermine it. He neither wills wickedness nor compels virtue.
18. Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109) — The will is the cause of its own falling. God does not make the creature fall.
19. Peter John Olivi (1248–1298) — The will retains power for opposites. First sin is from the created will, not from divine or intellectual necessitation.
20. John Duns Scotus (1266–1308) — Synchronic contingency: at the instant of choice the will can do otherwise. God co-causes the act as being, not the deformity of sin.
21. Gregory Palamas (1296–1359) — God foreknows but does not predetermine. His plan reflects what we freely choose.
22. William of Ockham (1287–1347) — God is not the author of sin. Created freedom is not a necessitated effect of the divine will.
23. Gabriel Biel (1420–1495) — The will is not determined ad unum to evil. The Fall is not the output of a necessitating premotion.
24. Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536) — Defended the power of human choice. Explicitly opposed early Protestant deterministic bondage.
25. Balthasar Hubmaier (1480–1528) — Radical Reformer who argued human choice was restored by the Word; if God necessitated the Fall, subsequent cosmic punishment would be fundamentally unjust.
26. Philip Melanchthon (1497–1560) — Luther’s right-hand man who later rejected absolute predestination, developing synergism to protect the universal offer of grace against divine determinism. Caveat is that he is only here by his later synergist phase.
27. Sebastian Castellio (1515–1563) — Early Swiss reformer who openly fought Calvin’s predestinarian system, arguing that a guaranteed blueprint turns God into a hypocrite and the true author of evil.
28. Luis de Molina (1535–1600) — God knows what Adam would freely do. He does not physically predetermine the choice.
29. Francisco Suárez (1548–1617) — Rejects physical premotion that makes the free act inevitable apart from the will.
30. Jacobus Arminius (1560–1609) — No absolute decree necessitating Adam’s fall. Adam could have stood.
31. Benjamin Whichcote (1609–1683) — Moral evil is not necessitated by God. Divine government does not cancel created liberty.
32. Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688) — Attacks “neoteric” divine fatalism: decrees that make all actions necessary are contrary to the ancient church.
33. John Wesley (1703–1791) — Championed universal prevenient grace. Fiercely resisted the Westminster model of unconditional election.
→

33 Key Voices First 1,600 yrs of Christendom whose theological metaphysics opposed Westminster’s Guaranteed Fall of “Not By Bare Permission”

1. Justin Martyr (c. 100–165) — Angels and men created free. Foreknowledge is not causal determination.
2. Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 130–202) — No coercion with God. Man is cause to himself of becoming wheat or chaff.
3. Tertullian (c. 155–220) — Adam willed the sin he committed. The Fall is not a necessity God imposed.
4. Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–215) — Virtue and vice require real choice. Fate does not author the first sin.
5. Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253) — Autexousion against Valentinian determinism. God does not create anyone wicked.
6. Methodius of Olympus (d. c. 311) — God is not the author of evil. Evil begins in a will that could have kept the command.
7. Archelaus (c. 320) — Anti-Manichaean: devil and man fall by refusing the commandment, not by nature or fate.
8. Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373) — Creatures are mutable by nature, not predetermined to sin. Defilement is from turning, not from God’s making.
9. Cyril of Jerusalem (c. 313–386) — The soul is inherently autexousios (self-governed) as the image of its Creator. Humans do not sin by necessity, cosmic fate, or biological drive, but entirely by the exercise of real-time choice.
10. Cyril of Alexandria (c. 376–444) — God’s eternal foreknowledge neither restricts nor compels the human will; human nature “fell ill” in Adam with mortality, but individual destiny is determined by real-time choice, not an arbitrary divine blueprint.
11. Basil the Great (c. 330–379) — Evil is a voluntary choice. It originates entirely inside the creature’s defect.
12. Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335–395) — Image of God includes being without a master. Ruin and return hang on deliberate choice.
13. John Cassian (c. 360–435) — Free will actively cooperates with grace. God does not force salvation or damnation. Not Bañezian but Western resistance to extreme predestination.
14. Vincent of Lérins (d. c. 445) — Opposed extreme predestinarian views. Preserved the baseline consensus of moral accountability. Not Bañezian. Western resistance to extreme predestination.
15. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407) — The call is not forced. Not all who were called obeyed.
16. Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662) — Created will is a real power of self-determination. God does not necessitate the gnomic turn to evil.
17. John of Damascus (c. 675–749) — God foreknows what is in our power; He does not predetermine it. He neither wills wickedness nor compels virtue.
18. Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109) — The will is the cause of its own falling. God does not make the creature fall.
19. Peter John Olivi (1248–1298) — The will retains power for opposites. First sin is from the created will, not from divine or intellectual necessitation.
20. John Duns Scotus (1266–1308) — Synchronic contingency: at the instant of choice the will can do otherwise. God co-causes the act as being, not the deformity of sin.
21. Gregory Palamas (1296–1359) — God foreknows but does not predetermine. His plan reflects what we freely choose.
22. William of Ockham (1287–1347) — God is not the author of sin. Created freedom is not a necessitated effect of the divine will.
23. Gabriel Biel (1420–1495) — The will is not determined ad unum to evil. The Fall is not the output of a necessitating premotion.
24. Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536) — Defended the power of human choice. Explicitly opposed early Protestant deterministic bondage.
25. Balthasar Hubmaier (1480–1528) — Radical Reformer who argued human choice was restored by the Word; if God necessitated the Fall, subsequent cosmic punishment would be fundamentally unjust.
26. Philip Melanchthon (1497–1560) — Luther’s right-hand man who later rejected absolute predestination, developing synergism to protect the universal offer of grace against divine determinism. Caveat is that he is only here by his later synergist phase.
27. Sebastian Castellio (1515–1563) — Early Swiss reformer who openly fought Calvin’s predestinarian system, arguing that a guaranteed blueprint turns God into a hypocrite and the true author of evil.
28. Luis de Molina (1535–1600) — God knows what Adam would freely do. He does not physically predetermine the choice.
29. Francisco Suárez (1548–1617) — Rejects physical premotion that makes the free act inevitable apart from the will.
30. Jacobus Arminius (1560–1609) — No absolute decree necessitating Adam’s fall. Adam could have stood.
31. Benjamin Whichcote (1609–1683) — Moral evil is not necessitated by God. Divine government does not cancel created liberty.
32. Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688) — Attacks “neoteric” divine fatalism: decrees that make all actions necessary are contrary to the ancient church.

text:
🇺🇲 🇨🇦 Trump spent his first year threatening to make Canada the 51st state. Wednesday, von der Leyen invited Canada to become the EU's first-ever associate member instead, a status the bloc has never used before, and by Thursday morning Carney was standing in Strasbourg accepting it to a lengthy standing ovation.

Neither leader said Trump's name once. They didn't need to. Carney's line, "economic integration is now being used as a weapon, and tariffs as a means of leverage," and von der Leyen's own invitation a day earlier landed the same day Trump told reporters he'd consider the whole arrangement a "hostile act" and threatened "very serious tariffs" on Europe in response, an explicit threat against the EU triggered by an offer extended to a third country. That is Washington threatening to punish Brussels for what Ottawa might accept.

⚠️ The polling is the number that should worry Washington more than the speech itself. Abacus Data found 56% of Canadians now feel they have more in common with the EU than the US, just 16% say the reverse, and 81% support deeper Canada-EU integration. That's not elite diplomatic maneuvering running ahead of public opinion, it's public opinion that has already moved, with Ottawa catching up to where Canadians already are.

What makes this genuinely new, not just Davos rhetoric repeated, is that "associate member" is undefined and unprecedented, which is precisely the point. Carney was careful to say Canada isn't pursuing full EU membership, and his own government spent the past week downplaying the label after it leaked via the Wall Street Journal. 

But the substance he outlined, deeper integration on trade, defense, critical minerals, AI, energy, space and financial services, is a hedging strategy explicitly built to reduce Canada's dependency on a single unpredictable partner, dressed in language about sovereignty rather than realignment.

The Atlantic Council's Batchik framed the mechanism precisely: Trump has been "pulling his punches toward adversaries, top of mind Russia and China, and doubling down and taking a rather gleeful approach to needling previous would-be allies." 

A trade war intended to bring Canada to heel instead helped elect the government now negotiating its way into Europe's institutional orbit, a result opposite to the one the pressure campaign was built to produce.

text:
‘Reasonable grounds’ to believe US committed war crimes in Iran – UN
Indiscriminate attacks, such as the strike on an elementary school in Minab, went beyond negligence, a new report has found
Published 17 Sep, 2026 (FULL)
https://t.co/3XSP8oHeeE
A UN fact-finding mission has found reasonable grounds to believe the US committed war crimes by carrying out indiscriminate strikes on civilian targets in Iran, according to a new report.
The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran released its findings to the UN Human Rights Council on Thursday, focusing in part on two strikes it described as “emblematic” of the conflict and involving “significant violations” of international law.
The first was the February 28 double strike on an elementary school in Minab. The mission said credible information confirmed 157 deaths, including 123 children aged 13 and younger.
Investigators identified the weapon as a Tomahawk Land Attack Missile (TLAM), used only by the US during the conflict. Citing evidence including internal Pentagon investigations and Washington’s failure to explain the incident, the mission concluded that the school had been deliberately targeted, apparently on the basis of outdated intelligence.
The site had been part of an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) compound before 2016, but the school had been separated from the military facility by a wall for more than a decade. Investigators said it was clearly identifiable as a civilian site and found no evidence it was being used for military purposes.
The second incident involved a strike on a sports complex and surrounding residential area in Lamerd, Fars Province. The mission said the attack killed and injured 22 civilians and damaged nearby homes and a school.
Investigators said a US-made Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) detonated in the air, dispersing around 180,000 tungsten pellets over a wide area.
In both cases, the mission concluded that US conduct went beyond negligence and amounted to the war crime of launching an indiscriminate attack resulting in civilian deaths, injuries or damage to civilian property. It said the US had failed to adequately verify targeting information despite the risk to civilians.
The report also cited rhetoric from senior US officials, including President Donald Trump and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, which investigators said indicated a “deprioritization of civilian harm mitigation” and compliance with international humanitarian law.
Hegseth had called for the US military to be “more lethal” and said American forces would give “no quarter” to their enemies, drawing criticism from lawmakers and legal experts over the implications for prisoners of war.
Trump has repeatedly criticized the UN, accusing it of failing to resolve international conflicts and of bias against Israel, which joined the US in launching the war against Iran. His administration has also withdrawn Washington from several UN bodies and agencies.
The fact-finding mission separately accused Iranian authorities of serious violations during their 2025-2026 crackdown on mass protests, concluding that some abuses amounted to crimes against humanity.
Trump publicly backed the protesters and offered them US protection, while Tehran accused Washington of supporting unrest as part of a failed regime-change effort.

text:
CALIFORNIA IDLE: Iconic reality show ditches Hollywood after 24 seasons https://t.co/0BCPloE5MV 

California chasing businesses from the State. 

"American Idol" will move production to the Atlanta area for its 25th season, ending a left-coast run that dates back to its 2002 debut, according to Deadline.

And the reason for the move makes the timing particularly awkward for the Golden State.

California has been desperately trying to stop film and television productions from fleeing to states such as Georgia and New Jersey. Last year, lawmakers dramatically expanded the state's film and television tax-credit program and, for the first time, opened it to a new category: large-scale competition shows.

You'd think “American Idol” might qualify; it didn't.

Under California's expanded incentive program, a “large-scale competition show” can qualify for tax credits if contestants compete over multiple episodes for money or another prize, with winners selected by judges, an audience, or another competitive mechanism.

That certainly sounds like “American Idol.” But California's rules also exclude “traditional reality, game shows, talk shows, or docufollow television programming” from the new category, and Deadline reports that “Idol” did not qualify for the state's credit.

Georgia presents a considerably more attractive proposition. The state offers qualifying film and television productions that spend at least $500,000 in Georgia a 20% base tax credit, with another 10% available under certain conditions. Unscripted and reality productions can qualify.

For a sprawling production such as “American Idol,” that's real money.

text:
There is no scientific evidence that mind-altering drugs enhance productivity or creativity in the tech industry; in fact, research indicates the opposite. 

Productivity vs. Drug Use Reality
•Decreased Cognitive Function: Scientific studies show that substances like cannabis and LSD impair divergent thinking, the core component of creative problem-solving.  High doses of THC decrease creative capacity, while psychedelics like LSD reduce the brain's ability to organize and categorize information, hindering the application of novel ideas.
•Short-Term Gains, Long-Term Loss: While stimulants like Adderall and cocaine may provide a temporary boost in focus or energy, experts warn these offer short-term gains at long-term costs.   As tolerance builds, users experience reduced concentration, missed deadlines, and buggy code, ultimately derailing careers and health.
•Myth of Enhancement: The belief that microdosing or other drugs boost creativity is largely considered a myth and anecdotal.   Research suggests that creative individuals possess their abilities despite, not because of, drug use, and that substances primarily serve to help users escape reality rather than confront complex problems. 
Industry Context
Despite the lack of productivity benefits, drug use remains prevalent in Silicon Valley due to a high-pressure culture that prioritizes innovation and long hours. 

 Approximately 15–20% of software developers in the region use mind-altering substances to cope with work demands, and 35% of developers have used cannabis while coding. 

 However, this culture is increasingly criticized for glamorizing burnout and chemical shortcuts, which are described as "shortcuts to collapse" rather than paths to genuine innovation.

USTR Greer told CBC on camera that French discoverability was not a U.S. red line. He said the press treated it like a hill Washington died on. “That’s not true at all.” What the U.S. actually objected to was Canadian streaming rules that make U.S. platforms hand a cut of revenue to their Canadian competitors and force “discoverability” placement. More properly, that is an industrial subsidy dressed up as culture. LeBlanc then announced the U.S. had “withdrawn” positions on language so Ottawa could pretend they had defended French and used that pretext to leave the table.

Labeling is the same trick. Bilingual labels were not the collapse. Autos, trucks, steel rates, and who added asks after Aug. 18 were. Carney denied Canada made last-minute requests. Greer said LeBlanc came back from Ottawa with new ones just hours before the agreement was set to be signed.

“Any deal must be approved by the U.S.” is also inflated. The live fight was whether Canada would align on third-country tariffs and China backdoors not a colonial veto stamp. And “first refusal on critical minerals” was listed by Greer as cooperation in the offer, not the reason Canada walked.

If those three terms really sank the deal, Leblanc should publish the term sheet. Until then this is sovereignty theater after Canada refused an Article 34.7 review.

Crypto rebounds after Fed hike; tax bill advances and portfolio reaches $126,200

Bitcoin rose 0.9% over 24 hours to about $76,600, while Ether gained 1.1% to roughly $2,444 in CoinDesk�s market report. The recovery extended well beyond the two largest coins: 94 of its 100 index constituents were higher, and smaller tokens outpaced the largest assets. Equity futures also advanced. US spot Bitcoin ETFs nevertheless recorded another roughly $296 million of net outflows, showing that the price rebound has yet to coincide with renewed demand through those funds.

The Federal Reserve raised its policy rate by a quarter point to 3.75%�4.00%, with all 12 voters supporting the decision. Its statement described solid economic activity and persistently elevated inflation. CoinDesk reported that policymakers� median projections implied only one further quarter-point increase through the end of next year. That limited projected tightening helped frame the market response, although the forecasts are conditional and the rally cannot be attributed to one announcement alone. Higher rates continue to make cash and short-term government debt more competitive with risky assets.

In Washington, the House Ways and Means Committee approved the Digital Asset Tax Certainty Act by 38 votes to five and sent it to the full House. The proposal addresses small transactions, income recognition, staking, mining and broker requirements. Clearer treatment could reduce the accounting friction of using crypto for ordinary payments. This is a committee advance, with further legislative steps still required before any provisions become law. The bipartisan vote gives crypto tax legislation some momentum following the separate market-structure bill�s Senate setback.

Bitnomial would create and administer the markets and clear the contracts, while NinjaTrader Clearing would carry approved customer accounts. Regulatory approval remains a condition. The proposal could connect a public blockchain order book with regulated US derivatives infrastructure and expand access to onchain products. It does not open Hyperliquid�s existing markets to all US users, and Payward has not announced a launch date.

text:
Now let’s do the same comparison for the USA. We’ll assume a single person in Columbus, Ohio, receiving

Average annual salary $69,770.

Assuming only single coverage, average health insurance cost $8650, over which employers typically pay 83%, adding $7179.50 to the gross

For this person, there’s a state unemployment tax on employers of $256.50 per year

Now let’s run the numbers for, say, a single person living in Columbus, OH.

Federal income tax: $6798
FICA tax: $5337 (social security and medicare) (employer-matched)
State income tax: $1145
Local income tax: $1744
Health insurance contribution: $1471

So total deductions:

$16,495

What about the gross?

$69770 + $5337 + $7180 + $256.50  = $82,543.50

Take-home is $69770 - $16495 = $53275

So the dedication from gross employer costs is ($82543.50-$53275)/$82543.50  = 0.355

36%

But it isn’t as simple as that, is it? The worker here will still have a substantial deductible to pay on all health costs, does not get proper holiday pay, and doesn’t receive a range of other benefits.

And most companies offer family cover; if our person has dependents, the company is likely to be paying substantially more - single people are prized by employers for their lower cost of employment!

So I don’t think it is reasonable to say that the European experience is fundamentally different to the US experience.

Another $8000 in our example is not unusual, and would make the total like-for-like cost the same as Europe.

text:
GayCities asked this week if gay-exclusive resorts are still a thing.

The answers split the way they always do.

Some men want a week where nobody has to translate themselves. Same pool. Same bar. Same assumption that the guy next to you already knows the code.

Others say the exclusive resort now feels like a museum of a version of gay life that used not to have options.

Both can be true at the same time.

The old circuit existed because the regular world was not safe or interesting. The new circuit exists because some men still do not want to spend vacation explaining their presence to a honeymoon couple from Ohio.

What changed is not the desire for a room full of other gay men. What changed is that plenty of us can now get that energy in ordinary cities, ordinary hotels, ordinary Tuesday nights.

So the exclusive resort has to offer something the algorithm cannot: actual proximity without a profile.

If the place is just rainbow merch and a DJ who peaked in 2014, it is finished.

If it is still one of the few rooms where you do not have to perform being fine with being the only one, it will keep selling out.
The question was never whether gay resorts should exist.

It is whether they still know what they are for.

text:
A client accused me of respecting his customers' privacy.

I was an Active Listening salesman at Cox Media Group. Naturally, I asked him to lower his voice.

He owned a roofing company. I had explained that our service could identify nearby people talking about needing a new roof. Their phones would hear them. Our technology would find them. He would get there before the other roofers.

He liked this very much. He had spent 19 years answering the phone whenever it rang and was ready for the phone to do some of the work.

Then he asked to hear somebody.

This had never been my favorite part of the presentation.

We sold email addresses bought from data brokers. You could sort them alphabetically. You could email them. If you put your ear to the file, you would have a difficult afternoon.

But the brochure offered listening, and he had brought his own mouth.

"I need a roof," he said to his phone.

We waited.

"I need a NEW roof."

He looked at my laptop. I looked at it too. A meeting invitation arrived. I moved it off the screen before he could see that somebody had contacted us on purpose.

He asked how long it took.

I said the system looked for natural conversations. He was delivering a command.

He accepted this criticism. Roofers understand the importance of preparing a surface.

He called his wife.

"I've been thinking about our roof," he said.

She reminded him that he had replaced it himself in March.

He covered the microphone and asked me whether the algorithm could hear her undermining the sale.

I said contradictions could affect the result.

He uncovered it.

"Nevertheless, as a homeowner within 10 miles of Orlando, I am dissatisfied."

His wife asked if he had been drinking.

I took this as evidence that the conversation sounded spontaneous.

He tried again with the receptionist's phone. She wanted to know why. I told her we were demonstrating a product. She wanted to know which product required him to breathe directly into her charger port.

I asked her to give us a moment.

The client had a fair objection. If I could find strangers discussing their roofs in their kitchens, I should be able to find a roofer discussing a roof in front of me.

I explained that he was already a roofing professional. The system might have recognized him as supply.

He took off his company fleece.

I respected that. He was meeting us halfway.

Underneath he had another shirt with the company name on it. His wife had ordered them in bulk. He turned it inside out and sat down again.

"My roof," he said, carefully, "is fucked."

The receptionist looked up.

I asked her to stop contaminating the demonstration with responses.

By then he wanted to see the audience list. I opened it. There were people all over the country.

He pointed to an address in Minnesota.

I asked whether he had considered expansion.

He said he had 2 vans.

I said I admired a business with room to grow.

He asked me to draw the 10-mile territory he was buying. I drew it around his office. He moved the center slightly to include a new development, then slightly again to exclude his own street.

His family had conversations there.

I made the adjustment.

After 70 minutes, he still hadn't received a lead.

He put his fleece back on.

"What am I actually paying you for?"

I started to explain the technology partnership. He said he had heard that part. I started to explain buyer intent. He said he had demonstrated that part.

Then the receptionist came over.

Her brother needed a roofer. Water was coming through the kitchen ceiling. She had been trying to ask whether the man shouting about roofs was available on Thursday.

I asked where her brother lived.

8 miles away.

I held up a finger. I needed everyone to appreciate what had just happened before anybody described it accurately.

Local. Real need. A conversation.

The client looked at me.

I looked at the phone.

He booked the job.

I put the brochure back between us and asked whether he wanted to reserve his territory before another roofer did.

He signed.

I took the receptionist to lunch. I asked whether anybody else in her family owned a house.

I expensed her as a data broker.

text:
“The Dirty Duchess”

The breathtaking Margaret Whigham, photographed by Cecil Beaton in 1934. On 22 March 1951, Margaret, who was England’s premier socialite and a reigning beauty, became the third wife of Ian Douglas Campbell, 11th Duke of Argyll. She wrote later: “I had wealth, I had good looks. I was constantly photographed, written about, flattered, admired. I had become a duchess and mistress of a historic castle. All was roses.” But not for long. She had married a stinker. Before their wedding, the Duke had forged a deed of sale (which offered items from his castle as security) in exchange for Margaret’s money, which he used to restore his family home. He also wiretapped her car. Margaret retaliated by faking letters that sowed doubt about the fatherhood of her husband's sons, and even tried to acquire a baby she could pass off as his rightful heir. Within a few years, the marriage was over. The Duke was known to be addicted to alcohol, gambling and prescription drugs, and was physically violent and emotionally abusive. He suspected Margaret of having lovers - do you blame her? - and, while she was in New York, broke open a cupboard in their Mayfair home. The evidence discovered resulted in an infamous 1963 divorce case, in which the Duke accused his wife of serial infidelity and produced a set of Polaroid photographs of the Duchess nude, except for a pearl necklace, in the company of another man. There were also pictures of Margaret fellating a lover, whose face was not shown. It was speculated that the “headless man" was the Minister of Defence, Duncan Sandys, who offered to resign from the cabinet. Dismayed, Margaret counter-petitioned, accusing the Duke of adultery with her stepmother, Jane Corby Whigham. She dropped the case the day of the hearing due to the lack of witnesses, and later had to pay her stepmother £25,000 in damages. A list of the 88 men with whom the Duke claimed his wife had consorted was then produced in court, creating an absolute frenzy. It was said to include two government ministers, Douglas Fairbanks Jr. and three members of the royal family. The judge commented, in a rather sexist manner, that the Duchess had indulged in "disgusting sexual activities". The government tried to identify the "headless man", comparing the handwriting of the five leading "suspects", (Duncan Sandys; Douglas Fairbanks Jr.; John Cohane, an American businessman; Peter Combe, a press officer at the Savoy Hotel; and Sigismund von Braun, brother of the German scientist Wernher von Braun) with the captions written on the photographs. It was claimed that the analysis proved it was Fairbanks, then married to his second wife, but the allegation was kept secret. Granting the divorce, Lord Wheatley, the presiding judge, said the evidence established that Margaret “was a completely promiscuous woman whose sexual appetite could only be satisfied with a large number of men". He continued: "Her attitude to the sanctity of marriage was what moderns would call 'enlightened' but which in plain language was wholly immoral." The Duchess never revealed the identity of the "headless man", and Fairbanks always denied it was him. text:
I moved to Florida in 2022 in search of my own little sliver of the Florida Dream and boy did I find it!

Since arriving in the Sunshine State, I have expanded my public relations firm, launched additional business ventures, developed a growing television career as a Newsmax contributor and built a life in a place where ambition and hard work is celebrated and rewarded rather than punished.

My experience is hardly unique. Millions of people have chosen Florida because they recognize what David Jolly apparently cannot: This is the greatest state in the nation and we have absolutely nothing to apologize for.
Yet Jolly has talked about apologizing to the nation “on behalf of Florida.” 

More recently, he declared on MSNBC that Floridians are “desperate” for change.

Desperate for what, exactly?

Are we desperate to become New York, where families and businesses are driven away by high taxes, crime and suffocating government? Are we desperate to become California, where radical policies have produced homelessness, lawlessness and an affordability crisis? Are we desperate to surrender the freedom, safety and opportunity that have made Florida one of America’s most desirable destinations?

No, David. We are not desperate. We are proud of our state and the values we champion.

Florida’s population has exploded in recent years because Americans have been voting with their feet. During the four years following the 2020 Census, Florida added roughly 1.8 million residents. From July 2023 to July 2024 alone, our state gained more than 467,000 people.

People do not pack up their families, leave behind their communities and move hundreds or thousands of miles because they are attracted to failure. They come here because Florida offers something increasingly difficult to find elsewhere in our upside down world: freedom, opportunity, safety and the chance to build a better life.
They come here to pursue the Florida Dream.

Jolly’s “apologize to the nation” tour is falling flat because it fundamentally misunderstands the people he is asking to govern. Floridians are not ashamed of our state. We are fiercely proud of it. Ask any of my friends around the country and the world how I speak about Florida. I’ve become a de facto Ambassador for the State of Florida telling the world how amazing life is here!

We will not apologize for supporting the men and women of law enforcement who put their lives on the line to protect our communities.

We will not apologize for expanding access to high-quality education, empowering parents and ensuring that a child’s future is not dictated by his or her ZIP code.

We will not apologize for defending women and girls by drawing a clear line in the sand: Biological males should not compete in female sports or take athletic opportunities away from our daughters.

We will not apologize for confronting radicalism. Florida has taken action against the Council on American-Islamic Relations and designated it a terrorist organization under state law. While politicians elsewhere bend the knee to activist pressure, Florida has demonstrated that protecting its residents must come before political correctness.

And as a Jewish American, I will never apologize for living in a state where Jewish families can worship, raise their children and walk through their communities with pride. At a time when Jews in places such as New York and Michigan are confronting frightening antisemitism, harassment and intimidation, Florida has made clear that Jewish residents will not be abandoned.

That is not something requiring an apology. It is something worth defending at all costs.

Jolly’s rhetoric also reveals the central choice in this election. He looks at Florida and sees something embarrassing that must be changed. Byron Donalds sees a successful state that must be protected and made even stronger.

Byron understands the Florida Dream because he has lived it. He believes in supporting law enforcement, defending parental rights, protecting women’s sports, strengthening Florida’s economy and ensuring that Jewish families can live, worship and raise their children without fear.

Most importantly, Byron Donalds does not believe Florida should be remade in the image of failed blue states. He believes our next governor must build upon the foundation that has made Florida a beacon of freedom for the entire country.

That is the leadership Floridians deserve. We certainly face real challenges. Housing and insurance costs are too high. Traffic and infrastructure must keep pace with our growing population. Families need relief, and our economy must continue creating opportunities for the next generation.

But solving those problems does not require apologizing for Florida. It requires fighting for Florida.

David Jolly may have spent too much time in MSNBC’s studios to understand why Americans are flocking here. Perhaps he has forgotten what makes this state so exceptional. But the people building families, businesses and futures here have not. We know exactly what Florida represents.

Florida represents freedom. Florida represents security. Florida represents opportunity. Florida represents the belief that hard work, faith and personal responsibility still matter.

No, David Jolly, we are not desperate for your version of change. We are not apologizing for anything.

We are proud to be Floridians, and we are going to keep Florida free by electing Byron Donalds as our 47th governor.

If Jolly finds that so embarrassing, he can always go back to MSNBC.

text:
WHEN A LOVED ONE LEAVES BEHIND A HOME
Losing a family member is difficult enough. Having to figure out what happens to their home can make an already emotional time even more overwhelming.
Is there a Will or Trust? Does the property have to go through probate? Who has authority to sell it? What happens to the mortgage, insurance, HOA and belongings? Should the property be repaired or sold as-is? Can it be listed immediately, or does the family have to wait?
As a Certified Probate Specialist (CPS) and Real Estate Concierge, I can help families navigate the real estate side of this process in coordination with their probate attorney and title professionals.
Where should a family begin?
1. Locate the estate documents. Find the Will, Trust and other estate-planning documents.
2. Gather the property documents. This may include the deed, mortgage information, insurance, property taxes, HOA/condo documents, leases and other records.
3. Determine how the property is titled. Property owned individually may be handled differently from property owned jointly, with survivorship rights or through a Trust.
4. Consult a qualified Florida probate attorney. The attorney can determine whether probate is necessary, who has legal authority to act for the estate and whether Florida homestead or other estate issues apply.
5. Protect the property. Secure the home and maintain appropriate insurance, utilities, A/C, landscaping, pool service and other essential maintenance.
6. Confirm who has authority to act. Being an heir or beneficiary does not necessarily mean someone presently has authority to list or sell the property.
7. Coordinate with the probate attorney and title professionals before selling. Confirm who may sign the listing agreement, negotiate and accept an offer, execute the contract and ultimately transfer title.
8. Develop the appropriate real estate strategy. Should the property be sold as-is? Would repairs improve its value? Does it need a cleanout, estate sale, inspection or professional preparation? What is it worth in today's market?
THIS IS WHERE I CAN HELP.
My role is to organize and manage the real estate side of the process.
I can assist with property valuation and market analysis, property condition assessment, as-is versus repair strategy, inspections, contractors and property maintenance, cleanout and estate-sale resources, preparation and marketing, offer evaluation, and coordination with the family's probate attorney and title professionals through closing.
I've also developed a structured probate real estate process using:
Family Probate Real Estate Intake Probate Attorney Transaction Questionnaire Probate Listing Intake & Agent Audit
The objective is to identify potential issues early, establish who has authority to act, and make sure the real estate transaction does not get ahead of the probate and title process.
The probate attorney manages the estate. I help manage the property.
If your family is dealing with real estate after the loss of a loved one, you don't have to know every step before contacting me. I can help you organize the real estate side of the process and coordinate with the appropriate professionals.

This information is for general educational purposes and is not legal, tax, accounting or financial advice. Probate, homestead, inheritance, trust and title matters should be reviewed by qualified Florida professionals.

Myrtice Cato: Sworn for the State, Wednesday, August 20, 1913

Her testimony, the defense’s objections, and the court’s rulings

Myrtice Cato and Maggie Griffin testified for the prosecution concerning Leo Frank and Rebecca Carson’s visits to the fourth-floor women’s dressing room. Their evidence directly contradicted Carson’s denial of entering the room with Frank (Brief of Evidence, 4).

The Atlanta Constitution, Thursday, August 21, 1913: Girls Testify to Seeing Frank Enter Dressing Room With Woman

The Constitution reported Cato’s answer concerning how often she had seen Frank and Carson enter together: “Twice.” Under questioning by defense attorney Luther Rosser, she placed the occasions at “About 10 o’clock one morning and one afternoon.” Asked for the date, she answered, “I don’t remember exactly, but it was this year.”

The defense formally protested the court’s decision permitting questions about Frank’s sexual character. Solicitor Hugh Dorsey argued Frank’s claim of a virtuous life permitted the prosecution to challenge his character. He also sought to discredit Carson’s testimony through witnesses who contradicted her denial.

The Constitution separately attributed three or four sightings to Griffin, together with estimates of 15 to 30 minutes inside the room. Rosser objected to retaining the duration testimony. Dorsey argued the length of the visits could support an inference about the pair’s conduct. Judge Leonard S. Roan ruled the time question irrelevant to contradicting Carson’s denial. The duration estimates therefore cannot be presented as evidence the judge allowed the jury to consider (AC, 1).

The Atlanta Journal, Wednesday, August 20, 1913: Testimony May Close Wednesday

The Journal supplied additional reasons for Rosser’s objections. He argued the defense’s female witnesses had been called to answer Jim Conley’s testimony. He also maintained Carson’s earlier testimony concerned conduct in Frank’s office. Before Dorsey could contradict her concerning the dressing room, Rosser demanded her recall for questioning about the specific incident.

Roan permitted evidence contradicting a defense witness, while continuing to exclude evidence offered to establish a separate crime of adultry. Carson was recalled and denied entering the dressing room with Frank.

When Cato was recalled, Rosser rose to object to Dorsey’s question about seeing the pair enter together. Cato answered before he could finish. Following an argument, Roan allowed her answer to remain.

The Journal quoted Cato describing two sightings: “I never saw it but twice,” before volunteering additional knowledge. Rosser interrupted: “Wait a minute!” Later, when she again suggested she had seen more, he interrupted: “Wait a minute! Stop!”

These interruptions occurred alongside formal objections, but the report does not record a separate ruling on each interruption. Rosser also challenged Cato’s speculation about whether other workers noticed the incident. She acknowledged she did not know (AJ, 2).

The Atlanta Georgian, Wednesday, August 20, 1913: State Closes. Frank Case Near Jury

The Georgian described the defense’s objection to questions concerning lasciviousness, meaning sexually improper conduct. Rosser relied on the court’s earlier restrictions and requested the jury’s removal during the legal argument:

“Let the jury retire if he is going to argue this, but your honor has already ruled.”

Dorsey argued Frank’s own statement permitted further questioning. He also proposed using the dressing-room incident to challenge a defense witness’s credibility. Roan allowed questions about Frank’s general reputation for sexual conduct and directed the prosecution toward questioning Carson before contradicting her.

Rosser then asked whether the court was permitting this character inquiry in a murder trial. Roan answered: “I do.”

The Georgian’s summary assigned two sightings to Cato. Its question-and-answer account instead attributed “Three or four times” to her. This internal inconsistency prevents treating its reported count as uniform.

The Georgian also recorded sustained objections during Griffin’s questioning about the visits’ duration and time of day. The Constitution and Journal identify the duration evidence as excluded (AG, 3).

The Brief of Evidence: What the Joint Entry Records

The Brief of Evidence combines Cato and Griffin’s dressing-room testimony in one paragraph. It identifies both as sworn witnesses for the State and records their claim of seeing Rebecca Carson enter the fourth-floor women’s dressing room with Leo M. Frank “two or three times during working hours.” Other women were working on the fourth floor when the incidents occurred.

The joint entry contains no duration estimate and no description of sexual activity inside the room. It preserves the allegation of repeated entry during working hours. Carson’s denial and the women’s contrary testimony presented a question of credibility for the jury. The defense secured limits on the questioning, but Cato and Griffin’s central allegation remained in the recorded evidence (Brief of Evidence, 4).

text:
You won't believe Duop's story: 

Reath, whose NBA journey began as a 27 year old rookie, battled an uphill climb from day one.  

Born in what is modern day South Sudan during a second Civil War, he lived in a small hut— no shoes, no bed. In 2001, forced into a Kenyan Refugee camp, his parents provided the best they could & searched for a better future. 

In 2005, he & his family moved 8,000 miles to live with his uncle in Australia. He didn't know English, couldn't read or write, was homesick, & missed his friends. 

In Perth, Duop's interests shifted from soccer to basketball where he thrived. He was discovered through tournaments & was offered a scholarship to Lee college from Marcus King.

He was pushed hard, but worked harder. Playing against strong competition, his skills developed fast & so did his recognition from scouts. From Lee college he transferred to LSU, put up solid numbers, but went undrafted in the 2018 NBA draft. 

From a Dallas Mavericks Summer league chance, European league teams, a Brooklyn Nets Summer league stint, back to the NBL, a Phoenix Suns Summer league that ended with an ankle injury, to China & West Asia; Reath never gave up on his dream. 

After improving & impressing every stop along the way, finally, Duop got his fourth Summer league invite— this time with the Portland Trail Blazers. 

He averaged 13 points & 7.4 rebounds, earning his spot. Although he was among the Blazers' final Summer cuts. Portland then gave him a two-way contract. He didn't disappoint. 
After just one superb G-League game scoring 37 points, 10 rebounds & 2 blocks, Duop played the rest of his games that season with the Blazers, never looking back to the G-league. 

When it came time that Reath's 50 game eligibility expired, Portland signed him to a three year, $6.2 million contract converting him to a full-time roster spot. 

Finally, his life-long journey from South Sudan to Kenya to Australia to Texas to Louisiana to Serbia to China to Lebanon back to Australia then finally to Portland— Duop Reath had truly made it.

His story is one of resilience & overcoming the odds, turning his struggle into success.

Portland will always love & appreciate what you gave on the floor & what you stand for. 

Thank you Duop. Good luck in Phoenix!
— #ripcity

Seattle’s Business Chamber Still Begging Katie Wilson to Do Something About Crime
Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce President and CEO Joe Nguyen — a former Democratic state senator — co-signed a letter with more than 30 business leaders from Microsoft, Nordstrom, Starbucks, Costco, and Alaska Airlines demanding a 100-day public safety action plan from Mayor Katie Wilson.

The letter highlighted a damning statistic: Nordstrom’s downtown flagship receives a police response to just 29% of its 911 calls, compared with 100% at its Bellevue and Southcenter locations. Nguyen called the number a clear example of how the city is failing to deliver basic services.

Nguyen, who once supported taxes the business community opposed, now says progressive leadership too often offers “lip service” instead of results. He pointed to the temporary public-safety improvements during the World Cup that quickly faded, and noted that similar jobs cost $12,000 to $17,000 more in Seattle than in Bellevue according to the mayor’s own office.

He argued that a strong economy and progressive values are not separate — nearly 70% of Seattle’s tax base comes from economic activity — and that elected officials have “abdicated their responsibility to govern” by outsourcing leadership to advocates instead of serving the people who elected them.

This is what progressive governance in Seattle has produced: major employers and a former Democratic lawmaker publicly pleading for the city to restore basic police response and economic stability. When even the Chamber has to beg for a 100-day plan, the failure of the current approach is impossible to ignore. Read more at https://t.co/jlHYgSio6j.

text:
📜 HOOK & AUTHENTIC QUOTE

"We are tired because we are living in a culture that measures human worth by economic output, mistaking exhaustion for virtue."

Franz Kafka captured the quiet horror of this a century ago in *The Metamorphosis*: 

"I have to get up at five. The trains leave at five. If I don't catch that train, I'm done for... It's the torture of traveling, the worries of changing trains, the irregular, bad meals, human relationships that are perpetually changing, never taking root, never warming you."

Gregor Samsa didn't wake up transformed into a monstrous bug because of bad luck. He woke up that way because he was already a cog, consumed by the relentless demands of his employer, running on an endless treadmill of compliance and output. 

⚡ THE MODERN MIRROR

Fast forward to today, and Kafka’s 1915 nightmare has been rebranded as "lifestyle design." 

We no longer just work jobs; we perform our productivity for an invisible jury. Hustle culture took the Protestant work ethic, stripped it of its spiritual meaning, and weaponized it into an aesthetic of self-exploitation. 

We wake up with our phones in our hands, answering emails before our feet touch the floor. We glorify the 80-hour work week, drink chemical stimulants to mimic energy, and wear chronic fatigue like a badge of honor. "Rise and grind" is just Kafka’s traveling salesman mantra repeated back to us through a ring light. 

🧠 DEEP ANALYSIS

1. The Internalized Overseer
In the past, tyrants whipped workers from the outside. Today, we have internalized the plantation owner. We police our own rest. If we take an afternoon to sit idly, a low-grade panic sets in—the terrifying sensation that we are falling behind in a race with no finish line.

2. The Commodity of the Self
Under the tyranny of modern productivity, everything must be monetized. Hobbies must become side hustles. Rest must be optimized ("sleep hygiene" so we can perform better tomorrow). When your entire existence is viewed through the lens of ROI, you stop being a human being and become a human resource. 

3. The Illusion of Agency
We are told we "chose" this path—that the gig economy and side-hustle life offer ultimate freedom. But as Kafka understood, true tyranny is when the prisoner falls in love with his chains, proudly showing them off to other prisoners on LinkedIn to prove how hard he is working.

4. The Death of Depth
When you are perpetually exhausted, your capacity for deep thought, empathy, and genuine connection withers. Burnout creates a population too tired to question the structures keeping them enslaved. Exhaustion is the ultimate social sedative.

💡 THE PHILOSOPHICAL TAKEAWAY

Kafka’s tragedy wasn't that Gregor woke up as an insect. It was that Gregor's first thought, upon realizing he had transformed into a monstrous bug, wasn't "I am suffering," but rather: *"How am I going to explain this to my boss and catch the 5:00 AM train?"*

We are doing the exact same thing. Our bodies scream at us with autoimmune disorders, brain fog, and chronic anxiety—and our response is to look for a better productivity app or a stronger cup of coffee.

True freedom is not found in the next milestone, the side-hustle revenue, or the optimized schedule. It is found in the radical, terrifying act of stepping off the train. Sometimes, the most revolutionary thing you can do is simply to rest, remember your humanity, and let the world wait. 

#HustleCulture #Burnout #Philosophy #MentalHealth #Kafka #DeepWork #ModernSociety

text:
My father opened his door before I knocked.

He lived in a small brick house in Decatur, the same house where I grew up after my mother’s funeral turned him from a husband into a widower overnight. He was sixty-eight, retired from the postal service, and still the kind of man who ironed his jeans on Sunday evenings.

When he saw me soaked from the rain, suitcase in one hand and Maple’s leash in the other, his face changed.

Not with surprise.

With recognition.

As if some part of him had been waiting for the night I finally came home.

He did not ask questions at first. He took the suitcase, wrapped a towel around my shoulders, and made tea the way he used to when I had the flu as a child. Maple jumped onto his couch despite never being allowed on furniture, and my father said nothing.

Only after I had changed into dry clothes did he sit across from me and ask, “Did he hurt you?”

I knew what he meant.

“No,” I said. “Not like that.”

My father’s jaw tightened. “There are many ways to hurt a person.”

Then I cried.

I cried so hard I could not speak. Eleven years of swallowed shame came out of me in ugly, breathless pieces: the failed treatments, the comments, the humiliation, Madison in my kitchen, Nathan telling me I could not give him a family.

My father listened without interrupting.

When I finished, he stood, walked into his bedroom, and came back with an old cardboard box. Inside were folders, receipts, papers, and things he had saved from my childhood because he believed documentation mattered even when life felt emotional.

He placed an empty folder on the table.

On the tab, he wrote one word.

Nathan.

“From now on,” he said, “we keep records.”

That was the most American sentence my father ever spoke.

Not because Americans are cold, but because in this country, when a marriage becomes a legal fight, memories are not enough. You need bank statements, text messages, mortgage records, insurance documents, medical files, emails, dates, screenshots, and a lawyer who understands the difference between being hurt and being protected.
My lawyer’s name was Denise Carter.

She worked out of a small office near downtown Atlanta with a receptionist who called everyone “honey” and a conference room that smelled faintly of coffee and printer ink. Denise wore navy suits, asked direct questions, and did not blink when I told her my husband had thrown me out for a younger woman.

But when I told her he planned to claim the house was his alone, she looked over her glasses.

“Did you contribute to the household?”

“Yes. I paid utilities, groceries, insurance, some renovations.”

“Do you have records?”

“My father says we will.”

Denise smiled slightly. “I like your father.”

Nathan’s first offer was insulting.

He wanted to keep the house, the savings account, both cars, and most of the furniture. He offered me what he called “a clean break,” which meant enough money for a few months’ rent and nothing else.

He also wanted Maple.

Denise read the proposal and said, “He is not asking for a divorce. He is asking you to disappear.”

That was exactly what Nathan wanted.

He wanted me gone quietly so he could move Madison into the house, repaint the spare room, and tell people our marriage had ended because I could not handle the pain of infertility. He wanted sympathy without accountability. He wanted to be both the wounded husband and the romantic hero starting over.

For a while, he got away with it…..

NIGERIAN NAVY APPLAUDS FEDERAL HIGH COURT, UYO CONVICTION OF NINE CRUDE OIL THIEVES ARRESTED UNDER OPERATION DELTA SENTINEL

The Nigerian Navy @NigerianNavy has welcomed the conviction of nine crude oil thieves by the Federal High Court, Uyo, describing it as a major boost in the fight against economic sabotage.

The court on 14 September 2026 sentenced the nine to five years on Count One and 10 years on Count Two, without option of fine. The convicts were arrested on 7 February 2026 during an intelligence-led operation for allegedly stealing crude from wellhead ASABO-D in Ibeno LGA, Akwa Ibom State.

The conviction underscores the impact of matching operational action with effective prosecution. Under Operation DELTA SENTINEL launched in January 2026, the Navy has dismantled over 241 illegal refining sites, recovered more than 6.44 million litres of stolen crude and refined products, and arrested over 230 suspects.

The renewed momentum is driven by the strategic leadership of the Chief of the Naval Staff, Vice Admiral Idi Abbas, in support of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s directive to raise crude oil production to 2.5 million barrels per day by 2027.

The Navy commended the Judiciary for the landmark judgment and the Department of State Services for diligent prosecution. It stressed that interdictions at sea only achieve full value when they lead to convictions that deter criminal networks, and called for accelerated adjudication of pending crude theft cases.

The Service warned all individuals and syndicates engaged in crude oil theft and illegal bunkering to desist, noting that remoteness of creeks and oil installations offers no cover from justice. It urged law-abiding citizens and host communities to continue providing credible information to protect critical national infrastructure.

The FBI’s 1970 summary of the career of former U.S. Marine turned mercenary and adventurer Gerald Patrick Hemming, Jr., notably leaps from early November 1963 to the summer of 1967, and reports the collapse of INTERPEN, his right-wing, anti-communist paramilitary group, as taking place several months before the assassination of JFK: “In September, 1963, INTERPEN no longer existed: HEMMING’s followers lost interest and felt HEMMING would never be able to launch any military action against Cuba. The majority of the recruits left Miami, others were run out of town by the police, and others were arrested for burglary, larceny, and vagrancy. During this period, HEMMING visited leading Cuban exile political figures and a number of American right-wing conservatives for donations. He travelled to Dallas, Texas; Chicago, Illinois, and other places but was unable to raise money.”

The FBI also assigned to the self-styled “Major” George W. Tanner, Jr., a leading or even founding role in creating what would become INTERPEN, in early 1961. Tanner’s version of the group was called the Anti-Communist Legionnaires, with significant financial support offered by a prominent Cuban exile leader in Miami, the Batista-era spy-master Rolando Masferrer Rojas. The ACL had numerous problems, outlined in a 1961 FBI memo: “…It soon became apparent TANNER had no knowledge of military affairs [and] was considered psychopathic, and the training camp was disbanded. TANNER left the organization, which was then taken over by GERALD PATRICK HEMMING.” (It has been suggested that Tanner and Hemming ran two different organizations at the same time, but several FBI reports indicate Hemming succeeded Tanner in the same group.)

text:
Those are actually two very important questions, because they address two different bottlenecks that existed in the original $NWBO #DCVax-L trial: the patient may not have enough functioning lymphocytes left to respond to the vaccine, and the patient may not have usable stored tumor tissue from which to manufacture DCVax-L.

1) Why IL-7 rather than IL-15 when radiation and temozolomide deplete the lymphocyte pool?

Because the immediate problem is not simply that there are too few killer cells. The problem is that the immune army itself has been depleted and narrowed.

Radiation and temozolomide can produce profound and persistent lymphopenia in GBM. In the classic prospective study of patients receiving RT/TMZ, 73% fell below 300 CD4 cells/mm³ and 40% fell below 200 at two months. Those with CD4 counts below 200 had a median survival of 13.1 months versus 19.7 months in patients with higher counts. Importantly, most deaths were from tumor progression, not opportunistic infection. (PubMed)

That matters enormously for a dendritic-cell vaccine. DCVax can present an extremely broad library of tumor antigens, but the dendritic cell still needs a sufficiently broad population of T cells capable of recognizing those instructions. DCVax-L has been shown to process and present hundreds of tumor-associated peptides through both MHC class I and class II, and vaccination produces expansion of large numbers of T-cell clonotypes.

So after lymphodepletion, you do not merely want to push the remaining cells harder. You want to rebuild the repertoire.

That is where IL-7 is fundamentally different.

IL-7 is the principal homeostatic survival signal for naïve T cells and is also important for long-lived memory populations. Human recombinant IL-7 studies showed sustained increases in both CD4 and CD8 cells, preferential expansion of naïve T cells and recent thymic emigrants, increased BCL-2 survival signaling, and, critically, a broadening of T-cell receptor diversity. The proportion of senescent CD8 effectors actually declined as the repertoire became more youthful and diverse. (PubMed)

And we now have something even more relevant: this has actually been tested in newly diagnosed high-grade glioma patients receiving radiation/TMZ.

The Phase I NT-I7 trial published in Clinical Cancer Research in July 2026 found that long-acting IL-7 increased absolute lymphocyte counts for more than 12 weeks, increased CD4 and CD8 cells, produced early expansion of T-stem-cell-memory cells followed by naïve T cells, and caused selective expansion of CD8 T-cell clonotypes. The investigators specifically concluded that IL-7 warrants further investigation in combination with immune-based therapies in high-grade glioma. (PubMed)

That is almost exactly the biological problem we have been discussing.

IL-15 is different.

IL-15 is extremely important immunologically, and it absolutely participates in memory CD8 biology. But its dominant effect is on NK cells and already antigen-experienced CD8 T cells. It is much more of an effector amplifier than a repertoire-rebuilding cytokine. Human IL-15 trials illustrate this vividly: systemic IL-15 causes dramatic proliferation of NK cells and memory CD8 cells. Continuous infusion produced roughly a 38-fold increase in NK cells but only a 5.8-fold increase in CD8 T cells. (PubMed)

That may be very useful when the objective is to amplify cytotoxicity. It is not the same thing as reconstructing the broad naïve and renewable T-cell compartment that chemotherapy and radiation have damaged.

There is also an important exhaustion issue. It would be too absolute to say that IL-15 inherently causes exhaustion, because IL-15 can support memory CD8 cells and, under some conditions, even progenitor-exhausted T cells. But dose, timing and antigenic context matter enormously. New 2026 experimental work under repetitive TCR stimulation found that high-dose IL-15 drove CD8 cells toward an exhausted phenotype through STAT5, with increased inhibitory-receptor expression and loss of stem-like characteristics. (PubMed) That is precisely the direction one would want to avoid in a cancer like GBM, where antigen is persistent and durable immune surveillance matters more than a short burst of cytotoxic expansion.

So I would frame the distinction very simply:

IL-7 rebuilds the army and restores its diversity.

DCVax teaches that army what the tumor looks like.

IL-15 can amplify selected fighters, but amplification is not the same as reconstruction.

That is why IL-7 makes much more biological sense as the lymphopenia-recovery layer around a broad dendritic-cell vaccine. You want naïve cells, stem-like memory cells, CD4 help, CD8 precursors and broad TCR diversity available when the dendritic cells arrive with hundreds of tumor targets. You do not want to merely inflate the ALC by preferentially expanding a restricted set of NK and previously activated CD8 cells.
And this makes Thomas’s outcome even more interesting. He achieved more than a decade of survival without IL-7 rescue. The point is not that IL-7 explains Thomas. It does not. The question is whether restoring the immune architecture that many other trial patients lost to RT/TMZ could allow a greater fraction of patients to generate the kind of durable response represented by that long survival tail.

2) What about the many patients whose tumor was never preserved properly? How can DCVax-Direct use their blood?

This is where one distinction is essential:

The blood supplies the dendritic cells. The tumor supplies the antigens.

DCVax-Direct does not attempt to find the complete tumor antigen library in a blood sample.

In the Phase I trial, patients underwent leukapheresis to collect monocytes, the precursor cells from which their autologous dendritic cells were manufactured. Those cells were differentiated, partially activated, cryopreserved, and subsequently injected directly into an accessible tumor. (PubMed Central (PMC))

Unlike DCVax-L, they are not loaded beforehand with surgically preserved tumor lysate.

That is the brilliance of the Direct concept. The dendritic cells are manufactured in a state that retains antigen-uptake capacity and then injected directly into the patient’s tumor. Northwest Biotherapeutics describes Direct as autologous, unloaded, partially activated dendritic cells, with maturation deliberately controlled so they can capture antigen after injection and subsequently mature and generate cytokines.

In other words:

the living tumor becomes the antigen source.

The injected dendritic cells encounter living and dying malignant cells, ingest their proteins and cellular material, process those antigens, and present the resulting peptides to T cells. They therefore sample the tumor in situ, instead of requiring the tumor to have been removed, frozen correctly, preserved for years and later converted into lysate.

That has another potentially important advantage: the tumor they are sampling is the tumor that exists now. A recurrent GBM may have been shaped by surgery, radiation, temozolomide and years of immunologic selection. Its antigenic landscape may therefore differ materially from the original surgical specimen. Direct theoretically allows the immune system to read the current tumor rather than relying entirely upon an archival snapshot.

And the response is not necessarily restricted to the injected lesion. In the Direct program, T-cell infiltration increased in tumors after injection, and T-cell sequences appearing in the tumor were also found in peripheral blood, supporting a systemic immune response. In the published Phase I study across diverse advanced solid tumors, increased lymphocyte infiltration occurred in 54% of assessed patients, and higher IL-12p40 and IL-8 production by the injected dendritic cells correlated with survival. (PubMed)

So for patients whose original tumor was discarded, inadequately frozen, consumed by pathology, mostly necrotic, or simply never collected for vaccine manufacture, DCVax-Direct offers a completely different solution to the antigen problem:

DCVax-L says, give me the tumor and I will teach the dendritic cell outside the body.

DCVax-Direct says, give me the patient’s dendritic-cell precursors from blood and I will send the dendritic cells into the tumor to learn the antigen library there.

That is why Direct could be so consequential practically if later trials establish efficacy. The bottleneck changes from “Did somebody preserve enough tumor years ago?” to “Is there an accessible tumor lesion that can be injected?”

And when you connect the two questions, the larger architecture becomes clear.

DCVax provides the instruction.

DCVax-Direct can obtain that instruction without requiring archived tumor lysate.

IL-7 restores the diverse, renewable T-cell population capable of receiving and remembering those instructions after chemoradiation has depleted it.

IL-15 may still have a role downstream when selective cytotoxic amplification is desired, but it is not a substitute for rebuilding the repertoire.

That is why IL-7 and Direct address two of the most important practical limitations of the original-generation platform: one restores the student population, and the other removes the requirement that the textbook have been saved at the original surgery.

text:
Cuba's economy faces its worst contraction in three decades, as inflation climbs

ECLAC projects Cuba's real GDP will contract 10.3% in 2026 (Table 1), the sharpest drop since the pandemic (-10.9% in 2020, per ONEI). That figure may be conservative. Using our own methodology, CER calculates an even steeper contraction: 15.5%. The gap reflects the weight we assign to the deteriorating value added in the state sector, which is falling even in current pesos, despite inflation. Economist Pedro Monreal, working from the official 13.4% drop in state production, puts the real contraction higher still, at 26% to 31%.

Either figure points to a worsening trajectory: GDP will post its third consecutive year of deepening contraction in 2026, and its fifth year of decline in the last seven. At our estimate of -15.5%, 2026 would surpass the pandemic and nearly match the worst year of the Special Period. Chaining the official rates since 2019, the economy would have lost about 28% of its output on our estimate, or 23% on ECLAC's.

Inflation, meanwhile, is picking up again in 2026. After closing 2025 at 14.1% year-on-year—the lowest level since 2021—it accelerated once more: from 14.4% in July 2025 to 20.7% this past July, with ECLAC projecting a year-end close near 27%. The increase stems mainly from a supply shock: the oil blockade, shortages of goods, the depreciation of the informal peso (down 56.3% so far in 2026), and monetary financing of the deficit. This is inflation that no longer responds to demand: the ongoing adjustment, which cut real current spending by 8.6% in 2025, has used up most of the room to control it through that channel.

📷

Sectoral performance depends, above all, on energy availability. The UNE's daily reports describe a year worse than 2025. On September 3, the grid had 990 MW available against peak demand of 3,250 MW — a deficit of 2,060 MW — with simultaneous blackouts across 64% of the country and nine of sixteen thermoelectric units offline. The national grid (SEN) collapsed completely six times between January and early August 2026, against five times in the previous fifteen months (October 2024 to December 2025). The new capacity installed at solar parks isn't being fully used because conventional plants and the transmission grid are in poor condition.

That bottleneck hits the two sectors that had been sustaining hard-currency income. Tourism — one of the country's main sources of foreign exchange and the engine of services exports — is deepening a slide already underway. The starting point was bad: 2025 closed with 1.8 million visitors, the lowest since 2002 and far short of the official 2.6 million target. But the 2026 pace points to fewer than 800,000, and seasonality works against it, since the first half of the year includes the high season. With hotel occupancy at 12.9% (Table 2), the capacity built up over a decade of priority investment now sits practically empty.

Nickel and cobalt mining ground to a halt —first from fuel and input shortages, then from U.S. sanctions on the Canadian company that runs the island's main plant. Sherritt reports that extraction stopped toward the end of the second quarter, and that on June 22 its refinery in Fort Saskatchewan (Alberta) ran out of feedstock, halting refining as well. With the oil blockade unresolved and the company in a corporate crisis, what was produced in the first half could end up being, in effect, all of 2026's output. Cuba had already closed 2025 with 25,240 tonnes of nickel, 17% below both 2024 and the company's own target.

📷

With external income in that state, the only flow that's growing is purchases from the United States: $674 million between January and July 2026, up 61.8% from the same period in 2025 and already 83% of everything exported to Cuba in all of 2025 ($809.6 million), compared with $404 million in all of 2023. The shift in composition is more telling than the amount. Frozen chicken, which accounted for 71% of those U.S. exports in 2023, fell to 18% in January–July 2026 and is no longer the leading item. Fuel, almost nonexistent three years ago, now adds up to more than chicken ($156.9 million versus $124 million), and used vehicles went from 2% of exports in 2023 to 13%, or $34.9 million.

Fuel deserves separate mention. Sales of gasoline and diesel — authorized for the private sector but not for the state's CUPET and UNE — surged in the second quarter: $100.6 million between January and July (a subset of the $156.9 million total fuel figure above), a pace already approaching the daily-equivalent volumes of a year like 2023. That's real relief for private transportation and logistics, but not for the core of the power deficit: the crude oil, fuel oil, and liquefied gas that feed power generation and home cooking remain scarce.

That composition portrays a two-speed economy. The state sector — roughly 80% of GDP — is retreating on nearly every front: its nominal gross value added (basic prices) fell 4.6% in the first half of 2026, a considerably larger drop in real terms once inflation is factored in. Meanwhile, a segment of the private sector is growing on the back of solvent demand: it imports diversified food, vehicles, and now fuel to sell to those with access to hard currency — MIPYMEs imported more than $2 billion in 2025, according to official figures — not as a policy of general supply. The surge in used-car purchases in the U.S. shows the mix adjusting to match demand.

For the rest of the year, the outlook isn't encouraging. With sanctions unchanged, no meaningful recovery is likely, even as the 176 measures approved in June are rolled out. The private sector remains a small slice of the economy and isn't growing evenly: even as more activities open up, the crisis itself limits the solvent demand that sustains it. Much of that purchasing power rests on remittances, and there the margin is thin, because emigrants are taking on rising costs to help their families cope with the energy emergency, leaving less money for everything else. No external lifeline is in sight either: the XVIII BRICS Summit produced expressions of "profound concern" over Cuba but no economic agreement of any real weight. It's not realistic to expect support from any allied power to grow enough to materially change the situation on the ground.
Cuba is thus heading toward its worst economic performance in more than three decades, and the damage is being distributed very differently than during the Special Period: this crisis is far more unequal. Families with no support from abroad, dependent on shrinking peso incomes, are also living alongside a state with less capacity to support them, one that has already announced a shift toward far more targeted social policies. And there the problem is twofold: amid so many material constraints, the support on offer is usually not enough to cover even basic needs, and it doesn't reach everyone who needs it either.
Sources: ECLAC, “Cuba's Macroeconomic Performance in 2025 and Outlook for 2026” | ONEI | Sherritt International, Second Quarter 2026 Report | Unión Eléctrica, informational bulletins | OnCubaNews | U.S. Census Bureau, USA Trade Online | author's calculations.

text:
US Marines climbing down the nets into landing craft during the Battle of Peleliu, September 15, 1944.

Peleliu is a small coral island, one of the southern most islands of the present-day Republic of Palau, situated in the western Pacific Ocean, east of the Philippines.

The Battle of Peleliu, codenamed Operation Stalemate II, involved marines of the First Marine Division and later soldiers of the US Army 81st Infantry Division. The aim was to take the airstrip used by Japanese bombers, and which was considered to be of vital strategic importance for the US if they were to continue the liberation of Japanese-occupied Pacific islands, particularly the nearby Philippines.
However, the island proved incredible difficult to secure and the original estimated four-days dragged on in to a bloody two month campaign due to strong Japanese fortifications. The resulting US casualty rate was the highest for the Marine Corps during the Pacific War.

USMC Colonel Merwin Silverthorn, one of the commanders involved in the operation, later remarked that "everything about Peleliu left a bad taste in your mouth."
Eighteen-year-old Eugene Sledge, who was in the second wave ashore, offers a vivid account of the landings:
"We moved ahead, watching the frightful spectacle. Huge geysers of water rose around the amtracs [landing vehicles] ahead of us as they approached the reef.
The beach was now marked along its length by a continuous sheet of flame backed by a thick wall of smoke. It seemed as though a huge volcano had erupted from the sea, and rather than heading for an island, we were being drawn into the vortex of a flaming abyss. For many it was to be oblivion ...."

Photographer: Griffin
Image courtesy of the United States Marine Corps History Division, Peleliu 117058

(Colourised and researched by Benjamin Thomas)

Churchill later wrote that Britain had guaranteed “that very Poland which with hyena appetite had only six months before joined in the pillage and destruction of the Czechoslovak State” (The Gathering Storm, 1948).
Munich was Britain, France, Italy, Germany. Czechoslovakia was not in the room.
