text:
Most know Socrates as the father of Western philosophy, but few realise he was also a seasoned Athenian hoplite, a heavy infantryman who fought in the Peloponnesian War.

Like other young Athenian citizens, Socrates was trained in martial and military disciplines from his youth. On reaching adulthood, he entered the military obligations of Athenian citizenship, bound to defend Athens, obey its laws, and honour the Gods.

Socrates would go on to serve until nearly fifty years old, taking part in at least three major military campaigns: Potidaea, Delium, and Amphipolis. He gained a reputation among his comrades for his toughness, composure, endurance, and courage under fire.

At Potidaea, Socrates famously saved the wounded Alcibiades, refusing to abandon him and bringing both him and his armour safely away from the fighting. Alcibiades later recalled that Socrates deserved the prize for valour, yet Socrates supported Alcibiades receiving the honour instead. His physical endurance was equally remarkable. During the bitter winter at Potidaea, Alcibiades remembered Socrates enduring hunger and cold better than the other soldiers, even walking barefoot over the ice while others wrapped and protected their feet.

At Delium, Socrates again distinguished himself during the chaotic Athenian retreat. While others fled in disorder, he withdrew calmly under arms alongside the general Laches, watching both friend and enemy with such composure that opponents were reluctant to attack him. Laches later praised Socrates’ conduct and declared that, had the rest of the army behaved as he did, Athens would not have suffered such a defeat.

Socrates was known not only as a warrior, but as a source of wisdom on military training, leadership, and tactics. Plato and Xenophon portray him discussing the duties of generals and the qualities necessary for command, from courage and discipline to judgement, organisation, endurance, and strategy.

One of the most iconic moments in Socrates’ military life also occurred during the campaign at Potidaea. At dawn, he became absorbed in contemplation and stood motionless in silence throughout the entire day. As night fell, soldiers noticed him. Some, out of curiosity, even brought out their bedding to see whether he would remain standing through the night. By morning, he was still standing. Then, at sunrise, Socrates offered a prayer to the Sun and walked away.

text:
The oldest surviving movie ever directed by a Black American spent fifty years lost in a Spanish vault, under a name its maker never chose. Oscar Micheaux, a former Pullman porter, taught himself filmmaking because Hollywood would not tell the truth about Black life, and his 1920 Within Our Gates put a lynching on screen to answer The Birth of a Nation.

The country nearly buried it for good, and only a chance discovery in Madrid brought it back. Sit with how close we came to never seeing it.

The label on that print read La Negra. The name the man who made it had given it, back in 1920, was Within Our Gates.

His name was Oscar Micheaux, and he was born in Metropolis, Illinois, in 1884, to parents who had been enslaved. Nothing in his early life pointed him toward making movies.

Before he ever stood behind a camera, he waited tables, worked in a steel mill, and portered on Pullman railroad cars. Then he went west and broke ground as a homesteader in South Dakota, one of the only Black farmers for miles.

Out there on the plains, he started to write. He wrote novels drawn from his own life, including a thwarted love affair with a white rancher's daughter that he never fully got over.

Then he did the thing almost no one in America was doing. He sold those books himself, on foot, door to door, town by town, across the Midwest and down through the South.

He was writing for an audience the publishing world had decided did not exist. He once put it simply, saying he had always tried to view the colored heart from close range.

When a film company offered to turn one of his novels into a movie but refused to let him direct it, he walked away and built his own film company instead. In 1919 he released that book as The Homesteader and became the first Black American ever to direct a feature film.

That first film is gone now. Not a single frame of it is known to exist anywhere on earth.

His second film very nearly went the same way. He shot Within Our Gates in 1919 on close to no money, in borrowed houses and out on the streets of Chicago, with borrowed costumes and, by most accounts, a single take of every scene.

He was building something the film industry had no room for. White studios were not making honest films about Black life, and across much of the country Black moviegoers were turned away from white theaters or pushed up into the balcony.

So he made films for them, and they played where Black audiences could actually gather, in Black-owned theaters and church halls and rented rooms. He was making movies for the people Hollywood had decided to ignore.

He was also working in the long shadow of another film. Four years earlier, The Birth of a Nation had become the most celebrated movie in the country, popular enough to be screened inside the White House, and it told white America that Black men were a danger to be feared.

Micheaux set out to make the answer to it. For most of its length, Within Our Gates follows a young teacher named Sylvia Landry, played by Evelyn Preer, who travels north to raise money for a struggling school for Black children in the South.

Then, near the end, the story breaks open. The film reveals that Sylvia's family was lynched by a white mob over a false accusation, and it cuts that scene against a white man attacking a Black woman.

It was a made-up story, but it was built out of what was happening to real people all over the country in those years. And the crosscutting was the entire point.

Griffith's film had sold the lie that lynching existed to shield white women from Black men. Micheaux turned the camera the other way and showed the truth, that it was Black women and Black families who were being blamed, hunted, and killed.

He finished his film at the most dangerous possible moment to release it. In the summer of 1919, Chicago had erupted into days of racial violence, part of a wave of bloodshed that swept the country that year.

Months later, when Micheaux brought a film with a lynching scene to the Chicago censors, the city was still reeling from that summer. A movie like his, in that city, in that year, frightened people badly.

The Board of Censors rejected it. The Chicago Defender later reported that it took two solid months of fighting before the picture finally cleared the censor boards.

He got it onto a Chicago screen in the first weeks of 1920. Then the same battle followed it from city to city.

After its first run, more than a thousand feet of film were cut away. He showed shorter and shorter versions in different towns to calm nervous officials, fought to screen it in Shreveport and in Omaha, and never even tried to open it in New York.

He could afford to strike only four prints of the entire film. Four copies, to carry a story the country did not want told, across the whole country.

And then, for roughly half a century, Within Our Gates simply disappeared. So did nearly everything else he ever made.

Film in those years was printed on nitrate stock, which rots and catches fire, and most American silent films have crumbled or burned away. Whole careers vanished like that.

Micheaux directed more than twenty silent films in his life. Only three of them still exist today.

Evelyn Preer, the woman at the heart of this one, made eight more silent pictures with him. Every single one of those eight is lost.

The rescue, when it finally came, came by accident and from far away. In 1956, a film archive in Madrid bought an old American nitrate print for four thousand pesetas, filed under its Spanish title, La Negra.

No one in that building knew what they actually had. The print sat there, unrecognized, for more than twenty years.

Then, in the late 1970s, an American film historian named Thomas Cripps looked at that Spanish print and realized what it was. It was Oscar Micheaux's lost Within Our Gates, the oldest surviving feature ever directed by a Black American, hiding under a name that was not its own.

In 1990 the print finally came home to the Library of Congress. In 1993 the Library set out to bring the film back to life.

But there was one wound no restoration could close. When the film had been shipped to Spain decades earlier, Micheaux's English title cards, the actual words he had written, were stripped out and replaced with Spanish ones.

His own words were gone. All of them, except four.

The Spanish distributor who swapped the cards had been careless, and in four places had left a single surviving frame of the original English titles. Four frames of his own writing, out of a whole film of it, survived by mistake.

So a scholar named Scott Simmon set out to rebuild the rest. He translated the Spanish cards back into English, and when he needed Micheaux's true voice, he turned to the novels Micheaux had once sold door to door and drew the man's own phrasing from his own books.

That patched-together version is the film we can watch now. It is real, and it is his, and it is also, in part, a translation of a translation, his voice rebuilt out of his old novels.

A short stretch in the middle of the film is gone for good, marked today by a single card that explains what is missing.

Add up everything it took for one Black man's answer to a national lie to reach us at all, and the wonder is not that the film is rough in places. The wonder is that any of it reached us.

It came back to us in pieces. Four accidental frames of his own writing were nearly all that survived of exactly what he had wanted to say.

We have the film tonight because a few people went looking for it, and because an archive in Madrid once happened to hold on to a print nobody there could even name. That is a thin thread for something this important to have hung by.

The least the rest of us can do is carry the name forward now that it is back.

His name was Oscar Micheaux, the film is Within Our Gates, and it is sitting there waiting. Put it on, and let it run.

text:
More debunking your idiotic lies.

This is long but worth the read, especially if you don't believe Trump hasn't accomplished anything.
Trump’s Top 25 Achievements: The List Every Conservative Should Know and Use
Donald Trump doesn’t have an accomplishment problem. Republicans have an information problem. It’s on each of us to change that.
With the midterms coming, an astonishing number of Republican voters cannot name three things President Trump has accomplished. Which is remarkable when you consider that Donald Trump has accomplished more in a year and a half than any other president ever did in four.
Indeed, he has accomplished so much, so fast, across so many fronts that most people cannot keep up. The Enemedia buries the victories, while Republicans do an abysmal job of explaining them.
So here is the cheat sheet. It barely scratches the surface. And yet each and every item here is a game-changer.
This is not a list of promises. It’s a list of laws enacted, cases won, policies implemented, agreements secured, and measurable results.
You don’t have to memorize all 25. Learn five. And when somebody says Trump “hasn’t done much,” show them the receipts.
Trump Restored American Safety and Sovereignty
1. He made the border a real border again.
In a matter of months, Trump reduced illegal border crossings to their lowest level in half a century. Catch-and-release is finished. The wall is going up and even being expanded, “Remain in Mexico” is back, and the Administration reduced releases into the country by an incredible 99.9 percent.
2. He reversed mass migration.
America recorded negative net migration in 2025 for the first time in at least half a century. So far, nearly 3 million illegal aliens have left the country, whether voluntarily or involuntarily: more than 675,000 forcibly deported and the rest “self-deported.”
Many of those self-deportations were facilitated by the President’s innovative program to offer plane tickets and cash bonuses for illegals to leave, not only incentivizing good behavior but significantly reducing the cost of deportations. Citizenship and the law actually mean something again.
3. He signed the Laken Riley Act — and required detention of criminal illegal aliens.
Named for an innocent girl murdered by an illegal alien, the Laken Riley Act requires federal authorities to detain illegals arrested for theft, burglary, shoplifting, assaulting police, or any crime causing death or serious injury. It also lets states sue officials who refuse to enforce it.
Laken Riley should still be alive. This law will prevent tragedies like hers.
4. History’s biggest drop in violent crime, and the lowest violent crime rate in 126 years.
According to FBI data, violent crime in America dropped an incredible 9.7 percent in 2025 — the largest one-year decline in history. Murder fell 18.1 percent, robbery fell 18.5 percent. And America’s violent crime rate is its lowest since 1900.
This is what happens when you put the National Guard on the streets in crime-ridden blue cities: fewer victims, safer streets, and better futures for America’s poorest.
Trump Launched an American Industrial Supercycle
5. He made the 2017 tax cuts permanent…and better.
The One Big Beautiful Bill locked in the largest tax cut in modern history, including the doubled standard deduction, the expanded Child Tax Credit, and 100 percent expensing for factories and equipment. It also delivered No Tax on Tips, No Tax on Overtime, an abolition of most taxes on Social Security benefits, and major relief for seniors.
Every Democrat voted no. With the 2017 act set to expire in December 2025, that would have resulted in the largest tax hike in American history.
6. He repealed 129 regulations for every new one.
In fiscal 2025, federal agencies finalized 646 deregulatory actions and just five regulatory actions: 129-to-1, and in nearly every case, the “one” was to repeal the others! OIRA says the savings exceeded those of Trump’s entire first term. That is more freedom, lower costs, and less bureaucratic sabotage.
Of these, the crown jewel was the repeal of Obama’s 2009 “Endangerment Finding”, the legal foundation for the Green New Scam’s vehicle mandates. EPA calls it the largest deregulatory action in American history and estimates that by itself, it will save Americans more than $1.3 trillion. Trump also killed the federal EV mandate, restored Americans’ freedom to buy the cars and trucks they actually want, and even eliminated the incentives behind the almost universally hated start-stop button.
7. He secured $18 trillion in announced investment commitments.
That’s nearly two-thirds the size of the entire American economy, building American factories, chip plants, data centers, energy projects, steel mills, shipyards, and supply chains employing American workers. Apple, Meta, NVIDIA, Micron, Hyundai, U.S. Steel, Ford, Taiwan Semiconductor, and many corporations and sovereign wealth funds are betting big on Trump’s America.
No President has ever done anything remotely like it. And it’s just getting started.
8. He made “reshoring” and “reindustrialization” real, not a slogan.
Ford is moving Lincoln production out of China. Toyota is shifting Tacoma production from Mexico to Texas. GM, Honda, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and others are expanding U.S. production. The capital equipment pouring into the country is the machinery that’s building the growing boom.
9. He replaced lopsided trade deals with balanced, reciprocal trade.
Trump used tariffs as leverage to reverse 80 years of lopsided trade deals that favored everyone but America, and to win new or improved agreements with trading partners accounting for more than half of global GDP. Those agreements open foreign markets, attack non-tariff barriers, defend strategic industries, and make it more profitable to build in America than to export American jobs.
10. He shifted global energy dominance from the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of America.
Once the world’s largest energy importer — “exporting” $700 billion a year to our enemies — America now outproduces Saudi Arabia and Russia combined. The U.S. is also setting new records in oil, natural gas, and LNG exports, becoming the first country ever to export more than 100 million metric tons of LNG in a year.
Trump also opened land, accelerated permits, expanded pipelines and export terminals, and made American energy a tool for prosperity and peace.
11. After four decades of nuclear paralysis, Trump brought five new reactors online in a single year.
For more than 40 years, not one new privately developed non-light-water reactor reached criticality in America. Trump ordered at least three by July 4, 2026. DOE delivered four by the deadline, then a fifth just one month later.
Decades of zero. One Trump summer: five. That is a genuine nuclear renaissance.
Trump Made Elections Matter Again
12. He broke the Deep State’s power to defy the elected branches.
In Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court ruled for the first time in 90 years that Article 2, Section 1 is still part of the Constitution: the President may fire subordinate officials in the executive branch, overturning the 1935 precedent that insulated “independent” agencies from voters’ control.
Ever wonder why elections often seem to change nothing? How about one President and 5,000 political appointees vs. 2.8 million unfireable, unaccountable bureaucrats? THAT is the “Deep State”.
Trump then made that victory real. For the first time in a century, all policy-making bureaucrats can now be fired for misconduct, incompetence, or defying lawful directives. The permanent bureaucracy no longer gets to veto the voters.
13. He ended nationwide injunction abuse.
In Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court sharply limited nationwide injunctions. A single, local, district judge should not be able to block a national policy for everyone, everywhere; and yet that’s exactly what they’ve done, nonstop, ever since Trump (and only Trump) took office in 2017.
In restricting that unconstitutional power, the Court kneecapped the Black Robe Bureaucracy’s favorite tool of unlawful judicial supremacy.
14. He shut down USAID as a left-wing slush fund and shadow government.
USAID had become a taxpayer-funded machine for exporting abortion, gender ideology, censorship, and left-wing politics. It had a bigger budget than the CIA and the State Department combined, absolutely no accountability whatsoever, and a penchant for overthrowing governments.
Trump terminated it — completely — and moved real humanitarian aid under the State Department. Immediately, seven socialist Latin American governments lost re-election. Coincidence?
15. He shrank Federal employment to its lowest level in 60 years.
From a high under Biden, the federal workforce is now its smallest since 1966. Workforce reductions, agency closures, and spending cancellations mean fewer bureaucrats paid to resist the voters.
What’s more, when Biden left office, 94 percent of federal employees “worked” from home. The Trump administration cracked down: as Elon Musk put it, “you can work from the office or you can pretend to work somewhere else.”
16. He expelled DEI from the federal government.
Trump eliminated federal DEI offices and barred race- and sex-based preferences across the executive branch. Government hiring and contracting are returning to merit and equality under the law, ending the grotesque Democrat idea that “fighting discrimination” requires the federal government to discriminate.
He Defended Faith and Family
17. He delivered sweeping pro-life reform.
In his first term, Trump delivered the judges that overturned the abominable Roe v. Wade. Hardly anyone believed it could be done, or that Trump would do it. But he did, and a half-century nightmare finally ended.
Since returning to office, Trump has enforced the Hyde Amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to pay for abortions, reinstated and expanded the Mexico City Policy prohibiting federal funding of foreign abortions, ended federal fetal-tissue research, strengthened conscience protections, protected Medicaid from funding large abortion providers, and pardoned 23 pro-life activists prosecuted by Biden’s weaponized Justice Department.
He’s also done everything within the Executive Branch’s power to defund Planned Parenthood. It would be nice if Congress did likewise.
No President has ever done more to protect life. No one.
18. He got men out of women’s sports, and restored biological reality to federal policy.
The United States government once again officially recognizes two sexes: male and female. Trump ended federal support for the chemical and surgical gender mutilation of children, stopped taxpayer funding of such irreversible abominations, and forced more than three dozen health systems to end or suspend their programs as well.
Trump also enforced Title IX as written: women and girls deserve their own teams, trophies, scholarships, and locker rooms. The NCAA and other athletic organizations changed their rules in response. After years of Democrats doing everything they could to destroy women’s sports and ruin girls’ lives, Trump’s administration protects women and girls again.
19. He enacted America’s first nationwide school-choice program — and launched Trump Accounts.
As part of the President’s One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump enacted America’s first-ever nationwide school choice program. The new Education Freedom Tax Credit helps fund scholarships for tuition, books, and other educational costs.
That’s on top of the new Trump Accounts, which give every child a tax-advantaged stake in America’s future, including a $1,000 federal seed for eligible newborns. Parents gain power. Bureaucracies lose it. And children learn first-hand about free markets and future orientation.
20. He targeted anti-Christian bias and discrimination.
Trump created the White House Faith Office, Religious Liberty Commission, and Task Force to Eradicate Anti-Christian Bias. He restored conscience protections and made clear that Christians do not surrender their First Amendment rights merely by entering public life.
He Restored Peace Through Strength and Put America First
21. He forced NATO to stop freeloading and increase defense spending by 250 percent.
For decades, wealthy European governments underfunded their militaries, effectively sending America the bill and using American taxpayers to subsidize their bloated welfare states. Trump forced NATO to replace its old two-percent-of-GDP spending target with an enormous five percent by 2035.
Allied spending is rising, American defense orders are soaring, and Europe is becoming a partner instead of a dependent.
22. He drove China out of the Caribbean.
China spent years building strategic beachheads at both ends of the Panama Canal, in Cuba, and in Maduro’s Venezuela. Trump forced Panama out of Belt and Road, expanded American security access around the Canal, and captured Maduro, who now sits in a New York jail cell awaiting trial.
Beijing’s planned encirclement of the United States collapsed. The Monroe Doctrine is back. Call it the Donroe Doctrine.
23. He brokered eight peace deals in just eight months.
In eight months, Trump brokered peace in eight conflicts spanning four continents, including wars that had gone on for as much as 40 years. It’s a record unmatched by any other President.
24. He launched and funded Golden Dome, the first-ever true missile defense for the U.S. population.
Ronald Reagan dreamed of making nuclear missiles obsolete through his Strategic Defense Initiative. Today, Trump is actually building it: a layered homeland shield with space-based sensors and interceptors, conventional defenses, and new technologies including microwave systems to destroy drone swarms and directed-energy weapons (yes, lasers) that can replace an $11 million missile with $2 of electricity.
Congress has funded the initial $25 billion, with far more on the way once it passes the NDAA this fall. Better a shield than a sword.
25. He restored the warrior ethos — and reversed the recruiting crisis.
After years of missed targets under Biden, every active military component met or exceeded its 2025 recruiting goal. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth refocused the newly renamed Department of War on actually winning wars, while pouring resources into shipbuilding, munitions, drones, missile defense, and America’s atrophied industrial base.
Young Americans once again believe their Commander-in-Chief is worth serving. And they’re showing up en masse.
Now Act Like It Matters
Those are not tweets or campaign promises. They are changes in law, power, investment, sovereignty, culture, and the structure of the Republic itself. And they’re just the top 25: I could give you hundreds more.
Midterms are turnout elections. We do not need to convince Democrats to love Donald Trump. We need Republicans and friendly independents to understand what is at stake — and to show up.
And let’s be clear. When you say (as some of you will) “the Republicans need to do a good enough job telling this story”, you’re pointing at yourself. You are “the Republicans.”
So tell people our story. Donald Trump is delivering great things, whether or not heaven on earth has broken out quite yet. Do the work, send the team he needs to Washington to finish the job, and get ready for 2028 afterward.
Take the time to learn at least five of these victories. Share this list with someone who needs it. And vote as though the most consequential Presidency in modern history depends on what you do.
Because it does.

text:
AGE LIMITS OR TERM LIMITS?

by Bill Kochman    09-18-2026

I have mixed feelings regarding this issue because we run into a variety of different situations and conditions. If you really stop to think about it, it is really a rather complex and complicated issue.

First of all, I think we need to make a distinction between term limits and age limits.

A term limit would mandate that an individual can only run and serve in a specific government position x number of times.

An age limit would establish a clear legal age after which one can no longer run or serve in any government position.

To complicate the issue even further, there is also the difference between being sound in mind, or sound in body, or both.

For example, would you tell Governor Greg Abbott that he can no longer be the governor of Texas simply because he is in a wheelchair?

Do you see my point? As long as a person maintains sharp mental acuity, what does the condition of their physical body really matter?

On the other hand, if their mental faculty is clearly in decline — as occurred with Joe Biden — then, yes, I agree, something needs to be done for the benefit of the nation as a whole.

Furthermore, think of all of the individuals who accomplished great things in the latter years of their lives. Imagine if they had been told, “No, you can’t do that because you are too old!” What a tragedy that would have been, right?

But there are still other problems. For example, career politicians who are milking the system for all it’s worth with little positive fruit to show for their time in office, versus good, longterm politicians who continue to serve the nation well, and who put the interests of the country first.
 
In short, whether they are some politician or some company boss, if they are still doing a good job, why restrict them or forcefully remove them from their position?

People dedicate their lives to a certain job, they do it with their whole heart and with full dedication, and it gives real meaning to their life. Are we to tell them that they can no longer do it — even though they really want to — because of some invented legal age restriction?

And the clincher is this: We live in a hybrid constitutional republic which operates under the democratic voting system.

So if people keep electing the same individual term after term because they like that person’s job performance, who are we to say otherwise?

So as you can hopefully see, this is a lot more complex situation than what at first appears on the surface.

Personally, I am not sure what a fair, equitable and lawful solution would look like.

The most I can offer is that we should judge, determine and decide each situation on a case-by-case basis.

These are my personal reactions as I just now thought about this issue. You may or may not agree with me. That is obviously your right and choice.

text:
New technology that looks powerful enough to change everything always produces the same reaction. People start talking as if the invention itself is a loaded question about whether the species gets to continue. The talk is meant to scare the public into slowing the work or stopping it. The work does not stop. The same thing happened when scientists first built the atomic bomb.

In 1942 Edward Teller raised a question that rattled the small group of physicists then thinking about a fission weapon. An atomic explosion would create temperatures hotter than the center of the sun. Nitrogen nuclei make up most of the air. Under those temperatures two nitrogen nuclei might fuse and release still more energy. If that reaction ran away it could set the atmosphere on fire or even start something in the oceans. The earth would be vaporized. That would be the end of the world.

Hans Bethe sat down and did the arithmetic by hand almost immediately. He later said he did not believe the idea from the first minute. Two nitrogen nuclei colliding hard enough to fuse in ordinary air was incredibly unlikely. The energy would leak away as radiation faster than it could build. Oppenheimer was still uneasy enough to go see Arthur Compton. Compton later recalled they agreed that if there were even a remote chance of that catastrophe they would not proceed. Better to accept the slavery of the Nazis than to draw the final curtain on mankind.

Compton told the story years afterward that they set a hard line. If the calculations showed more than about three chances in one million that the earth would be vaporized they would shut the project down. The figures came back slightly under that line so the work continued. Other physicists who actually ran the detailed numbers rejected the idea that this was ever a probability question. Bethe later called the three in a million story a misunderstanding. Ignition is not a matter of odds. Under the conditions of the bombs they were building it was simply impossible. A classified report finished around the time of the first test showed that energy losses always overcompensated any energy the fusion reactions could produce. You could not reach the temperatures needed unless you used weapons far larger than anything then under consideration.

They built the bomb anyway. On July 16 1945 they detonated it at Trinity in the New Mexico desert. The night before and the morning of the test the old worry was still in the air as dark humor. Enrico Fermi offered to take bets on whether the blast would ignite the atmosphere and if it did whether it would destroy only New Mexico or the entire world. General Groves was annoyed. When the device went off the flash was brighter and lasted longer than some men expected. Emilio Segrè later wrote that for a moment he thought the atmosphere might have caught fire even though he knew the calculations said it could not. James Conant had the same instant of fear. Then the light faded into a mushroom cloud. The atmosphere did not burn. The world did not end.

They used the weapon on Japan a few weeks later. The scare had not stopped the project. The calculations had been used to justify going forward not to halt it. The people doing the work already had the money the talent the wartime pressure and the conviction that the other side might get there first. Public talk about world ending chances arrived as a story after the fact. It did not change what they did.

That is the pattern. New technology that looks like it could remake or unmake the world always generates claims that it might kill everyone. Scientists and engineers calculate the risk judge it small enough or impossible under the designs they actually have and they keep going. Saying the work is scary does not stop them. They will do it anyway.

Vance’s office pushes back on report claiming he offered Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign advice in 2016, in the hopes of enabling her to defeat Trump.

Vice President JD Vance privately sought contact with Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign in 2016 and offered advice aimed at preventing Donald Trump from reaching the White House, according to a new Vanity Fair report.
The account, published Wednesday as part of a lengthy profile of Vance, adds a previously unreported episode to the vice president’s well-documented opposition to Trump during the 2016 presidential race.
Vance, then best known as the author of Hillbilly Elegy, ultimately voted for independent candidate Evan McMullin rather than either Trump or Clinton.

Vanity Fair cited a person who said they acted as an intermediary between Vance and Clinton’s campaign. According to that person, Vance repeatedly sought an introduction to Jake Sullivan, then a senior Clinton policy adviser who would later serve as President Joe Biden’s national security adviser.

The source recalled Vance making his opposition to both major-party candidates explicit but regarding Trump as the greater concern.

“I hate Hillary. But I hate Trump more. Trump can’t win,” Vance said, according to the intermediary.

The intermediary said Vance urged Clinton’s campaign to devote more attention to the industrial Midwest, specifically naming Ohio, Michigan, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania.

WATCH: Trump - 'Mojtaba Khamenei is still alive'
He reportedly argued that Clinton should travel to the region and address resentment over her 2002 Senate vote authorizing military force against Iraq, particularly among working-class communities whose families had served in the war.

Vance and Sullivan eventually spoke directly about six weeks before Election Day, Vanity Fair reported.

A second source described as close to Sullivan confirmed that a conversation took place, but did not remember Vance making the detailed argument about the so-called Blue Wall states attributed to him by the intermediary.

That source did remember Vance pressing Clinton’s campaign to address the political fallout from her remark that “half” of Trump’s supporters could be placed in a “basket of deplorables.” Vance’s message, the source recalled, was: “She’s got to focus.”
Vance’s office challenged Vanity Fair’s characterization of the contacts, rather than denying that Vance communicated advice to people connected with Clinton.

“A lot of people asked the Vice President for advice in 2016,” spokeswoman Taylor Van Kirk said. She said Vance “never worked for a campaign” and had encouraged politicians in both parties to pay greater attention to working-class communities such as his hometown of Middletown, Ohio.

“We 100 percent reject the characterization that he was trying to help Hillary win,” Van Kirk said.

Katz: No solution for Gaza without emigration, but Trump temporarily froze plan
Vance’s reported advice about the Midwest is notable in hindsight because Trump ultimately carried all four states the intermediary said Vance identified.

Official Federal Election Commission results show Trump defeated Clinton by just 10,704 votes in Michigan, 22,748 in Wisconsin and 44,292 in Pennsylvania. Trump won Ohio by a much wider margin of 446,841 votes. Michigan, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania proved central to Trump’s Electoral College victory even as Clinton won the national popular vote.

Clinton’s campaign was subsequently criticized for its strategy in the region, particularly its treatment of Wisconsin. Clinton herself did not campaign in Wisconsin during the general election, although running mate Tim Kaine made appearances there.

Trump won the state by less than one percentage point.

The newly reported outreach is consistent with Vance’s publicly expressed views of Trump at the time, though it goes further than what had previously been known about his involvement in the race.
“I’m a Never Trump guy. I never liked him,” Vance said in an October 2016 interview with Charlie Rose.

Other comments from the period were considerably harsher. Vance described Trump as “noxious” and “reprehensible” in public remarks and, in a private February 2016 message later made public by a former Yale Law School roommate, raised the possibility that Trump could become “America’s Hitler.”

Vance also wrote during the campaign that Trump amounted to “cultural heroin” for struggling white working-class communities — offering an emotionally satisfying response to economic and social decline without, in Vance’s view at the time, addressing its causes.

His relationship with Trump changed substantially in the years that followed.

When Vance launched his Ohio Senate campaign in 2021, he apologized for his earlier criticism and increasingly aligned himself with Trump’s political movement. Trump endorsed Vance in the Republican Senate primary in 2022, Vance won the seat, and Trump chose him as his running mate two years later. The Trump-Vance ticket won the 2024 presidential election, making Vance vice president.

Vance has publicly said his change of position resulted from his assessment of Trump’s first term rather than political convenience.

“I was certainly skeptical of Donald Trump in 2016,” Vance later explained, adding that Trump’s presidency “changed my mind.”

text:
Awesome... back to renting. Why do people use these companies? It is a nightmare. 

Marble Property Management most closely matches Marble (https://t.co/5JQXIyhx5o), a Seattle-based virtual/tech-enabled rental management company that offers flat-fee services (around $65/month per unit plus a leasing fee) for listings, tenant screening, rent collection, and 24/7 maintenance dispatch across the US.

Trustpilot (main review source)
1.9/5 from 83 reviews (rated “Poor”). Only 2 reviews in the last 12 months. The company has not invited recent reviews and generally does not reply to negatives.
Common landlord positives (especially earlier reviews): Low cost compared with traditional 8–12% managers, easy listing/syndication, rent collection, and hands-off approach for some owners. Some called the service “tremendous” or said they switched and were happy.
Common complaints (tenants and some landlords):Very poor or slow communication; no published phone number or working emergency contact.
App and portal bugs, scheduling problems, and system glitches (e.g., double-charging rent).
Slow or inadequate maintenance (handymen instead of specialists, issues recurring).
High security deposits, listing/price changes after application, deposit refund delays.
Difficulty reaching anyone, especially after hours or for urgent issues.
Some accusations of unresponsiveness on late rent, lease renewals, or inspections.

Recent reviews (2025–2026) trend more negative, focusing on lack of human contact and reliability.
Other platforms
Google Play app (“Marble - Renting Made Easy”): 2.0 stars from 47 reviews. Similar issues with maintenance requests, app functionality, and communication.
Reddit (r/realestateinvesting and r/PropertyManagement, mostly 2021–2022): Mixed. Some landlords liked the $50/month price and basic services when properties needed little work; others and tenants reported bait-and-switch listings, no-shows for tours, and poor follow-through. Limited recent discussion.
Capterra/Software Finder (software reviews, 8 total): 4.3/5, but these appear more focused on the platform features than full management experience. One recent 1-star review cited poor support and bugs.
Other companies with similar names

Marble Property / Marble Sales & Lettings (UK, e.g., London/Willesden): Generally positive older Trustpilot and GetAgent reviews (around 4.7 in some listings) praising staff responsiveness. One Trustpilot profile is closed.

Marblestone Property Group (Chicago): Strong 4.8/5 from 246 Google reviews, with praise for communication and professionalism.
Marble Properties, LLC (Ohio): A+ BBB rating, limited complaints.
Reviews for the Seattle virtual service are polarized and have declined in recent years. Landlords who want a cheap, mostly automated option sometimes report good results; tenants and owners needing reliable communication or maintenance often do not. Check current listings, Google reviews, and local BBB if this is a different local company. Always verify the exact business name and location.

text:
Coinbase and Circle didn't lose 10% in a day because of a hack or a scandal. A vote that failed did that.

The U.S. Senate failed to advance the Clarity Act, leaving the SEC and CFTC's roles in crypto regulation undefined and the country without a comprehensive federal framework. Coinbase and Circle shares each fell about 10% in the immediate aftermath. The EU's MiCA framework has been fully in effect since 2023, and the UK's rules take hold in late 2027. The SEC did roll out a new tokenized securities exemption the same week, but industry voices call agency rulemaking no substitute for actual legislation.

Capital and talent move toward wherever the rules are clearest, not toward the biggest market. This vote doesn't move volume out of the U.S. overnight, but every quarter without a framework is a quarter Europe and Asia get to compound a head start the U.S. handed them voluntarily. Agencies can patch some of the gap, but they can't offer the multi year durability that institutional money is actually asking for before it commits at scale.

This 25-litre Walstad cherry shrimp breeding tank started with just 15 shrimp, and over the last 15 months, I’ve given away hundreds while still having babies all over the aquarium.

In this video, I follow the tank from its original dirted setup through cycling, planting, algae problems, and breeding success, sharing what worked, what went wrong, and what I would change.

If you’re interested in breeding cherry shrimp, building a low-tech planted aquarium, or trying the Walstad method, this is a look at 460 days of experience with one of my smallest tanks.

The aquarium holds around 6.6 US gallons and started with half an inch of topsoil capped with roughly an inch of fine gravel, alongside Corbo wood, black lava rock, and a mix of aquarium plants.

I explain the planting choices, including Anubias ‘Coin Leaf’, Bucephalandra, Rotala H’ra, Hygrophila polysperma, Cryptocoryne albida ‘Brown’, and Staurogyne repens, as well as the problems I had getting the original foreground established.

One of the biggest lessons was choosing plants for the job you need them to do, because slow-growing decorative plants offer a different contribution from fast-growing stems in a filterless planted tank.

The topsoil released ammonia during the early weeks, so I carried out frequent water changes and waited for the tank to cycle before adding the cherry shrimp early in the second month.

Some plants were also adjusting from tissue culture or emersed growth, which made the early setup less straightforward than simply planting the tank and expecting everything to thrive.

I share the bacterial bloom, plant melting, and algae that appeared during this period, along with why I would choose more reliable fast-growing plants from the beginning if I built it again.

The Chihiros AII light was another learning experience, as I initially ran it too intensely for this setup and eventually reduced it to a maximum of 40%.

Adding Limnophila sessiliflora helped the tank develop, while Marsilea hirsuta eventually produced the carpet I had wanted without injected CO₂.

The green algae on the side and back panels also became part of the shrimp breeding setup, providing grazing areas while I kept the front glass clearer for viewing.

Starting with 15 cherry shrimp from my existing colony, the population grew enough for me to give away hundreds and move plenty into other aquariums without the tank looking empty.

I also cover a summer oxygen problem, when shrimp gathered near the surface and adding an air stone helped restore surface movement and gas exchange.

Although this aquarium began as a filterless Walstad tank, I later added a filter as backup after changing the main stem plants and noticing less predictable growth at room temperature.

That change involved Micranthemum umbrosum, sometimes sold as baby tears or giant baby tears, which grew at noticeably different rates in this tank depending on the temperature.

At the 15-month update, I look at the carpet, the remaining plants, the shrimp population, and why I’m preparing to replace this aquarium with a more accessible shrimp breeding setup.

I explain how removable contents should make catching shrimp easier, and why managing water hardness matters in my fish room, where I use shrimp salt to adjust my soft tap water.

This is the full story of a productive little Neocaridina shrimp tank, including the practical lessons I’ll carry into future low-tech aquariums and shrimp breeding projects at Glass Box Diaries.

# The Future of Market Resolutions: AI, Efficiency, and Real-World Lessons for Prediction Markets

Prediction markets thrive on one critical pillar: credible, timely resolutions. Without them, even the most liquid platforms like Polymarket and Kalshi lose their edge. As of September 17, 2026, discussions across X reveal accelerating momentum toward technology-driven resolution models that reduce human friction while increasing verifiability. This shift is not merely incremental; it promises to reshape market economics, expand the range of tradable events, and align prediction platforms more closely with institutional-grade standards.

## Onchain AI and the Push for Live, Verifiable Resolutions

Recent conversations highlight how onchain AI systems can fundamentally improve transparency in market resolutions. Projects such as GenLayer are drawing attention for enabling “live” resolutions—automated outcomes that update in real time based on verifiable data feeds rather than waiting for manual adjudication.

For platforms like Polymarket, which have historically relied on community-driven or oracle-based resolutions, this evolution offers clear advantages. Live resolutions minimize disputes and reduce the window for manipulation. In high-stakes markets—such as election outcomes or corporate events—AI-augmented verification could replace subjective interpretation with cryptographic proof. Early experiments suggest that once these systems mature, the utility of prediction markets extends beyond speculation into practical risk-management tools for institutions.

Kalshi, with its regulated framework, stands to benefit similarly. Regulatory acceptance often hinges on demonstrable fairness in resolution processes. Onchain AI provides an auditable trail that satisfies both retail traders and compliance teams, potentially accelerating the listing of more complex event contracts.

## Cost Reallocation: From Human Time to Computational Efficiency

A parallel theme in current discussions centers on the economics of resolutions. Traditional models carry significant human overhead—moderators, dispute panels, and manual data review. Shifting these costs to computation via agent layers and automated systems could permanently alter the viability of niche or low-volume markets.

Analysts point to platforms leveraging agent infrastructure, such as Somnia, as potential beneficiaries. By moving resolution workloads onto scalable compute, platforms can list markets that were previously uneconomical. This change directly impacts Polymarket’s long-tail offerings and Kalshi’s expansion into less liquid event categories. Lower marginal costs per resolution translate into tighter spreads and higher trading volume, creating a flywheel effect.

The implication is strategic: prediction markets that adopt these efficiencies first will likely capture market share from slower-moving competitors. Traders should monitor which platforms integrate agent-based resolution layers most rapidly, as this metric may soon rival liquidity as a leading indicator of platform strength.

## Corporate Insolvency as a Real-World Benchmark

While crypto-native upgrades dominate tech conversations, traditional finance offers instructive parallels. The recent NCLT approval of Standard Capital Markets’ resolution plan for Paymark Payment Technologies underscores how structured, rule-based processes can resolve complex claims efficiently. Though this case sits outside prediction markets, the underlying principle—clear criteria, transparent timelines, and enforceable outcomes—mirrors what onchain systems aim to replicate.

Prediction market operators can draw lessons here. Corporate resolutions succeed when participants understand the rules in advance and trust the adjudicator. Polymarket and Kalshi already publish detailed resolution criteria; the next step is embedding those criteria into automated, tamper-resistant code. Markets involving corporate actions—earnings misses, bankruptcy filings, or regulatory approvals—stand to gain immediate credibility from such integration.

## Implications for Polymarket and Kalshi Traders

For active traders, these developments suggest several near-term considerations:

- **Market Selection**: Prioritize contracts likely to adopt AI-assisted or onchain resolution mechanisms first. Early adoption often correlates with fewer disputes and faster payouts.
- **Risk Management**: Reduced resolution latency lowers opportunity cost. Capital tied up in pending markets becomes available sooner, improving portfolio turnover.
- **Information Edge**: Monitor technical updates from projects like GenLayer and agent-layer protocols. Public testnet milestones frequently precede mainnet integrations on major platforms.

The broader trajectory points toward hybrid models where human oversight remains for edge cases while routine resolutions shift to automated systems. This balance preserves regulatory comfort while unlocking scalability.

## Outlook

The conversations surfacing today are not isolated noise; they reflect a structural transition in how prediction markets will operate. Platforms that successfully blend onchain AI transparency, computational cost efficiencies, and lessons from traditional finance resolutions will define the next phase of industry growth. Traders positioned ahead of these changes—by favoring adaptable platforms and understanding the new economics—stand to capture the resulting alpha.

As always, focus remains on credible sources and verifiable developments rather than speculation. The resolution layer is quietly becoming the most important competitive battleground in the space.

text:
Washington State 

Weaponized State Supreme Court 

NO NATURAL GAS FOR YOU

Washington high court tosses natural gas measure approved by voters

Justices, in a 6-3 decision, found Initiative 2066 unconstitutional because it dealt with multiple unrelated subjects

Sept. 17, 2026

In 2024, Washington voters approved Initiative 2066 that aimed to halt the state's push to end natural gas use in homes and buildings. On Thursday, the state Supreme Court found the measure unconstitutional. Shea White of Du Pont, Washington, pictured above, wrote in the number of signatures initially submitted for the measure in July 2024. 

The state Supreme Court on Thursday invalidated a ballot measure approved by voters in 2024 that sought to slow Washington’s shift from natural gas toward technology like electric heat pumps.

In a 6-3 decision, the justices affirmed a lower court ruling, finding Initiative 2066 “unconstitutional in its entirety” because it runs afoul of a provision limiting citizen initiatives to no more than one subject.

Because the measure includes “several provisions with markedly distinct purposes and regulatory effects, embracing four distinct subjects. It is not possible by judicial construction to sever and save any of the separate provisions and therefore I-2066 is unconstitutional in its entirety,” Chief Justice Debra Stephens wrote for the majority.

Justice Sal Mungia wrote a dissent that Justices Sheryl Gordon McCloud and Charles Johnson joined.  He argued he would find the initiative constitutional after removing three sections that “silently amend the law” in a way that voters could not understand their impact. 

“Courts are required to construe initiatives in favor of constitutionality when possible,” he wrote. “This court can uphold much of I-2066 as constitutional and should do so.”

The initiative was 21 pages and broken into more than a dozen sections. It aimed to unwind changes to the state energy code that offer builders incentives in the permitting process for choosing electric heat pumps – which provide both heating and cooling in the same unit – instead of natural gas furnaces.

And it sought to repeal provisions in a 2024 state law intended to accelerate Puget Sound Energy’s transition away from natural gas. The measure also would have prevented approval of utility rate plans that would end or restrict access to natural gas, or make it too costly. 

The Building Industry Association of Washington drew up the measure and enlisted Let’s Go Washington, a conservative political committee, to gather signatures to get it on the ballot. 

Nearly 52% of voters approved it as it passed in 34 of Washington’s 39 counties including Snohomish and Pierce.

A coalition including Climate Solutions, Washington Conservation Action, Front and Centered, King County and the city of Seattle filed its suit within days of the election’s certification.

Its attorneys argued in a court filing that the measure’s “most obvious constitutional infirmity” was that it violated a prohibition on what is known as “logrolling.”

This is a practice in which an unpopular policy is attached to a popular one to increase its likelihood of enactment. The measure, opponents argued, contained several distinct policy choices and required voters to enact all or none of them.

The state of Washington is the primary defendant. The Building Industry Association of Washington was allowed to intervene to defend the measure.

Greg Lane, executive vice president of the Building Industry Association of Washington, repeatedly said in the course of the legal fight 2024 that “every single section” addressed the broader policy of protecting consumers’ choice to access and use natural gas.

The case known as Climate Solutions vs. State of Washington/Building Industry Association was argued on Jan. 22.

This is a developing story.

Eighty per cent for “closer ties” is not eighty per cent for a people chapter. A poll is not a treaty.

I will give Abacus its due. After Washington edited the annex, Canadians soured on the neighbour. Eighty per cent for closer integration on foreign policy, defence and economic opportunity is a real mood. Forty-nine per cent for full membership is a real number. More than half saying Canada has more in common with Europe than with the United States is a feeling the trucks do not share. Sixteen per cent still name the United States. Geography has not moved. Seven-tenths of merchandise still goes south. Fifteen thousand trucks still roll that way on an ordinary weekday.

The Financial Post headline treats the mood as ratification. It is not. Von der Leyen offered a status the treaties do not contain. Capitals said the line was not run past them. Carney said Canada is not seeking membership and that nomenclature is a question for Europe. Then he praised mobilité de ses citoyens in French. Those sentences only sit together if the exclusions are published: no free movement of persons, CETA Chapter 10 stays temporary, no dynamic alignment, Parliament keeps the methane rule and the grocery bill. That page does not exist. The poll did not ask it.

“Closer ties” is a bundle. Defence cooperation through SAFE is one file. Minerals and LNG Europe actually wants to buy are another. Student mobility and qualification recognition that raise the stock while the levels plan looks cut are a third. Club arithmetic will not grant single-market privileges without single-market duties. Steel, autos, GM crops and Made-in-Canada preference are the files member states already named. A voter who likes NATO and hates Trump has not voted for Brussels as the last word on a Canadian plant.

Disillusionment with Washington is not a finished register. Phase 2 still has no public FID. The title map has not shrunk because a settlement closed. Barton chairs Invest in Canada and Rio Tinto. Ukraine outlays and the China car quota still sit in different drawers. Collective resilience that cannot get a second signature under one law before 1 January 2027 is a seating chart sold as strategy.

Poll the exclusions. Poll the corridor. Poll whether the House sees the chapter list before Montreal. Until then, “broadly supported” is a lighting line on an undefined noun. Rooms do not move cargo. Plants and pipelines do. Or they do not.

text:
⚠️ 🇨🇦 🇪🇺 ⚜️ Carney courts Europe while Quebec and Canada pay the price of a trade war

Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday welcomed in Strasbourg the idea of Canada becoming an “associate” member of the European Union, a move presented as a shield for sovereignty even as Donald Trump already threatens new tariffs and Quebec remains the biggest loser of a federal strategy far removed from its interests.

Ursula von der Leyen proposed Wednesday that Canada become the EU’s first “associate member,” a status that does not yet exist in European treaties. Carney answered the next day before the European Parliament by praising that “ambition” and speaking of an alliance for the future, while stressing that Canada is not seeking full membership. The Canadian Parliament will have to debate and vote, he added.

The opening comes amid a full-blown trade war with Washington. Talks collapsed in August, 50 percent U.S. tariffs took effect, and Ottawa replied dollar for dollar. Trump called the Canada-EU rapprochement a “hostile act” and “laughable,” threatening Europe with heavy tariffs if the intention is bad.

Carney insists Canada is not in a position to become a full member and that the alliance would actually strengthen its partnership with the United States. He spoke of deeper cooperation on critical minerals, energy, defence, artificial intelligence and youth mobility. He also offered Canadian LNG and hydrogen to help Europe.

For Quebec the calculation is colder. The EU already piles up debt, regulation and declining competitiveness in several member states. A too-tight alignment with Brussels risks importing those rigidities without guaranteeing a real outlet for Quebec exports already hard hit by American tariffs. Quebec’s identity, language and powers are not negotiated in Strasbourg.

Carney frames the gesture as an assertion of sovereignty. Yet it is still Ottawa that decides the country’s strategic direction. Quebec needs solid, predictable trading partners, not another layer of European bureaucracy while the American market, even strained, remains the closest and most important.

Trump is right to recall that intentions matter. A more autonomous and realistic Canada in its alliances would serve Quebec better than a rush toward an Europe that is itself in difficulty. The Canadian Parliament will have to ask the real questions before signing anything.

🔥Hollywood almost left California for good — and the fight isn't over.

By last year, the state had lost roughly 40,000 production jobs in two years. Newsom himself called the industry "on life support." California's answer: more than double its film tax credit, from $330 million to $750 million a year, raising the base rate to 35% — with an added relocation bonus for productions moving back from elsewhere.

But California isn't just competing with Georgia anymore. It's competing with the world. Canada offers around 36%. Australia pays up to 40%. And even Georgia — which built an entire "Hollywood of the South" industry on tax credits — is losing ground. Marvel, which filmed over 20 projects near Atlanta, is now making its next Spider-Man and two Avengers films in the UK instead. The reason isn't the incentive. It's that the UK doesn't require studios to cover health insurance, so labor is simply cheaper there regardless of tax breaks.

Tax credits buy location. 

That's the part tax credits can't fix. States can outbid each other on percentages. They can't outbid universal healthcare on cost.

text:
Virginia Data Center Boom Is Delivering a Major Tax Benefit to Homeowners

As the debate over AI and massive data centers continues across the country, one Virginia county is showing why communities are also looking closely at the potential financial benefits.

Loudoun County, Virginia, has become one of the biggest data center hubs in the world. According to figures cited in a new Fox News report, data centers now generate roughly 45% of the county's local tax revenue while occupying only about 3% of its land.

That revenue is having a major impact on homeowners. Jared Walczak of the Tax Foundation estimates that without the data center industry, the average Loudoun County homeowner could be paying about $5,800 more per year in property taxes.

The money generated by the industry also helps fund schools, public safety, roads and other local services while reducing how heavily the county has to rely on residential property taxes.

There are still legitimate concerns surrounding large data centers, including electricity demand, new transmission infrastructure, water use in some facilities and how quickly communities should allow them to expand.

But Loudoun County offers an important part of the discussion that often gets overlooked. AI infrastructure does not only bring power demand and massive construction projects. When the tax structure is handled properly, it can also bring enormous new revenue into a community and potentially take some of the pressure off homeowners.

I will reprint this from another response I gave earlier. It is what has been reported as the deal.
Here is what was reportedly offered:  
1. Cut the headline tariff on Canadian-built passenger vehicles from 25% to about 15%, with U.S. content deducted (effective rate lower). Medium- and heavy-duty trucks were later carved out of that relief.  
2. Cut steel tariffs from 50% to 25%, but only up to a quota (figures around 4 million tonnes were reported); above-quota steel would stay at 50%.  
3. Cut aluminum tariffs from 50% to 25%, generally without the same quota.  
4. Drop or suspend a 10% Section 232 lumber tariff (existing anti-dumping/countervailing duties would remain). 
5. Suspend the new 50% Section 338 tariffs that then took effect on about $20–28 billion of Canadian goods (alcohol, dairy, clothing, hockey equipment, etc.). Open formal talks on updating USMCA/CUSMA and some cooperation on critical minerals, export controls, and security.  
What was expected from Canada:  
1. Drop remaining retaliatory tariffs on U.S. steel, aluminum, and autos.  
2. Press provinces to restore U.S. alcohol on liquor-board shelves and ease “Buy Canadian” procurement.  3. Administrative changes around dairy supply management without dismantling the system or changing U.S. quota volumes.  
4. Possible alignment of some Canadian steel/aluminum tariffs on third countries with the U.S. approach.  
5. U.S. side also pressed issues Canada treated as red lines: French-language labelling and streaming discoverability, limits on Canada’s other trade deals, and (in some accounts) influence over Canadian tariffs on non-U.S. partners. 
Washington later downplayed culture as a “red line.”  
What Carney said: 
Last-minute U.S. changes made the package uneconomic for autos/steel/aluminum, threatened sovereignty and culture, and called the reliability of any deal into question. 
U.S. officials said Canada walked back earlier terms and added late asks (especially trucks). 
No complete term sheet was released to the public.  
Not much doubt, Carney is engaged in theater for political purposes.

text:
Jon Ossoff decided the best way to attack President Trump was to smear a 35-year-old cancer survivor who carries a portable printer around the White House.

Natalie Harp grew up in a Christian family in San Diego County.

She earned a business degree from Point Loma Nazarene University in 2012 and an MBA from Liberty University in 2015.

That same year, while she was fighting stage II bone cancer, a nurse accidentally put sterile water into her IV line instead of saline.

The mistake left her housebound, in a wheelchair, and in constant pain. She was in her early twenties.

She failed two rounds of chemotherapy.

She was turned away from clinical trials because she was one of the youngest patients with her rare form of the disease.

By her account, her providers offered her opioids, medical marijuana, and counseling on ending her own life. She wanted none of it. She wanted to live.

Then President Trump signed the Right to Try Act in May 2018. Harp found an oncologist willing to treat her with an immunotherapy drug that had not been approved for her condition.

She credits that law, and the president who signed it, with saving her life.

She told her story in 2019, and the country took notice. President Trump invited her to speak at the Faith & Freedom Coalition and at the 2020 Republican National Convention.

She served on his campaign advisory board, hosted at One America News, and joined his team full time in 2022.

Colleagues call her the human printer because she hands the president whatever he needs on paper, wherever he is.

That is what loyalty and hard work look like in Washington, and it is rarer than it should be.

Now Ossoff is using her name as a punchline at campaign rallies, and his allies in the media are running with sleazy innuendo about a staffer who has done nothing wrong.

Even some Democrats admit he went too far.

Let’s be honest about what is happening here. Natalie Harp is an attractive young woman, and that is exactly why they think the smear will stick.

If she were plain or fat, no senator would put her name in a stump speech and no reporter would type a word of insinuation about her travel schedule.

Her looks are the whole play.

The same people who lecture the country about respecting women decided a pretty conservative was fair game.

Ossoff will not debate the record on the economy or the border, so he traffics in innuendo about a devout Christian woman who beat cancer, earned two degrees, and shows up to work every day.

Georgia deserves better than that. So does Natalie Harp.

Canada has every right to diversify. America has every right to demand reciprocity and protect access to its enormous market. That isn’t hostility. That’s sovereignty.

Brussels can offer Ottawa an associate badge, regulatory romance and a standing ovation, but it still can’t move Europe across the Atlantic.

Canada is basically leaving the supermarket next door because the owner got tougher on prices, then proudly announcing it found a lovely grocery store 4,000 miles away.

And if Washington ever pulls the plug on USMCA preferences, Canada will have the perfect new accessory for Brussels: an EU associate badge pinned right over the hole where preferential access to the U.S. market used to be. 😂🇺🇸

Canada can enjoy the badge. Shipping into USA will extra :)

During a recent event at the @MiddleEastInst (MEI), U.S. Congressman @RepLaHood  (Darin LaHood) offered candid remarks about Lebanese Speaker of Parliament Nabih #Berri and the question of sanctions. When asked about Berri’s role in consolidating state control over arms in Lebanon, LaHood described the Speaker’s influence as “mixed,” and expressed surprise that Berri has not faced U.S. sanctions, particularly during the Trump administration.
“I am still a little surprised that he has not been sanctioned by the government,” LaHood said, noting that while Berri may have played a valuable role with the United States in the past, “his time has passed. I don’t think he’s been very conducive to the process moving forward.”
LaHood emphasized his skepticism about Berri’s current value to Lebanon’s political process, citing the changing dynamics in the region, including developments in Syria and Iran, as well as the weakening of Hezbollah’s influence. He argued that the Shia community and the Amal Movement, led by Berri, would benefit from new leadership to move Lebanon forward.
“The only reason why he’s been somewhat cooperative is because of what happened in Syria, what happened to Iran, [and] Hezbollah being weakened,” LaHood added. “He’s a creature of circumstances in many ways.”
The congressman’s remarks highlight ongoing debates in Washington about the effectiveness of U.S. policy toward Lebanon’s political leaders and the broader question of accountability in the country’s fragile political landscape.

❗️ DAMNING UN FACT-FINDING MISSION REPORT ON IRAN –– The International Fact-Finding Mission told the Human Rights Council today that Iran committed crimes against humanity in the 2025-2026 protest crackdown.

PROTESTS THAT BEGAN DECEMBER 28, 2025

   • Spread to all 31 provinces and more than 200 cities. Started as economic grievances. Became calls for political change.

   • Mission: crackdown produced at least 3.5 times the injuries and 5.5 times the deaths of the September 2022 “Woman, Life, Freedom” protests.

   • Government official toll: 3,038 killed. 25,000 injured. More than half required surgery.

   • Mission: lists from independent groups do not match the government’s names. Government lists lack location, gender, and age breakdowns. Mission says it cannot yet certify a final number under its standard of proof. It has “strong grounds to believe” the true dead and injured are “significantly higher.”

   • Highest reported fatalities: Tehran, Karaj, Mashhad, Isfahan, Rasht.

   • Deadliest window: January 8-9, immediately after the nationwide communications blackout.

INTERNET SHUTDOWN

   • Nationwide shutdown of internet and mobile communications from about 8 p.m. on January 8. No prior warning.

   • Mission calls it the longest nationwide internet shutdown on record. Lasted more than five months.

   • January 8-9: complete suspension of all digital communication except landline telephone.

   • Partial restore from late January. Connectivity did not exceed 30 percent and stayed uneven.

   • Tightened again without warning on February 28 after the US-Israeli attack. Broad restore only on May 27. Restrictions, censorship, and state control continue.

   • National Information Network stayed up except on January 8 and the days after. “White SIM” cards kept selected users online from February 28, mainly officials, plus some journalists and businesspeople.

   • Some civilians used Starlink. Authorities banned unauthorized use, seized terminals, and arrested users.

   • Government line: shutdown was needed to “protect the public from riots” and disrupt “violent groups.”

FORCE USED

   • Recurring pattern: tear gas, then shotguns loaded with metal pellets at people who presented no imminent threat. Pellets to eyes, head, chest, and upper body.

   • Farabi Hospital in Tehran: 700+ people sought treatment for eye injuries between January 8 and 10.

   • State-TV doctor: small-diameter metal shotgun pellets were “specifically used to create injuries severe enough to cause death or permanent disability.”

   • Verified video: automatic rifle fire from rooftops and police stations in Tehran Pars and Gohardasht, Karaj, toward crowds with no visible return fire.

   • Witnesses: people shot from behind while fleeing.

   • Security forces entered hospitals, searched for wounded protesters, and arrested patients and companions. Some injured stayed away and later died of wounds.

   • One human rights group has named at least 221 children killed, including six under age 10 and two who were two years old. Most were boys. A 16-year-old girl was shot in the chest and killed in Karaj on January 8.

ARRESTS AND DEATH PENALTY

   • State media on January 16: 3,000 arrested. Judiciary on February 17: 10,538 summoned. 8,843 indicted. Rights groups: tens of thousands detained.

   • Since the start of 2026 the government has announced at least 58 executions on security charges: 29 tied to the 2025-2026 protests, 14 espionage, 14 alleged membership in MEK or other banned groups, 2 from the 2022 protests. Five of the protest-related hangings were public.

   • More than 70 people remain at imminent risk of death sentences or execution over the protests, including at least five women and three boys.

   • Mission is aware of at least three people sentenced to death who were under 18 at the time of the alleged offense. International law bars the death penalty for child offenders.

   • Cases charged under moharebeh, efsad-e-fel-arz, and the 2025 espionage law. Forced confessions, closed Revolutionary Court trials, denial of chosen counsel.

   • Death-row protest cases were excluded from the February 2026 pardon.

WAR THAT BEGAN FEBRUARY 28, 2026

   • WHO sitrep cited in the report, through April 7: 2,362 civilians killed, 32,314 injured, more than 3.2 million displaced.
   • Tasnim chief on August 9: 3,519 deaths, including 517 women and 270 students.

MINAB SCHOOL STRIKE, FEBRUARY 28 

   • Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in Minab. Children 6 to 13. Struck mid-morning as the US-Israeli attack opened. About 72 meters from an IRGC naval site, behind a separating wall. Mission: functioning school. No evidence of military use. 

   • Two Tomahawk strikes. Mission says the school itself was the intended impact, not collateral. Prosecutor: 156 dead, 120 of them children. Independent count: 157 dead, 123 children. About 110 injured. 

   • Preliminary DoD inquiry and CENTCOM’s Brad Cooper tied the strike to a US shot after outdated targeting data treated the building as part of the base. Mission wrote Washington in June. No reply. Finding: reasonable grounds the US carried it out.

LAMERD SPORTS CENTER, FEBRUARY 28 

   • Civilian sports complex next to, but separate from, an IRGC compound. Mission: PrSM airburst with tungsten pellets. CENTCOM confirmed first combat use of PrSM, then denied this strike and blamed an Iranian Hoveyzeh. Analysts in the report rejected that ID.

WHAT THE MISSION SAYS IT COULD NOT DO

   • Iran has never granted access. 47 information requests since 2022. 34 unanswered.

   • Requests to the US and Israel in June also unanswered.

   • Nationwide shutdown, displacement, fear of reprisals, and restricted satellite imagery after US concerns limited interviews and imagery. Secretariat staffing at or below 60 percent under the UN recruitment freeze.

   • 73 interviews for this report. Standard of proof: “reasonable grounds to believe.”

LEGAL FINDINGS

   • Iran: gross violations of the rights to life, freedom from torture, liberty, fair trial, assembly, expression, health. Many amount to crimes against humanity of murder, imprisonment, torture, and other inhumane acts as part of a widespread and systematic attack on protesters and perceived opponents.

text:
Protect Children, Protect Liberty Too

The Gays for Liberty Perspective

There is a lesson here that should not require either side of the culture war to surrender its principles.

Children deserve protection.

Parents deserve a meaningful role in what their children are exposed to.

Pornography does not belong in children’s programming.

Sexual exploitation and grooming should be prosecuted aggressively.

None of that requires the government to pretend that gay people themselves are sexually explicit material.

That is the distinction liberty demands.

A government should be capable of saying:

This material is pornographic.

This material promotes exploitation.

This material is inappropriate for this age group.

But government should need more justification than simply saying:

There is a gay person in it.

Conservatives do not have to abandon parental rights to recognize that distinction.

Gay-rights advocates do not have to oppose every child-protection law simply because politicians occasionally misuse that label.

The issue should be what the law actually regulates.

Hungary’s previous government said its restrictions protected children.

The European Union’s highest court concluded that the measures went far beyond that purpose and unlawfully restricted LGBT-related expression.

Hungary’s new government is now attempting to retain protections against genuinely harmful sexual material while removing restrictions based simply on homosexuality or LGBT representation.

That is a distinction worth watching.

Because liberty does not mean that children should have unrestricted access to everything.

And protecting children does not mean government should have unrestricted authority to censor everyone.

The difficult work of a free society is drawing the boundary between the two.

Hungary Draws a New Line Between Child Protection and Gay Censorship 

https://t.co/5Tvc88q3IA

Hungary’s new government is moving to repeal Orbán-era restrictions that treated depictions of homosexuality as inappropriate for minors while retaining tougher protections against pornography, exploitation and genuinely harmful sexual material. The debate offers a useful test of whether governments can protect children without censoring peaceful LGBT expression.
