text:
Jamal Khashoggi walked into the Saudi consulate in Istanbul on October 2, 2018. He was killed inside. Intelligence services confirmed the order came from the top. Forensic evidence was extensive. And not one senior Saudi official has faced criminal accountability for it. Not one.

That's not a failure of evidence. It's a failure of architecture.

A legal analysis circulating through academic repositories has now mapped that architecture in detail, and the picture is bleak. The study looks at transnational repression through targeted killing across multiple authoritarian state programs, including Russia, Saudi Arabia, Iran, and China, and finds that international law as currently structured is not just imperfect at deterring state-sponsored assassination of exiled dissidents. It is structurally incapable of doing so. The accountability gap isn't incidental. It's load-bearing.

Start with the sovereignty problem, because it's the most cynical part. Sovereignty norms exist in international law partly to protect individuals within a state's territory from external interference. Authoritarian states have figured out how to run that logic in reverse. When Russia, Iran, or Saudi Arabia kills someone abroad and faces accountability claims, they invoke sovereignty doctrine to argue the operation falls within legitimate state security functions, or constitutes a counterterrorism action, or is simply an internal matter. The same legal framework designed to protect people becomes the shield for killing them. The analysis documents this as a systematic feature of how these states construct their justifications, not an occasional rhetorical convenience but a deliberate and recurring inversion of the doctrine.

Then there's the evidence problem. To prosecute a state-sponsored killing, you need evidence about who ordered it, who conducted it, and through what chain of command. That evidence lives inside the operational security of the state that committed the killing. International investigative mechanisms have no compulsory process against sovereign states. You can't subpoena Moscow. You can't demand Riyadh turn over communications. So unless the perpetrating state cooperates (it won't), or a significant intelligence disclosure occurs (rare, and intelligence services protect sources), the evidentiary foundation for prosecution is structurally unavailable before the case even gets to a courtroom.

Alexander Litvinenko was poisoned with polonium-210 in London in 2006. The trail of radioactive contamination across London hotels and aircraft was, if anything, almost comically thorough evidence of Russian state involvement. A British public inquiry concluded in 2016, a full decade later, that the operation was "probably approved" by Putin and then-FSB director Patrushev. No Russian officials have faced criminal prosecution. The Salisbury poisoning of Sergei Skripal in 2018 followed the same pattern: nerve agent, confirmed GRU officers identified by open-source investigators, formal attribution by the British government, and still no accountability beyond diplomatic expulsions that Russia absorbed without notable consequence.

The host state problem compounds this. Even where a killing occurs on the territory of a state that theoretically has jurisdiction, prosecuting it requires confronting the perpetrating state directly. Smaller nations with trade dependencies or security relationships with authoritarian powers face a genuine calculation: pursue accountability and absorb the economic or diplomatic retaliation, or let it go. The analysis is clear-eyed about this. Political will is not uniformly distributed. Countries in Russia's near abroad, or states economically dependent on Chinese investment, or Gulf states tied into Saudi regional security networks, face structural incentives to not push.

Universal jurisdiction is the theoretical escape valve here. The doctrine holds that for the most serious international crimes, any state can prosecute regardless of where the offense occurred or the nationality of the perpetrator. In practice, courts and governments have been deeply reluctant to apply it to state-sponsored assassination because of what it implies: placing foreign state officials on trial for acts conducted in an official capacity. The precedent concern is real and not entirely cynical. States that extend universal jurisdiction aggressively expose their own officials to reciprocal claims. So even the broadest jurisdictional tool available runs into sovereign immunity questions and political hesitance that have, in practice, kept it from being meaningfully applied to this problem.

The reform proposals surveyed in the analysis are reasonable as far as they go. Expand universal jurisdiction. Create a dedicated international accountability mechanism for state-sponsored assassination. Improve Interpol protocols to stop Red Notice abuse, which authoritarian states routinely use to harass exiled dissidents through law enforcement channels as a complement to physical targeting. Establish mandatory host state investigation obligations enforceable through international court proceedings.

The analysis is honest about the ceiling on all of this. Legal mechanisms are downstream of political will. If states are not willing to confront authoritarian allies and competitors over extraterritorial killing, then better legal architecture produces better-documented impunity, not accountability. The Khashoggi case made this visible in real time. The evidence was overwhelming. The intelligence was public. The forensics were damning. And the conclusion reached by the international system was, functionally, that Saudi Arabia's role in regional security and its economic relationships were worth more than imposing criminal consequences on the people who ordered a journalist dismembered in a consulate.

Iranian operations across European jurisdictions have continued despite repeated diplomatic consequences including sanctions and expulsions. The pattern is consistent: Iran plots against exiled opposition figures and former officials, gets caught, takes a diplomatic hit, and continues. The cost-benefit calculation for the Iranian state has not, so far, been altered by the accountability environment.

What the analysis contributes is a precise account of why this keeps happening. It's not that the world lacks human rights conventions or sovereignty law or extradition frameworks. All of those exist. They interact in ways that collectively fail to reach the problem. Sovereignty norms that should protect dissidents get weaponized by the states killing them. Evidence necessary for prosecution stays locked inside those states. Host states lack capacity or will. Universal jurisdiction doctrine stalls on sovereign immunity. Each gap reinforces the others.

The architecture of international law was built around a set of assumptions, including that states would mostly operate within their own borders, that the most serious violations would involve non-state actors or rogue officials rather than systematic state programs, and that diplomatic and economic consequences would function as deterrents. State-sponsored transnational assassination stress-tests all of those assumptions and, in the cases documented here, breaks them.

The people being killed are the ones who left. Exiles. Journalists in foreign cities. Opposition figures who thought distance meant safety. Dissidents who relocated to allied Western states expecting that the territorial protection of those states would extend to them. The gap the analysis documents is the gap between what those people reasonably believed the law offered and what it actually delivers.

That gap is not closing on its own.

SAPS Rejects DA’s R500,000 Top-Up Reward for Ekurhuleni Murders Probe 

The South African Police Service (SAPS) has firmly rejected a R500,000 cash reward offer made by the Democratic Alliance (DA), stating that the state will not be drawn into political matters.

Deputy National Police Commissioner Lieutenant General Tebello Mosikili clarified the police's stance on Thirsday explaining that law enforcement cannot accept or combine funds from a political party.

"This is a state issue," Mosikili stated during a media briefing.

 "I don't know what they are combining, but it cannot be combined. It has never been done before." 

She added that the police do not know the specific intentions or conditions behind the opposition party's monetary pledge and must remain independent of political influence.

The DA's financial gesture followed an announcement by Acting National Police Commissioner Puleng Dimpane, who put forward an official R400,000 state reward for information leading to the arrest and conviction of those responsible for a horrific string of murders in Ekurhuleni. 

The DA’s proposed top-up would have brought the total bounty to R900,000.

The DA’s Ekurhuleni mayoral candidate, Khathutshelo Rasilingwane, previously mentioned that the party's intention was to supplement law enforcement's efforts and that the money would only be released directly to informants upon a successful criminal prosecution, rather than handed over to the police directly. 

However, SAPS maintains that only established state authority channels will be used

text:
Massacre on the Mosa (55 BC) ... 

In the winter of 56/55 BC, two Germanic tribes, the Usipetes and the Tencteri, crossed the Rhenus (Rhine) in the present-day Netherlands. According to Caesar, they had been on the move for three years, after having been driven from their tribal homelands by the Suebi, a highly aggressive confederation of Germanic tribes. When they reached the Rhenus, the Menapii, a Belgic tribe that lived on both sides of the river, tried to block their crossing. The invaders feigned a retreat, but when the Menapii returned to their homes, the Germani reappeared with a vengeance, putting the locals to the sword and capturing their villages, to wait out the winter there.

When the thaw set in, the Germani started sending out their cavalry force to raid neighbouring tribes—the Eburones, the Condrusi and the Ambivariti. Caesar, who had campaigned in the area by the end of the previous campaigning season, but was now wintering in Aremorica (Britanny and Normandy), readied his troops and supplies and sprang into action earlier than in previous years. He called the leaders of many Gallic tribes together and told them that he would deal with this outside threat. He claims that he privately knew that some of the Gauls had sent envoys to the Germani to conspire with them, but he did not confront them with it.

Upon his arrival in the region, the Germani sent envoys, stating that they would settle wherever Caesar wanted, and could be powerful allies to him. Caesar said that he could not settle them in Gaul, but that he could try to secure land for them with the Ubii, another Germanic tribe that he had recently befriended. The Usipetes and Tencteri asked for three days to consider this offer, and Caesar wrote that he thought they were stalling for time because a large portion of their cavalry were raiding elsewhere. The return of these mounted warriors would surely improve their bargaining position.

Whether this was true or they were acting in good faith, Caesar kept advancing, ignoring their repeated pleas. During these tense negotiations and hostile forces at close proximity, a skirmish broke out between the Roman auxiliary cavalry and the cavalry the Germani still had at their disposal. The Roman cavalry performed poorly against the Germani and lost the engagement. Caesar blames this breach of truce on the Germani, but we cannot be sure of this.

The following morning, many of the senior leaders of the two tribes came to Caesar, claiming they were innocent of any wrongdoing regarding the cavalry skirmish. Caesar promptly ordered these leaders to be arrested, and immediately attacked the two tribes, now virtually leaderless. The Germani were in camp and not prepared to fight. What followed was more a massacre than a battle. The tribesmen put up a brief resistance but their army soon collapsed into a rout, and the women and children fled as well. Caesar sent his cavalry to run them down or drive them into the Mosa (Meuse) river. The remainder of the Germanic cavalry that had been out raiding fled across the Rhenus and joined the Sugambri, another Germanic tribe.

Caesar’s actions, particularly his imprisonment of envoys during negotiations, caused an uproar in Rome and were grist to the mill of his enemies in the Senate. Nominally, Romans held acting with ‘fides’ (‘good faith’) in high regard, which they thought set them apart from barbarians, who acted duplicitously. Cato, one of Caesar’s greatest enemies, led the clamour against him, urging the Senate to surrender Caesar to those he had wronged, so as not to let the pollution of his crime fall upon the city. Although Caesar’s behaviour here was certainly dubious, Cato did not succeed.

text:
Cannae 216 BC August 2nd

"...if no one shall give him battle this year, the man will remain in Italy only to perish, or will leave it in flight"
Fabius Maximus on Hannibal's chances if Rome did not offer him battle in 216, by way of Plutarch.

All of Rome rejected this advice. Romans were warriors; man per man, with virtuous commanders and competent leadership, they believed they could beat anyone, especially the degenerate Carthaginians. 

Terentius Varro and Paulus Aemilius were elected consuls, and it was for them that Rome mobilized around 90,000 men. We are told that Varro was eager for battle and Paulus wanted to follow the same tactics that Fabian had followed the year before. If this is not simply a product of hindsight, Rome as a people and the Senate were with Varro, and the command structure of rotating command between Varro and Paulus guaranteed Varro's aggression would win out. 

There was no great chase as Hannibal wanted battle and soon enough, near Cannae, the two armies came together. Hannibal crossed the river Aufidus to help constrict the size of the battlefield, anchoring his left against the river bank. The size and might of the Roman army made even Hannibal's veterans uneasy, but he steadied them with humor and charisma. 

We are told that Paulus delayed the battle a day, but then Varro took command and offered battle as Hannibal wished. Famously, Hannibal and his brother Mago took their most expendable troops; the Gauls and the light infantry Spanish stood with them in an arc pointed at the Roman center with the best troops on his flanks. 

Varro and Paulus set their army in a tried and true Roman fashion and then unleashed 80,000 soldiers burning with a fury of a thousand suns against the Punic army that had made a mockery of Rome.

Hannibal had placed his and his brother's lives firmly in the hands of his officers, and he and Mago pulled off a miraculous feat that stuns even today. In the face of this massive Roman killing machine the Spanish and Gallic troops made a controlled fighting retreat; the only two men in the whole world capable of command such a feat were Hannibal and Mago. 

The Roman army, like a street fighter throwing haymakers from too far out, lurched and stumbled forward when the Numidians and Libyan heavy infantry smashed the Roman army from the flanks. Hannibal and Mago, with supernatural generalship, got their troops to stand and fight!  Trapping thousands of Romans in a killing salient.

The Roman army's momentum was too much, and the rear ranks pushed in the front ranks whose front was now narrowed to the point that Roman soldiers could not move to fight, and every minute 10,000 Punic spears were thrust into that mass and withdrew red with Roman blood.

While this was bad and thousands of Romans were doomed, Varro and Paulus could have still saved the situation by getting the rear ranks to reform, lengthen their line again, but for Hannibal's cavalry. Sweeping aside the Roman horse, Maharbal rallied his men and swept to the Roman rear. 

Cavalry, at the time, could not charge into mass cavalry, but they could prevent any movement and maneuver, kill any soldier coming out of formation, and shoot missiles into the packed ranks of the Romans. The soldiers that saw that slaughter then turned and thought their only salvation was to push forward away from the cavalry.

In this way, trapped in Hannibal's brilliant design, the Romans in the rear doomed the Romans in the front, and by the end of the battle up to 70,000 Romans were dead and another 10,000 captured. With their men died Paulus and 80 other senators as well as 29 senior commanders. Varro, with the few men he could gather, escaped the slaughter. 

Rome mobilized an unprecendented army with the desire to prove once and for all that no one could beat them on their home turf in a fair fight. It did prove something but it was that Hannibal with his army in fights of his choosing not the Romans ruled the battlefield.

text:
A polite note for clarity and to inform the debate,
First, the U.S. already has a lasting presence in Poland, including Army Garrison Poland and the V Corps forward headquarters in Poznań since 2023, along with Aegis Ashore at Redzikowo and sizable prepositioned stocks. What’s currently being negotiated isn’t an initial American footprint but a larger, family-friendly base. Most of the nearly 10,000 U.S. personnel in Poland still rotate in; Poland is working to establish a permanent status.

Secondly, a defence tripwire is a double-edged sword. It’s designed to deter Russia by making it costly to attack Americans, and it also ensures that future U.S. administrations can’t easily devalue Poland as a mere eastern outpost if U.S. priorities shift. Poland’s approach is a strategic hedge: it wants American forces on its soil, not just talk of autonomy over dinner in Europe.

Contrary to some claims that this is about Trump parking tanks wherever he pleases, Poland crafted this offer, is footing the bill for the infrastructure, and has clear reasons for hosting these forces—reasons that go well beyond European debates over autonomy. 🤔🇪🇺

text:
I'm sure they did 🙄😂

What never ceases to amaze me is how often Scotland's own enormous role in the British Empire gets quietly replaced with the story of "the English" doing everything.

Scots weren't spectators to the Empire. They were soldiers, merchants, colonial administrators, settlers, politicians, missionaries and businessmen throughout it. Even National Museums Scotland describes Scots as both participants in and drivers of the imperial project.

You can condemn aspects of the Empire if you want. That's a legitimate historical argument.

But rewriting a British enterprise into an exclusively English one so modern Scots can inherit all the victimhood while none of the responsibility is just bad history.

If we're going to discuss the past, let's at least own all of it.

text:
I find the Christian enthusiasm for rebuilding a Third Temple fascinating—and theologically difficult to reconcile.

The Temple and its sacrifices belonged to a covenantal system that Christians believe was fulfilled in Jesus Christ. Hebrews could hardly be clearer: Christ offered Himself “once for all,” and “where there is forgiveness… there is no longer any offering for sin.” (Hebrews 10)

Some dispensational Christians believe prophecy predicts a future Temple and even renewed sacrifices, sometimes explaining those sacrifices as “memorial” rather than atoning.

But there is an important distinction between believing prophecy predicts a Temple and actively advocating its rebuilding.

If Jesus Christ is the final and sufficient sacrifice for sin, why would Christians enthusiastically desire the restoration of the very sacrificial system His death fulfilled?

For me, that is a theological question worth asking.

text:
New Mexico Friends

I think this plays a roll in the Homelessness Economy.

Did you know that New Mexico also runs a statewide Harm Reduction Program through the Department of Health (NMDOH), authorized under the Harm Reduction Act. It focuses on reducing overdoses, infectious disease, and other health harms from drug use by distributing supplies and training rather than requiring abstinence. https://t.co/7r51ps93jx 
Services include:
•  Syringe services and “safe use” kits developed with the state: sterile needles and syringes (plus exchange and disposal), cookers, tourniquets, foil, smoking/inhalation supplies, wound-care items, and related materials. These are available at public health offices, partner clinics, and community organizations such as Casa de Salud in Albuquerque, Alianza in Roswell and Las Cruces, the New Mexico Harm Reduction Collaborative, and The Mountain Center. Some areas offer home delivery. https://t.co/aO17hujz5f 
•  Free naloxone (Narcan) plus training on how to recognize and reverse an overdose. Distribution channels include mail-order at no cost through https://t.co/gZ2RZ4sC0s, vending machines at Income Support Division offices and high-need sites, “naloxboxes” in places like Rio Arriba County, public health offices, and partner programs. Early data from Rio Arriba suggested fewer 911 overdose calls after boxes were installed. https://t.co/hZdHg9oLG3 
•  Fentanyl and xylazine test strips, plus an adulterant-checking (drug-checking) program at selected sites. https://t.co/7r51ps93jx 
•  Overdose-prevention education, referrals to medication for opioid use disorder (MOUD/buprenorphine) through the NM Pathways program at public health offices, HIV/hepatitis testing and care, and connections to housing, food, and treatment. https://t.co/7r51ps93jx 
Additional efforts include culturally tailored work with Native nations and organizations (naloxone, language translation, ceremonies, and peer support) and virtual training programs such as CORE through UNM Project ECHO that mail supplies after a short course. https://t.co/9BmptWYKJB 
New Mexico does not currently operate supervised consumption or overdose-prevention centers. A 2025 bill (HB 355) to create an “Overdose Prevention Program” with monitored spaces by 2027 did not advance. A later legislative proposal called for a feasibility study instead. https://t.co/YuQ50s7DQE 
Statewide overdose deaths declined for two years after a 2021 peak (from 1,029 to 948 in 2023), though some northern counties later saw increases and local EMS data show continued high call volume. The state attributes part of the earlier drop to expanded treatment and harm-reduction access. https://t.co/PxQGfDiMcp

text:
Live updates: Bitcoin continues near $76,000 as stocks surge following Fed rate hike

The US government just gave crypto one of its biggest regulatory green lights ever. And the market seems to be paying attention.

Bitcoin is sitting near $76,000 today, holding steady while stocks are also climbing after the Federal Reserve raised interest rates. But the real story is what just came out of Washington.

What happened

The SEC officially launched its so-called "innovation exemption" on September 17, 2026. This is a set of rules that explains exactly how blockchain-based platforms can legally offer tokenized securities. Tokenized securities are basically real financial assets, like stocks or bonds, that are turned into digital tokens on a blockchain.

For years, crypto companies have been asking regulators to tell them what is and is not allowed. Now, for the first time, there is a real roadmap. Companies no longer have to guess whether they might get sued or shut down for building these kinds of products.

Why it matters for you

If you hold crypto, this is the kind of news that can bring more serious money into the space. When big financial companies feel safe that the rules are clear, they are more likely to build products and invest. More investment usually supports prices, though nothing is guaranteed.

For everyday crypto holders, it also means the world of tokenized assets, think owning a fraction of a stock or a bond on a blockchain, could actually become a real option in the near future. That is a pretty big shift from where things stood just a year ago.

What to watch next

Keep an eye on how major financial firms and crypto exchanges respond to the SEC's new framework. If big players start announcing tokenized securities products in the coming weeks, that would be a strong signal that this exemption is being taken seriously and not just filed away as a press release.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the SEC's innovation exemption good for Bitcoin?
It is generally seen as a positive sign because it shows regulators are becoming more open to crypto. That kind of clarity tends to attract more institutional money into the whole market, which can support Bitcoin's price.

What is a tokenized security in simple terms?
It is a traditional financial asset, like a stock or bond, that has been converted into a digital token on a blockchain. It works like the real thing but lives on a crypto network instead of a traditional exchange.

Does this mean crypto is finally fully legal in the US?
Not exactly. This exemption covers a specific area, which is blockchain platforms offering tokenized securities. The broader crypto regulatory picture in the US is still being worked out, so more rules are likely coming.

text:
“Just watch me” is what you say when the statute is about to do something ugly. It is not a substitute for the statute.

I will give the clip its due. Trump prices partners in public. A prime minister who answers that he will not be told what language to speak, what culture to keep, or with whom he may sign is doing the job the cameras hired him for. “Complementary partnerships that reinforce sovereignty” is a fair sentence if the paper behind it is a trade-and-defence annex Canada can repeal. Matching a price with a posture is what a middle power does when the neighbour has become a price-setter.

That is not what happened in Strasbourg, and it is not what “just watch me” meant the last time a Liberal government used the line as a governing theory.

Watch what, Andrew.

Watch the Prime Minister tell the same week that Canada is not seeking membership, that the precise noun is “a question for Europe,” and that the Union is to be admired for mobilité de ses citoyens. Those sentences only live together if Ottawa publishes the exclusions before Montreal: no free movement of persons, no dynamic alignment with rules the House does not write, no unvoted contribution, no European court as last word on a Canadian plant. That page does not exist. Nomenclature that belongs to Europe is the opposite of nobody dictating with whom we strike agreements. It is the dictation outsourced, then sold as spine.

Watch the Gazette, not the ovation. Comments on listing Mackenzie Valley and Roberts Bank under the Building Canada Act close 1 October. Listing is not a permit. A permit is not a term sheet. A term sheet is not a second bank. Referral was sold as delivery last year. Listing will be sold as delivery next month. Neither pours concrete. Phase 2 at Kitimat still has a limited notice to proceed and a potential FID. PetroChina still holds 15 per cent of the plant Europe is being offered as diversification. The 49,000-car quota and the Ukraine outlays still sit in different drawers. The title map has not shrunk because a settlement closed.

Watch the staffing. Barton chairs Invest in Canada and Rio Tinto. Wiseman is in Washington. The growth theory that treats people and inbound capital as interchangeable substitutes for output per hour is running both desks. The levels plan was cut. The people chapter has no ceiling. A voter who likes NATO and hates Trump has not voted for Brussels as the author of the next methane rule.

“Just watch me” in 1970 preceded the War Measures Act. In 2022, a column called a protest sedition and the cabinet reached for the Emergencies Act. Two courts later said the national-security test failed. This government is still appealing. He did not sign that order. The method is the point. If the ordinary statute is slow, write around it. If the chapter list is unfinished, collect a noun and tell Andrew Coyne to watch.

I watched. Geography did not attend the speech. Seven-tenths of the merchandise still goes south. Fifteen thousand trucks still roll that way on an ordinary weekday. CETA has been provisionally applied since 2017 and is still not fully ratified. Member states said the associate line was not run past them. Club arithmetic will not grant single-market privileges without single-market duties. That is not Trump’s vulgarity. That is how clubs survive.

Sovereignty is a corridor a second lender will finance under one law before 1 January 2027. It is a title map that shrinks because a settlement closed. It is a deduction that exists the day a firm writes the cheque. It is a House that can fire the people who write the grocery bill.

Until those move, “just watch me” is lighting. Rooms do not produce results. Capacity does. Or it does not.

text:
**Responses from India and China**
India's position has been articulated by its Ministry of External Affairs, centering on the priority of ensuring "energy security for 1.4 billion people." The MEA stated: "India is firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people... and will continue to do so through diversified sourcing and by responding to evolving market dynamics." India made it clear that it had "conveyed to the US the potential impact of this move on bilateral relations and international energy markets" and would "take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests."

China’s response was more direct. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun stated: "China consistently opposes long-arm jurisdiction that lacks a basis in international law and has not been authorized by the UN Security Council." He emphasized that China's economic and trade cooperation with other nations "is not directed at any third party, nor should it be subject to interference or coercion by any third party."

Expert Assessment: Threat Outweighs Action
Many analysts believe it is unlikely that Trump will immediately implement these tariffs. Martin Chorzempa of the Peterson Institute for International Economics told CNBC that if the tariffs were actually imposed, "China would certainly retaliate." Stephen Olson of the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore predicted that "the US is unlikely to take any destabilizing actions," noting that Washington might leave "wiggle room" regarding the timing or scale of the tariffs.

Ajay Srivastava, founder of GTRI, offered a sharper assessment: the bill represents a "crude and dangerous attempt" to "turn sanctions into a trade weapon against India," aimed at forcing India to "sign a bilateral trade agreement on unilateral terms." He specifically pointed out that India might face greater risks than China, citing a precedent for "differential treatment": in July 2025, the US imposed a 25% Russia-related tariff on Indian goods while exempting China from similar measures.

Sensitivity of Timing
The timing of the bill's passage is highly sensitive. A summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and Trump is expected to take place in Washington on September 24–25. Dan Wang, Director of China Research at Eurasia Group, assessed that China would "ignore the restrictions and continue importing Russian oil to ensure energy security," as any substantial reduction in purchases would be "politically unacceptable." Meanwhile, Olson of the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute predicted that Washington would not take actions that escalate tensions prior to the summit.

In short, the "tariff war" remains in the authorization phase rather than the implementation phase. However, this bill does provide Trump with a tool of leverage that can be deployed at any time, whereas both India and China have clearly indicated that they will not yield to external pressure regarding energy security.

text:
🇺🇸🇮🇷 Neither America nor Iran is actually trying to win this war.

6 months into the Iran war, Ian Bremmer sees something strange beneath all the escalation:

Restraint.

Iran has not launched major attacks on critical Gulf infrastructure.

The U.S. has not sent ground troops, attacked Kharg Island, resumed leadership assassinations or unleashed the full economic campaign threatened against countries still dealing with Tehran.

Bremmer calls what is happening instead “price discovery.”

Washington and Tehran want incompatible outcomes in the Strait of Hormuz, but both are probing for how much pain the other side can absorb.

So they escalate just enough to demonstrate leverage, while trying not to trigger the regional war neither side appears to want.

That is why Bremmer remains less worried about a sudden massive escalation than many other analysts.

“Neither the Iranians nor the Americans are actually trying to win.

They're trying to avoid losing.”

That distinction explains a lot.

Iran keeps enough pressure on shipping and regional infrastructure to preserve leverage. Washington keeps enough military and economic pressure on Iran to deny Tehran control of the outcome.

Neither can force the other to surrender.

Neither wants to pay the price of trying.

So the war continues, not because either side sees a clear path to victory, but because neither has yet found an acceptable way to lose.

text:
POWER MAKES MEN BLIND: WHAT I LEARNED IN MONROVIA

Letters from Stockholm
By Kio Amachree

Many years ago, I found myself in Monrovia, Liberia, because my father had substantial business interests there.

Liberia fascinated him. It used the American dollar, and instead of constantly flying all the way to the United States to generate dollar income, he established business interests closer to home: mining, grocery stores and other investments. He also had a beautiful penthouse overlooking the sea.

I was never as enchanted with the arrangement as he was.

I had dealt with Liberians at university, and I had already developed a deep suspicion about doing business where politics, money and personal relationships could become dangerously intertwined. I repeatedly warned my father that powerful political friends of mine in the United States were telling me the same thing:

“Tell your father to get out of Liberia.”

But advising a powerful man is not easy—even when you are his eldest son.

My father would dismiss my warnings. Liberia, he reminded me, had extraordinarily close historical ties with America. He believed those ties offered a degree of protection.

There was certainly some truth behind his confidence. Liberia and the United States had unusually close strategic relations. Declassified American records show just how important Liberia was to Washington: U.S. officials described American access and facilities there as extremely valuable, while President Jimmy Carter authorized covert CIA advice and assistance to Liberia’s government and intelligence and security services. Samuel Doe himself later maintained close relations with Washington and received considerable American financial support. (Office of the Historian⁠￼)

But history teaches us something else:

Foreign friendship is not immortality insurance for an African president.

THE DAY I WALKED TOO CLOSE TO THE MANSION

One afternoon in Monrovia, I made what appeared to be a very simple mistake.

I walked too close to the Executive Mansion, where President Samuel Doe exercised power.

Suddenly I was surrounded by about ten Liberian soldiers.

Rifles were pointed at me.

They were shouting questions in thick Liberian patois, demanding to know who I was and why I was walking there. Their behaviour frightened me because several appeared to me to be intoxicated or otherwise impaired, and there was something unpredictable about the whole encounter.

I am six-foot-one, and physically I towered over several of them. But height means absolutely nothing when the smaller man is holding an automatic rifle.

What struck me most was the atmosphere. I had the unmistakable feeling that my life could disappear over some misunderstanding and these men might sleep perfectly well that night.

My foreign accent initially made them more suspicious.

Then I gave them my name.

The Amachree name was known within the Liberian establishment and to President Doe’s circle. A telephone call was made.

Suddenly everything changed.

I was allowed to continue on my way.

I never forgot that afternoon.

THEN THE PALACE COULD NOT SAVE ITS OWNER

Not long afterwards, the political order around Samuel Doe collapsed.

Charles Taylor’s rebellion had begun in December 1989. Prince Y. Johnson subsequently broke from Taylor and established his own armed faction. On 9 September 1990, Johnson’s forces captured Doe. He was tortured and killed, and images of his final ordeal became some of the most horrifying footage to emerge from Africa’s wars. (https://t.co/twOC93atGo⁠￼)

I watched some of that footage.

Even today it turns my stomach.

Here was a man who had occupied the presidency, commanded soldiers, enjoyed a relationship with Washington and once appeared untouchable.

Then suddenly he was powerless before armed men.

The United States had indeed been close to Doe. He had met President Ronald Reagan twice and received substantial American support. But when his political and military world collapsed, those relationships did not save him. (https://t.co/twOC93atGo⁠￼)

That lesson stayed with me.

POWER IS A DRUG

Africa has seen this story too many times.

Men enter office and gradually convince themselves that the palace belongs to them.

The security services belong to them.

The country belongs to them.

Foreign governments need them.

Their political allies will never desert them.

Their inner circle loves them.

And therefore they are untouchable.

That is the great deception of power.

Samuel Doe discovered it brutally.

His fall also helped destroy the business environment my father had invested in. Foreign investors fled, businesses collapsed and Liberia descended into years of catastrophic civil war. The 1989–1996 conflict killed more than 200,000 people and displaced around a million, according to the U.S. State Department’s historical account. (https://t.co/twOC93atGo⁠￼)

That was the real tragedy—not merely the death of one president, but the destruction visited upon ordinary Liberians.

WHY I REMEMBER LIBERIA WHEN I LOOK AT NIGERIA

When I look at Nigeria today, Liberia comes back into my mind.

Not because I want Nigeria to experience Liberia’s horrors. I emphatically do not.

Political change in Nigeria must come through constitutional institutions, elections, courts, public scrutiny and peaceful civic pressure—not torture, assassination or civil war.

But there is a warning from history that every powerful political leader should understand.

No president should confuse the loyalty surrounding his office with permanent loyalty to himself.

No leader should assume Washington, London or any other foreign capital guarantees his survival.

And no politician should imagine that the people standing closest to the throne will necessarily remain there when circumstances change.

When I look at President Bola Tinubu, therefore, my concern is not that Nigeria should repeat the fate of Samuel Doe. It is precisely that Nigeria must avoid ever reaching such a point.

My suspicion is that if Tinubu eventually faces a serious political rupture, some of the decisive pressure could come from people presently inside or close to his own political coalition. That is my assessment, not a prediction of violence.

History is littered with powerful men who believed their entourage was permanent.

It never is.

I remember those armed soldiers outside the Executive Mansion in Monrovia.

I remember the rifles.

I remember giving my name.

And I remember being allowed to walk away.

Months later, the enormous machinery of presidential power that had frightened me could not protect the man sitting at its centre.

That is the lesson I brought home from Liberia: power can make a man believe he is untouchable precisely when he should be watching the ground beneath his feet.

Asked a simple question about Americans, Rep. Derrick Van Orden narrowed his answer to one specific racial group - with no data to back it up.
TMZ asked Van Orden directly whether he thinks America is ready to elect a gay president, following Pete Buttigieg's comments that the country is. Van Orden's answer immediately pivoted: "Traditionally, if you look at statistics, if you're doing political science, African Americans don't want to vote for homosexuals." When pressed, he doubled down: "Statistically speaking, if you look at their actual, you know, polling stuff, African Americans are not ready to vote for a gay candidate." He never cited a specific poll, study, or pollster to support the claim.
Asked to clarify whether he thinks a gay Republican president is more likely than a gay Democrat, Van Orden said: "Well, if you wanna look at it objectively, yeah" - reasoning that Democrats need Black voters to win elections.
Van Orden also mentioned he's endorsed by the Log Cabin Republicans, a group representing gay conservatives, and said a candidate's sexuality is personally "irrelevant" to him. But this isn't his first brush with LGBTQ-related controversy - Wisconsin Watch reported that before his election, he confronted library staff over a Pride Month children's display, checking out nearly all the books before returning them days later. At the time, he said in a statement: "I unequivocally support equal rights for all Americans."
A congressman asked about the country, answering instead about one racial group - with zero data offered to back the claim.

text:
Elon, Just Send It To Me. I’ll Pass It On. By Dan
So Elon Musk offered Rupert Lowe “as much money as we want” for Restore Britain.

As much as we want. From the richest man on Earth. Most politicians would have fainted into the bank account and woken up in a new office.

Rupert said no.

Not because he hates money. Because taking a foreigner’s cash — even a friendly foreigner’s cash — would not sit right. Optics. Principle. And under UK law a foreign donation over five hundred quid is not a tip, it is illegal unless you send it back. Lowe deliberated, then rejected it. He will take Musk’s moral support and the megaphone on X. He will not take the cheque that turns Restore Britain into “bankrolled from California.”

That is what an English spine looks like.

Now look at Labour.

They clutch pearls about “foreign money” and “oligarchs” while the green gravy train runs on a loop. Dale Vince / Ecotricity — reported £120–145 million in renewable subsidies over roughly two decades, paid for by your bills — then he and his firms donate past £5 million into Labour’s pocket, plus the GLA contracts. Consumers fund the “eco” empire. The eco empire funds the party. The party sells Net Zero as virtue. Britain’s energy bills are not a tip jar for Labour donors. That is not transparency. That is recycling with a wind turbine sticker on it.

And Nigel?

Farage’s Reform machine has been swimming in big money — Christopher Harborne alone into the tens of millions, Thailand-based crypto wealth, other overseas British billionaires wiring in record sums. Labour screams “fascist oligarchs” at Reform’s donors while living off union pipelines and their own rich mates. Farage takes the cash and still will not say remigration without choking. Different brand. Same game: follow the money, not the speech.

So here we are.

Rupert will not take Elon’s cheque because it would be foreign money into a British party and he will not wear it. Labour takes green subsidy loops and calls it climate leadership. Farage takes the big cheques and calls it winning.

Fine.

Elon — if Rupert will not accept it, send it to me.

I am English. Registered. Permissible. Living in Hampshire, not Mars. You send it to Dan Reed. I forward it to Rupert Lowe. Then it comes off an English person. Problem solved. Optics fixed. Law happy. Restore Britain funded. Musk still helpful. Lowe still clean.

I will even write “from Elon, via a bloke in Basingstoke on the transfer note so nobody can say I was subtle.

Serious bit under the joke: a man who turns down unlimited foreign money because it would stain the cause is rarer than a Home Office that stops boats. Labour will never understand that. Farage will never match it. That is why Lowe is the only way forward.

Elon — my DMs are open. Or my account. Or a carrier pigeon. I am not proud.

Restore Britain. Rupert Lowe. One country. One law. And if the money has to arrive via a Hampshire postcode first — so be it.

text:
Yes.  I think it's the best model of linear (linguistic) consciousness.

Now, we can still enrich it with adjacent thinkers, which Adam did (David R. Olson, Wierzbicka, and a long list of others) and which I would do myself (Stiegler, Deleuze, Heidegger, Habermas, and others I would discover in passing, particularly within philosophy of mind and theory of probability).

To be sure, there were other philosophers of language who had compelling criticisms of declarative metaphysics and how it can lead to inorganic, inhuman ideology, which is one of the principal problems of the last 2,000 years of civilization, but I think Gans' unique contribution was providing a grammatical mechanism.

Adam's contribution was extending this mechanism into institutions which will of course involve politics.  I still stand by all my prior praise of Adam and intend to use key areas of his work and cite and credit him.

---

But whatever he's doing with this anti-Vance schizoposting I can't understand, outside of one reason.  For a long while our group and adjacent groups prophesized a rising tech Red elite, which would naturally ally with military interests and have a mature understanding of freedom as delegation and dignity, not suffer from liberal ontology.

Well, now that that rising tech Red elite has appeared, he's suddenly against its primary face.  Why?  I guess because for Adam it's about Israel before it can be about anything else, and if America's commitment to Israel fades even moderately, he does not want this new American Right to succeed.

It's very unfortunate to watch a man you respected go down with the dinosaurs and believe me, he and I batted heads for several months about this and I with a few others near him, who also see it as unfortunate and likely to make Adam share the dinosaurs' fate.

---

I wrote above 'linear consciousness'.  There's another dimension to my research project that does not believe all intelligence is linguistic (e.g. mysticism) or temporally linear.

You can look into Franklin Merrell-Wolff if you want to explore the idea.  He does a good job decomposing the dimensions of thought.

Adam never understood it when I explained the intuition toward philosophical Idealism to him, but oh well.  I'll keep going.

---

Another aspect is of course the operationalization of all of this: financing, investing, information brokering, teaching other operators, but I think in terms of the academics there are these two hemispheres: temporal and ever-present.  And as goes the temporal, historical, GA offers interesting mechanisms and tools.

text:
Topic: The Value Ladder — Turning One-Time Clients into Long-Term Partners

Most tech solution providers sell a single service and then hope the client comes back. That's leaving money and relationship depth on the table. A value ladder gives clients a clear path to deepen their relationship with Samp-Tech — starting small, then growing over time. Each step delivers more value, builds more trust, and increases revenue per client.

Today's Framework;
The 4-Rung Value Ladder:

Design your services as a progression, from low-commitment entry to high-value partnership:

1. Rung 1: The Entry Point (Low Risk, Quick Win)
      A small, low-cost offer that solves one immediate problem. It's easy for the client to say yes.
      Examples: Free 15-point IT audit, one-time network health check, cybersecurity assessment, or a paid 1-hour consultation.
      Goal: Demonstrate competence and build trust quickly.

2. Rung 2: The Core Solution (Main Offer)
      Your primary service — the thing your business does best. This is where most clients start after the entry point.
      Examples: Managed IT support, network setup and monitoring, cloud migration, ongoing cybersecurity management.
      Goal: Deliver consistent value and become embedded in their operations.

3. Rung 3: The Retainer (Recurring Revenue)
      A monthly or quarterly agreement that covers ongoing support, monitoring, or strategic guidance.
      Examples: Monthly managed services retainer, priority support package, quarterly tech strategy sessions.
      Goal: Create predictable revenue and deeper dependency on your expertise.

4. Rung 4: The Strategic Partnership (High Value, High Trust)
      The top of the ladder — where you become their outsourced tech department or trusted advisor.
      Examples: Full managed IT department, multi-year technology roadmap, board-level advisory, equity or revenue-share partnerships.

      Goal: Maximum loyalty, maximum revenue, minimum churn.

Dear members of the American press!

Steve Jobs once said, "If you can convince the press of your technology, and the press convinces us, we'll pay attention."

That's why I'm reaching out to you.

For years, the development of personal devices has been driven by advances in smartphones, tablets, and virtual reality technologies. However, all of these solutions still require people to adapt to the device. I've developed a concept based on the opposite principle: the device should adapt to the user and interact with them as naturally as possible.

I believe this technology has the potential to be the next major step in the development of consumer electronics. It offers a fundamentally new way to interact with the digital environment and has the potential to replace many existing devices that accompany people in their daily lives today.

If my assessment is correct, this isn't just another gadget, but a platform capable of transforming the market in the same way that the personal computer, iPod, and iPhone once did. Such opportunities arise extremely rarely, and that's why they deserve independent attention and objective assessment.

I believe Apple has the experience, engineering culture, and vision necessary to turn this idea into a world-class product. Moreover, the successful implementation of such technology could strengthen the leadership of the American tech industry at a time when global competition is becoming increasingly fierce.

I'm not asking you to take my word for it. I'm asking only one thing: help draw Apple's attention to this development and give it the opportunity to be considered by those capable of objectively assessing its potential.

If the technology truly represents the value I see in it, ignoring it could be a missed opportunity. If not, that will become clear after a professional evaluation. But in either case, the idea deserves to be heard.

Thank you for your attention.

Sincerely,

Alexander.

text:
A $1.8M Pipeline Built Overnight With Kimi K3 And A Single Prompt Chain

Kimi K3 costs a few dollars in API tokens per run. One prompt chain, left running overnight, generated a qualified pipeline worth $1.8M for a B2B seller who used to pay a team of five SDRs $340K a year to do the same research and outreach by hand.

Kimi K3 has a 1,048,576 token context window and an Agent Swarm mode that runs up to 300 subagents on a single task. Together those two features do for outbound sales research what a team of analysts used to do over a month, except it runs while you sleep and costs less than the coffee budget for that team.

Why one prompt chain beats one prompt, one answer

Most people use Kimi K3 the way they use any chatbot. One question, one answer, close the tab, forget the context. That is fine for a single email draft. It is the wrong tool for building a pipeline, because a pipeline is not one task, it is a sequence of dependent tasks that all need to share the same context: who the buyer is, what they care about, what was already said to them, what stage they are at.

Old approach:

Find leads -> new tab -> research each one -> new tab
-> write outreach -> new tab -> track replies -> spreadsheet
context lost between every step

New approach:

One prompt chain -> Kimi K3 holds the entire pipeline state
Step 1 defines the target -> Step 2 researches at scale
Step 3 personalizes -> Step 4 sequences -> Step 5 scores
nothing gets re-explained, nothing gets lost

A prompt chain is not a fancier prompt. It is a single continuous session where each step's output becomes the next step's input, and the million token context window means the model never forgets the ICP definition from step one by the time it is writing outreach copy in step four.

What the million token context is actually for

A big context window is not for pasting one giant document. It is for holding a full campaign's worth of state without re-explaining it every time: the ideal customer profile, the disqualification rules, the tone guide, the list of accounts already contacted this month, the objection library. Once that is loaded, every downstream step in the chain inherits it for free.
https://t.co/uUr0wRBMpw

Kimi K3 is an open weight model with 2.8T total parameters and 104B activated per token through a mixture of experts architecture, which is what makes holding that much state and still running fast at scale realistic instead of theoretical.

What Agent Swarm does that the chain alone cannot

https://t.co/jKotMg1NHl

Moonshot documents Agent Swarm running up to 300 subagent instances and over 4,000 tool calls in a single task. The chain defines the strategy once. The swarm executes the research step in parallel instead of one company at a time.

"Research 400 target accounts"

Single agent:
1 agent x 400 sequential lookups -> takes most of a day

K3 Swarm:
K3 decides to parallelize automatically
80 Research Agents simultaneously
-> synthesis and qualified list
-> 6x faster

Each subagent researches one account: funding stage, recent hires, tech stack signals, trigger events. Context Sharding means each subagent works in its own context and returns only the conclusion, not the raw research, back to the main chain:

Agent 1 -> 30K tokens researched -> 1K token conclusion  ->
Agent 2 -> 45K tokens researched -> 2K token conclusion  ->
Agent 3 -> 20K tokens researched -> 1K token conclusion  -> Orchestrator
Agent 4 -> 50K tokens researched -> 2K token conclusion  ->

The orchestrator, still the same prompt chain from step one, never sees the raw research. It sees 400 clean conclusions and scores them against the disqualification rules it was given in step one.

The full chain, step by step

STEP 1: Define ICP, disqualifiers, tone, offer
   |
STEP 2: Agent Swarm researches N target accounts in parallel
   |
STEP 3: Chain scores each account against ICP, drops disqualified
   |
STEP 4: Chain writes personalized first-touch for every qualified account
   |
STEP 5: Chain sequences follow-ups based on the trigger event found in step 2
   |
STEP 6: Human reviews and sends
   |
RESULT: qualified pipeline value

The chain never restarts. Step 6 is the only human checkpoint, and it exists on purpose, not because the system needs it to function, but because sending unreviewed outbound at scale is how accounts get suspended.

The math that makes this a business

Assume a target list of 400 accounts, average qualified deal size of $30,000, and a realistic 15% of researched accounts clearing the disqualification bar.

400 accounts researched          -> Agent Swarm, overnight
60 accounts qualify (15%)        -> disqualifiers applied by the chain
60 x $30,000 average deal size   -> $1,800,000 pipeline value
Infrastructure cost              -> ~$40 in API tokens for the run

That $1.8M is pipeline, not closed revenue. It is 60 qualified conversations that did not exist yesterday, at a token cost close to zero, versus the old cost of an SDR team spending weeks to hand-research and hand-write the same volume.

Old cost: 5 SDRs x $68K/year salary -> $340,000/year for this volume
New cost: one prompt chain, run monthly -> ~$480/year in tokens

Real businesses built on this exact chain

Outbound-as-a-service for B2B SaaS, where the chain researches and qualifies a client's target list weekly and hands back a ranked, pre-written outreach queue:

Price: $2,000 per month per client
25 clients = $50,000 per month
Infrastructure: ~$300 per month
Margin: ~99%

Account-based marketing research for agencies, where the swarm researches 200 target accounts per campaign and the chain writes the personalization layer for every channel:

Price: $4,000 per campaign
15 campaigns per month = $60,000 per month
Infrastructure: ~$400 per month
Margin: ~99%

Pipeline audits for sales teams, where the chain re-scores an existing CRM's open pipeline against the real disqualification rules instead of the ones reps convinced themselves of:

Price: $1,500 per audit
40 audits per month = $60,000 per month
Infrastructure: ~$200 per month
Margin: ~99%

How to build it overnight

0:00 - 0:15   Write the ICP and disqualification rules as one document
              This is step 1 of the chain, get it precise, everything
              downstream inherits its mistakes

0:15 - 0:30   Connect Kimi K3 via API
              https://t.co/uUr0wRBMpw
              Load the ICP document as the first message in the chain

0:30 - 0:45   Set up Agent Swarm for the research step
              https://t.co/jKotMg1NHl
              Test on 20 accounts before running the full list

0:45 - 1:00   Wire step 3 through 5 as continuations of the same
              chain, not new sessions. Confirm context carries forward

1:00 - 1:30   Run the full target list overnight

1:30 - 1:45   Morning review: human checks the top 20 by deal size
              before anything gets sent

1:45 - 2:00   Send the first batch, log results, feed replies back
              into the chain for the next run's disqualification rules

The honest part

This is not a guaranteed $1.8M and it is not magic. There are real limits to understand before anyone builds a business on this.

More parallel agents does not mean better research. Moonshot itself documents problems like serial collapse and fake parallelism, where subagents duplicate work instead of genuinely dividing it. A badly defined step 1 produces 300 confidently wrong research conclusions just as fast as it produces good ones.

Pipeline is not revenue. Sixty qualified conversations is not sixty closed deals, and nothing about this chain replaces the human part of a sales cycle: trust, negotiation, timing.

A million token context does not mean the chain should use all of it. Context Sharding exists precisely because long unstructured context degrades output quality even inside a model built to hold it.

The volume this produces is also the risk. An outreach chain that can personalize four hundred first-touches overnight can violate a platform's outbound limits and get an account flagged just as fast, if the human checkpoint in step 6 gets skipped because the numbers looked good.

The businesses built on this are not the ones running the biggest swarm. They are the ones with the most precise step one, because everything after it just executes what step one defined, at a scale no team of humans could match for the price of the API calls it took to run.

The chain does not replace the sales team. It replaces the week they used to spend finding out who was worth calling.

GIRL OR BOY - what do you see in this clip?

Look again. The face, body, hair, skin and tiny expressions are convincing enough that your brain picks an answer almost instantly. But the longer you watch, the less obvious it gets.

So... girl or boy? What's your final answer then?!

What if the person you're looking at doesn't exist at all?

She doesn't.

The girl in this video is AI-generated.

And that's where things get interesting from a business perspective. AI models are no longer just pretty images. People are building recognizable digital characters, growing audiences around them and turning that attention into money.

Subscriptions, paid content, affiliate offers, brand deals, digital products. One character can produce new content every day without another photoshoot, another model or another location.

The real value isn't generating one realistic girl.

It's building an AI character people want to keep watching.

And once attention is there, monetization follows.

Many prominent scientists appear in the released Epstein files (court documents from the Giuffre v. Maxwell case, later DOJ batches, emails, flight logs, and related records). Mentions typically involve funded conferences, donations, emails, visits to properties, or flight records. Appearance does not imply criminal involvement.

Physicists and cosmologists
Stephen Hawking: Attended the 2006 “Confronting Gravity” conference in the U.S. Virgin Islands (funded by Epstein). Mentioned in a 2015 email in which Epstein offered a reward to disprove an allegation (later described as unfounded). Photos from the event appear in releases.
Lawrence Krauss: Organized the 2006 conference. Extensive email correspondence (including after Epstein’s 2008 conviction). He asked Epstein for advice on handling sexual misconduct allegations in 2017–2018.
Kip Thorne: Attended the 2006 conference (as previously noted).
Lisa Randall (Harvard): Years of emails and phone contact. Flew on Epstein’s jet and briefly visited Little St. James in 2014.
Alan Guth, David Gross, Frank Wilczek, and Gerard ’t Hooft (several Nobel laureates): Attended or were invited to the 2006 conference or related events.
Lee Smolin: Correspondence into 2013; listed among scientists supported by Epstein’s foundation. He later paused a professional affiliation amid scrutiny of the files.
Murray Gell-Mann: Mentioned in reporting on Epstein’s scientific network.

Other scientists and academics
Marvin Minsky (MIT AI pioneer): Organized a conference; named in a Virginia Giuffre deposition allegation (he died in 2016).
Martin Nowak (Harvard mathematician/biologist): Led a program that received major Epstein funding; thousands of document hits and ongoing contact. Harvard later sanctioned him.
George Church (Harvard geneticist): Meetings and dinners with Epstein.
Steven Pinker (Harvard psychologist): Appears in flight records and emails.
Noam Chomsky (linguist): Correspondence after 2008.
Additional names include Richard Axel (Nobel biologist), Joscha Bach (AI researcher), Nathan Wolfe(virologist), Eric Lander, Oliver Sacks, Stephen Jay Gould, Jack Horner, and others in evolutionary biology, neuroscience, and related fields.

Epstein cultivated these connections through donations, invitation-only events (often mixing science talks with leisure on or near Little St. James), and personal outreach, frequently via literary agent John Brockman. Later document releases showed some relationships continuing after Epstein’s 2008 conviction. Several institutions (Harvard, MIT, others) later reviewed or sanctioned affiliated researchers. Public searchable indexes and news analyses of the files list hundreds of scientific names in total, most in passing or in the context of funding/events.

text:
Democrats reluctantly support Trump’s fraud initiative targeting Tim Walz 

The US House of Representatives voted 352–72 on Wednesday to make President Donald Trump’s National Fraud Enforcement Division a permanent body within the Department of Justice.

More than 140 Democrats, including Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, joined Republicans in backing the bill. The division, created in January 2026 to address fraud in federally funded programs, was previously used to refer Minnesota Governor Tim Walz and Attorney General Keith Ellison for potential criminal investigation over alleged welfare fraud. Democratic Representative Jamie Raskin offered “tepid support,” noting a fraud unit already existed, while Republican Jeff Van Drew called the measure a “nonpartisan commitment.”

Raskin also pressed Republicans over Trump’s pardons of white-collar offenders, questioning whether victims would receive restitution.

Ernest Obodo and Most Rev. Donatus Ogun on their appointments, by the Holy Father, as Apostolic Administrators of Abakaliki Diocese and Benin-City Archdiocese, respectively. The dignity of the human person is the very foundation of human rights and religious liberty, rooted in both human reason and the revealed Word of God (Dignitatis Humanae, 1). We continue to pray especially for all who hold political positions, as recommended by St. Paul (1Tim.2, 3-6).
 
We offer prayers for all men and women of our country that we may lead a productive and peaceful life, godly and respectful in every way. May our Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of all Consolation and Hope, and Patroness of Nigeria, continue to intercede for us. Amen

2026 On this Constitution Day and Citizenship Day the 239th anniversary of the signing of the U.S. Constitution Oregon stands at a crossroads between two visions of liberty and the limits of government.
Governor Tina Kotek, the Democratic incumbent and longtime House Speaker, has governed since 2023 with emergency declarations, expansive social programs, and a philosophy of aggressive state intervention. Supporters call it compassion. Critics point to persistent disorder in Portland, soaring costs, struggling schools, and a progressive experiment that has left ordinary families feeling less free and less secure. To her opponents, she represents a political class that confuses ever larger government with true citizenship.
State Senator Christine Drazan, the Republican who nearly defeated Kotek in 2022 and is running again, offers the opposite path. A mother and former House minority leader, she campaigns on a simple message: the status quo is failing. She focuses on affordability housing, taxes, energy costs and insists government must live within its means the way families do. Public safety, she argues, is a foundational duty, not an afterthought. True citizenship means the active exercise of rights and responsibilities, not passive dependence on programs.
Constitution Day reminds us that the document signed in 1787 was a charter of limited power. Oregon’s 2026 race has become a live test of that principle. Kotek stands for continuity. Drazan stands for course correction. The Constitution waits to see which vision Oregon will choose. 🇺🇸 🐺

text:
From Karl Streed -

I BET YOU DIDN'Y KNOW ABOUT THIS: AFTER FLIGHT 77 HIT THE PENTAGON ON 9/11, THE FOLLOWING HAPPENED.

A daycare facility inside the Pentagon had many children, including infants who were in heavy cribs. The daycare supervisor, looking at all the children they needed to evacuate, was in a panic over what they could do.

There were many children, mostly toddlers, as well as the infants who would need to be taken out with the cribs. There was no time to try to bundle them into carriers and strollers.

Just then a young Marine came running into the center and asked what they needed. After hearing what the center director was trying to do, he ran back out into the hallway and disappeared. The director thought, "Well, here we are, on our own."

About 2 minutes later, that Marine returned with 40 other Marines in tow.

Each of them grabbed a crib with a child, and the rest started gathering up toddlers.

The director and her staff then helped them take all the children out of the center and down toward the park near the Potomac .

Once they got about 3/4 of a mile outside the building, the Marines stopped in the park, and then did a fabulous thing - they formed a circle with the cribs, which were quite sturdy and heavy, like the covered wagons in the Old West.

Inside this circle of cribs, they put the toddlers, to keep them from wandering off. 

Outside this circle were the 40 Marines, forming a perimeter around the children and waiting for instructions. There they remained until the parents could be notified and come get their children.

The chaplain then said, "I don't think any of us saw nor heard of this on any of the news stories of the day. It was an incredible story of our men there.” There wasn't a dry eye in the room.

The thought of those Marines and what they did and how fast they reacted; could we expect any less from them? It was one of the most touching stories from the Pentagon.

It's the military, not the politicians that ensures our right to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. 

It's the military who salutes the flag, who serves beneath the flag, and whose coffin is draped by the flag.

If you care to offer the smallest token of recognition and appreciation for the military, please pass this on and pray for our men and women, who have served and are currently serving our country, and honor the memory of those who have given the ultimate sacrifice!

God Bless The USA!

Never forget!!!

33 Key Voices First 1,600 yrs of Christendom whose theological metaphysics opposed Westminster’s Guaranteed Fall of “Not By Bare Permission” 
→
1. Justin Martyr (c. 100–165) — Angels and men created free. Foreknowledge is not causal determination.
2. Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 130–202) — No coercion with God. Man is cause to himself of becoming wheat or chaff.
3. Tertullian (c. 155–220) — Adam willed the sin he committed. The Fall is not a necessity God imposed.
4. Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–215) — Virtue and vice require real choice. Fate does not author the first sin.
5. Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253) — Autexousion against Valentinian determinism. God does not create anyone wicked.
6. Methodius of Olympus (d. c. 311) — God is not the author of evil. Evil begins in a will that could have kept the command.
7. Archelaus (c. 320) — Anti-Manichaean: devil and man fall by refusing the commandment, not by nature or fate.
8. Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373) — Creatures are mutable by nature, not predetermined to sin. Defilement is from turning, not from God’s making.
9. Cyril of Jerusalem (c. 313–386) — The soul is inherently autexousios (self-governed) as the image of its Creator. Humans do not sin by necessity, cosmic fate, or biological drive, but entirely by the exercise of real-time choice.
10. Cyril of Alexandria (c. 376–444) — God’s eternal foreknowledge neither restricts nor compels the human will; human nature “fell ill” in Adam with mortality, but individual destiny is determined by real-time choice, not an arbitrary divine blueprint.
11. Basil the Great (c. 330–379) — Evil is a voluntary choice. It originates entirely inside the creature’s defect.
12. Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335–395) — Image of God includes being without a master. Ruin and return hang on deliberate choice.
13. John Cassian (c. 360–435) — Free will actively cooperates with grace. God does not force salvation or damnation. Not Bañezian but Western resistance to extreme predestination.
14. Vincent of Lérins (d. c. 445) — Opposed extreme predestinarian views. Preserved the baseline consensus of moral accountability. Not Bañezian. Western resistance to extreme predestination.
15. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407) — The call is not forced. Not all who were called obeyed.
16. Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662) — Created will is a real power of self-determination. God does not necessitate the gnomic turn to evil.
17. John of Damascus (c. 675–749) — God foreknows what is in our power; He does not predetermine it. He neither wills wickedness nor compels virtue.
18. Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109) — The will is the cause of its own falling. God does not make the creature fall.
19. Peter John Olivi (1248–1298) — The will retains power for opposites. First sin is from the created will, not from divine or intellectual necessitation.
20. John Duns Scotus (1266–1308) — Synchronic contingency: at the instant of choice the will can do otherwise. God co-causes the act as being, not the deformity of sin.
21. Gregory Palamas (1296–1359) — God foreknows but does not predetermine. His plan reflects what we freely choose.
22. William of Ockham (1287–1347) — God is not the author of sin. Created freedom is not a necessitated effect of the divine will.
23. Gabriel Biel (1420–1495) — The will is not determined ad unum to evil. The Fall is not the output of a necessitating premotion.
24. Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536) — Defended the power of human choice. Explicitly opposed early Protestant deterministic bondage.
25. Balthasar Hubmaier (1480–1528) — Radical Reformer who argued human choice was restored by the Word; if God necessitated the Fall, subsequent cosmic punishment would be fundamentally unjust.
26. Philip Melanchthon (1497–1560) — Luther’s right-hand man who later rejected absolute predestination, developing synergism to protect the universal offer of grace against divine determinism. Caveat is that he is only here by his later synergist phase.
27. Sebastian Castellio (1515–1563) — Early Swiss reformer who openly fought Calvin’s predestinarian system, arguing that a guaranteed blueprint turns God into a hypocrite and the true author of evil.
28. Luis de Molina (1535–1600) — God knows what Adam would freely do. He does not physically predetermine the choice.
29. Francisco Suárez (1548–1617) — Rejects physical premotion that makes the free act inevitable apart from the will.
30. Jacobus Arminius (1560–1609) — No absolute decree necessitating Adam’s fall. Adam could have stood.
31. Benjamin Whichcote (1609–1683) — Moral evil is not necessitated by God. Divine government does not cancel created liberty.
32. Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688) — Attacks “neoteric” divine fatalism: decrees that make all actions necessary are contrary to the ancient church.
33. John Wesley (1703–1791) — Championed universal prevenient grace. Fiercely resisted the Westminster model of unconditional election.
