h/t Rod D. Martin
@RodDMartin
25 More Trump Achievements: The First List Was Just the Beginning The Top 25 barely scratched the surface. Here are 25 more laws, victories, reforms, and measurable results from the most consequential Presidency of the modern era. My original list of Trump’s Top 25 achievements was supposed to be a cheat sheet. Instead, it drew a million views on X, thousands of new followers, and coverage from Dan Bongino’s show to Roger Stone’s.  Why? Because millions know something extraordinary is happening, but almost no one gives them the receipts. The Enemedia buries every victory. Republicans announce today’s win and forget yesterday’s. Voters sense that Trump is transforming the country but can’t explain how.  So here's the sequel. These are achievements, not promises.  You don’t have to memorize all 25. Learn five. And when somebody says Trump “hasn’t done much,” show them how wrong they are.  Trump Restored Speech, Sovereignty, and Safety 1. He dismantled the federal censorship machine at home—and confronted government censorship abroad. On his first day back in office, Trump prohibited federal employees and agencies from coercing or paying private companies to censor constitutionally protected speech. He ordered an investigation of the Biden Administration’s abuses, gutted CISA’s censorship apparatus, and made free speech a foreign-policy priority. He also imposed visa restrictions on foreign officials and NGO operatives who pressured American platforms to silence Americans.  2. He ended state-run “public” broadcasting. Not only was government unconstitutionally censoring Americans’ free speech: it was subsidizing Democrats’ talking points. Republicans have talked for decades, but Trump delivered, cutting off funding for the Corporation for Public Broadcasting. Now PBS and NPR must compete for audiences and donors like everyone else.  3. He ended catch-and-release. Sealing the border was No. 1 in my first list. But what happened after illegal aliens were caught deserves its own place. Under Biden, arrest often meant a bus ticket, a court date years away, and easy disappearance into the country.   Under Trump, it means detention and removal. The Border Patrol has now recorded 15 consecutive months without releasing a single apprehended illegal alien into America.  4. He helped drive fentanyl trafficking—and fentanyl deaths—sharply downward. Under President Trump, fentanyl trafficking at the southern border fell 56 percent compared with the same period in 2024. CDC figures showed synthetic-opioid deaths falling from 48,913 in 2024 to 38,084 in 2025 — a 22 percent plunge.  5. He designated the cartels as terrorists—and took the counter-narcotics war to sea. Trump designated eight cartels and transnational criminal organizations as terrorist groups, thus unlocking powerful sanctions, intelligence, and enforcement tools. He stopped treating them like ordinary criminals and started treating them as the government-sponsored paramilitary forces they actually are.   The Coast Guard also set an all-time record, seizing nearly 510,000 pounds of cocaine across the Eastern Pacific and Caribbean in fiscal 2025, and blowing up even more.  6. He crushed Washington, D.C.’s violent-crime wave. Trump refused to let America’s capital remain a cesspool of murders, rapes, carjackings, and municipal incompetence. He flooded Washington with federal law-enforcement resources and forced cooperation among police, prosecutors, and federal agencies. One year later, homicides are down 45 percent, carjackings 64 percent, and authorities have seized nearly 2,000 illegal guns.  Urban violence disproportionately victimizes the poor. Restoring order is not oppression: it’s liberation.  7. He restored Second Amendment rights. Trump ordered the entire executive branch to identify and reverse policies that infringed the right to keep and bear arms. DOJ created a Second Amendment Enforcement Task Force. ATF repealed Biden’s punitive “Zero Tolerance” policy for gun dealers and other unreasonable restrictions on selling firearms.  Then Trump’s DOJ filed the first affirmative civil-rights lawsuit in Department history, forcing Los Angeles County to end nine-month delays for concealed-carry permits. It also restored the congressionally authorized process through which deserving Americans may regain federal firearms rights — and zeroed out the $200 federal tax on suppressors.  Trump Encouraged Work, Savings, and Ownership 8. He ended federal income tax on tips and overtime pay. Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill allows eligible workers to deduct up to $25,000 in qualified tips through 2028. It also created a deduction for the overtime premium — up to $12,500 for an individual or $25,000 for a married couple. It’s hard to think of a more pro-working-class reform than that.  9. He eliminated the tax on Social Security for nearly all seniors. Under the One Big Beautiful Bill, seniors may deduct an additional $6,000 apiece or $12,000 for a qualifying married couple. For most seniors, that eliminates federal income tax on retirement income, including Social Security.  The fact that Democrats taxed Social Security in the first place is obscene. Trump reversed it.  10. He made Opportunity Zones permanent. Trump’s Opportunity Zones steer private capital toward distressed communities by rewarding long-term investment. The One Big Beautiful Bill made them permanent and established recurring qualifying rounds, giving investors and local leaders the certainty to build for decades.  The Left’s answer to poverty is always another federal program. Trump’s is capital, ownership, businesses, homes, and jobs.  11. He protected farms and family businesses from the death tax. The death tax can force a grieving family to sell family farms, homes, and businesses just to pay Washington. But Trump made it easier to pass a lifetime’s work and dreams on to the next generation. He increased the federal estate-and-gift-tax exclusion to $15 million per person in 2026, with inflation adjustments and no scheduled expiration — potentially $30 million for a married couple.  Trump Put Families and Good Health First 12. He expanded Health Savings Accounts — and created a $50 billion rural-health fund. Thanks to the One Big Beautiful Bill, millions more Americans can use Health Savings Accounts. The result? More personal control and fewer gatekeepers between doctor and patient.  Trump also created a $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program, reversing years of rural hospital closures under Biden.  13. He used TrumpRx and most-favored-nation agreements to force down drug prices. For decades, Americans paid the world’s highest drug prices while socialist governments imposed price controls and freeloaded on American innovation. Trump turned that arrangement on its head, securing most-favored-nation agreements with 26 drugmakers covering 89 percent of the branded-drug market.   It’s not a price control: it’s the end of a free ride. Foreign governments must now pay more for American drugs so Americans can pay less.  Moreover, the President’s new TrumpRx program gives patients direct access to steep discounts. Patients have already saved more than $700 million, while the latest nine deals added $19.6 billion in American manufacturing commitments.  14. He turned MAHA from a slogan into reality. Trump, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and MAHA forced a reckoning. HHS and FDA began moving manufacturers away from petroleum-based dyes, approved natural alternatives, changed labeling rules, and created a public tracker of corporate promises.  For the first time in generations, Washington is asking why American children are fat and sick — and fixing the problem instead of prescribing another drug.  15. He prioritized adoption and family formation. Trump made the adoption tax credit partly refundable, allowing eligible families to receive up to $5,000 per adopted child even when they owe less tax. He also raised tax-free dependent-care assistance from $5,000 to $7,500 in 2026. Trump is forcing government to stop making it harder to adopt, care for dependents, or build families.  16. He stood up for victims of revenge porn and sexual deepfakes. The TAKE IT DOWN Act criminalized specified nonconsensual intimate imagery, including AI-generated sexual deepfakes. Covered platforms must now provide a reporting process and must remove all qualifying images within 48 hours. Perps go to prison.  17. He stopped federal support for dangerous gain-of-function research in sketchy foreign labs. Wuhan should have ended this debate. Instead, the Fauci-led bureaucracy doubled down on reckless experimentation and dangerous gain-of-function research, not just in the United States but in sketchy foreign labs, even in China. Trump put a stop to it, terminating projects in countries of concern and suspending other high-risk programs.  Trump Built America’s Economic Future 18. He turned valuable access to the world’s largest consumer market into leverage and revenue. Washington treated access to the richest consumer market on Earth into a global entitlement, while allowing them to maintain huge trade barriers against U.S. producers. Trump turned that on its head. By January 2026, the Administration reported $300 billion in gross tariff collections.  The President used those tariffs to negotiate new trade deals with countries representing two-thirds of the global economy. In the process, he opened their markets, increased their purchases of U.S. energy, farm produce, and goods, supported industries vital to national security, and made companies begin building factories here.  19. He began breaking China’s rare-earth chokehold. China dominates the minerals and magnets inside everything from smartphones to submarines. It controls 92 percent of global rare-earths refining. That’s not free trade: It’s a strategic hostage situation.  Trump’s Pentagon partnered with MP Materials to expand American rare-earth separation and magnet production, backed by long-term purchases and a domestic price floor. He also made deals with allied nations to bring their own production and refining online.  20. He created a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve — and made America the center of digital finance. Trump created a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve by ordering the government to keep, rather than auction off, Bitcoin forfeited in criminal and civil cases. He also championed and signed the GENIUS Act, America’s first national framework for dollar-backed stablecoins, replacing Biden’s war on crypto with rules establishing global leadership and dollar dominance.  A stablecoin is a digital dollar that anyone with a smartphone can hold and spend, anywhere on Earth, without all the expensive banking fees. Under Trump’s law, the companies issuing those coins must back them with safe dollar assets, especially short-term U.S. Treasuries. So as stablecoins spread, they expand the dollar’s reach and dominance, even in countries with strict currency controls.  In short: instead of depending on the goodwill of foreign central banks, America can distribute the dollar system directly to billions of people and businesses.  21. He launched the AI Action Plan and Genesis Mission. Trump’s AI Action Plan attacks the energy, permitting, infrastructure, and regulatory bottlenecks that could hand this century’s most important technology to China. Genesis brings federal data, national labs, supercomputers, and private AI companies together to accelerate discovery. So far, the Energy Department has secured more than $800 million in partner commitments.  22. He restored the Moon to the center of American national strategy. Trump ordered America back to the Moon by 2028, with initial elements of a permanent base at its strategically vital South Pole by 2030. He also directed development of space-based nuclear power and nuclear rockets, and greater use of America’s unmatched commercial-space industry.  The Moon is the high ground of twenty-first-century industry, science, logistics, and defense — the first great arena of Astropolitics. Trump gave America the means to beat China and make the future free.  Trump Reasserted American Power Around the World 23. He brought American hostages home. By March 2026, the Administration had secured the release of 105 detained Americans. Marc Fogel came home after years in a Russian prison. George Glezmann came home after two years in Taliban captivity. So did prisoners held by Hamas, Belarus, Venezuela, and others.  24. He replaced foreign aid with investment and trade. For a century, Washington measured compassion by how many dollars it spent, regardless of the often abysmal results. Trump put a stop to that: his “Trade Over Aid” doctrine offers not a handout but investment, markets, infrastructure, and partnership.  The December 2025 agreement with the Democratic Republic of the Congo is a perfect example. It tied American investment to secure critical-mineral supply chains. This creates Congolese jobs and infrastructure while rewarding American investors and securing American supply chains. It also rescues impoverished Third World countries from Chinese Communist debt traps.  25. He launched a $76.6 billion American undersea buildup — and began rebuilding the shipyards to sustain it. China is on track to outnumber the U.S. submarine fleet by 2030. Biden did nothing about it. But in July 2026, Trump’s Navy awarded contracts for five Columbia-class ballistic-missile submarines and nine Block VI Virginia-class attack submarines. The package totals $76.6 billion — an historic contract allowing shipbuilders to expand production lines and train skilled workers.  The President also ordered plans for a fifth Navy shipyard — the first new one in more than 80 years — along with acquisition, workforce, and repair reforms.  Now Act Like It Matters Trump produced all of these “25 more” accomplishments in just a year and a half, while also accumulating that earlier Top 25 achievements list, accomplishments so consequential that these didn’t make the original cut.  The Republican Party’s greatest political problem this fall is not a lack of victories. It’s that too many Republicans have no idea what — or how much — they’ve accomplished.  It’s up to each of us to tell our story. Donald Trump is delivering great things, whether or not heaven on earth has broken out quite yet. Do the work, send him the team he needs to finish the job, and then get ready for 2028.  Take the time to learn at least five of these victories. Share this list with someone who needs it. Take friends to the polls. And vote as though the most consequential Presidency in modern history depends on what you do.

text:
ESPN's College GameDay is in Oxford, Mississippi this Saturday for LSU and Ole Miss, and the celebrity guest picker is Morgan Freeman.

He's there because he's a Mississippi guy. He grew up in the state and has lived in Charleston, a Delta town of about 2,100 people, since 1991. He's said he feels safer there than anywhere else in America.

Here's what he did in that town that almost nobody outside of it knows.

Mississippi integrated its public schools in 1970. Charleston High School integrated with them. Black students and white students went to class together, played on the same teams, grew up side by side from kindergarten on.

But the prom stayed separate.

It wasn't school policy. Parents organized it privately. One prom for the Black students, one for the white students, every single year, for decades after the classrooms had been integrated.

That was still happening in 1997.

So Morgan Freeman went to the school and made an offer. He would personally pay for the entire senior prom. Every dollar. One condition.

Everybody comes.

The school ignored him.

He let it sit for eleven years. Then in 2008 he went back and offered again.

This time the school board said yes.

Charleston High School had 415 students, about 70% Black and 30% white, in Tallahatchie County, the poorest county in Mississippi. In April 2008, they held the first racially integrated prom in the school's history.

Freeman paid for all of it and then mostly got out of the way. He didn't want it to be about him.

Not everyone came along. A group of white parents held a secret meeting and organized a separate whites-only prom at a local National Guard facility, and some of them forbade their kids from attending the integrated one.

Freeman was clear-eyed about why.

He said the parents were the hard part, that they'd settled into a that's-the-way-it-is attitude that doesn't move. The kids were different.

"In other words, you can sell them another idea."

A Canadian filmmaker named Paul Saltzman heard about it, moved his family to Charleston for four months, and filmed the whole thing. The documentary is called Prom Night in Mississippi. HBO aired it in 2009.

The prom happened. The kids had a great night. Several of them said afterward they couldn't understand what the adults had been so afraid of.

Freeman was 71 years old when he finally got that yes. He'd been offering since he was 60.

On Saturday he'll be on a stage in Oxford in front of a few hundred thousand people, picking football games.

He already did the harder thing, in a town of 2,100, where nobody was watching.

A Houthi spokesman says Saudi Arabia carried out about 450 air strikes on Yemen this week, and that the Houthis hit back at the Red Sea oil port of Yanbu and an air base in southern Saudi Arabia.

Earlier attacks damaged Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline. That is the line that carries crude oil across the country to the Red Sea, so tankers do not have to sail out through the Gulf. Saudi Arabia has not said when it will run again.

text:
“Trump Must Not Win”: The Advice Vance Gave Clinton’s Campaign Before the 2016 Election

Current U.S. Vice President JD Vance tried through unofficial channels in 2016 to offer Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign advice on how to defeat Donald Trump, Vanity Fair reports, citing sources.

“I hate Hillary. But I hate Trump even more. Trump must not win,” a Vanity Fair source recalled Vance saying.

According to the magazine, Vance asked to be connected with Jake Sullivan, who was then a senior policy adviser to Clinton. About six weeks before the election, Vance and Sullivan spoke directly.

Vance reportedly urged Clinton’s campaign to devote more attention to the crucial Midwestern battleground states, including Ohio, Michigan, Wisconsin, and Pennsylvania. According to a source, he also advised Clinton to apologize publicly for her support of the Iraq War.

A source close to Sullivan confirmed that the conversation with Vance took place, although the source did not recall discussing a strategy involving the traditionally Democratic “blue” states. According to the source, Vance did urge Clinton to repair the political damage caused by her controversial “basket of deplorables” remark about some Trump supporters.

At the time, Vance publicly said that he intended to vote for neither Trump nor Clinton. He ultimately cast his ballot for independent candidate Evan McMullin.

Vance’s spokesperson did not deny that such contacts took place but told Vanity Fair that in 2016 Vance offered advice to people in both parties and encouraged them to pay more attention to America’s working-class communities.

Vance’s relationship with Trump later changed dramatically: from being a public Trump critic, he became one of his political allies and eventually Vice President of the United States.

text:
🏈Bison Host Penn in Family Weekend Game Presented by Giant Saturday

Bucknell football is back at home for its Family Weekend game presented Giant. The Bison are playing host to Penn on Saturday, Sep. 19 at 3 p.m. in Christy Mathewson-Memorial Stadium.

This will be the 39th time in program history that the Quakers and Bison will face off. Penn currently holds the overall series 33-5 over Bucknell and are 8-2 when playing in Lewisburg. The Quakers are on a 10-game winning streak over the Bison with the most recent contest in 2024 ending in a 31-21 victory for Penn. The last time Bucknell came away with a win against Penn was in 1999, when the Bison won 23-16.

An interesting connection between the Quakers and the Bison is that Bucknell football’s head coaching position is named after Bob Odell, a former head coach for Bucknell and former football player for Penn. Odell served as the head football coach at Bucknell from 1958-64. While playing at Penn in the 1940s, he was an All-America halfback, won the Maxwell Trophy and was runner-up for the Heisman in 1943 for his prowess on the field. After leaving Bucknell, Odell was the head coach for his alma mater Penn from 1965-70.

In addition to it being Family Weekend at Christy Mathewson-Memorial Stadium on Saturday, it is also the vs Cancer game presented by Geisinger and JRBC Day presented by Knoebles.

GAME DAY GUIDE FOR FANS

Tailgating Policy | Clear Bag Policy | Join the Gridiron Club | VS Cancer Donation
NEW Clear Bag Policy
Only small clutch bags (no larger than 4.5” by 6.5”) and bags made of clear plastic (any size) will be allowed inside Christy Mathewson-Memorial Stadium.
Exceptions will be made for Bucknell employees and vendors whose work requires event-related supplies or equipment. In addition, strollers, diaper bags, and medically-necessary equipment are permitted, but will be subject to search upon request.

NEW Rusty Rail Biergarten

Bucknell Athletics and the local brewery Rusty Rail have announced an exciting new partnership that will bring a beer garden to select Bison football games this fall. The new feature will be located on the west side of the Pascucci Team Center at the north end of Christy Mathewson-Memorial Stadium. All fans are invited to the area but must be 21 years of age or older to purchase beer. Gates open 90 minutes prior to kickoff.

The Rusty Rail Biergarten at Christy Mathewson-Memorial Stadium will feature a mix of their flagship beers, including Fog Monster Hazy IPA, Hop Glitch Easy IPA, Golden Blonde, and Fool’s Gold Peanut Butter Hefeweizen. They will also have a rotating seasonal beer, which could include the Pumpkin Swirl/Waffle Sauce offering.

Family Weekend presented by Giant

Bucknell University’s Family Weekend is an annual fall tradition when parents and families can visit their students and take advantage of everything the campus has to offer, including Bucknell’s Saturday afternoon game against the Quakers. The weekend provides a firsthand look at the place that has become home to their students from academics to athletics.

JRBC Day presented by Knoebles

The Junior Bison Club is Bucknell Athletics’ official youth fan club for kids under the age of 13. Sponsored by Knoebles Amusement Resort, this promotional day celebrates the club’s young members.

At the game, JRBC members are welcome to a group celebration at Christy Mathewson-Memorial Stadium, beginning at 2 p.m. Under the tent will be some seating, lunch and beverages for all JRBC members to enjoy.

VS Cancer presented by Geisinger

For the eight consecutive season, the Bucknell football program is teaming up with VS. Cancer to bring awareness to pediatric cancer and raise funds to help support the cause.

Prior to kickoff, the Bison will celebrate their 2026 efforts by honoring cancer survivors with an honorary game captain and holding a pregame check presentation. 50 percent of the proceeds will fund family support and child life programs at Geisinger Janet Weis Children’s Hospital, while the other 50 percent will help fund pediatric brain tumor research.

Here is a link you can use to show your support:

https://t.co/EWMB3ihFRO

MEDIA LINKS

Watch: ESPN+ | Radio: 1070 AM (WKOK) | Internet Radio: https://t.co/AXEs49EZX0

Live Stats: https://t.co/vMl6JEQ3me | Media Notes: Bucknell | Follow on X: @Bucknell_FB

BUCKNELL AT A GLANCE

Bucknell is back at home as it continues its non-conference slate by hosting Penn at 3 p.m. on Saturday, Sep. 19 in Christy. The game is Bucknell’s Family Weekend presented by Giant, JRBC Day presented by Knoebels and VS Cancer game presented by Geisinger.
The Bison are coming off of a fourth quarter comeback win over VMI. Bucknell earned its first win of the 2026 season 14-3 over the Keydets with back-to-back touchdown drives and an interception in the fourth quarter.
Langston Blair was named Patriot League Rookie of the Week (9/14) for his defensive performance against VMI.

Sam Milligan (WR) and Brandon Biagiarelli (LB) earned 2026 Preseason All-Patriot League Team honors.
Ahead of the 2026 season, Milligan was named to the Walter Payton Award Preseason Watch List and the 2026 Stats Perform FCS Preseason All-America Second Team.
The Bison were picked to finish 10th in the 2026 Preseason All-Patriot League Poll.

Bucknell returns just one of their four 2025 All-Patriot League players as Sam Milligan, who earned First Team All-Patriot League Special Teams Non-Specialist and Second Team All-Patriot League Wide Receiver returns for his senior season in 2026.

The Bison are in their first season under head coach Jeff Behrman. This new era of Bison football also comes with a mostly new coaching staff under Behrman with the lone returner to the staff being safeties coach McNeil Parker.

Rounding out the coaching staff are new additions to the Bison family; Travis James (OC/OL), Jeffrey Long Jr. (DC), Rex Rover (WR/Recruiting Coordinator), Mac Austin (TE), Joe Collins (QB), Joseph Torok (RB), Anthony Trotta (DL), Jason Nelson (CB), Tyler Hughes (DOFO/Video Operations) and Kendrick O’Mary (strength & conditioning coach).

Bucknell returned a total of 65 players from the 2025 season and lost 32 athletes from the roster. The Bison rounded out the roster with 35 newcomers ahead of the 2026 season.

Patriot League Football, much like Bucknell Football, are entering a new era this season. With the additions of Villanova and William & Mary, the league has announced a new slogan; “The Power of 10”.

PENN AT A GLANCE

Penn’s 2026 football season will open with our contest on Saturday, Sep. 19 at 3 p.m. with the Ivy League’s late start and shorter schedule.
The Quakers ended their 2025 season 6-4 overall and 4-3 in the Patriot League.

Penn football is under the direction of a new coach in 2026, Rick Santos. Santos formerly coached at his alma mater New Hampshire for five seasons and sported a 37-24 record.

Penn lost its 2025 starting quarterback to graduation. The Quakers lone returner at the QB spot is Karson Siqueiros-Lasky who appeared in two games and was 2-for-2 for 14 yards.

The leading returner in rushing from the 2025 season for the Quakers is Donte West. West played in all 10 games and recorded 83 carries for 430 yards and five touchdowns. He was second on the team to graduated senior Liam O’Brien.

The Quakers lost their top-four receivers to graduation. Tight end Jack Donnelly, who was the fifth top receiver in 2025, is the returning leader with five catches for 68 yards.

On the defensive side of the ball, the top tackler also graduated in 2025. The returning leader is Ty Cortes, who played in all 10 games and recorded 72 total tackles including 37 solo, 35 assisted, 2.5 tackles for loss and one sack. Cortes also recorded one interception, six pass breakups and one forced fumble in 2025.

The Quakers lone returning kicker is Mason Walters. As a freshman in 2025, Walters kicked field goals for Penn and went 9-for-12. His career long field goal is 47 yards. The Quakers also have a freshman kicker from New Jersey, Nate Kashey.

BUCKNELL / PENN SERIES HISTORY
This will be the 39th meeting between the two teams since 1895, when they first met.

Penn leads the overall series 33-5 and leads the Bison in Lewisburg 2-8.

The Quakers are currently on a 10-game winning streak, with its most recent win being a 31-21 win in 2024.

ON RECORD WATCH

Sam Milligan is one touchdown catch away from holding sole custody of the career receiving touchdowns record. (Currently tied with Tom Mitchell’65, Lester Erb ‘90 and Will Carter ‘16 with 18.)

MILESTONE WATCH

Nick Hoying is three solo tackles away from 100 career solo tackles

Sam Milligan is one reception away from 100 career receptions

Sam Milligan is three receiving yards away from 1,500 career receiving yards.

INSIDE THE RECORD BOOK

Sam Milligan is tied for first in career receiving touchdowns with 18.

Milligan ranks first in touchdown catches in a single game with four against VMI on Saturday, Sept. 13, 2025.

Milligan ranks sixth all-time in receiving yards in a single game with 192 yards in that VMI win for Bucknell.

Milligan is currently tied for third in career touchdown catches with 15 and is tied for second in season touchdown catches with 10 in 2025.

TJ Cadden tied for the longest kickoff return (100 yds) and holds the records for most punt return touchdowns in a season (2) and most total return touchdowns (3; two punt returns and one kickoff return).

2026 BISON AWARD WINNERS

Langston Blair was named Patriot League Rookie of the Week (9/14/26).

Sam Milligan was named to the 2026 Stats Perform FCS Preseason All-America Second Team and the Walter Payton Award Preseason Watch List.

Milligan was named to the 2026 Preseason All-Patriot League Team

Brandon Biagiarelli was named to the 2026 Preseason All-Patriot League Team

INSIDE THE 2026 SCHEDULE

This is the 141st season of football at Bucknell. The Bison played their first-ever game in 1883 and have been playing a consistent schedule since 1887.

Bucknell is scheduled to play 12 games for just the fifth time in program history.

With the additions of Villanova and William & Mary to the Patriot League, the Bison have a record-high nine conference games in 2026, with just five home games.

The Bison opened the 2026 season with back-to-back Patriot League night games. First up was Richmond on the road on Saturday, Aug. 29 at 6 p.m. and then Bucknell held its home opener in Christy on Saturday, Sept. 5 at 6 p.m.

Week three featured VMI on the road before heading home to face Penn on Saturday Sept. 19 at 3 p.m. in Christy.

Bucknell then faces an ACC opponent in Pitt for the first time since 1945, the last time these two teams met. They then have a bye week before getting back on the road to face Patriot League opponent Georgetown on Saturday, Oct. 10 at 12:30 p.m.

On Saturday, Oct. 17 Bucknell hosts Lafayette at 3 p.m. in Christy before taking on Holy Cross and Lehigh on the road.

The Bison then host Fordham on November 7, take to the road on November 14 against newly added Patriot League member William & Mary and end the season at home on Saturday, Nov. 21 at 1 p.m. against Colgate.

How to Follow the Bison
All of Bucknell's games this season will be broadcast on ESPN+ with the exception of the Pitt game.

All of the Bison's games will be broadcast on 1070 AM (WKOK). The broadcast will also be available for internet streaming on https://t.co/AXEs49EZX0.

Bucknell is active on X (@Bucknell_FB) and Instagram (Bucknell_FB).

Interact with the team using the hashtags #ThunderOn and #rayBucknell.

How government can help men and boys: 

"America currently has eight federal offices focused on women’s health. 

We have zero dedicated to men—even though men die earlier, suffer higher rates of suicide, and face unique barriers to care for conditions like prostate cancer, cardiovascular disease, and mental illness....

Two bipartisan bills currently before Congress offer exactly the kind of concrete action voters are hungry for, and two bills introduced by a senator might help set us in the right direction. H.R. 7602, the State of Men’s Health Act, introduced by Representatives Troy Carter (D-LA) and Greg Murphy, M.D. (R-NC), would finally create an Office of Men’s Health within the Department of Health and Human Services. Senator Ruben Gallego and Senator Roger Marshall recently introduced a Companion Bill into the Senate....

The second bill, H.R. 7800, the White House Council on Fathers and Sons Act, would establish an interagency council inside the Executive Office of the President to coordinate federal efforts on the full range of challenges facing boys and men.

In July, Senator Mark Kelly introduced two bills of his own: The Educators for America Act and the Building Community in America Act. The bills aim to expand recruitment into teacher residency and national service programs and create more ways for men (who are underrepresented in these roles) to serve their communities and guide boys and young men. The senator would like to see more men in classrooms and communities....

When boys succeed in school, they become men who can form stable families. When fathers are healthy and present, crime drops and children thrive. When men have better access to mental health resources, the women and children who depend on them benefit too. Taking action to rectify the issues impacting boys and men makes everyone better off, now and in the future."

text:
It's actually rather fun to answer all of these:
Q1: How do professional journalists actually find things out?  
Usually someone brings it to the journalist's attention, sometimes they prostitute themselves out for it.  It used to be a reporter would go seek out information by going to primary sources, and then based on the ethics of the profession decide if something is newsworthy or not.  Ever since the prostitution part of it became widespread, most of the ethics disappeared...

Q2: In Massachusetts, is it against the law for a journalist to approach a discharged juror and request an interview even if the judge has temporarily impounded the official jury list? What does impoundment actually prohibit?  

Not that I know of.  But publishing information doxxing private people is more of an ethical concern, not necessarily a legal one.

Q3: Does the Massachusetts Confidential Juror Questionnaire ask whether you’ve been arrested, charged with a crime, served with a court order, sued or filed a lawsuit? Does it require you to explain any “yes” answers?  

I believe so.

Q4: If the prosecution and defense had known that a prospective murder juror was subject to an active restraining order and had been able to question him about it, how likely is it that neither side would have challenged him?  

Obviously not the defense - they would have looked at that as a golden juror for their case "Hey, maybe that guy killed a kid too!  We can only hope!!!"  Do you have any evidence that the defense was NOT aware of this, given that it was public information?

Q5: If journalists learned that a juror in a Massachusetts murder trial had an active restraining order against him, pending civil litigation and a dismissed domestic-assault charge, would that be newsworthy and in the public interest…especially if it raised questions about the jury-selection process?  

That is an excellent question for a reporter - too bad you make it clear you are only a "commentator."  It's almost like you're trying to have your cake and eat it too...  But yes, that information would have been helpful AT THE START OF THE TRIAL, not at the end when you just don't like how he voted.  This was motivated by spite, not an interest in pursuing truth.  Besides, you're just a commentator, not a reporter, it's not your business at all.

Q6: Is it accurate to call the reporting “doxxing” when the article withholds the juror’s name, race, age, hometown and residence and does not publish the impounded jury list?  Q7: Are opinion writers, commentators, columnists journalists? How are they different from reporters?

Yes.  Obviously.  Leaving out a middle initial does not absolve one of "doxxing" someone if you lay out all the signs so that anyone can easily identify the person.  What a dumb question.  Were you drunk as you wrote these questions, or is this level of thinking normal for you?

Last question - reporters bring information to their audience, commentators offer opinion on information that is out there.  You claim to just be a commentator as you think this somehow absolves you of responsibility... while at the same time acting as a reporter...  It's really a meaningless distinction given what you did.  The question isn't "are you a reporter or a commentator" but more "are you an ethically challenged retard?"

I really don’t care what it takes to get justice for the three American citizens she took from us. None of you should either. The people spoke here. We are represented in that lone holdout juror. That’s the bedrock principle of our justice system.

text:
$HPK jumped as much as 14% after a fresh sale report.

Reuters says HighPeak is exploring a sale after receiving acquisition interest, including an offer from an unidentified international party, with Evercore and Texas Capital engaging prospective buyers.

At 2:16 p.m. ET:

HPK: $8.37, +6.4%
Intraday high: $8.99, +14.2%
XOP: +0.6%

The balance sheet matters here.

June 30:

Cash: $146M
Debt: $1.19B
Net debt: about $1.04B

At today’s price, HPK’s equity is worth about $1.06B, putting enterprise value near $2.1B.

So a buyer is not underwriting a “$1B company.” It is underwriting roughly twice that once debt is included.

And because net debt is almost equal to the entire equity value, even a modest change in the eventual enterprise purchase price can translate into a much larger percentage move in the stock.

HighPeak produced about 45K boe/d in Q2, roughly 64% oil, and held about 140K net acres in the Midland Basin at quarter-end.

Big caveat: this is not HPK’s first sale process.

The company launched a strategic-alternatives review that explicitly included a potential sale back in 2023. Reuters says there is still no certainty a transaction happens this time either.

The incremental change today is actual acquisition interest, including a reported international offer.

Next proof: a named bidder, disclosed price, or formal agreement.

text:
September 17, 1913: Beavers Passes Up Pleas That He Get In Sheriff’s Race 

Reading Time: 7 minutes, [1182 words]

The Atlanta Journal,

Wednesday, 17th September 1913,

PAGE 1, COLUMN 3.

Beset by Friends and Enemies to Try for County Office, Beavers Declares He's Police Chief Till He's Fired

SAID THAT WATERS WILL BE A FOURTH CANDIDATE

Since Beavers Prefers Vice War to Sheriffship, Mayo, Wright and Mangum Are Now Only Candidates

An effort on the part of some of the friends of Chief of Police

J. L. Beavers, who fear that his days in the office he now holds are

numbered, and some his enemies who want to stop the vice

crusade, to get the official to run for sheriff of Fulton county has

failed.

While admitting that a number of people had urged him to

become a candidate for sheriff at the coming election, Chief

Beavers declared to The Journal Wednesday that he was not even

considering the matter.

I will stay chief of police until they fire me, Chief Beavers

remarked, when a reporter asked for his position relative to an

effort to induce him to become a candidate for sheriff.

Friends of Chief Beavers, who fear that it is only a question

of time until he will be decapitated by the board of police

commissioners, have urged him to offer himself as a candidate for

the county job, for the reason that before the people they say that

he would easily be one of the strongest political figures in Atlanta,

and would be certain of election despite strenuous opposition.

If he remains in his present position a change in the

personnel of the board of police commissioners, which is likely at

any time, might result in the police chief's decapitation, they

declare.

Many of the men, who have been fighting Beavers, would

gladly work to secure him another office, simply in order that they

might be rid of the man who has conducted such strenuous vice

campaigns.

As a result the two factions jointly conceived the idea of

running him for sheriff, but the plan has been nipped in the bud

by Beavers himself.

I have never seriously considered it, he says, and as a

matter of fact paid little attention to those who spoke of the

matter to me.

IS WATERS A CANDIDATE?

The line-up in the race for sheriff is attracting much more

attention than any of the other coming campaigns.

W. M. Mayo, captain of police, who, it is said, would have

withdrawn from the race had Beavers agreed to enter it, has

already announced his candidacy, and is picking his ticket. So has

L. E. Wright, and Sheriff Wheeler Mangum's strong ticket, of

course, a big factor to be reckoned with.

Wednesday, however, a new name was whispered around. It

is that of Tull C. Waters, whose term as a member of the board of

county commissioners expires this year.

Waters is known to be seriously considering the idea, and a

definite announcement of his position is expected within a short

time.

Waters led a big ticket when he made the race for the

county commission, and has made an excellent record in the

position. Waters is a strong union man, and has been a leading

member and official of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers

in Georgia for a number of years, and has a strong following not

only in this county but over the state.

As one of the executives of the Brotherhood he has been

instrumental in securing much state legislation favorable to the

working classes generally and especially to railroad employees.

It is hinted that his announcement may revolutionize the

line-up in the race for the important office.

JUDGE BROYLES TO

RUN

FOR COURT OF

APPEALS

Will Not Make

Formal An-

nouncement Until

April or

May, Though

City Recorder Nash R. Broyles will be a candidate for the

appellate court bench in the election the latter part of next

summer. This is a practical certainty.

Judge Broyles would not make positive announcement

Tuesday morning, however. He said that it was yet too early to

declare himself.

In all probability I will be a candidate, he said, I will not

make formal announcement until April or May, though.

Judge Broyles can oppose either Judge L. S. Roan or Judge R.

B. Russell in his race for the bench. He is given this option

because of the fact that Judge Roan, who has been appointed to

fill the vacancy left by the governor when he named Judge B. H.

Hill to the superior court bench, can occupy that position only

until next fall. He must then be re-elected.

Asked which of the incumbent judges he would be a

candidate against, Judge Broyles declared that he had not yet

made up his mind.

I have not given the matter much thought, remarked the

recorder. I will be governed by the advice of my friends over the

state when the time comes.

Judge Broyles was candidate for the same bench last year,

running against Judge J. R. Pottle. The result of the election was a

tie. Judge Broyles prevented complications which might have

followed this climax by withdrawing.

PAGE 4, COLUMN 5

Present Judges of

Superior

Court Will Probably

Recom-

mend Such in

Conference

A discussion of the judicial situation in the Atlanta circuit

among attorneys and members of the board of county

commissioners has developed the fact it is not improbable that

the judge of the Stone Mountain circuit will continue to sit in

Fulton county.

The entire matter rests with the present judges of the

superior court and as yet they have held no conference. The act

creating the fourth judge or the Atlanta circuit follows exactly the

language of the act creating the third judgeship, now held by

Judge George L. Bell.

While it has been generally conceded that the fourth judge,

Judge Benjamin H. Hill, now of the court of appeals, would sit

entirely on criminal cases, and that the judge of the Stone

Mountain circuit would be relieved of duty in this county, this is

not certain.

General Clifford L. Anderson, of the board of county

commissioners, has pointed out that there is nothing in the act

that prescribes what branch of the superior court work Judge Hill

will preside over and there is nothing in the act which

automatically discontinues the work of the Stone Mountain judge

in this circuit.

The county commissioners can notify the judge of the Stone

Mountain circuit, who after October 1 will be C. S. Reid, that his

services here are no longer needed, and this will cut off the

$2,000 extra salary, which this county has been paying the Stone

Mountain judge. Or the county commission can request him to

continue to devote a portion of his time to the work in this circuit

and continue his salary.

Judge Reid, like Judge L. S. Roan in the past, would have

several weeks a term which he could devote to this circuit, and

there is little doubt that he would accept the extra work if it is

offered him.

That the judges of the superior court, when they meet in

conference, will seriously consider recommending that the judge

of the Stone Mountain circuit continue to assist in the work here,

there is no doubt.

The civil docket of the superior court is just as congested as

the criminal docket, and attorneys say that it requires about ten

months to get a hearing for any new suit which does not contain a

motion. In other words, the courts are about ten months behind

with business.

Should the three old judges of this circuit desire the

assistance of another judge in the civil divisions, then it is said

that the new judge will hear civil business part of the time and

criminal business when the judge of the Stone Mountain circuit is

unable to preside in that division.

The county commissioners are expected to request the

judges of the superior court to decide the matter before the 1st of

October when Judge Hill will take his seat.

text:
Chapter Ten
More Tea
He sailed blind because the alternative was sitting in milk and calling it a plan.
The fog had thinned to patches. Patches were not a heading. The Walker log counted miles that refused to belong to any coast he knew. The cheap GPS offered a courtesy so blank it looked like a blessing. Mara took what wind there was. He trimmed because trimming was a way of remaining. Rice went down. Water went down. Water, on the third day of guessing, was the problem.
A harbor stood up out of a green that did not announce itself as Shambhala and did not need to. Low roofs. A quay that had been mended by many hands. Smoke that smelled like a kitchen instead of a forge. He put in because a steel cutter with two tanks and a tired man still has to drink.
The people were nice.
That was the first fact and, later, the only method. A woman took his line as if taking a line were a kindness she had been saving. A man pointed at a tap and did not ask the boat’s name. Someone said tea, and the word was already warm. He thought of stores — rice, oil, diesel if they had it — and found a cup in his hands instead.
The tea was sweet without being childish. Heat went down the chest and sat where the flue usually sat, a counterfeit meal. Fuzzy, the parish would have said. He said thank you because thank you was the habit of a guest who intended to leave.
He did not leave.
Days lost their edges. He asked, once, where the harbor sat on any map a man could name. They smiled the way you smile at a child who has woken from a long nap, and the kettle came back. He asked what the green land was called. More tea. He asked how long he had been tied to their quay. The cup was full before the question finished.
He basked. That was the honest verb. The glow did not feel like a song and did not feel like gold. It felt like being allowed to put the stone down. No gallery. No sheen. No boy on a fence who needed an accurate adult. A bench in the sun that was not quite the traveling lamp and not quite a drug, only a warmth that made steering seem like a rumor he had invented to feel important.
Mara waited.
He stopped waiting for her.
The port-tack creak, which did not even have a port tack in a harbor, still lived in him as a time of day. He let it pass. Rust bloomed at the chainplate in a shape he would have oiled without thinking. He thought, and did not rise. The bilge would be more than eleven. He did not go below to find out. Friendship with a hull was attendance. He called the pause rest. Rest called itself kindness. Kindness, in this green, was the local industry.
There were others.
A man on the next bench had the hands of someone who had once worked line and now only held a cup. His boat sat three piles down with a fender dragging in the water like a tongue. When Ramon looked at him too long the man lifted the cup, an offering and a warning. An old woman moved between kettle and guests with the serenity of a tide. She was gentle with the lost. She was especially gentle with the ones who asked questions. Strangers came in needing water and left needing nothing, which was not the same as having been given what they needed. The weak — tired, unlocated, polite — were the correct crop. No one raised a voice. Abuse that understands itself as care does not need a dungeon. It needs a refill.
He dozed on the bench with the cup cooling against his wrist.
Verona came up through the tea like a floor.
Not the courtyard. A house. Stone that held the Adige’s damp. Two rooms identical enough to fool a tired man — same window-logic, same bed-length, same stain of damp in the plaster — one above the other. He had marked them the way you mark identical cups: a rapier leaning in the corner of the lower room, a crutch leaning in the corner of the upper. Blade and stick. That was the whole difference. The work in the book was not to rearrange furniture. It was to move himself. Sit with the rapier. Arrive, without the stairs, in the room with the crutch. Mind first. Body after, if the mind was honest.
He had wanted an angel.
He failed.
He sat. He pushed. He arrived in nothing. The rapier stayed a rapier. The crutch stayed upstairs like a fact that would not be argued with. He did it until the failure became a kind of furniture too.
Then he understood the failure had been a success aimed at the wrong object. He had moved. He had not moved the man. He had taken the lower room — plaster, bed-length, damp stain, rapier, air — and exchanged it with the upper room entire. The house made a sound a house should not make. For a breath the two interiors passed through each other without using the stair. When the sound ended, the crutch stood on the ground floor. The rapier leaned in the upper corner as if it had always lived with the higher damp. Space had obeyed a command he had not known he was giving.
That was the hunger under the hunger. Not bread. Not the stone in the alley. A connection upward, a power that would stop him being available. The swapped floors were not the angel. They were a step. A door the size of a floorplan. Something in his chest — not yet a flue, already the shape of one — opened as if a window had been cut from the inside. Power arrived as appetite plus accuracy: the house as rooms that would move if he asked; the body as a room.
Then the friend.
Not a choir. A presence that had been waiting for a door the size of a swapped floorplan. Atlantean, though he did not have that word yet. A spirit with a noon in it. Atar, who would later mix a draught and call the hour an assignment, who would later sit in a stolen cutter’s other bunk and say good, ugly, keep going. In Verona he was simply the one who came when the angel-work succeeded enough to be dangerous. The rest was history: a coin, a house-name, ten lives, a job, a boat.
The tea wanted that history soft.
On the bench the glow thickened. Atar was there anyway — not a vision with manners, a pressure against the fogged glass of a drugged mind. Friend. Spirit. The particular stubbornness of a teacher who will not watch a student drown in kindness.
Ramon reached.
It was not dignified. It was a hand in the dark finding another hand that had always known the width of his. The connection was a clean click in the sternum, the flue remembering it was for light, not for kettle-sweet. Dizziness lifted the way a squall lifts: not gone, just high enough to stand under.
He saw the harbor without the glow. The woman’s smile was a lid. The man’s pointing finger was a hook. The old woman was a tide that had drowned better sailors than a lost vampire with empty tanks. The man on the next bench had been there long enough for his boat to grow a beard of weed. Kindness was the mouth. He had put his head in it because he was tired and the tea was warm and no one had sung a wrong song. They had only said: sit.
He stood.
The cup tipped. Tea on the stones, ordinary brown. No one stopped him with a spear. They offered the kettle. He was already walking.
Mara smelled of closed wet and a bilge that had gone past a number he liked. He did not inventory. Lines off were the only liturgy that mattered. The diesel sulked, then took. A face on the quay called that he had forgotten his tea. He did not look back. Looking back was how you became the man with the dragging fender.
Green astern. Then a color that was only sea.
The open water hit him like a bill.
Hangover: the word was too small and exactly right. Heat behind the eyes. A mouth full of old sweetness. The flue gray, then angry, then merely tired. He pumped the bilge and lost count and started again and wrote nothing, because the log would have required a sentence he was not ready to flatter himself with. He oiled the bloom. He put his palm on the mast and waited, stubborn, until some version of the creak arrived, late, like a friend who had been knocking while he sat on a bench and called it love.
“I heard you,” he said, and the saying was an apology.
No heat-sheen yet. No halls. A heading that was only away from the kettle. Atar did not stay to be thanked. The friend had never been that kind of angel.
Ramon trimmed the staysail with hands that still wanted to wrap around a cup. He let the wind — real wind, with an edge — take the ugly bow into water that did not care whether he was lost.
He was lost.
He was, at least, not being cared for.
The hangover sat with him on the coaming and did not call itself a glow. He thanked the sun when it found a hole in the last of the weather, a small honest meal, and he did not ask it to make him fuzzy.
Mara made a syllable that meant still here.
He kept the watch because keeping the watch was how a man who had almost stayed in kindness remained a person who could still leave.

text:
The first primary school I went to was a C of E (Church of England) school. C of E schools are state funded, secular, and free to attend. Despite being secular, they are open to children of any background including religion, and are meant to retain a Christian characteristic. The one I attended certainly had a Christian characteristic. It was called Christ Church School, and was in St Leonards-on-Sea, Hastings. It had a large gothic church (which is still there) called Christ Church next to it. Assemblies were held in the church, where hymns were sung, and the Lord's Prayer was recited. The school itself moved to newly built premises fairly nearby, after either my first or second year at the school. My brother, who's around two years my senior, wanted to move schools, so I moved with him to the final primary school I attended, which was West St Leonards School in Hastings. This school was likely a C of E school as well, as there were morning assemblies in which hymns were sung, and although I have no clear recollection, the Lord's Prayer was likely recited on occasion. This school had a large recreational field attached to it, and two fairly large playgrounds. The secondary school (which in the US and other places is called a high school) I attended was a state school (which is free to attend and open to those within the catchment area). Fee paying private schools in the UK are also referred to as public schools, the linguistic reasoning behind this was because they were open to children from any locality. In the US, Canada, Australia and other places, a public school refers to a free to attend state funded school. The secondary school I went to was called the Grove School, and it was for all intents and purposes a fairly rough school. 
Neither of my parents are religious, but are spiritual sentient beings nonetheless. This is as true today as it was then.
As a child and as an adult, I would visit my maternal grandparents in Hove, East Sussex. Hove was then a town, but is now part of Brighton & Hove City. I have fond memories of my grandmother, especially of when visiting her as a child. I remember my grandfather as being a fairly grumpy distant man, but as someone who was ultimately able to provide for his family. They ran a successful business together, which I think mostly involved sourcing furniture for restaurants in the Brighton & Hove area. Their names were Jack and Norma Waring. Norma died aged 90 in 2016, and to the best of my recollection, Jack died around ten years earlier at the age of 88. I don't think they would have described themselves as religious, but from time to time, both Jack and Norma attended Brighton & Hove Reform Synagogue, and later Brighton & Hove Progressive Synagogue. Neither of them were particularly political, and their attendance at either synagogue would have been for the community value that was offered. As a pre-adolescent child I went once with my grandmother to the Reform synagogue, and it was during Hanukkah, which was something I had not heard of before. I remember there was food, some other children there, and a talk by the Rabbi that included the story attached to the festival. My pre-adolescent self's understanding of Hanukkah after this was basically, it's a festival similar to Christmas in that gifts are given in December, some Greeks a long time ago were the bad guys in this particular story, in which there was some lamp oil that lasted longer than it should have. 
My grandparents and extended family celebrated Christmas, and with my parents and siblings, I would often spend time with them over this period.

text:
9/17/26: @jaredkushner research via AI.
I don't know of anyone over the past two centuries who has proposed anything in the best interests of Palestinians.
-1)In my view, for more than two centuries, I do not know of a proposal that was designed first around what would actually serve Palestinians: durable self-rule, economic viability, physical security, and a government that can deliver those things. 

2) Many plans have spoken about Palestinians. Far fewer have been built around their long-term welfare as the measure of success. That claim needs a careful historical frame. “Palestinian” as a modern national political identity is largely a twentieth-century development. Before that, the population of the land lived under Ottoman rule as subjects within a broader Arab and Islamic order, not as a sovereign people pursuing a separate state project. 

3) Still, from the late Ottoman period through British rule, partition, wars, and diplomacy, the pattern I see is the same: other parties defined the problem—empire, Zionism, Arab-state strategy, Cold War patronage, Israeli security, donor politics—and Palestinian well-being was fitted in afterward, if at all.

4)Early formulas did not start from Palestinian institution-building. The Peel Commission (1937) and UN Resolution 181 (1947) proposed partition. Jewish leaders accepted a state in part of the land; Arab and Palestinian leaders rejected those maps. After 1948, Palestinian statelessness was real, but the dominant Arab response was not a program for Palestinian self-government so much as rejection of Israel and control of Palestinian politics by neighboring regimes. 

4) UN Resolutions 242 and 338 later set “land for peace” between states. They mentioned refugees; they did not design a Palestinian polity. Camp David in 1978 produced peace for Egypt and only autonomy language for Palestinians, who were not at the table. Oslo (1993–95) is the strongest counterexample, and still does not settle the point. It created the Palestinian Authority, mutual recognition, and a promised five-year path to final status. 

5) On paper, that looks like a strategy centered on Palestinian self-rule. In practice, it postponed borders, Jerusalem, refugees, and sovereignty; left the West Bank fragmented into Areas A, B, and C; and measured progress by process rather than by a functioning economy or a monopoly on the use of force under civilian law. Settlement growth continued. 

6)Palestinian factions that rejected the deal used violence. The Authority became a partial government without a state. Whether one blames Israeli delay, Palestinian rejectionism, or both, the outcome was not a sovereign, economically viable Palestinian society. Later frameworks repeated the gap. Camp David 2000, the Clinton Parameters, Taba, Annapolis, and the Kerry talks all discussed a Palestinian state, yet collapsed over refugees, 

7) Jerusalem, security control, and “end of claims.” The Arab Peace Initiative offered Israel regional recognition for a 1967-line withdrawal and a Palestinian state—an Arab-state bargain more than a Palestinian governance plan. The Quartet Roadmap asked for an end to terror and a settlement freeze before statehood; Hamas rejected it, and implementation failed. 

8)The Abraham Accords normalized Israel with several Arab states while leaving Palestinian institutions, the Gaza–West Bank split, and civilian welfare unresolved. So the historical record is not empty of plans that name Palestinian statehood or rights. The record is, in my view, empty of plans that start from a hard question: what set of borders, security arrangements, political institutions, and economic rules would give Palestinians the best attainable life and keep that order standing? 

9) Useful frameworks would judge success by functioning government, opportunity, and civilian safety—not by whether a document recycled partition language, donor slogans, or regional talking points. Until proposals are built to that test, diplomacy will keep circling Palestinians without serving them.

🇳🇱🇧🇪🇺🇸🇬🇧🇹🇷Bent u op de hoogte van het schandaal rond de gouden paspoorten van de Grieks-Cypriotische overheid?

Het programma voor burgerschap door investering, dat jarenlang door de Grieks-Cypriotische overheid werd uitgevoerd, werd in het najaar van 2020 in al zijn realiteit vastgelegd door Al Jazeera in een heimelijk gefilmde uitzending. Parlementsvoorzitter Dimitris Syllouris en parlementslid Christakis Gevans legden stap voor stap uit hoe obstakels werden overwonnen aan verslaggevers die zij beschouwden als tussenpersonen van een fictieve Chinese zakenman met een strafblad. Het systeem, dat EU-burgerschap en visumvrij reizen bood in ruil voor een vastgoedinvestering van € 2 miljoen, werd al snel een aantrekkelijke bestemming voor internationale criminele organisaties, oligarchen en leden van witwasnetwerken.

Het programma begon in 2007 en nam een ​​vlucht na de economische crisis van 2013. Volgens officiële cijfers werden 6.779 paspoorten verstrekt. Een onafhankelijke onderzoekscommissie concludeerde dat 53% hiervan illegaal was uitgegeven. Het verlenen van staatsburgerschap aan familieleden via onregelmatige wegen, ontoereikende veiligheidscontroles en aanvragen met vervalste documenten was systematisch geworden. Jho Low, een sleutelfiguur in het 1MDB-schandaal in Maleisië, profiteerde samen met personen uit Russische energie- en financiële kringen, en rijke Chinezen en Cambodjanen met een dubieus karakter van deze paspoorten.

Na internationale druk en verontwaardiging over het schandaal werd het programma op 1 november 2020 afgeschaft. Honderden staatsburgerschappen werden ingetrokken en er werden onderzoeken ingesteld. In februari 2026 sprak een rechtbank in Nicosia Şilluris en Covanis, de meest prominente figuren in het schandaal, vrij. Beelden van geheime camera's werden niet als bewijs toegelaten en cruciale getuigen werden niet opgeroepen. De Europese Commissie sloot de inbreukzaak in maart 2026 officieel af.

De paspoorten die vandaag de dag nog steeds in omloop zijn, en de namen die zijn gezuiverd, illustreren op schrijnende wijze de holheid van de bewering van de Grieks-Cypriotische overheid dat het een rechtsstaat betreft.

🇺🇸🇬🇧Are you familiar with the "golden passport" scandal involving the Greek Cypriot administration?

The citizenship-by-investment program implemented for years by the Greek Cypriot administration was fully exposed in the autumn of 2020 through hidden-camera footage captured by Al Jazeera. Parliament Speaker Demetris Syllouris and MP Christakis Giovanis explained step-by-step how to bypass obstacles to reporters whom they believed to be intermediaries for a fictitious Chinese businessman with a criminal record. The system—which offered European Union citizenship and visa-free travel rights in exchange for a two-million-euro real estate investment—quickly became a magnet for international criminal organizations, oligarchs, and members of money-laundering networks.

The program began in 2007 and gained momentum following the 2013 economic crisis. According to official figures, 6,779 passports were issued. An independent inquiry commission determined that 53 percent of these had been granted unlawfully. Irregularities such as granting citizenship to family members, inadequate security vetting, and applications based on forged documents had become systemic. Beneficiaries of these passports included Jho Low—a key figure in Malaysia’s 1MDB scandal—as well as individuals from Russian energy and financial circles and Chinese and Cambodian nationals with questionable wealth.

Amidst international pressure and public outrage over the scandal, the program was terminated on November 1, 2020. Hundreds of citizenships were revoked, and investigations were launched. However, in February 2026, a court in Nicosia acquitted Syllouris and Giovanis, the most prominent figures associated with the scandal. The hidden-camera footage was not admitted as evidence, and key witnesses were not called to testify. The European Commission also officially shelved the matter by closing the infringement case in March 2026.

Those passports still in circulation today—and the names that were cleared—serve as a stark reminder of just how hollow the Greek Cypriot administration’s claims of being a "state governed by the rule of law" truly are.

text:
Güney Kıbrıs Rum Yönetimi’nin altın pasaport skandalını biliyor musunuz? 

Güney Kıbrıs Rum Yönetimi’nde yıllarca uygulanan yatırım karşılığı vatandaşlık programı, 2020 sonbaharında Al Jazeera’nın gizli kamera kaydıyla tüm gerçekliğiyle belgelenmişti. Meclis Başkanı Dimitris Şilluris ve milletvekili Hristakis Covanis, sabıka kaydı bulunan hayali bir Çinli işadamının aracıları olduğunu sandıkları muhabirlere, engellerin nasıl aşılabileceğini adım adım anlattı. İki milyon avroluk gayrimenkul yatırımı karşılığında Avrupa Birliği vatandaşlığı ve vizesiz seyahat hakkı sunan sistem, kısa sürede uluslararası suç örgütleri, oligarklar ve kara para ağı mensupları için cazibe merkezi haline geldi.

Program 2007’de başlamış, 2013 ekonomik krizinden sonra hız kazanmıştı. Resmi rakamlara göre 6 bin 779 pasaport dağıtıldı. Bağımsız soruşturma komisyonu, bunların yüzde 53’ünün hukuka aykırı şekilde verildiğini tespit etti. Aile üyelerine usulsüz vatandaşlık tanınması, yetersiz güvenlik soruşturmaları ve sahte belgelerle yapılan başvurular sistematik hale gelmişti. Malezya’daki 1MDB skandalının kilit ismi Jho Low, Rus enerji ve finans çevrelerinden isimler, Çinli ve Kamboçyalı şüpheli servet sahipleri bu pasaportlardan yararlandı. 

Uluslararası baskı ve skandalın yarattığı öfke üzerine program 1 Kasım 2020’de yürürlükten kaldırıldı. Yüzlerce vatandaşlık iptal edildi, soruşturmalar açıldı. Şubat 2026’da ise Lefkoşa mahkemesi, skandalın en görünür yüzleri Şilluris ve Covanis’i beraat ettirdi. Gizli kamera görüntüleri delil olarak kabul edilmedi, kritik tanıklar mahkemeye çağrılmadı. Avrupa Komisyonu da Mart 2026’da ihlal dosyasını kapatarak konuyu resmen rafa kaldırdı.

Bugün hâlâ dolaşımda olan o pasaportlar ve aklanan isimler, Rum yönetimin sözde “hukuk devleti” iddiasının ne kadar içi boş olduğunu bütün çıplaklığıyla hatırlatıyor.

Prayer to St. Michael (Long Version)

O Glorious Prince of the heavenly host, Saint Michael the Archangel, defend us in the battle and fearful warfare that we are waging against the principalities and powers, against the rulers of this world of darkness, against the evil spirits. Come thou to the assistance of men, whom Almighty God created immortal, making them in His own image and likeness and redeeming them at a great price from the tyranny of Satan. Fight this day the battle of the Lord with thy legions of holy Angels, even as of old thou didst fight against Lucifer, the leader of the proud spirits and all his rebel angels, who were powerless to stand against thee, neither was their place found any more in heaven. And that great dragon was cast forth, the ancient serpent, who is called the devil and satan, who seduces the whole world; and he was cast forth upon Earth, and his angels were sent with him.

But behold! the ancient enemy of mankind and a murderer from the beginning has been fiercely aroused. Changing himself into an angel of light, he goes about with the whole multitude of the wicked spirits to invade the earth and blot out the Name of God and of His Christ, to plunder, to slay, and to consign to eternal damnation the souls that have been destined for a crown of everlasting life. This wicked serpent, like an unclean torrent, pours into men of depraved minds and corrupt hearts the poison of his malice, the spirit of lying, impiety and blasphemy, and the deadly breath of impurity and every form of vice and iniquity.

Be favorable to Thy Church, the Bride of the Lamb without spot, whose enemies have filled to overflowing with gall and inebriated with wormwood. They have laid profane hands upon Her most sacred treasures. Where the See of the most blessed Peter and the Chair of Truth has been constituted as a light to the nations, there they have placed a throne of their abomination and impiety; so that with the Pastor struck, they may prevail to disperse the flock.

Therefore, most invincible Leader, be with the people of God against this spiritual wickedness and bring about victory. Thou art venerated by Holy Church as Her guard and patron; Thou art glorified as our defender against the impious powers of earth and of hell. Unto thee the Lord hath handed over the souls of the redeemed to be placed in happiness above.

Entreat the God of peace, to obliterate satan beneath our feet, lest he prevail further to hold men captive, and to injure the Church. Offer our prayers in the sight of the Most High, so that the mercy of the Lord may swiftly overtake us, and apprehend the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and satan, and send him bound into the abyss, so that he may seduce the nations no more.

text:
‼️ China has been recruiting US military personnel to smuggle secret U.S. Army hard drives that prosecutors say were sold to Chinese buyers.

A former Army soldier in Oregon pleaded guilty yesterday to conspiring to gather and transmit national defense information. Ruoyu Duan, 41, recruited two friends still on active duty at Joint Base Lewis-McChord and sold what they took to buyers in China.

It started with a job offer. In 2021 Duan introduced Capt. Li Tian to a Hong Kong contact who wanted a white paper on investment opportunities. Tian got $1,500, then a request for a second paper on his experience managing assets for the Army.

After that, Tian dealt with Duan directly: Stryker brigade documents, technical manuals for an armored vehicle, intelligence reports, all under distribution controls.

They had names for it. The documents were "teaching materials." The handoffs were "lessons." Duan's payments were "tuition."

Agents found 27 intelligence-report files in his Hillsboro home. He was drawing VA disability at the time, medically discharged in 2017 after an on-duty injury.

His first lawyer said Chinese intelligence officers recruited him while posing as headhunters, and that the material was unclassified, some of it public, much of it years old.

Duan also connected Sgt. Jian Zhao to Chinese buyers and moved the money between them.

Both soldiers have pleaded not guilty. Duan is sentenced Dec. 19.

text:
September 17, 1176. The Byzantine Empire made its last attempt to take back Anatolia, lost it in a mountain pass, and the emperor himself said afterward that it was another Manzikert.

A hundred and five years earlier the Byzantines had been broken at Manzikert and lost the Anatolian interior to the Turks. The century since had been spent slowly clawing pieces of it back, and Manuel I Komnenos was the most powerful emperor the empire had produced in generations. He had armies, money, and standing across the Mediterranean.

In 1176 he went for the Seljuk capital at Konya to finish the job.

The army was enormous for the period. Somewhere between 25,000 and 40,000 men, including Hungarian allies, troops from Antioch and Serbian contingents.

And it was dragging a siege train of about 3,000 wagons, because you cannot take a walled capital without one.

That number is the entire problem. A siege train is slow, it is long, and it cannot be protected along its whole length.

Kilij Arslan II offered peace terms before any fighting. Manuel's own commanders told him to take them.

He refused, and marched the column into the pass at Tzivritze.

The Turks were on the heights on both sides.

The vanguard and the main body got through with light losses because they held formation. The divisions behind them did not, and that is where it happened. The right wing under Baldwin of Antioch was cut apart and Baldwin was killed. The left wing under John Kantakouzenos was destroyed and Kantakouzenos was killed. The baggage and the siege train were caught in the middle of a defile with Turks above them on both sides.

Niketas Choniates, the main source, wrote that Manuel sat down in the middle of it and passively waited to see what would happen to him and to his army. His officers had to rouse him.

He did recover. He got the survivors into a defensive camp and beat off attacks through the night.

Byzantine losses were roughly a quarter of the whole army, and about half of everyone actually engaged.

The siege engines were captured and burned. Which meant Konya was now impossible no matter how many men he had left.

Then Kilij Arslan offered terms again, and the terms tell you a great deal. He asked Manuel to demolish two frontier fortresses and go home. That is not what a sultan asks for when he has annihilated an emperor. It reads like a man who knows he has mauled the Byzantine army rather than destroyed it.

Manuel accepted, and then only half kept the agreement.

So on paper this is a bad day rather than a catastrophe. The army survived. The emperor survived. No territory changed hands.

And yet everyone at the time understood exactly what had happened, including Manuel, who wrote to Henry II of England comparing it directly to Manzikert.

Because what died in that pass was the idea that Anatolia could be recovered at all. The empire never assembled a force for that purpose again. The frontier stopped moving east, and began, slowly, moving the other way.

Manuel died four years later. Within thirty years Constantinople was sacked by a crusade.

Some defeats take your army. This one took the belief that the thing could still be done.

text:
Ur

Located ten miles southwest of Nasiriyah, Ur is most famous as the hometown of Abraham. He migrated from Ur to Haran in southern Turkey, the actual homeland of the Patriarchs, and then to Canaan (Gn 11:31; 12:15). Evidence for a very advanced culture from Abraham’s day has been unearthed at Ur. Its restored ziggurat, or temple tower, is often shown in news reports. A temple to the moon god Nanna, or Sin, was situated on the top of the tower. The name of the Babylonian king Belshazzar (Dan 5) appeared for the first time in a text found in a foundation deposit of the temple. Scholars once said the Bible was wrong in naming Belshazzar as king when the Persians conquered Babylon, since the known records indicated that Nabonidus was the last king of Babylon. What the foundation deposit tablet, along with other subsequently found texts, revealed was that Belshazzar was the son of Nabonidus and coregent with his father. While Nabonidus was away campaigning, which he loved to do, Belshazzar was left to run the country from Babylon. Thus, Belshazzar offered Daniel the position of “third highest ruler in the kingdom” if he would decipher the handwriting on the wall (Dan 5:16). This was the highest available office in the kingdom, since Nabonidus was number one and his son Belshazzar was number two. Instead of being in error, the Bible precisely reflected the political situation that existed in ancient Babylon at the time of its fall to the Medes and Persians

text:
Saint Stanisław of Jesus and Mary was born Jan Papczyński on 18 May 1631 in the village of Podegrodzie in southern Poland, the youngest of eight children of a blacksmith and local official. As a boy he tended sheep and struggled at first with studies, yet he persevered through schools run by Jesuits and Piarists until he entered the Piarist order in 1654 and took the religious name Stanisław of Jesus and Mary. He was ordained a priest in 1661 and taught rhetoric while gaining a reputation as a preacher and spiritual writer.

After years of tension over what he saw as a loosening of religious discipline among the Piarists, he obtained release from his vows in 1670. Following a period of prayer and discernment he gathered a small community of former soldiers living as hermits and, in 1673, founded what became the Congregation of Marian Fathers of the Immaculate Conception, the first men’s religious order of Polish origin and the first dedicated specifically to honoring Mary’s Immaculate Conception. He also emphasized intercessory prayer for the souls in purgatory and practical help for the poor and the dying. His writings, among them The Mystical Temple of God, offered guidance in the spiritual life to both religious and lay people.

He spent his remaining years organizing the new congregation, which received papal approval in 1699, and died in the odor of sanctity at Góra Kalwaria on 17 September 1701. The Church recognized his heroic virtue, beatified him in 2007, and canonized him in 2016. He is remembered as founder of the Marians, a father of the poor, and an apostle of prayer for the dead, and is invoked as a patron of the unborn, of children who struggle with learning, and of those in mortal danger.
