text:
SELLING SCOTLAND

Castle and estate for £9 million, Isle of Mull

A castle is yours for a mere £9 million, complete with historic architecture and dramatic views of the Atlantic coastline. The perfect get-away-from-it-all for a wealthy yank, a millionaire on-the-run on the Epstein list.

Situated at the northern tip of Mull, Glengorm Estate, wants offers 'over' the stated sum but offers " rugged, natural beauty with peace and quiet. It is within easy reach of Mull's principal town, Tobermory, and mainland Scotland.

Helicopters are able to land on the estate lawn, and a nearby airstrip at Salen can accommodate light aircraft. You will need a heft lawn mower, and at least two large dogs as daily companions.

At the heart of it all is Glengorm Castle, a B-listed Baronial residence constructed in 1860. It has turreted façades, ornate decorations and built from locally quarried granite, with sandstone dressings and biblical inscriptions carved into the exterior. Holy Moses!

On the inside, Glengorm Castle blends its historic Victorian glamour with modern comforts. The bedrooms are arranged over several floors, turrets and self‑contained apartments, of which there are four. The drawing room features a large bay window with coastal views, while a formal dining room is well suited to entertaining, and a library provides a more intimate atmosphere.

Throughout the castle, original features and open fireplaces add to the grandeur of the building. There is also a modern biomass central heating system, installed in 2014, to provide efficient and sustainable warmth throughout the property.

The estate itself extends to 3,702 acres, encompassing pasture, rough grazing, hill and coastline, and around 260 acres of woodland.

The estate's shoreline is more than three miles long with secluded bays, rocky headlands and sheltered anchorages at Loch Mingary and Laorin Bay, complete with a historic pier, mooring and boathouse.

Glengorm has a pedigree livestock enterprise: the Highland cattle at Glengorm have been maintained for more than 170 years. Residential properties across the estate include a portfolio of 17 properties, including a combination of long‑term rentals and short‑term holiday lets.

What are you waiting for? The Scots have no regulations on how much you sell it on for, or if you want to turn it into a hotel and 18-hole gold course..

text:
(Mat 5:23-26 NIV)  "Therefore, if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, {24} leave your gift there in front of the altar. First go and be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift. {25} "Settle matters quickly with your adversary who is taking you to court. Do it while you are still with him on the way, or he may hand you over to the judge, and the judge may hand you over to the officer, and you may be thrown into prison. {26} I tell you the truth, you will not get out until you have paid the last penny.

a. Leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way: Jesus considers it far more important to be reconciled to a brother than to perform a religious duty. Jesus says we must first be reconciled to your brother. We can’t think that our service towards the Lord justifies bad relationships with others. We should do what Paul commanded in Romans 12:18: If it is possible, as much as depends on you, live peaceably with all men.

b. Agree with your adversary quickly: Jesus commands us to quickly settle anger and malice with another. When we ignore it or pass it off, it genuinely imprisons us (and you be thrown into prison).

i. Paul expresses the same idea in Ephesians 4:26-27 (do not let the sun go down on your wrath). When we hold on to our anger against another, we then sin – and we give place to the devil.

c. Assuredly, I say to you, you will by no means get out of there till you have paid the last penny: Jesus here spoke with figures of speech. The ultimate penalty one pays at the hands of the judge, the officer, and in the prison could never be satisfied with money (the last penny). Yet the reality suggested by these strong figures of speech reminds us that the suffering of eternity is indeed eternal.

i. “Let our merit-mongers first go to hell for their sins, and stay all eternity there; then afterward, if God will create another eternity, they may have liberty to relate their good works, and call for their wages…A child with a spoon may sooner empty the sea than the damned in hell accomplish their misery.” (Trapp)

text:
The issues I care about most begin with first principles. The foundations that allowed this country to prosper—individual liberty, self-reliance, and the chance to become a product of one’s own effort—need to remain intact. Life is not equally fair at birth. Genetics and environmental circumstance differ. What America uniquely offered was possibility. That possibility is narrowing in much of the West under regulation, collectivist policy, and a slow erosion of freedom.
When liberties are taken incrementally, democracy itself is weakened. 
Many Americans were shaken when the southern border was effectively opened. No one voted for that. That sense of being governed without consent is a large part of why the last election went the way it did. I believe the rise of the right was a counter balance to the overreach of the left.
The reforms I want are practical. Education should return to fundamentals, with individualized plans and real pathways into trades or college that do not require a lifetime of debt—without lowering standards. Healthcare, which I know from a career in the field, needs more than patchwork repairs. The architecture of the system itself has to be overhauled. Immigration is welcome when it is lawful, orderly, and vetted. Laws exist because they mark the difference between what defines a civilization and not. I do not excuse abuse from either side of that argument— all people need to follow the laws.
I believe in a hand up, not a handout. Well intended programs can over incentivize dependency, and human nature being what it is, people stop reaching when needs are met for them. That is not hardness or coldness of heart. It is the opposite. I care about people keeping their dignity and their drive, reaching personal fulfillment. 
National security matters. So does the fact that our own government is so consumed with battling itself that it can barely govern. A healthy democracy cannot function that way. 

So there’s your glimpse into the mind of a moderate Republican voter. Thank you for asking, by the way. I think many people have lost their way with civility and manners, which is a disturbing symptom in itself, but you appear not to be that person. So many people are playing games online right now, like antagonizing or baiting people. Not my style. I block if needed.

The US faces a projected shortage of up to 157,000 semiconductor workers by 2030, according to McKinsey and the SEMI Foundation. This deficit occurs during the fastest US chip manufacturing buildout in history, driven by AI demand.

Only 3% of US engineering graduates enter the semiconductor industry annually. 73% of chip employers report significant difficulty in filling engineering roles. Jon Taylor, Executive VP at Samsung's semiconductor division, noted insufficient technical people in the pipeline.

While the US leads in chip design, advanced chip manufacturing talent pipelines have historically been stronger in Asia. US chip jobs often offer lower salaries compared to the substantial bonuses available to workers in countries like South Korea.

Industry and academia are mobilizing to address this. Purdue University and Arizona State University are investing millions in new chip-focused programs. Samsung, Intel, and TSMC fund university initiatives and K-12 pathways. The CHIPS Act has also enabled over 80 community colleges to expand semiconductor programs.

Accelerating these workforce development efforts is necessary for the US to maintain its competitive position in advanced chip production.

text:
Joey Porter Jr.’s name has come up a lot recently, with some believing his injury is really cover for wanting a contract extension.

We don’t know what goes on behind closed doors, but there’s also speculation teams are sniffing around about a trade, including a rumor that Detroit offered a second and fourth-round pick.

Folks, I cannot be clear enough:

THAT IS NOT WORTH IT.

Quarterbacks and the guys who stop them play the premier positions in the NFL. Edge rushers and, yes, cornerbacks. There’s a reason there’s big money at the position.

People act like Porter isn’t worth it, but forget he was picked 32nd overall: technically a second-rounder, but a first-round pick in any other draft.

Then there’s the “not elite” talk, even though he doesn’t give up touchdowns. The penalties? That reputation is overblown, with many of the memorable ones coming against Bengals receivers who draw flags against EVERYONE.

Now try replacing Porter.

Take Detroit’s second and fourth. Unless the Lions suddenly go 6-11, those picks are probably LATE in each round.

Some speculate Omar Khan could use them to move up for a QB, but who’s dying to take something like pick 62 to let Pittsburgh jump from around pick 20? You’re not getting one of the top QB prospects with that.

The draft is a lottery. Maybe you get another Kenny Pickett. Or mortgage multiple drafts moving WAY up and hope you didn’t do it for the next Anthony Richardson, Zach Wilson or Trey Lance.

This thought process also assumes Pittsburgh is already giving up on developing Drew Allar and Will Howard, who BOTH made the roster.

All of that risk to give up a top-tier corner... over money?

Make it make sense.

I’m also sick of the revolving door at CB: Artie Burns. Ross Cockrell. Coty Sensabaugh. Steven Nelson. James Pierre. Ahkello Witherspoon. Levi Wallace. Patrick Peterson. Donte Jackson. Darius Slay.

Heck, even William Jackson III was a Steeler for a hot minute.

Remember how badly everyone wanted Pittsburgh to finally stabilize this position?

They did.

Stop the nonsense. Joey Porter Jr. became exactly what everyone was begging for on draft night years ago: now pay the man.

I am familiar with the rich history of who/what/when/where/why in the state of Utah. Utahn's have been following my journalism since I worked in Cedar City in 1996, at ABC4 sarting in 2001 and here at KUTV. I have integrity in journalism.

Just so you understand my position I am currently the main evening anchor at KUTV. I am a journalist and also a reporter and podcast host. I have spent decades reporting, working specifically on investiagtions- that is no longer the  main focus of my day. 

I do deep dives when I can. But I anchor three newscasts a day — and up to seven depending on the day of the week when someone is on vacation. If you do the math that leaves a few minutes for bathroom breaks in between. Anchoring is far more than reading a teleprompter. Throughout my shift, I write, research and develop stories for air and online; make calls; conduct interviews; post on social media; host and produce my podcast; and help manage our nightside crew.

My paid shift is 2:30 to 10:30, but I work much of the day before I arrive. There simply are not enough hours in the day to investigate everything I'd like.

Local newsrooms today have less than half the staff they had a decade ago and more work to cover. Our Salt Lake market covers all of Utah and parts of Nevada, Idaho and Wyoming. 

For Example- I have an investigative story on crime at Pioneer Park that I shot this spring and still have not had time to produce it. I also have six weeks of unused vacation because I work so much.

KUTV has a team of reporters and specific investigative journalists. Tyquan Thornton (WR, KC): 2026 outlook

Tyquan Thornton enters his fifth professional season holding down a projected starting spot as the third receiver for Kansas City. Last year across twelve games, he managed 6.73 points per game on a 39 percent snap share and a 9 percent target share, translating to 3.08 opportunities a game. The raw production remains modest, but the structural opportunity has quietly improved around him. Kansas City enters the year with 38.5 percent of the position room work and 31.9 percent of the team targets now vacant from the offense. That kind of available volume offers an opening for a deeper rotation piece to carve out a steady role, even if the primary weapons command the bulk of the attention. The offensive environment provides a strong foundation. Kansas City operates with a pass rate over expected of 4.0 and an implied team total of 25.2 points per game while running 61.6 plays a game. That volume keeps the floor somewhat elevated for anyone running routes in the system. The underlying profile carries a very specific archetype. His depth of target sits at an extreme 26.9 yards, which signals a clear vertical role designed to stretch the defense rather than collect high-frequency underneath catches. That kind of usage naturally brings volatility. A deep threat survives on efficiency and splash plays, which introduces a high bust rate when the downfield connections do not materialize. He occupies a deep bench tier where weekly reliability is difficult to trust, but the combination of a high-octane passing offense and significant vacated targets in the room leaves a pathway for occasional spike weeks if the deep ball connects.

Colby Parkinson steps into his seventh NFL season locked in as the primary tight end for Los Angeles. His projected opportunity sits at three targets per game, which leaves very little margin for error when targets do not convert. The opening week performance yielded just one catch for two targets and 1.6 fantasy points against San Francisco, falling well behind his preseason expectations and signaling that efficiency will dictate his weekly value. He is fundamentally a touchdown dependent tight end functioning as a secondary option in a loaded passing offense. The schedule strength index sits at 0.982, representing a neutral to slightly tough overall slate for the position over the remaining games. While the depth chart spot is secure as the starter, his fantasy utility remains tied to high value touches inside the red zone where he averaged nearly 1.6 red zone opportunities per game last season. Managers should expect a low floor with touchdown dependence as the primary path to relevance.

What to watch:

text:
A mandatory tax bill is coming due for pre-2027 Opportunity Zone investors.

Per IRC Section 1400Z-2 and IRS Notice 2026-40, all capital gains deferred into a legacy QOF must be recognized on the 2026 return, with December 31, 2026, as the inclusion date.

It applies whether the fund has distributed liquidity or not.

The key balance-sheet mechanics allocators need to know:

The FMV Valuation Cap:

▪ Taxable gain is calculated on the lesser of the deferred gain or the fund's FMV on December 31, 2026. 
▪ For underperforming, unencumbered funds, a year-end appraisal can permanently reduce the recognized gain with no recapture. 
▪ The Catch: For leveraged real estate partnerships, Treasury Regulations factor in debt relief, which can dilute the benefit of a lower FMV.

Estate & Wealth Planning Reality:

▪ Deferred gains are Income in Respect of a Decedent (IRD). Heirs get zero basis step-up on the deferred gain; they inherit the 2026 tax liability. 
▪ Gifting a QOF interest accelerates the gain immediately; transfers to revocable grantor trusts do not. 
▪ Legacy gains cannot be rolled over into new "QOZ 2.0" vehicles.

The Action Item:

This is a phantom tax event. Coordinate proactive loss harvesting across public equity portfolios and adjust Q4 estimated payments with your CPA before December 31.

Sources: IRC Section 1400Z-2, IRS Notice 2026-40, Treasury Regulations. Analysis by Momentum Wealth Management.

text:
Canada has been invited to become an associate member of the European Union.

Associate member.

Not a member. An associate member. A status that, to be precise, does not legally exist.

Ursula von der Leyen invented it on stage. NPR saw her prepared remarks and the line was not in them. She added it live, with Carney sitting right there like a man proposed to at a restaurant where the staff had not been told.

Canada is not in Europe. That is not a technicality, it is a hemisphere.

There is already a trade deal. CETA eliminated 99 percent of tariff lines back in 2017. The tariffs were handled nine years ago. What is new is the title.

And the title comes with a model, which is Norway and Switzerland. Both follow the rules. Neither votes on them.

Ukraine was offered this same arrangement earlier this year and turned it down, because Ukraine wants the real thing and understood the difference immediately.

Canada looked at it and asked when they start.

But 51st state was an outrage. A national insult. Sovereignty under siege, flags in windows, boycotts of bourbon.

Associate member of a club on another continent, with no vote, is dignity.

I have been sitting with what associate member really means, and I have landed on it.

It is the guy in the band who is not in the band.

Plays keyboards on tour. Not on the album cover. Introduced fourth, by first name only. No vote on the setlist and absolutely no cut of the publishing.

Canada is now the touring keyboardist of Western civilization.

I want this to work out, so here are the other options.

Join the United Kingdom. Enormous vacancy, everybody else left, the paperwork is right there.

Junior Mexico. Better food, better weather, the winters would be a revelation.

Almost China. Fewer benefits than it sounds, but the branding is honest.

Or take the band seriously. Somebody out there needs a country. I do not know if Canada can sing, the evidence is mixed, but forty million people and one of them can play drums.

Now, there is a scheduling problem nobody in Strasbourg mentioned.

Alberta votes on October 19.

Thirty two days from now, Albertans go to the polls on whether to remain a province of Canada or to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving it.

So Mark Carney flew to France to sign his country up for the most aggressive climate regulatory bloc on earth, thirty two days before the province that produces the oil votes on whether to start the paperwork.

That is not timing. That is a man booking a honeymoon during the custody hearing.

I will be fair, because the numbers deserve it. Separation is a minority position. Polling has run near 36 percent in Alberta and 34 in Saskatchewan, and the share who would definitely vote to leave is about half that. Smith has said she would vote to remain. This is not a province with its bags packed.

It is a province with a very well organized grievance and a date on the calendar.

And an EU relationship is a strange gift to hand them. Brussels regulates carbon the way Texas regulates cattle theft. Alberta's economy is bitumen. Somebody is going to have to explain to Fort McMurray that the plan is closer alignment with the people who want it in the ground.

So here is the American offer, and it is sincere.

Alberta and Saskatchewan can be Junior Associate States. Non-voting, obviously, we learned that from Brussels. But with an option to buy.

Full statehood available at the exercise price. No environmental review on the paperwork. We will even throw in a Senate seat, which is two more votes than Brussels is offering the entire country of Canada.

Carney says there will be debates, plural, and a vote in Parliament, and that this is the start of a road.

Start of a road. On another continent. As an associate.

Somewhere in Ottawa a man is explaining that this is completely different from being the 51st state.

And he is right.

The 51st state came with voting rights.

"Saudi Arabia suspends Yanbu loading, offers more crude via Oman
Three pumping stations along Saudi East-West Pipeline damaged in recent attack, sources say
Ukraine drone attack damages oil refinery in Russia's Yaroslavl, governor says.

 Oil prices settled about 1% lower on Thursday, but ​stayed above $100 a barrel, as investors weighed the disruption from strikes by Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis against reports ‌that additional Saudi crude barrels could reach global markets and ease supply concerns.
Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis exchanged fresh strikes across their border on Thursday, with the spread of the Middle East war to Yemen and Saudi Arabia threatening to worsen the global energy supply shortage caused since the United States and Israel attacked Iran ​in February.

Brent crude futures closed down $1.01, or 0.95%, at $104.82 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate futures fell 52 cents, or ​0.5%, to $101.91 a barrel. Both benchmarks had fallen about 3% on Wednesday.
Brent had fallen over $3 earlier in the session ⁠to its lowest since September 10, while WTI also fell over $3 to its lowest since September 11 after reports that Saudi Arabia was offering more ​crude cargoes to Asian refiners through ship-to-ship transfers off Oman's Sohar port. This will offset some of the disruption caused by attacks on the ​East-West pipeline to the Red Sea.

Saudi Arabia was also seeking to return about half the capacity of its East-West oil pipeline within days after the link was halted last week following drone attacks, Bloomberg reported.

Oil prices had climbed to around four-month highs this week after shipping industry sources said crude loadings at Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ​export hub of Yanbu had been suspended and Riyadh had canceled some cargo deliveries to European customers. The East-West pipeline supplies Yanbu.

Three pumping stations serving the East-West pipeline were damaged in an attack last week, and the repair timeline remained unclear, according to assessments from three oil and security sources.

Singapore's DBS Bank said its base-case scenario for the fourth quarter assumes tensions between the ​US and Iran will ⁠ease, allowing Brent to stabilize in an $85 to $95 a barrel range.

DIESEL MARKET FEELS THE SQUEEZE
While crude supply disruptions remain the market's main concern, tightening diesel supplies have emerged as another source of pressure as disruptions to energy infrastructure in the Middle East and Russia constrain fuel availability.
European gasoil futures , a benchmark ⁠for diesel prices, ​settled at a record high on Tuesday. US ultra-low sulfur diesel futures also settled ​at a record high.
A Ukrainian drone attack damaged a refinery in the Russian city of Yaroslavl, causing a fire that was later extinguished, regional Governor Mikhail Yevrayev said on  Principles."

text:
In 2009, Jason Brown signed a five-year contract with the St. Louis Rams worth $37.5 million. At the time it was the richest deal ever given to a center in the NFL.

Three years later, at 29 years old, in the prime of his career, he quit.

Not for another team. Not for injury. He quit to become a farmer.

"My agent told me, you're making the biggest mistake of your life," Brown said. "And I looked right back at him and I said, no I'm not. No I'm not."

The Baltimore Ravens called and offered him a way back into the league. He turned it down.

Then he bought a thousand acres of an old dairy farm in Louisburg, North Carolina, and sold his 10,000 square foot mansion in St. Louis to pay to develop it.

Here's the part that makes it insane.

Jason Brown had never farmed anything. Not once. He knew nothing about crops, soil, equipment, seasons, any of it.

So he taught himself. On the internet.

"I went to the online University of YouTube while I was still playing football," he said. "I watched hours and hours of film every single day."

He named the place First Fruits Farm, because of what he intended to do with it. The plan was to give away the first harvest of every crop to local food banks and keep the rest.

That plan didn't survive contact with reality. Once he saw how much hunger there actually was around him, the Browns started giving away all of it.

His first sweet potato harvest was 100,000 pounds. Every pound went to food pantries.

Since then, First Fruits Farm has donated more than a million pounds of fresh produce to families who needed it.

Now here's why he did any of this.

Jason Brown had an older brother, Lunsford Bernard Brown II. In 2003, Lunsford was killed in Iraq while serving in the Army. He was 27.

Brown was in college when it happened. Years later, sitting on an enormous contract, he did the math on his own life and realized he'd already outlived his brother, and he wasn't sure he'd done anything with it that mattered.

He'd been given a talent and a fortune. Lunsford had been given 27 years.

"People tell me I'm crazy," Brown said. "They downright tell me that I'm stupid, to walk away from millions of dollars. Because if you have the opportunity to play in the NFL then it's supposed to be a no-brainer."

He and his wife have eight children, and they all work the farm.

"Seeing my children out there in the farm field, knowing that they're learning life skills to help feed them and their families for generations to come, that is the blessing of a farm."

He could have played five more years. He could have bought a bigger house.

He grows sweet potatoes in North Carolina and gives them away.
